hunt_bio_general_information: The Henry's bison are truly free-ranging, held and managed under the public trust doctrine and are considered a Conservation Herd. They are genetically pure having ancestral roots from the last few dozen of the American Bison which were protected and saved in Yellowstone National Park in the late 1800's. It is remarkable that this herd makes its home now on the Henry Mountains and the surrounding canyons, mesas, and valleys. The herd is a treasure, thanks to those early conservation minded sportsmen who got them here. This is truly a once in a lifetime hunt, with challenges, as most hunts are. With beautiful vistas of the area while hunting such an iconic animal the rewards are memorable for those who are able to draw this permit or participate in the hunt. Realize too that you will have company on the hunt; it can feel crowded, especially early on in the hunt, this will taper off if you are still hunting later on as more and more hunting camps take their buffalo home.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: ***PLEASE DO NOT SEARCH FOR OR KILL COLLARED BISON*** The lower elevation bison range has been extrememly dry due to the ongoing drought. If the drought continues herds will most likely spend more time at higher elevations on the mountain where there is more available forage and where water is more available closer to the source. The past few years after coming off the winter range, bison have settled more on the slopes of Mt. Pennell and Mt. Ellen except that there has been less use on the east side. Often used lower elevation areas include the Airplane Springs, 5 and 7 Canyons of Tarantula Mesa, Apple Brush Flat, Stevens Mesa, Cedar Creek and Oak Creek Benches, and Sawmill Basin. There has been very little bison use on Mt. Hillers and Tarantula Mesa. Expect bison to move away from busy roads and hunting pressure while also traveling longer distances in search of forage. Traditionally herds eventually move south/southwest to the wintering areas of Cave Flat, Swap Mesa, Muley Creek and Bullfrog Creek drainages as hunting pressure increases through November and December. These areas have not received the precipitation needed to produce the forage for these herds. As a result bison may enter into Capital Reef National Park to find residual forage from the previous growing season, return to the mountain, or possibly venture to nontraditional areas to obtain forage. There is a seasonal road closure November 1 to May 15 on the Cave Flat road and hunting in this area usually requires horses. If you access the Cave Flat road prior to November 1st with vehicles, please do not venture off the designated Cave Flat road. Doing so threatens future access and can push bison farther away from the mesa making it more difficult to find bison. Please follow the BLM travel regulations and report anyone leaving a designated road. A bison is a big animal to take care of. A mature cow can weigh as much as a thousand pounds and a mature bull as much as 2000 pounds so it's a good idea to have at least two people to help with a harvested animal. There have been individuals who have done well on their own but the challenge is to keep the animal from spoiling and not wasting your meat. Most hunters have friends and family helping scout and share this once in a lifetime experience and make memories. As big as the Henry's Mountains are there are only so many roads, and with each person having transportation there can be a surprising number of vehicles traversing the mountain on any given bison hunt. Increasing pressure can move some bison towards or down onto the winter range where vehicular traffic is prohibited during the hunts. If you have difficulty locating bison and believe you have done everything you could do then consider hunting this area with horses or on foot especially later in November and during the December cow hunts. If this is not an option keep in mind that all the bison do not go out to the winter range while the hunts are going on. Bison are very good at hiding, holding tight, and sometimes moving a lot. Not all the bison leave the mountain even on the last hunt in December. The wintering area between the western and southern slopes of Mount Pennell and Capitol Reef National Park is an area large enough for bison to gather from heavy hunting pressure and remain on the landscape. The Cave Flat road which accesses the wintering area from the north through The Turn of the Bullfrog has a temporary road closure November 1st- May 15th. The closure is necessary to reduce hunter pressure that would push bison towards Capitol Reef National Park, the Boulder Mountains or around to the Sandy Ranch. The wintering area has geographical features that have aided the herd to naturally limit their free-ranging area and it is a refuge big enough that hunting has not moved them beyond the natural free-ranging area they have historically used. This is the reason why hunting is limited to horseback or foot travel during the hunting season. There is an orientation for cow hunters that may be of help to you. You may view the cow bison orientation course online at http://wildlife.utah.gov/dwr/hunting/hunting-information/big-game.html There you will find information on what to expect hunting bison, help in determining a bull from a cow, horn growth that can be helpful in deciding which animal you may want to harvest, and what equipment you might find useful. If you draw a permit you may receive a blood collection kit in the mail. By following the kits instruction you will play a critical role in the management and conservation of the Henry Mountains bison herd and North American bison in general by helping collect a blood sample for disease testing from your animal if you are successful. We are asking that you follow the instructions and make every effort to collect this sample correctly and send it in promptly. Not every hunter will receive a blood collection kit. During the winters of 2011 and 2013, 77 adult bison on the Henry Mountains were captured and fitted with GPS and/or VHF radio collars for a long-term research project monitoring bison movements and survival. If you harvest a collared bison, it is very important that we receive the collar(s) in order to download stored GPS data and reuse the collar/s. Please do not cut the collar off. Doing so makes the collar unusable, and they are very expensive to replace. A small adjustable wrench or multi-tool pliers can remove the collar fasteners/nuts. If the threaded posts are bent pliers may be needed to twist or break off the posts. The cape of a harvested collared bison may show some wear from a collar. After harvesting it is critical to get your buffalo skinned as soon as possible. A buffalo can spoil if left unskinned overnight, even in sub-freezing temperatures. Splitting or quartering will also facilitate cooling. Be prepared to saw through over two feet of backbone at the hump when splitting a bison. Minimum Hunting Checklist 1. Minimum of two individuals to help you 2. Large, sturdy meat saw/battery powered reciprocating saw plus extra batteries 3. Axe 4. Minimum of two sharp knives 5. Sharpening stone 6. Ton capacity block and tackle 7. Rope 8. Plenty of large sturdy game bags 9. Large tarp 10. Salt for cape and hide 11. Maps 1:100,000 scale (Hanksville, Hite Crossing, Escalante, Loa) 12. Tire chains Location of Harvest: Bison on the Henry Mountains are mostly found from 5,000'-10,000' elevation. During the November hunts much of the harvest the last few years has been on or around Mount Ellen except on the east side between Eagle benches and Pennellen Pass, and on the north and west side of Mount Pennell. Fewer are harvested on east and southern sides of Mt. Pennell as in years past; the southern end seems to hold bison each year. Except for the Stanton Pass area between Mount Hillers and Pennell there has been little harvest on Mount Hillers. Occasionally bison are harvested on the north and east sides/canyons of Tarantula Mesa. It is rare to find bison on top of Tarantula Mesa, it is large and a lot of time can be spent without success. The Mesa does provide some excellent glassing opportunities. As hunting pressure increases through the hunts generally between mid November through December, more bison move onto the winter range around Mt. Pennell either through the Turn Of The Bullfrog on the southwest side or around the Mud Springs area on the south side. From these areas bison move onto Cave Flat, Bullfrog Creek, Swap Mesa, and Muley Canyon areas where access is limited to horseback or on foot. Although there have been some hunters go in on foot and be successful it's not recommended unless you are prepared to stay overnight in cold temperatures and make numerous trips packing out your meat, hide, and head. Hunters that hunt these areas when bison are on the winter range have good success. Migration: In the spring, bison herds migrate back to the mountains from the southern winter range moving around the west and east sides of Mt. Pennell. In recent years these bison migrate on to the western/northwestern slopes and lower benches and flats of Mt. Ellen where they herd up in large numbers for the summer rut. They continue to stay in this area up until the first hunt. Not all the bison migrate however. Individual bulls and a small herd or two have wintered on the mountain at higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Locating bison is not always easy. The Henry Mountains are rough and there are plenty of areas for buffalo to hide out, so don't be surprised when you find that this really is a "hunt". Use good clean optics and glass often. Glassing often from vantage points that offer a wide expanse of country is a good strategy. From these vantage points you'll often see bison in areas that are inaccessible to vehicles. You can also easily miss them in smaller openings in the timber so glass often along your travels. Bison most often graze in open areas throughout the day. There are many chaining's/seeding's where pinion-juniper habitat has been mechanically altered and opened up in favor of grasses and shrubs. These are good places to look, as well as any high elevation meadows, pass's/saddles, or ridges. Although some bison herds are not bothered by vehicle traffic or people, the Henry Mountains herds usually avoid human activity. Prior to opening morning bison are often times easily located in larger herds but come opening morning, having been made wary of all the scouting activity in the area and the setting up of camps nearby, hunters often find that the bison are nowhere to be found. Subsequently harvest on opening weekend can be very low on the first hunt in November. Subsequently bison will move to secluded areas away from pressure where they are sometimes very difficult to find. As hunting pressure increases bison move towards the wintering areas of Cave Flat and beyond. A few hunters are lucky enough to harvest a bison close to a road, but for most it's much more difficult. Generally, bulls are considerably larger in body size with a more massive diameter horn base and overall horn size. Along the underside of the animal, the penile sheath is usually evident on mature bulls, but not a reliable characteristic of younger bulls. Yearling bulls have horns that have a large diameter base and grow outward more than female bison. Cows have similar shaped horns as younger bulls but are typically much thinner and appear slightly more curved. Young bulls, especially yearlings and two year olds, have some similar horn characteristics of younger and mature cows, are difficult to distinguish, and are sometimes taken for a cow during the cow hunt. When the time comes that you are determining what buffalo to shoot, make sure that you take your time and look at all the identifying characteristics (see the 'Identifying Characteristics' in the Cow Bison orientation.) before shooting. Being within a hundred yards can also help make the distinction between bulls and cows more clear. Behavior: Bison are active most of the day and generally water 1-2 times/day but they can go a couple days without water. They have been observed traveling 5 miles to water. Herds are composed of cows, calves and bulls, and will follow the lead of an older cow. Bison rut mid-July to early September. Not all bulls will leave the herd and form bachelor groups outside of the rut. In steeper terrain and when moving from danger they will single out and travel on the many trails that are available to them. Bison are highly mobile and can travel for miles without stopping when they decide to move. When grazing they will move together fanning out and when resting or loafing some will feed while others rest. Some older bulls are found alone or together in small numbers away from the herds, other bulls of varying age classes will also bachelor up into small groups. When hunted some larger herds will break-up into smaller herds and bulls will often times be in these herds throughout the hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Henry Mountain range is remote and services are many miles away. Have good tires with extra spares, the roads are known for flat tires and it is not uncommon to have a couple flats. Late fall rains can result in flash floods and very muddy conditions. Roads can be washed out from storms many miles away leaving you with few exit points so be prepared. On later season hunts high mountain roads can become iced up and unsafe to travel (chains may help to get you where you want to be). Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but will not always connect. Consider hand held radios and a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Use common sense. Be prepared to spend the night out if you get stuck or for some reason can't make it back to camp. Carry a survival kit. It's always a good idea to let someone know where you plan to camp and when you will return
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Keep abreast of the weather forecast. Be prepared for inclement weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Henry's bison are truly free-ranging, held and managed under the public trust doctrine and are considered a Conservation Herd. They are genetically pure having ancestral roots from the last few dozen of the American Bison which were protected and saved in Yellowstone National Park in the late 1800's. It is remarkable that this herd makes its home now on the Henry Mountains and the surrounding canyons, mesas, and valleys. The herd is a treasure, thanks to those early conservation minded sportsmen who got them here. This is truly a once in a lifetime hunt, with challenges, as most hunts are. With beautiful vistas of the area while hunting such an iconic animal the rewards are memorable for those who are able to draw this permit or participate in the hunt. Realize too that you will have company on the hunt; it can feel crowded, especially early on in the hunt, this will taper off if you are still hunting later on as more and more hunting camps take their buffalo home.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: ***PLEASE DO NOT SEARCH FOR OR KILL COLLARED BISON*** The lower elevation bison range has been extrememly dry due to the ongoing drought. If the drought continues herds will most likely spend more time at higher elevations on the mountain where there is more available forage and where water is more available closer to the source. The past few years after coming off the winter range, bison have settled more on the slopes of Mt. Pennell and Mt. Ellen except that there has been less use on the east side. Often used lower elevation areas include the Airplane Springs, 5 and 7 Canyons of Tarantula Mesa, Apple Brush Flat, Stevens Mesa, Cedar Creek and Oak Creek Benches, and Sawmill Basin. There has been very little bison use on Mt. Hillers and Tarantula Mesa. Expect bison to move away from busy roads and hunting pressure while also traveling longer distances in search of forage. Traditionally herds eventually move south/southwest to the wintering areas of Cave Flat, Swap Mesa, Muley Creek and Bullfrog Creek drainages as hunting pressure increases through November and December. These areas have not received the precipitation needed to produce the forage for these herds. As a result bison may enter into Capital Reef National Park to find residual forage from the previous growing season, return to the mountain, or possibly venture to nontraditional areas to obtain forage. There is a seasonal road closure November 1 to May 15 on the Cave Flat road and hunting in this area usually requires horses. If you access the Cave Flat road prior to November 1st with vehicles, please do not venture off the designated Cave Flat road. Doing so threatens future access and can push bison farther away from the mesa making it more difficult to find bison. Please follow the BLM travel regulations and report anyone leaving a designated road. A bison is a big animal to take care of. A mature cow can weigh as much as a thousand pounds and a mature bull as much as 2000 pounds so it's a good idea to have at least two people to help with a harvested animal. There have been individuals who have done well on their own but the challenge is to keep the animal from spoiling and not wasting your meat. Most hunters have friends and family helping scout and share this once in a lifetime experience and make memories. As big as the Henry's Mountains are there are only so many roads, and with each person having transportation there can be a surprising number of vehicles traversing the mountain on any given bison hunt. Increasing pressure can move some bison towards or down onto the winter range where vehicular traffic is prohibited during the hunts. If you have difficulty locating bison and believe you have done everything you could do then consider hunting this area with horses or on foot especially later in November and during the December cow hunts. If this is not an option keep in mind that all the bison do not go out to the winter range while the hunts are going on. Bison are very good at hiding, holding tight, and sometimes moving a lot. Not all the bison leave the mountain even on the last hunt in December. The wintering area between the western and southern slopes of Mount Pennell and Capitol Reef National Park is an area large enough for bison to gather from heavy hunting pressure and remain on the landscape. The Cave Flat road which accesses the wintering area from the north through The Turn of the Bullfrog has a temporary road closure November 1st- May 15th. The closure is necessary to reduce hunter pressure that would push bison towards Capitol Reef National Park, the Boulder Mountains or around to the Sandy Ranch. The wintering area has geographical features that have aided the herd to naturally limit their free-ranging area and it is a refuge big enough that hunting has not moved them beyond the natural free-ranging area they have historically used. This is the reason why hunting is limited to horseback or foot travel during the hunting season. There is an orientation for cow hunters that may be of help to you. You may view the cow bison orientation course online at http://wildlife.utah.gov/dwr/hunting/hunting-information/big-game.html There you will find information on what to expect hunting bison, help in determining a bull from a cow, horn growth that can be helpful in deciding which animal you may want to harvest, and what equipment you might find useful. If you draw a permit you may receive a blood collection kit in the mail. By following the kits instruction you will play a critical role in the management and conservation of the Henry Mountains bison herd and North American bison in general by helping collect a blood sample for disease testing from your animal if you are successful. We are asking that you follow the instructions and make every effort to collect this sample correctly and send it in promptly. Not every hunter will receive a blood collection kit. During the winters of 2011 and 2013, 77 adult bison on the Henry Mountains were captured and fitted with GPS and/or VHF radio collars for a long-term research project monitoring bison movements and survival. If you harvest a collared bison, it is very important that we receive the collar(s) in order to download stored GPS data and reuse the collar/s. Please do not cut the collar off. Doing so makes the collar unusable, and they are very expensive to replace. A small adjustable wrench or multi-tool pliers can remove the collar fasteners/nuts. If the threaded posts are bent pliers may be needed to twist or break off the posts. The cape of a harvested collared bison may show some wear from a collar. After harvesting it is critical to get your buffalo skinned as soon as possible. A buffalo can spoil if left unskinned overnight, even in sub-freezing temperatures. Splitting or quartering will also facilitate cooling. Be prepared to saw through over two feet of backbone at the hump when splitting a bison. Minimum Hunting Checklist 1. Minimum of two individuals to help you 2. Large, sturdy meat saw/battery powered reciprocating saw plus extra batteries 3. Axe 4. Minimum of two sharp knives 5. Sharpening stone 6. Ton capacity block and tackle 7. Rope 8. Plenty of large sturdy game bags 9. Large tarp 10. Salt for cape and hide 11. Maps 1:100,000 scale (Hanksville, Hite Crossing, Escalante, Loa) 12. hunt_bio_general_information: The Henry's bison are truly free-ranging, held and managed under the public trust doctrine and are considered a Conservation Herd. They are genetically pure having ancestral roots from the last few dozen of the American Bison which were protected and saved in Yellowstone National Park in the late 1800's. It is remarkable that this herd makes its home now on the Henry Mountains and the surrounding canyons, mesas, and valleys. The herd is a treasure, thanks to those early conservation minded sportsmen who got them here. This is truly a once in a lifetime hunt, with challenges, as most hunts are. With beautiful vistas of the area while hunting such an iconic animal the rewards are memorable for those who are able to draw this permit or participate in the hunt. Realize too that you will have company on the hunt; it can feel crowded, especially early on in the hunt, this will taper off if you are still hunting later on as more and more hunting camps take their buffalo home.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: ***PLEASE DO NOT SEARCH FOR OR KILL COLLARED BISON*** The lower elevation bison range has been extrememly dry due to the ongoing drought. If the drought continues herds will most likely spend more time at higher elevations on the mountain where there is more available forage and where water is more available closer to the source. The past few years after coming off the winter range, bison have settled more on the slopes of Mt. Pennell and Mt. Ellen except that there has been less use on the east side. Often used lower elevation areas include the Airplane Springs, 5 and 7 Canyons of Tarantula Mesa, Apple Brush Flat, Stevens Mesa, Cedar Creek and Oak Creek Benches, and Sawmill Basin. There has been very little bison use on Mt. Hillers and Tarantula Mesa. Expect bison to move away from busy roads and hunting pressure while also traveling longer distances in search of forage. Traditionally herds eventually move south/southwest to the wintering areas of Cave Flat, Swap Mesa, Muley Creek and Bullfrog Creek drainages as hunting pressure increases through November and December. These areas have not received the precipitation needed to produce the forage for these herds. As a result bison may enter into Capital Reef National Park to find residual forage from the previous growing season, return to the mountain, or possibly venture to nontraditional areas to obtain forage. There is a seasonal road closure November 1 to May 15 on the Cave Flat road and hunting in this area usually requires horses. If you access the Cave Flat road prior to November 1st with vehicles, please do not venture off the designated Cave Flat road. Doing so threatens future access and can push bison farther away from the mesa making it more difficult to find bison. Please follow the BLM travel regulations and report anyone leaving a designated road. A bison is a big animal to take care of. A mature cow can weigh as much as a thousand pounds and a mature bull as much as 2000 pounds so it's a good idea to have at least two people to help with a harvested animal. There have been individuals who have done well on their own but the challenge is to keep the animal from spoiling and not wasting your meat. Most hunters have friends and family helping scout and share this once in a lifetime experience and make memories. As big as the Henry's Mountains are there are only so many roads, and with each person having transportation there can be a surprising number of vehicles traversing the mountain on any given bison hunt. Increasing pressure can move some bison towards or down onto the winter range where vehicular traffic is prohibited during the hunts. If you have difficulty locating bison and believe you have done everything you could do then consider hunting this area with horses or on foot especially later in November and during the December cow hunts. If this is not an option keep in mind that all the bison do not go out to the winter range while the hunts are going on. Bison are very good at hiding, holding tight, and sometimes moving a lot. Not all the bison leave the mountain even on the last hunt in December. The wintering area between the western and southern slopes of Mount Pennell and Capitol Reef National Park is an area large enough for bison to gather from heavy hunting pressure and remain on the landscape. The Cave Flat road which accesses the wintering area from the north through The Turn of the Bullfrog has a temporary road closure November 1st- May 15th. The closure is necessary to reduce hunter pressure that would push bison towards Capitol Reef National Park, the Boulder Mountains or around to the Sandy Ranch. The wintering area has geographical features that have aided the herd to naturally limit their free-ranging area and it is a refuge big enough that hunting has not moved them beyond the natural free-ranging area they have historically used. This is the reason why hunting is limited to horseback or foot travel during the hunting season. There is an orientation for cow hunters that may be of help to you. You may view the cow bison orientation course online at http://wildlife.utah.gov/dwr/hunting/hunting-information/big-game.html There you will find information on what to expect hunting bison, help in determining a bull from a cow, horn growth that can be helpful in deciding which animal you may want to harvest, and what equipment you might find useful. If you draw a permit you may receive a blood collection kit in the mail. By following the kits instruction you will play a critical role in the management and conservation of the Henry Mountains bison herd and North American bison in general by helping collect a blood sample for disease testing from your animal if you are successful. We are asking that you follow the instructions and make every effort to collect this sample correctly and send it in promptly. Not every hunter will receive a blood collection kit. During the winters of 2011 and 2013, 77 adult bison on the Henry Mountains were captured and fitted with GPS and/or VHF radio collars for a long-term research project monitoring bison movements and survival. If you harvest a collared bison, it is very important that we receive the collar(s) in order to download stored GPS data and reuse the collar/s. Please do not cut the collar off. Doing so makes the collar unusable, and they are very expensive to replace. A small adjustable wrench or multi-tool pliers can remove the collar fasteners/nuts. If the threaded posts are bent pliers may be needed to twist or break off the posts. The cape of a harvested collared bison may show some wear from a collar. After harvesting it is critical to get your buffalo skinned as soon as possible. A buffalo can spoil if left unskinned overnight, even in sub-freezing temperatures. Splitting or quartering will also facilitate cooling. Be prepared to saw through over two feet of backbone at the hump when splitting a bison. Minimum Hunting Checklist 1. Minimum of two individuals to help you 2. Large, sturdy meat saw/battery powered reciprocating saw plus extra batteries 3. Axe 4. Minimum of two sharp knives 5. Sharpening stone 6. Ton capacity block and tackle 7. Rope 8. Plenty of large sturdy game bags 9. Large tarp 10. Salt for cape and hide 11. Maps 1:100,000 scale (Hanksville, Hite Crossing, Escalante, Loa) 12. Tire chains Location of Harvest: Bison on the Henry Mountains are mostly found from 5,000'-10,000' elevation. During the November hunts much of the harvest the last few years has been on or around Mount Ellen except on the east side between Eagle benches and Pennellen Pass, and on the north and west side of Mount Pennell. Fewer are harvested on east and southern sides of Mt. Pennell as in years past; the southern end seems to hold bison each year. Except for the Stanton Pass area between Mount Hillers and Pennell there has been little harvest on Mount Hillers. Occasionally bison are harvested on the north and east sides/canyons of Tarantula Mesa. It is rare to find bison on top of Tarantula Mesa, it is large and a lot of time can be spent without success. The Mesa does provide some excellent glassing opportunities. As hunting pressure increases through the hunts generally between mid November through December, more bison move onto the winter range around Mt. Pennell either through the Turn Of The Bullfrog on the southwest side or around the Mud Springs area on the south side. From these areas bison move onto Cave Flat, Bullfrog Creek, Swap Mesa, and Muley Canyon areas where access is limited to horseback or on foot. Although there have been some hunters go in on foot and be successful it's not recommended unless you are prepared to stay overnight in cold temperatures and make numerous trips packing out your meat, hide, and head. Hunters that hunt these areas when bison are on the winter range have good success. Migration: In the spring, bison herds migrate back to the mountains from the southern winter range moving around the west and east sides of Mt. Pennell. In recent years these bison migrate on to the western/northwestern slopes and lower benches and flats of Mt. Ellen where they herd up in large numbers for the summer rut. They continue to stay in this area up until the first hunt. Not all the bison migrate however. Individual bulls and a small herd or two have wintered on the mountain at higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Locating bison is not always easy. The Henry Mountains are rough and there are plenty of areas for buffalo to hide out, so don't be surprised when you find that this really is a "hunt". Use good clean optics and glass often. Glassing often from vantage points that offer a wide expanse of country is a good strategy. From these vantage points you'll often see bison in areas that are inaccessible to vehicles. You can also easily miss them in smaller openings in the timber so glass often along your travels. Bison most often graze in open areas throughout the day. There are many chaining's/seeding's where pinion-juniper habitat has been mechanically altered and opened up in favor of grasses and shrubs. These are good places to look, as well as any high elevation meadows, pass's/saddles, or ridges. Although some bison herds are not bothered by vehicle traffic or people, the Henry Mountains herds usually avoid human activity. Prior to opening morning bison are often times easily located in larger herds but come opening morning, having been made wary of all the scouting activity in the area and the setting up of camps nearby, hunters often find that the bison are nowhere to be found. Subsequently harvest on opening weekend can be very low on the first hunt in November. Subsequently bison will move to secluded areas away from pressure where they are sometimes very difficult to find. As hunting pressure increases bison move towards the wintering areas of Cave Flat and beyond. A few hunters are lucky enough to harvest a bison close to a road, but for most it's much more difficult. Generally, bulls are considerably larger in body size with a more massive diameter horn base and overall horn size. Along the underside of the animal, the penile sheath is usually evident on mature bulls, but not a reliable characteristic of younger bulls. Yearling bulls have horns that have a large diameter base and grow outward more than female bison. Cows have similar shaped horns as younger bulls but are typically much thinner and appear slightly more curved. Young bulls, especially yearlings and two year olds, have some similar horn characteristics of younger and mature cows, are difficult to distinguish, and are sometimes taken for a cow during the cow hunt. When the time comes that you are determining what buffalo to shoot, make sure that you take your time and look at all the identifying characteristics (see the 'Identifying Characteristics' in the Cow Bison orientation here.) before shooting. Being within a hundred yards can also help make the distinction between bulls and cows more clear. Behavior: Bison are active most of the day and generally water 1-2 times/day but they can go a couple days without water. They have been observed traveling 5 miles to water. Herds are composed of cows, calves and bulls, and will follow the lead of an older cow. Bison rut mid-July to early September. Not all bulls will leave the herd and form bachelor groups outside of the rut. In steeper terrain and when moving from danger they will single out and travel on the many trails that are available to them. Bison are highly mobile and can travel for miles without stopping when they decide to move. When grazing they will move together fanning out and when resting or loafing some will feed while others rest. Some older bulls are found alone or together in small numbers away from the herds, other bulls of varying age classes will also bachelor up into small groups. When hunted some larger herds will break-up into smaller herds and bulls will often times be in these herds throughout the hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Henry Mountain range is remote and services are many miles away. Have good tires with extra spares, the roads are known for flat tires and it is not uncommon to have a couple flats. Late fall rains can result in flash floods and very muddy conditions. Roads can be washed out from storms many miles away leaving you with few exit points so be prepared. On later season hunts high mountain roads can become iced up and unsafe to travel (chains may help to get you where you want to be). Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but will not always connect. Consider hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Use common sense. Be prepared to spend the night out if you get stuck or for some reason can't make it back to camp. Carry a survival kit. It's always a good idea to let someone know where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Keep abreast of the weather forecast. Be prepared for inclement weather.

You can also easily miss them in smaller openings in the timber so glass often along your travels. Bison most often graze in open areas throughout the day. There are many chaining's/seeding's where pinion-juniper habitat has been mechanically altered and opened up in favor of grasses and shrubs. These are good places to look, as well as any high elevation meadows, pass's/saddles, or ridges. Although some bison herds are not bothered by vehicle traffic or people, the Henry Mountains herds usually avoid human activity. Prior to opening morning bison are often times easily located in larger herds but come opening morning, having been made wary of all the scouting activity in the area and the setting up of camps nearby, hunters often find that the bison are nowhere to be found. Subsequently harvest on opening weekend can be very low on the first hunt in November. Subsequently bison will move to secluded areas away from pressure where they are sometimes very difficult to find. As hunting pressure increases bison move towards the wintering areas of Cave Flat and beyond. A few hunters are lucky enough to harvest a bison close to a road, but for most it's much more difficult. Generally, bulls are considerably larger in body size with a more massive diameter horn base and overall horn size. Along the underside of the animal, the penile sheath is usually evident on mature bulls, but not a reliable characteristic of younger bulls. Yearling bulls have horns that have a large diameter base and grow outward more than female bison. Cows have similar shaped horns as younger bulls but are typically much thinner and appear slightly more curved. Young bulls, especially yearlings and two year olds, have some similar horn characteristics of younger and mature cows, are difficult to distinguish, and are sometimes taken for a cow during the cow hunt. When the time comes that you are determining what buffalo to shoot, make sure that you take your time and look at all the identifying characteristics (see the 'Identifying Characteristics' in the Cow Bison orientation here.) before shooting. Being within a hundred yards can also help make the distinction between bulls and cows more clear. Behavior Bison are active most of the day and generally water 1-2 times/day but they can go a couple days without water. They have been observed traveling 5 miles to water. Herds are composed of cows, calves and bulls, and will follow the lead of an older cow. Bison rut mid-July to early September. Not all bulls will leave the herd and form bachelor groups outside of the rut. In steeper terrain and when moving from danger they will single out and travel on the many trails that are available to them. Bison are highly mobile and can travel for miles without stopping when they decide to move. When grazing they will move together fanning out and when resting or loafing some will feed while others rest. Some older bulls are found alone or together in small numbers away from the herds, other bulls of varying age classes will also bachelor up into small groups. When hunted some larger herds will break-up into smaller herds and bulls will often times be in these herds throughout the hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Henry Mountain range is remote and services are many miles away. Have good tires with extra spares, the roads are known for flat tires and it is not uncommon to have a couple flats. Late fall rains can result in flash floods and very muddy conditions. Roads can be washed out from storms many miles away leaving you with few exit points so be prepared. On later season hunts high mountain roads can become iced up and unsafe to travel (chains may help to get you where you want to be). Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but will not always connect. Consider hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Use common sense. Be prepared to spend the night out if you get stuck or for some reason can't make it back to camp. Carry a survival kit. It's always a good idea to let someone know where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Keep abreast of the weather forecast. Be prepared for inclement weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Henry's bison are truly free-ranging, held and managed under the public trust doctrine and are considered a Conservation Herd. They are genetically pure having ancestral roots from the last few dozens of the American Bison which were protected and saved in Yellowstone National Park in the late 1800s. It is remarkable that this herd makes its home now on the Henry Mountains and the surrounding canyons, mesas, and valleys. The herd is a treasure, thanks to those early conservation-minded sportsmen who got them here. This is truly a once in a lifetime hunt, with challenges, as most hunts are. With beautiful vistas of the area while hunting such an iconic animal the rewards are memorable for those who are able to draw this permit or participate in the hunt. Hunting a bison is challenging, especially with a bow due to the size and hardiness of the animal. The hunter who applies for this permit should be a very experienced and proficient archer having the confidence to place the arrow in the kill zone to minimize the suffering and wounding of the animal. Bison running around with arrows sticking out of them will likely result in negative public perception of archers and put in jeopardy the future of this archery hunt. Realize too that you will have company on the hunt. It can be very crowded, especially early on in the hunt, this will taper off if you are still hunting later on as more and more hunting camps take their buffalo home.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: ***PLEASE DO NOT SEARCH FOR OR KILL COLLARED BISON*** The lower elevation bison range has been extrememly dry due to the ongoing drought. If the drought continues herds will most likely spend more time at higher elevations on the mountain where there is more available forage and where water is more available closer to the source. The past few years after coming off the winter range, bison have settled more on the slopes of Mt. Pennell and Mt. Ellen except that there has been less use on the east side. Often used lower elevation areas include the Airplane Springs, 5 and 7 Canyons of Tarantula Mesa, Apple Brush Flat, Stevens Mesa, Cedar Creek and Oak Creek Benches, and Sawmill Basin. There has been very little bison use on Mt. Hillers and Tarantula Mesa. Expect bison to move away from busy roads and hunting pressure while also traveling longer distances in search of forage. Traditionally herds eventually move south/southwest to the wintering areas of Cave Flat, Swap Mesa, Muley Creek and Bullfrog Creek drainages as hunting pressure increases through November and December. These areas have not received the precipitation needed to produce the forage for these herds. As a result bison may enter into Capital Reef National Park to find residual forage from the previous growing season, return to the mountain, or possibly venture to nontraditional areas to obtain forage. There is a seasonal road closure November 1 to May 15 on the Cave Flat road and hunting in this area usually requires horses. If you access the Cave Flat road prior to November 1st with vehicles, please do not venture off the designated Cave Flat road. Doing so threatens future access and can push bison farther away from the mesa making it more difficult to find bison. Please follow the BLM travel regulations and report anyone leaving a designated road. A bison is a big animal to take care of. A mature cow can weigh as much as a thousand pounds and a mature bull as much as 2000 pounds so it's a good idea to have at least two people to help with a harvested animal. There have been individuals who have done well on their own but the challenge is to keep the animal from spoiling and not wasting any meat. Keep in mind that all the bison do not go out to the winter range while the hunts are going on. Bison are very good at hiding, holding tight, and sometimes moving a lot. Not all the bison leave the mountain even on the last hunt in December. Bison are very good at hiding, holding tight, and sometimes moving a lot. There is also an orientation for cow hunters that may be of help to you. You may view the cow bison orientation course online at http://wildlife.utah.gov/dwr/hunting/hunting-information/big-game.html There you will find information on what to expect hunting bison, help in determining a bull from a cow, horn growth that can be helpful in deciding which animal you may want to harvest, and what equipment you might find useful. If you draw a permit you may receive a blood collection kit in the mail. By following the kits instruction you will play a critical role in the management and conservation of the Henry Mountains bison herd and North American bison in general by helping collect a blood sample for disease testing from your animal if you are successful. We are asking that you follow the instructions and make every effort to collect this sample correctly and send it in promptly. Not every hunter will receive a blood collection kit. During the winters of 2011 and 2013, 77 adult bison on the Henry Mountains were captured and fitted with GPS and/or VHF radio collars for a long-term research project monitoring bison movements and survival. If you harvest a collared bison, it is very important that we receive the collar(s) in order to download stored GPS data and reuse the collar/s. Please do not cut the collar off. Doing so makes the collar unusable, and they are very expensive to replace. A small adjustable wrench or multi-tool pliers can remove the collar fasteners/nuts. If the threaded posts are bent pliers may be needed to twist or break off the posts. The cape of a harvested collared bison may show some wear from a collar. After harvesting it is critical to get your buffalo skinned and cooled as soon as possible. A buffalo can spoil if left unskinned overnight, even in sub-freezing temperatures. Splitting or quartering will also facilitate cooling, be prepared to saw through over two feet of backbone at the hump when splitting a bison. October temperatures can still be warm so be prepared to take care of your animal and get it cooled down as quickly as possible. Starter Hunting Checklist 1. Minimum of two individuals to help you 2. Large, sturdy meat saw/battery powered reciprocating saw plus extra batteries 3. Axe 4. Minimum of two sharp knives 5. Sharpening stone 6. Ton capacity block and tackle 7. Rope 8. Plenty of large sturdy game bags 9. Large tarp 10. Salt for cape and hide 11. Maps 1:100,000 scale (Hanksville, Hite Crossing, Escalante, Loa) 12. Pennell as in years past but the southern end has held a small bison herd each year. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Lower elevation bison range is extrememly dry due to the ongoing drought and herds will most likely spend more time at higher elevations on the mountain where there is more available forage and where water is more available closer to the source. The past few years after coming off the winter range, bison have settled more on the slopes of Mt. Pennell and Mt. Ellen except that there has been less use on the east side. Often used lower elevation areas include the Airplane Springs, 5 and 7 Canyons of Tarantula Mesa, Apple Brush Flat, Stevens Mesa, Cedar Creek and Oak Creek Benches, and Sawmill Basin. There has been very little bison use on Mt. Hillers and Tarantula Mesa. Expect bison to move away from busy roads and hunting pressure while also traveling longer distances in search of forage. Traditionally herds eventually move south/southwest to the wintering areas of Cave Flat, Swap Mesa, Muley Creek and Bullfrog Creek drainages as hunting pressure increases through November and December. These areas have not received the precipitation needed to produce the forage for these herds. As a result bison may enter into Capital Reef National Park to find residual forage from the previous growing season, return to the mountain, or possibly venture to nontraditional areas to obtain forage. There is a seasonal road closure November 1 to May 15 on the Cave Flat road and hunting in this area usually requires horses. If you access the Cave Flat road prior to November 1st with vehicles, please do not venture off the designated Cave Flat road. Doing so threatens future access and can push bison farther away from the mesa making it more difficult to find bison. Please follow the BLM travel regulations and report anyone leaving a designated road. A bison is a big animal to take care of. A mature cow can weigh as much as a thousand pounds and a mature bull as much as 2000 pounds so it's a good idea to have at least two people to help with a harvested animal. There have been individuals who have done well on their own but the challenge is to keep the animal from spoiling and not wasting your meat. Most hunters have friends and family helping scout and share this once in a lifetime experience and make memories. As big as the Henry's Mountains are there are only so many roads, and with each person having transportation there can be a surprising number of vehicles traversing the mountain on any given bison hunt. Increasing pressure can move some bison towards or down onto the winter range where vehicular traffic is prohibited during the hunts. If you have difficulty locating bison and believe you have done everything you could do then consider hunting this area with horses or on foot especially later in November and during the December cow hunts. If this is not an option keep in mind that all the bison do not go out to the winter range while the hunts are going on. Bison are very good at hiding, holding tight, and sometimes moving a lot. Not all the bison leave the mountain even on the last hunt in December. A bison is a big animal to take care of. Not all the bison leave the mountain even on the last hunt in December. There is an orientation for cow hunters that may be of help to you. You may view the cow bison orientation course online at http://wildlife.utah.gov/dwr/hunting/hunting-information/big-game.html There you will find information on what to expect hunting bison, help in determining a bull from a cow, horn growth that can be helpful in deciding which animal you may want to harvest, and what equipment you might find useful. If you draw a permit you may receive a blood collection kit in the mail. By following the kits instruction you will play a critical role in the management and conservation of the Henry Mountains bison herd and North American bison in general by helping collect a blood sample for disease testing from your animal if you are successful. We are asking that you follow the instructions and make every effort to collect this sample correctly and send it in promptly. Not every hunter will receive a blood collection kit. During the winters of 2011 and 2013, 77 adult bison on the Henry Mountains were captured and fitted with GPS and/or VHF radio collars for a long-term research project monitoring bison movements and survival. If you harvest a collared bison, it is very important that we receive the collar(s) in order to download stored GPS data and reuse the collar/s. Please do not cut the collar off. Doing so makes the collar unusable, and they are very expensive to replace. A small adjustable wrench or multi-tool pliers can remove the collar fasteners/nuts. If the threaded posts are bent pliers may be needed to twist or break off the posts. The cape of a harvested collared bison may show some wear from a collar. After harvesting it is critical to get your buffalo skinned as soon as possible. A buffalo can spoil if left unskinned overnight, even in sub-freezing temperatures. Splitting or quartering will also facilitate cooling. Be prepared to saw through over two feet of backbone at the hump when splitting a bison. Minimum Hunting Checklist 1. Minimum of two individuals to help you 2. Large, sturdy meat saw/battery powered reciprocating saw plus extra batteries 3. Axe 4. Minimum of two sharp knives 5. Sharpening stone 6. Ton capacity block and tackle 7. Rope 8. Plenty of large sturdy game bags 9. Large tarp 10. Salt for cape and hide 11. Maps 1:100,000 scale (Hanksville, Hite Crossing, Escalante, Loa) 12. Tire chains Location of Harvest: Bison on the Henry Mountains are mostly found from 5,000'-10,000' elevation. During the November hunts much of the harvest the last few years has been on or around Mount Ellen except on the east side between Eagle benches and Pennellen Pass, and on the north and west side of Mount Pennell. Fewer are harvested on east and southern sides of Mt. Pennell as in years past; the southern end seems to hold bison each year. Except for the Stanton Pass area between Mount Hillers and Pennell there has been little harvest on Mount Hillers. Occasionally bison are harvested on the north and east sides/canyons of Tarantula Mesa. It is rare to find bison on top of Tarantula Mesa, it is large and a lot of time can be spent without success. The Mesa does provide some excellent glassing opportunities. As hunting pressure increases through the hunts generally between mid November through December, more bison move onto the winter range around Mt. Pennell either through the Turn Of The Bullfrog on the southwest side or around the Mud Springs area on the south side. From these areas bison move onto Cave Flat, Bullfrog Creek, Swap Mesa, and Muley Canyon areas where access is limited to horseback or on foot. Although there have been some hunters go in on foot and be successful it's not recommended unless you are prepared to stay overnight in cold temperatures and make numerous trips packing out your meat, hide, and head. Hunters that hunt these areas when bison are on the winter range have good success. Migration: In the spring, bison herds migrate back to the mountains from the southern winter range moving around the west and east sides of Mt. Pennell. In recent years these bison migrate on to the western/northwestern slopes and lower benches and flats of Mt. Ellen where they herd up in large numbers for the summer rut. They continue to stay in this area up until the first hunt. Not all the bison migrate however. Individual bulls and a small herd or two have wintered on the mountain at higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Locating bison is not always easy. The Henry Mountains are rough and there are plenty of areas for buffalo to hide out, so don't be surprised when you find that this really is a "hunt". Use good clean optics and glass often. Glassing often from vantage points that offer a wide expanse of country is a good strategy. From these vantage points you'll often see bison in areas that are inaccessible to vehicles. You can also easily miss them in smaller openings in the timber so glass often along your travels. Bison most often graze in open areas throughout the day. There are many chaining's/seeding's where pinion-juniper habitat has been mechanically altered and opened up in favor of grasses and shrubs. These are good places to look, as well as any high elevation meadows, pass's/saddles, or ridges. Although some bison herds are not bothered by vehicle traffic or people, the Henry Mountains herds usually avoid human activity. Prior to opening morning bison are often times easily located in larger herds but come opening morning, having been made wary of all the scouting activity in the area and the setting up of camps nearby, hunters often find that the bison are nowhere to be found. Subsequently harvest on opening weekend can be very low on the first hunt in November. Subsequently bison will move to secluded areas away from pressure where they are sometimes very difficult to find. As hunting pressure increases bison move towards the wintering areas of Cave Flat and beyond. A few hunters are lucky enough to harvest a bison close to a road, but for most it's much more difficult. Generally, bulls are considerably larger in body size with a more massive diameter horn base and overall horn size. Along the underside of the animal, the penile sheath is usually evident on mature bulls, but not a reliable characteristic of younger bulls. Yearling bulls have horns that have a large diameter base and grow outward more than female bison. Cows have similar shaped horns as younger bulls but are typically much thinner and appear slightly more curved. Young bulls, especially yearlings and two year olds, have some similar horn characteristics of younger and mature cows, are difficult to distinguish, and are sometimes taken for a cow during the cow hunt. When the time comes that you are determining what buffalo to shoot, make sure that you take your time and look at all the identifying characteristics (see the 'Identifying Characteristics' in the Cow Bison orientation here.) before shooting. Being within a hundred yards can also help make the distinction between bulls and cows more clear. Behavior: Bison are active most of the day and generally water 1-2 times/day but they can go a couple days without water. They have been observed traveling 5 miles to water. Herds are composed of cows, calves and bulls, and will follow the lead of an older cow. Bison rut mid-July to early September. Not all bulls will leave the herd and form bachelor groups outside of the rut. In steeper terrain and when moving from danger they will single out and travel on the many trails that are available to them. Bison are highly mobile and can travel for miles without stopping when they decide to move. When grazing they will move together fanning out and when resting or loafing some will feed while others rest. Some older bulls are found alone or together in small numbers away from the herds, other bulls of varying age classes will also bachelor up into small groups. When hunted some larger herds will break-up into smaller herds and bulls will often times be in these herds throughout the hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Henry Mountain range is remote and services are many miles away. Have good tires with extra spares, the roads are known for flat tires and it is not uncommon to have a couple flats. Late fall rains can result in flash floods and very muddy conditions. Roads can be washed out from storms many miles away leaving you with few exit points so be prepared. On later season hunts high mountain roads can become iced up and unsafe to travel (chains may help to get you where you want to be). Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but will not always connect. Consider hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Use common sense. Be prepared to spend the night out if you get stuck or for some reason can't make it back to camp. Carry a survival kit. It's always a good idea to let someone know where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Keep abreast of the weather forecast. Be prepared for inclement weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is targeted at bison that migrate off of Tribal lands on the east side of the Green River on to the Nine Mile unit. Bison now only rarely migrate to the Nine Mile unit and occur in a few very remote and isolated portions of the unit. This hunt is a very, very difficult hunt as the vast majority of the area where bison occasionally inhabit is roadless. Hunters should not consider purchasing this permit if they are not able and willing to walk or backpack 10 to 20 miles per day in very rugged terrain. Most hunters never see a bison and hunt success is extremely low.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: UPDATED INFORMATION February 2026 1. PLEASE READ THESE UPDATES PRIOR TO PURCHASING A PERMIT! This portion of this Hunt Planner page is updated periodically with new information on road access and recent observations of bison. To view specific information about this hunt please refer to the main body of this page found below. This will be the last update of the season. 2. VEHICLE ACCESS TO THE RANGE CREEK AREA IS TRICKY. It is a very steep road that becomes impassible once there is significant snowfall. This can occur anytime between mid October and early December. There are tight switchbacks that make pulling a short horse trailer difficult but possible IF there isn't any snow. It is a very rough road. Check weather conditions before attempting to drive this road. This area is very remote with no cell service. 3. Access to the Green River in Desolation Canyon. The Green River typically ices over in late November preventing river access. The BLM does not issue river permits for launches after December 1. Early November tends to be the best window for boaters to both access the river and potentially see a bison 4. This was the fifth year of over the counter bison hunting on the Nine Mile unit. During the initial 2020-21 season the hunting was rather good with nearly 50% success and over 130 bison being harvested. However during the past 4 years, bison have changed behavior and rarely migrate to the unit. No bison were harvested during the 2025 season and only a handful of bison have been harvested in the past 4 years. Obviously, hunt success is very low. The vast majority of hunters did not see a bison last season despite spending countless miles by foot, horseback, or boat. There has not been a significant migration of bison from the adjacent Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation on to the Nine Mile unit during the hunting season for the past 3 years. This could be due to a variety of factors including the fact that the Ute Tribe has invested considerable effort in to preventing migration from the Reservation lands on to the Nine Mile unit including the construction of a bison proof fence. It is anticipated that hunting will likely be poor again during the 2026-27 season 5. Most of the area where a bison might occasionally be found require some sort of access permit. In the rare event that bison migrate on to the unit, they usually will show up in lower Desolation Canyon or in Range Creek. Desolation Canyon can only be accessed by floating this 90 mile stretch of the Green River. This requires a permit from the BLM. Most of these permits have already been taken. However, there are often cancellations so there may be some permits available. In addition, much of the Range Creek area is owned and controlled by the Natural History Museum of Utah. Access to these properties is by foot or horseback only and requires a permit as well. Most of these permits have already been issued but cancellations are possible here as well. Please see the details below on how to acquire these access permits. Neither of these areas allow any access after December 1 . GENERAL INFORMATION ABOUT THE HUNT Bison only rarely migrate on to this unit, and only in small numbers. If bison show up, they most likely will be foundin two major areas: Lower Range Creek and the area around Three Canyon along the Green River. Please see the attached maps of likely places to potentially find bison during October to December. There are also outlying areas that have rare sightings of a few individual bison. Bison are also occasionally observed on private lands atop the West Tavaputs Plateau but private property owners do not allow any public hunting of bison. By far your odds of finding a bison are much greater in the aforementioned Range Creek and Three Canyon areas. Range Creek Area: The Range Creek area is accessed via a very steep road over Horse Canyon. Elevation at the top of the pass is around 8400 feet. This road often gets inaccessible once significant snowfall occurs. It is strongly advised that all vehicles have 4 wheel drive and that you bring tire chains. Once you arrive at the bottom of Little Horse Canyon at Range Creek you will reach a locked gate. The area north of this gate is primarily private land. The area south of this gate is administered by the Natural History Museum of Utah (NHMU) The area is walk in or horseback access only. It is managed this way in order to protect the archaeological specimens common in this canyon. Hunters must first acquire an access permit from NHMU before entering this area. These are in short supply. Access permits can be found by going to the NHMU website at https://nhmu.utah.edu/range-creek/visitor-permits. There is no camping allowed on NHMU properties or surrounding BLM lands. This forces hunters to come back to the trailhead each day which will often require 10-20 miles of horseback riding or walking per day. The access permit season extends until November 30 each year. There is no access allowed after December 1. Please see the attached map of NHMU properties and Frequently Asked Questions. NHMU Frequently asked questions document An alternate access point to the Range Creek area is via the Turtle Canyon road. It is a long 26 mile bumpy road that reaches Range Creek below the NHMU properties. Please be advised that there is no access allowed to NHMU properties in Range Creek from the Turtle Canyon road. Bison might occasionally be found in the lower portions of Range Creek canyon from Lighthouse Canyon on the upper end to the Last Chance Bench at the lower end. Spots to look for bison are near the mouth of Lighthouse Canyon, Cherry Meadows Canyon, and Dilly Canyon and in the fields near the Field Station near Mitch's Canyon. Bison will often go down in to the bottoms in the mornings and evenings and then hide up in the side canyons during the middle of the day. Bison have also been observed on Last Chance Bench. There is a bison trail at the base of the red cliffs that connects the Green River area at Three Fords Canyon to the Range Creek area. This is how bison migrate to the Range Creek area. Three Canyon: Three Canyon is found along the Green River in Desolation Canyon. It is only accessible from boat and a river permit from the BLM is required. Please go to https://www.blm.gov/programs/recreation/passes-and-permits/lotteries/utah/desolationgray in order to secure a permit. It takes 2-3 days to arrive at Three Canyon and an additional 1-2 days to get to the takeout at Swasey's Beach. Floating the river in November can be very dangerous. It is advised that only experienced rafters attempt this. Low flows expose many rocks. Furthermore, the Green River can ice over as early as late November. Several groups of hunters were stranded in Desolation Canyon during the 2020 hunting season. These hunters had to be rescued by helicopter and leave their gear in the canyon for the winter. Bison are most likely to be found in the large valley at the mouth of Three Canyon. Occasionally if bison are present, they will migrate up Three Canyon 1 - 5 miles from the river. There have been a few sightings of small groups of bison just north of Three Canyon near the mouths of Calf Canyon and Rock Creek. They also have been observed downstream of Three Canyon in small groups near Three Fords. Bison usually cross the Green River at Three Canyon and downstream at Three Fords Canyon. These tend to be preferred migration corridors. Please be advised that everything on the east side of the river in Desolation Canyon is part of the Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation. Landing a boat, camping, and hunting is not allowed on these lands. Also please be advised that the Desolation Canyon corridor is managed as Wilderness Area or Wilderness Study Area. These areas have certain restrictions to be aware of. For example, it is unlawful to use carts in Wilderness Areas in order to retrieve game.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a hunt where numerous things could go wrong. The access roads in to the Range Creek area are very steep with numerous switchbacks. The Horse Canyon Road ascends a mountain pass that is nearly 8500 feet in elevation. Long horse trailers are not advised although shorter trailers and 5th wheel trailers are routinely taken over this pass. Be advised that it is very steep. Significant snowfall will make this road impassible. This can happen as early as mid October and at the latest by early to mid December. Tire chains are advised if there is any snow at all. The Turtle Canyon Road that accesses lower Range Creek is similar. Although the elevation is a little lower at 7500 feet, most of the ascent is on a north facing slope where snow tends to accumulate. The Turtle Canyon Road is 26 miles of very rough road from the Horse Canyon mine to the mouth of Range Creek. It usually takes several hours to get there. There is no cell coverage anywhere down in Range Creek or Desolation Canyon. Most areas will require extensive hiking or horseback riding in rugged terrain. Please be prepared.<br If you choose to hunt the Desolation Canyon area, please be aware that you must first secure a permit from the BLM in order to float the Green River in Desolation Canyon. These are in short supply. The link to acquire BLM river permits is found below in the Biologists Notes section. Boaters should be advised that floating Desolation Canyon in late fall/early winter has numerous hazards. There are numerous class II and III rapids on the river which are tricky to negotiate. These rapids get more technical at low flows common in October and November. The sun sets early and rises late in the bottom of the canyon. It is cold down there. Be prepared to spend some long, cold nights. If there is a significant cold stretch of weather, the slow moving portions of the river could freeze up and trap boaters on the river
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: If bison migrate to the unit, they do not begin migrating until late October at the earliest. Most years snow precludes access to most of the areas where bison might be found by mid December so the vast majority of the hunting opportunity is in the month of November. Please be prepared for short days as you are in the bottom of a deep canyon and long cold nights. Please bring tire chains. If it snows while you are there it may be very difficult to get out. As the vast majority of this area is roadless, please plan on spending all day every day out in the weather and prepare accordingly. If you harvest a bison, please be aware that they hold a ton of heat and can spoil if not taken care of immediately, even in relatively cold weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Book Cliffs offers a challenging landscape. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. Most of the canyons and ridges do not have roads or ATV trails to provide access. There are plenty of areas to hike and get away from the main roads. The South unit has very limited vehicle access. There are only game trails going up most canyons. There are several springs that the bison use to water out of in the canyons. Take every opportunity to scout for this hunt. I would bring a GPS, a good map that shows land status, or OnX maps. Make sure you are not trespassing on Ute Tribal land or private land. I recommended that we include the South unit for this hunt. One of the reasons for this is if the bison in the Roadless/Little Creek unit get pushed out of that unit; there are areas on the south that hold bison. Bulls will usually have large body size than cows. Judging bulls can be difficult especially if they are by themselves. Bulls' horns will be larger and will not curve in as much as cows. The bulls will have a tuft of hair that will hang down on their bellies. Most cows will have a calf or a yearling that will stay fairly close to them. The larger bulls can weigh over 2,000 lbs. and their hide is very thick, and if not skinned right away the meat could spoil even in cold temperatures. If possible, I would bring plenty of help, sharp knives, and a big bore rifle. This area has the potential for Boone and Crocket quality bulls.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Roadless/Little Creek area has four main drainages: West Willow Creek, She Creek, Little Creek, and East Willow Creek. All of these drainages are good for camping. The ridges that separate the drainages are: Went Ridge, and Little Creek Ridge. If hunting the roadless area I would camp in She Canyon, East Willow or West Willow. The bison can be found mainly in the bottom and heads of the canyons. I haven't seen many bison on the tops of the ridges. During the hunt I would expect to find them in She Canyon, Fish Creek, Little Creek, East Willow, and West Willow. They will move around the unit using the canyon bottoms. They will tolerate horse to a certain point. Numbers have steadily increased on this unit over the last 10 years. There are some great trophy quality bulls in this area. The South unit historically holds bison in select canyons in the higher elevations where water and feed is prevalent. I have not found any bison or sign east of Hay Canyon. There is no cattle grazing on the south so the access to the canyons is by game trails. Bison have used Diamond and Cherry Canyon on the South as well as the upper ends of the drainages in the Rattlesnake area. Behavior: During the late summer early fall bison rut. The bulls will mostly be in the large herds. During the rut there will be several mature bulls competing for herds of cows. Younger bulls will start to wander during this time to avoid the large mature bulls and look for other more available cows. Later in the fall bulls will start to bachelor back up into small herds of 2-7 animals. The cows and calves will be in larger herds but similar areas. I have observed calves of different sizes, suggesting that the cows could be coming into estrus outside of this time. Once the snow is deep enough they won't be tied to water sources. Bison are active most of the day. They will bed down in open areas where they have good visual vantage points to chew their cud. They will typically drink 1-2 times a day. They spend the majority of their time grazing. During the winter, they will use their large heads to burrow through the snow to reach grass and browse. During harsh winter months, they rely on their body's fat reserves to compensate for lack of nutritious vegetation. The bison are very good and smelling so make sure you try to keep the wind in your face. They will run when they spot you but its usually not for a long distance and most of the time they will stay in the bottom of the canyon. After they create distance, usually they'll go back to feeding. Eventually they will stop running and will move off to the far side of the canyon while you pass. Occasionally they will come right back at you on the trail. Usually there is enough space for you to get by them but occasionally they will push you off the trail.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a GPS type of messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and snow. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.
