hunt_bio_general_information: Please reference the Black Bear Guide Book and be familiar with the rules and regulations concerning hunting bears in Utah. This summer hunt allows you to hunt over bait, or you can spot & stalk hunt. For this hunt the use of dogs to track or pursue bears is not permitted and 'early baiting' prior to the opening of the hunt is also not permitted. Desirable bait site locations are almost always away from roads and atv trails and where there are denser conifer stands with water nearby. With that in mind do not violate Utah Code § 23-20-3 and Utah Admin. Rule R657-33-14: You may not place bait in either of the following areas: Within 100 yards of water, a public road or a designated trail. Or within a half-mile of any permanent dwelling or campground. There may be additional bait-placement restrictions, depending upon historical human and bear activity-especially nuisance complaints within any given area. The site that you choose to place a bait should not put other people using that same area at risk. Seek other suitable locations if other campers or resource users are nearby. Oftentimes, multiple bears will come into a bait station and hunters need to know how to tell whether it is a male or female. Be sure of the bear you are shooting, that it does not have cubs of the year with it or evidence that it is a female that has cubs. A female with new cubs is illegal to pursue or harvest. The required black bear orientation course can be found here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html If you find any illegal baits, please report them to the UDWR promptly. Apply early for a certificate of registration (COR) to run a bait station which a can take upwards of ten days.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: You can find resources on black bear habitat, diet, behavior, and natural history on the division's black bear hunting website here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html Hunting bears on or near sheep allotments on the south Manti is encouraged to help decrease the number of bears taken by Wildlife Services- Dept. of AG each year for killing domestic sheep. Not all bears kill sheep, but if sportsmen take some of the bears that do, there will be more opportunity for sportsmen to harvest bears. These allotments are generally higher in elevation reaching to Skyline Drive. Other areas on the S. Manti include Huntington and Cottonwood canyons and the following mountains: East, Trail, Candland, Heliotrope, Ferron, and the White Mtn area. Another area not to be overlooked is along the Price River between Woodside and Cedar Mountain; we have had a number of reports of black bear sign along this river corridor.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: You can find resources on safety in black bear country on the division's website here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html Cellular phone coverage can be spotty on this hunt unit. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service, it also allows a designated person with internet service to track you. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Expect muddy roads and cool springtime conditions at high elevations in June. Depending on winter conditions there may be snowdrifts that persist at high elevations along Skyline Drive into July. If using a tree stand, it is a good idea to wear a safety strap.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. Get your baits put out as early as legally possible. It typically only takes a few days for bears to find your bait station. Pastries, dog food, marshmallows are good baits. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present. It is illegal to harvest a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be cautious of bears when entering your bait station area. If using a tree stand, it is a good idea to wear a safety strap.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. During the early portion of the hunt rain and snow may be possible. You should also be prepared for hot, dry conditions throughout the hunt. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

Anthro Subunit
Public, Private and Tribal Lands. hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is meant to target black bears that are up higher in elevation during the spring hunt and inaccessible to hunters due to road closures during that season. Hunters should pick bait locations that won't interfere with campers or put people at risk. Oftentimes, multiple bears will come into the bait stations and hunters need to know how to tell the sex of the bear and make sure sows don't have cubs with them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Recommended areas to hunt: Greendale Junction, Eagle Creek, Meadow Park, Carter Creek, Goslin Creek, Mustang Ridge/Bare Top, Deep Creek, Summit Spring
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, wind, heat, and lightning. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Roads can become very muddy, and sometimes impassable, after spring storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The bear population on the Panguitch Lake/Zion unit has been slowly increasing over the past few years. The Panguitch Lake portion of the unit is primarily public land and the Zion portion is primarily private land. Make sure you have written permission before you access private land. Remember to apply for your baiting Certificate of Registration early. Don't wait until a few days before the hunt to apply. You will be delayed in beginning your hunt. If you are planning to hunt on private land you still have to register your bait station. Make sure to bring a copy of your written permission to submit with your COR application.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hunters will find bears primarily in the oak brush to mixed conifer habitats. Bear numbers and are increasing on the unit and bears can be found primarily from about the 7,000-9,500 foot elevation all around the unit. When locating your bait stations, please make sure to follow the rules do not apply for a bait station near homes/cabins, campgrounds and water sources. Sweet baits and meats that are very aromatic seems to work best for bear. Make sure to clean up after you self when you are done hunting or after you harvest. The use of dogs on this hunt is not permitted.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Make sure somebody at home knows where you are going and when you plan to return. Please be prepared with plenty of food and water if you plan to be out for an extended period of time.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Daytime temps should be mild during this season. Night time temps can still be below freezing at the the higher elevations but are typically in the high 30's. In can and will still snow in June at the higher elevations on this unit.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder mountain has a good bear population but is a rugged, large, tough place to hunt. Vehicle access is limited and the steep, rocky terrain makes it a challenging experience. The DWR has several GPS tracking collars on female bears and would ask that hunters not harvest a bear with a collar on this unit. These individuals provide important information for the unit and often have cubs with them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Please don't harvest our radio collared bears! Boars usually prefer the higher elevations on the Boulder and sows with cubs often don't leave the oak/mountain brush zones around the mountain. All parts of the mountain have populations of bears and pre-season scouting and hiking will help hunters find good areas. Game cameras can help bait hunters identify promising areas to select for bait sites and evaluate age class and sex of bears frequenting the area. There are many lakes and streams on the Boulder and these are areas where bears like to feed and lounge. Spot and stalk style hunting on this unit is incredibly difficult due to the topography and thick conifer stands covering the unit that prohibit hunters from being able to see far with optics. Hunting with a guide on the Boulder is a good idea for some hunters.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Boulder is a tough place to hunt. Take plenty of water and always tell someone where you plan to hunt. Be prepared to spend the night in the backcountry in case your hunt goes south on you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is unpredictable and can change suddenly. Snow can fall anytime of the year especially at high elevations. Nights can be very cold.

hunt_bio_general_information: The San Juan unit has one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. Get your baits put out as early as legally possible. It typically only takes a few days for bears to find your bait station. Pastries, dog food, marshmallows are good baits. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present. It is illegal to harvest a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Use caution when entering your bait station area. If using a tree stand, use a safety harness.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions can are typically hot and dry during this season, with afternoon thunder storms possible. Plan for all types of weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is meant to target black bears that are up higher in elevation during the spring hunt and inaccessible to hunters due to road closures during that season. Hunters should pick bait locations that won't interfere with campers or put people at risk. Oftentimes, multiple bears will come into the bait stations and hunters need to know how to tell the sex of the bear and make sure sows don't have cubs with them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Recommended areas on Diamond Mountain: Marshall Draw, Mail Draw, Warren Draw, Little Hole Recommended areas on Vernal: Iron Springs, Kane Hollow, Taylor Mtn, Mosby Mtn, Dry Fork, Red Cloud Loop Rd, East Park, and White Rocks Cyn.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, wind, heat, and lightning. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Roads can become very muddy, and sometimes impassable, after storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt allows you to hunt over bait using any legal weapon or you can use the Spot & Stalk method. You cannot use dogs. Early baiting is not allowed. Hunters should be aware of Ute Tribal Lands and not attempt to harvest a bear next to the tribal boundary.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bears are found across the entire unit. Hunters are encouraged to locate baits in areas not previously hunted if they are looking for a large boar. Harvesting bears in the same locations each year leads to over harvest of mature adults in that area. Be aware of air current flow as you pick your hunting spot. Bears have amazing noses and can wind hunters easily and then will only come to the bait after dark when it is not legal harvest them. Hunter success using the Spot & Stalk method has been very low on this unit. It is rare to see a bear on this unit without bait or hounds.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Any legal weapon is allowed for this hunt (including firearms). Be certain of your target before pointing your weapon. Rifle scopes should never be used as binoculars. Cellular phone coverage can be spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather during this season is normally warm with cool mornings. Unexpected weather is always possible during this season. Be prepared for hot and dry conditions or wet and cold.

Bait will not be approved on this unit if they are within 1 air mile of a previously approved bait.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There are bears across the whole unit. Look for areas away from campgrounds, roads, trails, and areas frequented by the general public. The more remote the area the better. Bears like areas close to water and cover. Streams flowing by conifers are good places to start. Use some kind of attractant such as anise oil or liquid fish fertilizer. Place attractant high in a tree so as to have the sent loft out. Bears can smell a mile away. Trail cameras are a good tool to use to find information on bears sex, age and time of day visiting the area. Some areas to look at are Strawberry valley, Sheep Creek, Diamond Fork, Hobble Creek, American Fork Canyon, but bears can be found in most all areas on the unit.. hunt_bio_general_information: Population is relatively small in comparison to other bear units. Higher densities seem to be observed on the South end of the unit, but bears can be found throughout their habitat on the unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There is a higher density of bears on the southern half of the mountain range. However, bears can be found all across the Pahvant. During this summer hunt, look for an area with a variety of open meadows, timber, and quaking aspen. In addition to eating meat and carrion, bears are omnivores and will feed on berries, grasses and other vegetation.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Some roads in the unit see a lot of traffic. Be aware of heavily used areas, camping locations, and other hunters especially in regards to bait placement. Depending on snow totals, access can still be difficult at higher elevations. Contact the local USFS office in Fillmore for up to date information on which roads are passable/open.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is typically nice and warm, but can change quickly at higher elevations. Be prepared for all weather conditions.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has a small bear population. There is only 1 bear permit for this season. Hunters should expect to work hard to locate animals. Bears can be found anywhere on this unit, historically the highest bear densities can be found in the central and Northern parts of the unit. Bears tend to be located in or near thicker stands of conifers and in the more difficult to access areas. Care should be taken when selecting bait sites. Sites will not be approved if they are near summer cabins or other areas frequented by people,
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell phone service is moderate in this unit. There are some areas where no service is available.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit unpredictable, but generally mild during this time of year. Summer monsoon rain storms may occur in July and August. Be prepared for snow, rain, lightning, and both hot and cold temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions.

Bear density on this unit is less known than for other units around the state, which my make for a challenging hunt. Know and follow the laws regarding bait sites. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: June is the height of mating season for bears. They are covering a lot of ground and should readily find baits. hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. Be sure to scout areas prior to the season and to get your baits put out as early as legally possible. It typically only takes a few days for bears to find your bait station. Bears have a great sense of smell, so using strong smelling bait will help bring bears in. Talk to your local bakery about getting day-old pastries to use as bait. Once you have a bear coming into bait, be sure to watch for any cubs that may be present. It is illegal to harvest a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be cautious of bears when entering your bait station area. If using a tree stand, it is a good idea to wear a safety strap.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. During the early portion of the hunt rain and snow may be possible. You should also be prepared for hot, dry conditions throughout the hunt. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

hunt_bio_general_information: Be prepared to cover several miles every day cutting tracks, and looking for sign. I would suggest hunting early instead of late. There have been complaints from houndsmen about the number of spike elk hunters in the field. I would try to use them as a resource of where they have been seeing bears. The south side of the divide can get very rugged and there is not much road access on that side. There are several houndsmen hunting during this time with pursuit permits as well. Some hunters prefer to spot and stalk. This can be considerably more difficult compared to hunting with hounds, but it can be an effective way to hunt. If you find any illegal baits please contact the UDWR in Vernal (435) 781-9453. I would focus my efforts in areas where I have good visual vantage points. Areas like: Rat Hole Cyn, Rail Road Cyn, Moon Ridge, and similar areas. Be prepared to hike in steep, rocky terrain. Put effort into locating a food source: berries, pine nuts, acorns, elk and deer carcasses. These are their main food sources this time of year. They will be up in the higher elevations looking for these food sources. The bears are usually holding close to their dens by early October and aren't moving far as they prepare to enter their dens. The majority of the region has a good deal of road access. This hunt unit offers some areas that are closed to vehicle access. These areas hold bears but can be difficult to hunt and don't receive as much pressure. The Meadow Creek WMA, and parts of the Bitter Creek WMA are two of these areas.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the fall the bears are trying to optimize there foraging strategy around pine nuts, remaining berries and acorns. They start to limit there movement to areas that provide them with these carbohydrates. I would try to hunt early and focus my hunting efforts in the higher country.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. There are no service stations for many miles. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and snow. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

The Book Cliffs offers a challenging landscape. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. Most of the canyons and ridges have roads or ATV trails to provide access. There are plenty of areas to hike and get away from the main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend.

There are two roads that allow you to drive across the majority of the Book Cliffs. The Kings Well Rd starts at the Seep Ridge Rd on the west side, and it can take you all the way to the Dragon Rd on the east side. The Indian Ridge Road starts at the Seep Ridge Rd and goes through the bottom of Sweet Water, top of McCook Ridge, Bitter Creek, and to Big Park. It is a great road to locate wildlife during this time of year.

Interstate 70 will provide access to most of the drainages on the south side of the Book Cliffs. Wildlife are found often found in these canyons. Major canyons and access points include Thompson/Sego Canyon, Nash Wash, Cottonwood Canyon, Hay/Middle/East Canyons, and Bryson Canyon. There are roads that will take you to the top of the Book Cliffs only in Sego Canyon, Hay Canyon, East Canyon, and Bitter Creek. The remainder of the roads dead end a short way up the canyons. hunt_bio_general_information: Bear habitat is plentiful across the unit. Road access is also very good
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bear habitat is plentiful across the unit. You really can not go wrong. There are some large blocks of private land on the northeast part of the unit near Scofield but some landowners are much more likely to allow a bear hunter than a big game hunter. It does not hurt to do some research and ask for permission to hunt on private lands. There are however an abundance of public land opportunities on USFS lands. Bears can be found from elevations of 6,000 to 10,000 feet and harvest is scattered across the mountain. We tend to find bears near the bands of domestic sheep on the mountain. Good areas to hunt include Trough Springs Ridge, North Skyline Drive, Fish Creek Ridge, C Canyon Ridge, Gentry Mountain, and Ford Ridge.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Big game hunters are in the field with you. Please be careful and considerate of other users.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: August and September tend to be the time when this area gets the most rain. Be prepared for afternoon thunderstorms that are sometimes severe. Temperatures tend to stay rather warm in during the early portion of the hunt. Very few people ever harvest during the November portion of the hunt. Plan to focus your efforts on August and September.

hunt_bio_general_information: Please reference the Black Bear Guide Book and be familiar with the rules and regulations concerning hunting bears in Utah. On this hunt, hounds and spot and stalk hunting are allowed. This hunt coincides with big game hunts, there will be many other users enjoying their pursuits, please be considerate of one another. Hunters need to know how to tell whether it is a male or female. Be sure of the bear you are shooting, that it does not have cubs of the year with it or evidence that it is a female with cubs less than one year old. A female with new cubs is illegal to pursue or harvest. The required black bear orientation course can be found here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html If you find any illegal baits, please report them to the UDWR promptly.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has a healthy bear population. Check out the black bear management plan and other resources to learn about black bears and their habitat, diet, behavior, and natural history on the division's black bear hunting website page here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html Few hunters harvest during the November portion of the hunt. Plan to focus your efforts on August. Hunting bears on or near sheep allotments on the south Manti is encouraged to help decrease the number of bears taken by Wildlife Services- Dept. of AG each year for killing domestic sheep. Not all bears kill sheep, but if sportsmen take some of the bears that do, there will be more opportunity for sportsmen to harvest bears. These allotments are generally higher in elevation reaching to Skyline Drive. Other areas on the S. Manti include Huntington and Cottonwood canyons and the following mountains: East, Trail, Candland, Heliotrope, Ferron, and the White Mtn area. Another area not to be overlooked is along the Price River between Woodside and Cedar Mountain; we have had a number of reports of black bear sign along this river corridor.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: You can find resources on safety in black bear country on the division's website here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html Cellular phone coverage can be spotty on this hunt unit. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service, it also allows a designated person with internet service to track you. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: August tends to be the time when this area gets a good amount of rain. Be prepared for afternoon thunderstorms that are sometimes severe. Temperatures tend to stay rather warm during the early portion of the hunt. Expect early snow during the November hunts.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Almost the entire unit is good bear habitat. Be aware of private land throughout the unit. Although in some cases private landowners tend to be a bit more amenable to allowing hunting for bears on their lands than they are for big game so it doesn't hurt to ask for permission if you have an area you'd really like to hunt. hunt_bio_safety_considerations: There is very little cell coverage on this mountain despite its proximity to the Wasatch Front.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Be careful of hot weather in the early half of the hunt and snowstorms in the late part of the hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the fall, focus on areas with berry patches or oak stands. Later in the season, bears will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet. They will look for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, along with scavenging dead carcasses. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear, suggesting that she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. You should be ready for anything from rain and sleet, to dry and hot conditions. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bears are common throughout much of the unit. They are much more visible and easy to locate during dry summers. Most of the best bear habitat is on private lands although bear are harvested on public lands occasionally. Bear can be found at relatively low elevations in the canyons east of Price including Coal, Soldier, Dugout, and Grassy Trail Creeks. There also tends to be a high concentration of bears in the upper portions of Argyle Canyon east of US-191. Bear are also common at high elevations along the West Tavaputs Plateau. The Cold Springs WMA is also a common place for sportsmen to encounter bears.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This unit is dominated by steep rocky canyons in very remote areas. Cell phone coverage is very poor throughout much of the unit. As much of the area is on private land, there is relatively little vehicle traffic on much of this unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is generally mild during the early fall. Monsoon rains can wash out roads and make access difficult

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt coincides with the bull elk and buck deer archery hunts and several other hunts, including muzzleloader elk and general season deer. The North Slope receives heavy hunting pressure during these hunts with a lot of campers in the unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Recommended areas to hunt: Greendale Junction, Eagle Creek, Meadow Park, Carter Creek, Goslin Creek, Mustang Ridge/Bare Top, Summit Spring
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, wind, heat, and lightning. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Roads can become very muddy, and sometimes impassable, after fall storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The bear population on the Panguitch Lake/Zion unit has been slowly increasing over the past few years. The Panguitch Lake portion of the unit is primarily public land and the Zion portion is primarily private land. Make sure you have written permission before you access private land.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hunters will find bears primarily in the oak brush to mixed conifer habitats. Bear numbers and are increasing on the unit and bears can be found primarily from about the 7,000-9,500 foot elevations all around the unit. Hunters can choose to use dog or spot and stalk on this hunt. When using dogs please be respectful of other public land users. There are several other big game hunts going on, on this unit during this hunts time frame.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Make sure somebody at home knows where you are going and when you plan to return. Please be prepared with plenty of food and water if you plan to be out for an extended period of time.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Daytime temps should be mild to warm during this season. Night time temps can still be below freezing at the the higher elevations but are typically in the high 30's to low 40's. It can and will still snow in September at the higher elevations on this unit.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder mountain has a good bear population but is a rugged, large, tough place to hunt. Vehicle access is limited and the steep, rocky terrain makes it a challenging experience. The DWR has several GPS tracking collars on female bears and would ask that hunters not harvest a bear with a collar on this unit. These individuals provide important information for the unit and often have cubs with them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Please don't harvest our radio collared bears! Boars usually prefer the higher elevations on the Boulder and sows with cubs often don't leave the oak/mountain brush zones around the mountain. All parts of the mountain have populations of bears and pre-season scouting and hiking will help hunters find good areas. There are many lakes and streams on the Boulder and these are areas where bears like to feed and lounge. When trailing bears with hounds, hunters can expect to cover lots of country through thick vegetation while pursuing. Spot and stalk style hunting on this unit is incredibly difficult due to the topography and thick conifer stands covering the unit that prohibit hunters from being able to see far with optics. Hunting with a guide on the Boulder is a good idea for some hunters.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Boulder is a tough place to hunt. Take plenty of water and always tell someone where you plan to hunt. Be prepared to spend the night in the backcountry in case your hunt goes south on you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is unpredictable and can change suddenly. Snow can fall anytime of the year especially at high elevations. Nights can be very cold.

hunt_bio_general_information: The San Juan has one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the fall, focus on areas with berry patches or oak stands. Later in the season, bears will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet. They will look for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, along with scavenging dead carcasses. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear, suggesting that she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. When hunting with bait, use caution when entering your bait station area. If using a tree stand, use a safety harness. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Plan for all types of weather conditions. Flash floods are common in this area, so pay attention to what the sky is doing miles away from you.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Recommended areas on Diamond Mountain: Marshall Draw, Mail Draw, Warren Draw, Little Hole Recommended areas on Vernal: Red Cloud Loop Rd, Kane Hollow, Taylor Mtn, Mosby Mtn, and White Rocks Cyn.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, wind, heat, and lightning. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Roads can become very muddy, and sometimes impassable, after spring storms.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bears are found across the entire unit. This is not considered a "trophy" bear unit by most hunters but good bears are harvested on the unit each year. Hunters need to be aware of Ute Tribal Lands which is closed to bear hunting for non-tribal members. Be aware of the tribal boundary and avoid turning out hounds close to the tribal boundary. If a hound crosses onto tribal land, hunters will need to contact the Ute Tribe Fish and Game Dept. and request access to enter tribal land to retrieve hounds on tribal land. Hunter success using the Spot & Stalk method has been very low on this unit. It is rare to see a bear on this unit without bait or hounds.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be certain of your target before pointing your weapon. Rifle scopes should never be used as binoculars. Cellular phone coverage can be spotty on this hunt unit. hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions during this hunt can vary from hot and dry to cold and snowy. The later in the fall the more likely it is for snow. Hunter should be prepared with 4 wheel drive vehicles.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt allows the use of any legal Weapon. This hunt does not allow the use of bait, including early baiting. Spot and stalk and the use of dogs are allowed for this hunt. No more than 16 dogs may be used to pursue a bear at any given time.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bears are found across the entire unit. Hunters are encouraged to locate baits in areas not previously hunted if they are looking for a large boar. Harvesting bears in the same locations each year leads to over harvest of mature adults in that area. Be aware of thermal air current flow as you pick your hunting spot. Cold air travels down hill in the morning and evenings and warm air rises up hill during the day. Bears have amazing noses and can wind hunters easily and then will likely only come to the bait after dark when it is not legal harvest them. Hunter success using the Spot & Stalk method has been very low on this unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This hunt now allows legal firearms to be used. Be certain of your target before pointing your weapon. Rifle scopes should never be used as binoculars. Cellular phone coverage can be spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather during this season is normally warm with cool mornings. Unexpected weather is always possible during this season. Be prepared for hot and dry conditions or wet and cold.

hunt_bio_general_information: The majority of harvest occurs the last 10 days of the hunt. Be prepared to cover several miles every day cutting tracks, and looking for sign. This area can be difficult to access in early April depending on the severity of the winter. There is no baiting during this hunt. If you find any illegal baits please contact the UDWR in Vernal (435) 781-9453. I would focus my efforts in areas where I have good visual vantage points. I have seen bears in the spring at the top ends of the canyons on grassy benches. They seem to prefer the grassy aspen stands relatively close to water. Be prepared to ride and hike in vertical, rocky terrain. The snow can cause delays in accessing certain parts of this unit. I would hunt later when the bears are more likely to be covering more country. Be prepared for a tough hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The bear's diet in the spring generally consists of grass, and forbs. They will be relatively close to water sources (creeks, or springs). They move the most during the early morning hours and the evening. The boars are more likely to come out of there dens first. They will continue to increase their movements as the hunt progresses.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote area with no vehicle access. Every year sportsmen injure horses and themselves while riding in the rough terrain. Be prepared for adverse weather, and limited cell phone coverage.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The spring can still be very cold and I would expect late snow storms. Depending on the severeness of the winter this unit can be difficult to access until mid to late April.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit is in a very remote location and can be difficult to access. The unit offers a high bear density. Look for scat piles and tracks on the trails. There are several riparian areas and springs the bears will be accessing. I would hunt on the opener to take advantage of elk and deer gut piles left by big game hunters. It is very common to find bears scavenging these kill sights. I would hunt on Little Creek Ridge.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bears will be on the move during this time of year. They will be looking for opportunistic meals along well used trails. The bears prefer low traffic areas. I have seen bears in Buck Cyn, Little Creek Ridge, West and East Willow, She Cyn, and Fish Creek. I would focus most of my effort on Little Creek Ridge.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote area with no vehicle access. Every year sportsmen injure horses and themselves while riding in the rough terrain. Be prepared for adverse weather, and limited cell phone coverage.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Be prepared for hot/dry conditions, with occasional thunder storms. The trails can get extremely slick and dangerous.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a new hunt in 2026. It was previously part of the La Sal unit, but wasn't being utilized by hunters. Bear density on this unit is less known than for other units, and my make for a challenging hunt. Be cautious and courteous of private property boundaries as well as state boundaries when hunting with dogs. This is a remote hunt that may be difficult to access at times of the year. Limited cell reception is is the norm in most areas.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Put effort into locating food sources like berries, pine nuts, acorns, and elk or deer carcasses. These are their main food sources this time of year. They will be up in the higher elevations looking for these food sources. The bears are usually holding close to their dens sites by early October and aren't moving far as they prepare to enter their dens. Try to hunt early to find bears that are still moving around.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote area that my be difficult to get access at certain times of the year. Be prepared for adverse weather conditions, and limited cell reception.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions can change quickly. Be prepared for early snow storms, thundershowers and occasional warm or days.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the fall, focus on areas with berry patches or oak stands. Later in the season, bears will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet. They will look for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, along with scavenging dead carcasses. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear that suggests she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. You should be ready for anything from rain and sleet, to dry and hot conditions. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

hunt_bio_general_information: The spring hunt historically has the highest success out of all the bear hunts in the Book Cliffs. Most hunters prefer to use hounds during this hunt. The majority of harvest occurs the last 10 days of the hunt. Be prepared to cover several miles every day cutting tracks, and looking for sign. It can be difficult hunting near the Colorado border and occasionally I have seen hunters have to retrieve their dogs across the hunt boundary. The bears will be close to there dens at the first of the hunt. They prefer the slopes with ledge rock to den in. I would hunt early in the day while the bears are out and the temps are cool. The snow level usually doesn't cause many problems during the spring hunt. Some hunters prefer to spot and stalk. This can be considerably more difficult compared to hunting with hounds, but it can be an effective way to hunt. There is no baiting during this hunt. If you find any illegal baits please contact the UDWR in Vernal (435) 781-9453. I would focus efforts in areas where I have good visual vantage points. Areas like: Rat Hole Cyn, Rail Road Cyn, Moon Ridge, and similar areas. Be prepared to hike in steep, rocky terrain. The majority of the region has a good deal of road access. This hunt unit offers some areas that are closed to vehicle access. These areas hold bears but can be difficult to hunt and don't receive as much pressure. The Meadow Creek WMA, and parts of the Bitter Creek WMA are two of these areas. I would hunt the spring hunt and put most of my resources into harvesting a bear during this hunt. The other hunts can be enjoyable, but have considerably lower success.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The bear's diet in the spring generally consists of grass, and forbs. They will be relatively close to water sources (creeks, or springs). They move the most during the early morning hours and the evening. The boars are more likely to come out of there dens first. They will continue to increase their movements as the hunt progresses.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for adverse weather conditions, and limited cell reception.

hunt_bio_general_information: Spring:The majority of harvest occurs the last 10 days of the hunt. Be prepared to cover several miles every day cutting tracks, and looking for sign. This area can be difficult to access in early April depending on the severity of the winter. There is no baiting during this hunt. If you find any illegal baits please contact the UDWR in Vernal (435) 781-9453. I would focus my efforts in areas where I have good visual vantage points. I have seen bears in the spring at the top ends of the canyons on grassy benches. They seem to prefer the grassy aspen stands relatively close to water. Be prepared to ride and hike in vertical, rocky terrain. The snow can cause delays in accessing certain parts of this unit. I would hunt later when the bears are more likely to be covering more country. Be prepared for a tough hunt. Bait Hunt:This hunt unit is in a very remote location and can be difficult to access to replenish baits. The unit offers a high bear density. Look for scat piles and tracks on the trails. There are several riparian areas and springs the bears will be accessing. Make sure you give yourself plenty of time to get your bait sites approved before your hunt starts. As soon as you can start baiting I would. There will also be archery deer and elk kills that bears will be visiting during this time.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The bear's diet in the spring generally consists of grass, and forbs. They will be relatively close to water sources (creeks, or springs) in the spring, summer and fall. In the late summer fall they will switch to carbohydrates like: pine nuts, acorns, and berries. They move the most during the early morning hours and the evening. The boars are more likely to come out of there dens first. They will continue to increase their movements as the hunt progresses. Their mating season takes place around the second week of June and can last several weeks.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote area with no vehicle access. Every year sportsmen injure horses and themselves while riding in the rough terrain. Be prepared for adverse weather, and limited cell phone coverage.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Be prepared for hot/dry/cold conditions, with occasional thunder storms. The trails can get extremely slick and dangerous.

hunt_bio_general_information: Please reference the Black Bear Guide Book and be familiar with the rules and regulations concerning hunting bears in Utah. The summer hunt allows you to hunt over bait, or you can spot & stalk hunt. For the summer hunt, the use of dogs to track or pursue bears and 'early baiting' prior to the opening of the hunt is not permitted. If you find any illegal baits during the Spring or fall hunts please report them promptly to the UDWR. Desirable bait site locations are almost always away from roads and atv trails and where there are denser conifer stands with water nearby. With that in mind do not violate Utah Code § 23-20-3 and Utah Admin. Rule R657-33-14: You may not place bait in either of the following areas: Within 100 yards of water, a public road or a designated trail. Or within a half-mile of any permanent dwelling or campground. There may be additional bait-placement restrictions, depending upon historical human and bear activity-especially nuisance complaints within any given area. The site that you choose to place a bait should not put other people using that same area at risk. Seek other suitable locations if other campers or resource users are nearby. Oftentimes, multiple bears will come into a bait station and hunters need to know how to tell whether it is a male or female. Be sure of the bear you are shooting, that it does not have cubs of the year with it or evidence that it is a female that has cubs. A female with new cubs is illegal to pursue or harvest. The required black bear orientation course can be found here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html If you find any illegal baits, please report them to the UDWR promptly. Apply early for a certificate of registration (COR) to run a bait station which a can take upwards of ten days.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: You can find resources on black bear habitat, diet, behavior, and natural history on the division's black bear hunting website here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html Hunting bears on or near sheep allotments on the south Manti is encouraged to help decrease the number of bears taken by Wildlife Services- Dept. of AG each year for killing domestic sheep. Not all bears kill sheep, but if sportsmen take some of the bears that do, there will be more opportunity for sportsmen to harvest bears. These allotments are generally higher in elevation reaching to Skyline Drive. Other areas on the S. Manti include Huntington and Cottonwood canyons and the following mountains: East, Trail, Candland, Heliotrope, Ferron, and the White Mtn area. Another area not to be overlooked is along the Price River between Woodside and Cedar Mountain; we have had a number of reports of black bear sign along this river corridor.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: You can find resources on safety in black bear country on the division's website here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/hunting-in-utah/hunting-information/black-bears.html Cellular phone coverage can be spotty on this hunt unit. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service, it also allows a designated person with internet service to track you. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Expect muddy roads and cool springtime conditions at high elevations in June. Depending on winter conditions there may be snowdrifts that persist at high elevations along Skyline Drive into July. If using a tree stand, it is a good idea to wear a safety strap.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the spring, focus on areas with green, grassy meadows. This typically means following the snowline up and glassing south facing hills. Bears will feed on the green grass soon after coming out of their dens. Later in the season, their diet will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet, looking for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, and then berries and acorns later on. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear, suggesting that she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. For those using bait, be cautious when entering your bait station area. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. During the early and late portion of the hunt rain and snow may be possible. You should also be prepared for hot, dry conditions throughout the hunt. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is not known for producing large bears, however, hunters can expect to see multiple bear tracks during their hunt. Due to the forest service road closures, this unit does not get hunted very heavily during the spring harvest objective season. The fall limited entry season overlaps several deer and elk hunts. This unit receives heavy hunting pressure and camping use.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Recommended areas to hunt: Greendale Junction, Eagle Creek, Meadow Park, Carter Creek, Goslin Creek, Mustang Ridge/Bare Top, Summit Spring
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, wind, heat, and lightning. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Roads can become very muddy, and sometimes impassable, after spring storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The bear population on the Panguitch Lake/Zion unit has been slowly increasing over the past few years. The Panguitch Lake portion of the unit is primarily public land and the Zion portion is primarily private land. Make sure you have written permision before you access private land. If you are planning to use bait and not dogs remeber to apply for your baiting Certificate of Registration early. Don't wait until a few days before the hunt to apply. You will be delayed in beginging your hunt. If you are planning to hunt on private land you still have to register your bait station. Make sure to bring a copy of your written permision to submit with your COR application.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hunters will find bears primarily in the oak brush to mixed conifer habitats. Bear numbers and are increasing on the unit and bears can be found primarily from about the 7,000-9,500 foot elivations all around the unit. Hunters can choose to use dogs, spot and stalk, or use bait on this hunt. If you choose to use bait during this hunt, please make sure to follow the rules do not apply for a bait station near homes/cabins, campgrounds and water sources. Also, if you end up using dogs, do not start them on a bear track within a several miles of your bait station. Sweet baits and meats that are very aromatic seems to work best for bear. Make sure to clean up after you self when you are done hunting or after you harvest. If you choose to use dogs please be respectfull of other public land users. There are several other big game hunts going on, in this unit during this hunts during the fall time frame. In the spring you will most likely encounter turkey hunters.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Make sure somebody at home knows where you are going and when you plan to return. Please be prepared with plenty of food and water if you plan to be out for an extended period of time.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Daytime temps should be mild to warm during this season during the summer and early fall portions of the season. In April, May and November you should expect cold temps and snow. Night time temps can still be below freezing at the the higher elevations but are typically in the high 30's to low 40's. It can and will still snow in May, June and September at the higher elevations on this unit.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder mountain has a good bear population but is a rugged, large, tough place to hunt. Vehicle access is limited and the steep, rocky terrain makes it a challenging experience. The DWR has several GPS tracking collars on female bears and would ask that hunters not harvest a bear with a collar on this unit. These individuals provide important information for the unit and often have cubs with them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Please don't harvest our radio collared bears! Boars usually prefer the higher elevations on the Boulder and sows with cubs often don't leave the oak/mountain brush zones around the mountain. All parts of the mountain have populations of bears and pre-season scouting and hiking will help hunters find good areas. Game cameras can help bait hunters identify promising areas to select for bait sites and evaluate age class and sex of bears frequenting the area. There are many lakes and streams on the Boulder and these are areas where bears like to feed and lounge. When trailing bears with hounds, hunters can expect to cover lots of country through thick vegetation while pursuing. Spot and stalk style hunting on this unit is incredibly difficult due to the topography and thick conifer stands covering the unit that prohibit hunters from being able to see far with optics. Hunting with a guide on the Boulder is a good idea for some hunters.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Boulder is a tough place to hunt. Take plenty of water and always tell someone where you plan to hunt. Be prepared to spend the night in the backcountry in case your hunt goes south on you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is unpredictable and can change suddenly. Snow can fall anytime of the year especially at high elevations. Nights can be very cold.

hunt_bio_general_information: The San Juan has one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the spring, focus on areas with green, grassy meadows. This typically means following the snowline up and glassing south facing hills. Bears will feed on the green grass soon after coming out of their dens. Later in the season, their diet will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet, looking for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, and then berries and acorns later on. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear, suggesting that she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. For those using bait, be cautious when entering your bait station area. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. During the early and late portion of the hunt rain and snow may be possible. You should also be prepared for hot, dry conditions throughout the hunt. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit receives a lot of public use throughout the hunts, including camping. During the spring hunt, expect forest service roads to be closed for most of the hunt. The fall hunt coincides with the bull elk and buck deer archery hunts and several other hunts, including muzzleloader elk and general season deer. This unit sees heavy hunting and camping use during these hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Recommended areas on Diamond Mountain: Marshall Draw, Mail Draw, Warren Draw, Little Hole
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting seasons. Be prepared for snow, rain, wind, heat, and lightning. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Roads can become very muddy, and sometimes impassable, after spring storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: Hunters with this permit are allowed to hunt all legal seasons during the year on this unit including the spring Hound and Spot & Stalk season, the summer Bait and Spot & Stalk season and the fall hunt which allows for Hounds, Spot & Stalk and bait.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bears are found across the entire unit. This is not considered a "trophy" bear unit by most hunters but good bears are harvested on the unit each year. Hunters need to be aware of Ute Tribal Lands which is closed to bear hunting for non-tribal members. Be aware of the tribal boundary and avoid turning out hounds close to the tribal boundary. If a hound crosses onto tribal land, hunters will need to contact the Ute Tribe Fish and Game Dept. and request access to enter tribal land to retrieve hounds on tribal land. Hunter success using the Spot & Stalk method has been very low on this unit. It is rare to see a bear on this unit without bait or hounds.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This hunt now allows legal firearms to be used. Be certain of your target before pointing your weapon. Rifle scopes should never be used as binoculars. Cellular phone coverage can be spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return if you camp out. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions can vary widely across the different hunts. The spring hunt is usually cool and wet. The summer hunt is normally fairly dry with cool mornings. The fall hunt starts out warm and dry but gets very cold and can even be snowy later in the season.

hunt_bio_general_information: Bear populations are doing well across the whole unit. This hunt allows you to hunt all legal seasons on the unit. Baiting is allowed on the May 27- June 30 hunt. Dogs are allowed March 30 - May 27, Aug. 1 - Aug. 31 & Nov. 4 - Nov. 10, 2024. You may not place bait in either of the following areas: •Within 100 yards of water, a public road or a designated trail. •Within a half-mile of any permanent dwelling or campground. Fore more information refer to the Utah Bear hunting guide book. https://wildlife.utah.gov/guidebooks/bear_guidebook.pdf
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There are bears across the whole unit. Look for areas away from campgrounds, roads, trails, and areas frequented by the general public. The more remote the area the better. Bears like areas close to water and cover. Streams flowing by conifers are good places to start. Use some kind of attractant such as anise oil or liquid fish fertilizer. Place attractant high in a tree so as to have the sent loft out. Bears can smell a mile away. Trail cameras are a good tool to use to find information on bears sex, age and time of day visiting the area. Make sure to follow all rules regarding the use of Trail cameras. Some areas to look at are Strawberry valley, Sheep Creek, Diamond Fork, Hobble Creek, American Fork Canyon, but bears can be found in most all areas on the unit.. Hunters are encouraged to locate baits in areas not previously hunted if they are looking for a large boar. Harvesting bears in the same locations each year leads to over harvest of mature adults in that area. Be aware of air current flow as you pick your hunting spot. Bears have amazing noses and can wind hunters easily and then may only come to the bait after dark when it is not legal harvest them. Hunter success using the Spot & Stalk method has been very low on this unit

Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Bears can be unpredictable and caution should be taken when hunting them.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather during this season is normally warm with cool mornings. Unexpected weather is always possible during this season. Be prepared for hot and dry conditions or wet and cold.

[{"BOUNDARY_ID":615,"ACREAGE":0,"LAND_OWNERSHIP":"The vast majority of the habitat from Argyle Canyon south is privately owned. Many of these properties are enrolled in the CWMU program where a separate hunting permit is required for big game on their property and they can not allow access. On this part of the unit there are only small isolated parcels of public lands on summer ranges to hunt. Prior permission must be secured before hunting on private lands. There is more public land on the northern third of the unit near Anthro Mountain. There is a mix of USFS and BLM lands in this area although wildlife densities tend to be lower in this area.

Anthro Subunit
Public, Private and Tribal Lands. The public lands are primarily US Forest Service lands managed by the Ashley National Forest and The Bureau of Land Management(BLM) managed out of the Vernal Field Office. This unit also includes large tracks of Ute Tribal lands that are closed to non-tribal members. The Tribal lands are mostly on the North end of the unit in the pinyon/juniper belt, with heavy oil field activity. The private land on the unit is primarily North of the Tribal boundary and in the low elevation desert areas and agricultural lands. There are two CWMU's on the unit (Antelope Creek and Cottonwood Ridge).

Range Creek Subunit
Most of the high elevation summer and early fall habitat is privately owned. Much of this private land occurs on 5 CWMU's (Preston Nutter Ranch, Patmos Ridge, Roan Cliffs, Conover-Jensen, and Minnie Maud CWMU's). Public lands occur at mid elevations and on the winter range. The vast majority of Nine Mile Canyon is privately owned. ","WMA_IN_UNIT":"The Cold Springs WMA exists on good habitat near the town of Sunnyside

The Cottonwood WMA exists on the Anthro subunit. ","CAMPGRND_INFO":"There are no known developed campgrounds on the unit. There are ample opportunities for dispersed camping on BLM and SITLA properties. No camping is allowed on the Cold Springs WMA. Please consult the Price BLM office for any camping restrictions at http://www.blm.gov/ut/st/en/fo/price.html

hunt_bio_general_information: Bears can be found throughout the entire unit. In general look for for areas away from heavy ATV access and popular camping locations.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bears seem to be equally distributed across the unit and can be found at different elevations. Most seem to be color phase with very little black coats being found. Depending on the year, oak brush can be a good place to look as acorns can be an important food source in the fall.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be cautious about baiting bears near campsites, try to always hunt with other people, be mindful of weather conditions. Cell phone coverage can be spotty.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: All types of weather can happen during this hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: Bear populations on these units have been increasing over the last 5-10 years but are still lower than other units in the State.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: With increasing bear densities, these units have provided hunters with more and more opportunity to harvest bears. Although there are not as many bears as other units in the Northern Region, bears are regularly showing up on trail cameras across the unit. Bears are using high elevation forested habitats from the Sinks area, Temple Peak, and Rock Creek on the Cache unit through the Monty Cristo area.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Bears are found in high elevation forested areas. Be prepared to be in the back country.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather in the spring and fall can change quickly, and can range from warm sunny days to cold snowy days.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal's have one of the highest densities of bears in the state, making for one of the best bear hunting units available. Please be respectful to private property, ask for permission before hunting on or turning dogs loose through private property. There are many different resource users on this mountain range, please be courteous to them. In order to reduce conflicts with others on the mountain, houndsmen are encouraged to keep the number of people and dogs in their hunting party to a minimum.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This can be a great hunt for trophy black bears. In the spring, focus on areas with green, grassy meadows. This typically means following the snowline up and glassing south facing hills. Bears will feed on the green grass soon after coming out of their dens. Later in the season, their diet will change to a more protein/carbohydrate based diet, looking for grubs and other insects by rolling rocks or logs, and then berries and acorns later on. Once you locate a bear, watch for any cubs that may be present, or look for evidence on a treed bear that suggests she may have cubs. It is illegal to harvest or pursue a bear with new cubs. There are bears with radio-collars or ear-tags on this unit. If you should happen to see one of these bears, the Division of Wildlife is interested. You can report the observation (eartag #, color) to the local biologist or Conservation Officer.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: When hunting bears with hounds, you can go from the bottom of the mountain to the top in a hurry. Use caution when trailing bears through steep, ledgy terrain. For those using bait, be cautious when entering your bait station area. Cell phone service is spotty throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt can change drastically. During the early and late portion of the hunt rain and snow may be possible. You should also be prepared for hot, dry conditions throughout the hunt. Be aware of what the sky is doing away from you, flash floods are common in this area and can begin many miles away.
