hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt is a great opportunity to hunt deer on the famed Paunsaugunt unit. This is a management hunt so an antler restriction is in place during this hunt. Throughout this hunt deer will be located on the northern 2/3's of the unit. You can hunt from the Glendale Bench road North to highway 12 on the north end. The deer like the higher elevation range up near Tropic Reservoir and south to the end of the pink cliffs. These deer can also be found at mid elevation ranges just below the pink cliffs. These deer often feed in the bitterbrush flats in the mornings and evenings, often bedding in the oak brush during the day. Hunting water and trails to water and feed could be a great way to harvest a buck. Also spot and stalk hunting will be very effective as deer are in their summer feeding habits, However depending on the year the migration will start occurring during this hunt. Deer on this unit migrate from high and mid ranges to lower desert ranges for the winter. If the migration is occurring you might want to focus on the mid ranges of this unit. You can find and hunt migration trails as a good tactic. If acorns are present on the oak brush during your hunting season focus on these areas as the deer really focus on eating the acorns as they migrate, and even cause them to hold up in these areas for several days.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell service is limited in certain parts of the unit
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Warm summer temperatures will likely occur during this hunt. Warm days followed up by cool nights are normal. It is also possible to receive heavy monsoon moisture during this time frame. Higher elevation temperatures could dip low enough that this moisture could change to snow.

These private lands will be more of an impact for deer hunters than pronghorn or bighorn sheep hunters. ","WMA_IN_UNIT":"Nash Wash WMA. It is accessed from Exit 204 off of Interstate 70. Firewood and water are relatively scarce. Plan on bringing your own water. ","SUGGESTED_MAPS":"The yellow 1:100,000 scale BLM maps named Westwater, Huntington, and Moab.","COUNTY_ROAD_INFO":"Grand County: http://www.grandcountyutah.net/pdf/roads/broadmap.jpg ","ATV_VEH_ACCESS":"ATV and Vehicle Access: allowed on approved roads and trails

Bighorn Sheep: Most roads and ATV trails on this unit are managed by the BLM and are covered on its Travel Management Plan. There are only a few roads that go on or near bighorn sheep habitat on the unit. The Hastings Road just east of the Green River in the town of Green River will take you along the east side of the Green River for about 15 miles until the road dead-ends near Rattlesnake Canyon. This road will provide the closest access to where most of the sheep live. This road is graded by the county and is generally in good shape. There are some tight spots along the river that you should be wary of if there is snowy or icy conditions. The Tushar Canyon road will go northeast off of the Hastings Road about 9 miles north of the town of Green River. It will access the right and left fork of Tushar Canyon and loop around along the bench to the east and provide access to Coal, Horse, and Floy Canyons. The Coal Canyon Road is the first right hand turn off of the Hastings Road while still in the town of Green River. It will go through a bunch of alfalfa fields and then up on the cliffs. the Horse Canyon and Floy Canyon roads can be access by following the frontage road along I-70 to the east. Despite all of these directions, most of your time will be spent on foot.

Deer: The main areas with the highest concentrations of deer include Nash Wash (Exit 204 off of Interstate 70), Cottonwood Canyon (Exit 214), Hay Canyon (Exit 221), and Bitter Creek (Exit 227)

Pronghorn: Use any exit off of Interstate 70 or drive the frontage road along the Interstate. Major access points include Green River (Exit 164), Floy Wash (Exit 175), Crescent Junction, Thompson, Yellowcat, Nash Wash (Exit 204), Cottonwood (Exit 214), Sulphur Canyon (Exit 221), and Bitter Creek (Exit 227)","PRIV_TRIBE_LAND_ISSUES":"Bighorn Sheep: The northern boundary of this unit adjoins Ute Tribal lands along Coal Creek. This is good bighorn sheep habitat and bighorns have been seen on both sides of the boundary near the mouth of Coal Creek. Take great care not to hunt or trespass on these tribal lands. The upper Tribal Boundary at upper elevations near Sego Canyon generally doesn't have bighorn sheep during November. There are small isolated pieces of private property in the mouths of Coal, Horse, Floy, and Thompson Canyons. County roads go through these properties so it is best to simply travel through them and park on public lands if you do not have written permission to hunt on these private lands. Bighorn sheep generally do not spend a great deal of time on these private lands.

Pronghorn: There is a large block of private land on the alfalfa fields near the town of Green River. Antelope use this area. Please secure written permission prior to hunting these private lands. The remainder of the private lands on this unit either do not occur in Pronghorn habitat or are scattered and unmarked.

Deer: Deer concentrate on private lands at the mouths of Cottonwood, Hay, and Bitter Creek Canyons. Please secure written permission prior to hunting these private lands. They are relatively small parcels so they are easy to avoid but they do concentrate deer. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 99% of land where hunters can expect to see deer in the eastern half of the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure. Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Most higher elevation Raft River Mountains deer will remain high on the range until snow depths push them down into the sagebrush flats. Access to higher elevations is through One Mile Canyon, George Creek Canyon, Johnson Canyon, and Wildcat Canyon. Deer are plentiful and hunting opportunities exist up every canyon. Deer along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range can be found up Kimbell Creek, Red Banks, and Keg Springs along the west side and near Devil's Playground and Rocky Pass on the east side. Mule deer in the higher elevations do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the Raft River Mountains to the southeast end of the Grouse Creek Mountains for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats from Kelton to Devil's Playground. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This is a very productive unit with one of the largest deer herds in the state. Muzzleloader hunters will find most success hunting on summer habitats at 7,500 feet and above. In some years hunting on water sources can be productive but water is generally not limiting on the Manti portion of this unit. Migration Patterns: There is very little deer migration during the muzzleloader hunt. Deer remain on summer ranges typically at 7,500 feet and above. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches east of SR-89 on the west and the sagebrush benches west of SR-6 and SR-10 on the east side of the mountain. There is very little seasonal movement of deer on the San Rafael portion of the unit. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: Upper Fish Creek and it's tributaries. The tributaries include Gooseberry Creek, Silver Creek, C Canyon, and the Straight Fork. This is a roadless area on the north end of the unit. This area has had some prescribed fires recently that has improved deer habitat. It can be accessed from North Skyline Drive on the west or from Scofield Reservoir on the east. The bottom two miles of Upper Fish Creek is privately owned and in a CWMU Bear Ridge and Fish Creek Ridge These ridges have roads going down them. They are northwest of Scofield Reservoir. The bottom 2 miles of these ridges are privately owned. This is excellent habitat in the Pondtown Creek drainage on the north end of the unit. It is best accessed from North Skyline Drive. Trough Spring Ridge This is accessed off of SR-264 southwest of the town of Scofield. It is just above the Skyline Coal Mine. This is the ridge on the east side of Electric Lake. There are some small pockets of private land that are posted well but the majority of the acreage is Forest Service. Much of this ridge burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 which has improved the deer habitat in this area. Gentry Mountain. This is accessed from SR-10 just north of the town of Huntington at Huntington Reservoir. Part of this mountain is privately owned and part of it burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 West of Skyline Drive All the small towns along the west face of the Central Mountains Manti Unit has a canyon road to connect to Skyline Drive. Some roads are fairly rough going with the better access up from Fairview, Ephraim and Mayfiled. Concentrate on side roads and trails from the main canyon roads to get to the more likely areas to find deer. The higher elevations in aspen and sagebrush meadows with water in close proximity will hold some of the mature bucks. Down low in the agricultural valleys many younger bucks will use the alfalfa fields in the evenings and early morning. Much of the adjacent property along the agriculture is either Forest Service or State lands and there will be a good opportunities there. East of Skyline Drive and South of Huntington Canyon There is a considerable amount of access along Skyline Drive, high elevation ridge tops, and lower canyons and valleys. There are also many areas where you can hike to get away from roads, much of it very steep, but where nice bucks hold up. Some preliminary scouting with maps is a great way to familiarize yourself with the unit. hunt_bio_general_information: This is a pre-rut/early rut hunt that highly depends on weather factors. If weather conditions are warm and/or there hasn't yet been a substantial snow storm bucks may be found solitary or in bachelor groups still at high elevations. Snow and cool temperatures may initiate deer migration to lower elevations as well as early rut behavior with bucks being found grouped up with does in transitional mountain brush habitats or winter range. Be flexible in hunting strategies for greatest chance of success.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This is a very productive unit with both road access to high elevations and backcountry hunting opportunities. If the weather has been mild throughout October then most hunters will find most success hunting on summer habitats at 7,500 feet and above. If there has been a few snowstorms then deer will often begin their fall migration and hunters find success on sagebrush and mid-mountain brush type habitats. Migration Patterns: Fall migration is very weather dependent on this unit. Most migration occurs in late November when significant snowfall typically occurs. However, big snowstorms in late October have prompted migration during the any weapon hunt. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to benches on both the east and west sides of the mountain. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. but pre-rut and early rut behaviors may be observed during this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: Nebo Loop, Loafer Mtn, Spencer Fork, and Mona and Santaquin Benches on the north Nebo, Chicken Creek, Log Hollow, Red Ledges, and Sage Flats on the Sanpitch Mtns are good places to start looking. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting deer. Find a high vantage point and glass a lot of terrain. If you find does with no bucks grouped up with them, keep checking on the area periodically as bucks will begin to group up with does more and more as the hunt goes on.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, snow, and cold. Early winter storms can create muddy or snowy roads and trails.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the La Sals typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Using quality binoculars or spotting scopes will be very valuable to you. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas for the muzzleloader hunt: Muzzleloader hunters will find bucks in the high country, but should also focus on mid to high elevations throughout the unit. Look for oak patches with intermixed sagebrush meadows and a healthy forbe component.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting deer in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of the bucks. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are several recovering burned areas that have produced large amounts of edge that is excellent for deer. Deer spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs. There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Panguitch Lake unit has a healthy deer population. Expect to see several bucks each day, with the majority probably being young deer. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. During the muzzloader hunt most deer are still in summer range with some deer in transition to their wintering habitat. Most deer will still be higher elevations on Forest Service and Private lands. This unit has a substantial amount of year-round range that will always have some deer. The eastern portion will have good numbers of deer on USFS lands and will generally see the heaviest hunting pressure. Some good areas to hunt include areas near Cedar Breaks National Monument, Red Desert, Sidney Valley, Hatch Mountain, Horse Valley, and Little Valleys. Migration Patterns: The migratory segments of this population may begin their fall movements in late September and October. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars can be helpful if you are unfamiliar with the area. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the muzzle loader season deer are scattered over the entire unit. Much of the buck movement is dictated by weather conditions. Bucks tend to remain higher in elevation than does until the rut begins. The Boulder Top is above 11,000 ft elevation and generally most deer move off the top by late September. Most of the deer tend to be at the intersection of the conifer/aspen habitats and the aspen/mountain brush/sage habitats. Hunters who want to hunt the Kaiparowits portion of the unit need to be prepared to see few deer and experience very difficult hunting conditions. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Abajos typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Once the rut starts, bucks will be found with and around does. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect these hunts. Recommended areas for the San Juan, Abajo subunit: Abajo Mountain - Muzzleloader hunters may find bucks in the high country, but should also focus on mid elevations. Look for oak-brush stands or sagebrush parks, surrounded by pinyon/juniper communities.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is managed as a General Season deer hunt and is not necessarily managed for trophy bucks, but every year a few nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The Uintah Mountain range can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also less deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. There are several four wheeler roads and dirt roads that provide a lot of access on much of the unit. The Bonanza unit has very low deer densities.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and tend to stay on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. Mule Deer rut: This hunt gets close to the the mule deer rut that usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Vernal: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. There is a variety of habitat to hunt during this late muzzleloader hunt. There is pinyon/juniper, sage brush savanna, thick lodge pole pine and areas above timber line. The larger openings on the forest are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and rocky terrain. During the hunts most of the deer on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. That zone across the South Slope is the most productive for deer. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit: Whiterocks Canyon- Whiterocks River is the western unit boundary, steep terrain. Paradise Park- Higher forest terrain, steep forested canyons. Mosby Mountain- High aspen forest, with large sagebrush bowls, excellent habitat. Red Cloud Loop Rd- Long road that starts in Dry Fork Canyon (west of Vernal). It takes you all the way through the Vernal unit, and comes out on Hwy 191.. Taylor Mountain- Great vantage points. Excellent area to glass and locate animals from far distances. Colton Ranger Station- Aspen/conifer mix forest. Limestone, Little V, and Range Study- These areas are east of Hwy 191 and border the Diamond Mountain limited entry deer and elk unit, know the boundary and your location.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: There is spotty cell service in some of the lower elevation hunting areas and typically on the faces overlooking the Uinta Basin. However, there are many areas with no phone service so let someone know where you are going and when you will be back.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for warm & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or snowy conditions. Early snow storms occur often during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: General Considerations: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. There are many CWMUs on this unit and a list of these can be found on the UDWR webpage. Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and typically from East to West, with most of the deer wintering on Wallsburg WMA, Sheep Creek and Diamond Fork canyons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. There are many CWMUs on this unit and a list of these can be found on the UDWR webpage. Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and typically from East to West, with good numbers of deer wintering on Wallsburg WMA, Sheep Creek and Diamond Fork canyons and the Wasatch face. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. After the general season deer hunt is over, bucks will begin to look for does to breed. Start looking on winter ranges as deer start to migrate at lower elevations at this time of year. Recommended areas to hunt: There are numerous areas to hunt on this unit. The areas surrounding Strawberry Reservoir, Sheep Creek, Diamond Fork, Hobble Creek, American Fork canyons, Mt. Timpanogos are excellent for deer hunting. They are easy to access with many roads and trails and camping areas. There are very few areas on this unit without a road in the general area. This unit has very large aspen stands, oak brush can hold a lot of deer in the early fall. In the summer there are deer in the more open higher areas, but once they get pressured by hunters they will move into the lower, thicker tree stands. These areas are difficult to hunt because of the leaves on the trees and fewer open areas to glass with optics. There are also many lower areas with several different browse species, including; oak brush, service berry, mountain mahogany, bitter brush, snow berry, sage brush, etc. These areas also have deer in them during the hunt, but at a lower density. All ways look for areas that deer are watering in. Some areas to hunt include the following: Strawberry Reservoir area- Try Indian canyon, Clyde Creek, Mud Creek, Squaw Creek, Horse Creek, Main canyon and Strawberry ridge. Sheep Creek area- Try any of the waters ( First to Sixth) along Ray's Valley road. Sheep Creek is a good winter range, Diamond Fork- Diamond Fork is a mixture of public and private and is a good winter range. Hobble Creek- Right Hand fork is mostly public land, Left Hand Fork is mostly private land. American Fork Canyon/Mt. Timpanogos-This area is steep and rugged. Timp WMA-This area is real brushy but can be good hunting. Wallsburg WMA-This WMA is mostly open sagebrush. Hunting can be good as the rut begins

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has a low deer population and is very remote with extreme topography. This is a very difficult unit to find deer. If you never have seen the Deep Creeks you better go look before your hunt. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting deer in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of the bucks along with everyone else. This is a popular unit to put cameras out. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset)unless pressured. Upper elevations deer spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. Consult with the Goshute Reservation for info on the reservation boundaries. The reservation expanded a few years ago and the public maps are not up to date. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a new Limited Entry muzzleloader only late buck hunt on a General Season hunt unit (not a trophy unit). This hunt is almost entirely private property. Do not apply for this hunt unless you have written permission to hunt private property within the boundary. The purpose of this hunt is to reduce mature buck density in an area with high prevalence of Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD). This hunt is primarily an agricultural area hunt. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt is intended to target mature bucks early in the rut in a private property area with high buck to doe ratios that has a high prevalence of Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD). The intent is to reduce the potential for mature bucks that may have CWD from dispersing into surrounding areas and spreading CWD. It's been found in other states that in areas with high buck to doe ratios older bucks are more likely to disperse to sounding areas during the rut and thereby spread CWD. Private landowners are not required to allow public access to hunt on their property. Hunters wanting to hunt this hunt must have written permission to hunt before applying. Obtaining permission after drawing the permit will be very difficult.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This hunt is primarily an agricultural area hunt. Extreme caution must be used to avoid shooting toward houses, agricultural structures or livestock.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a limited entry hunt on a general season unit. This hunt is comprised mostly of private lands. There are some roads/atv trails that allow access to both private and public land. This hunt is not managed to be a trophy hunt, but because of the high amount of private land and CWMU's there is a high ratio of bucks and a lot of mature bucks.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit experienced a hard winter this last year and we lost a big portion of fawns and adult deer to winter loss. You can expect to see fewer deer during the hunt. There is some forest land in the south east corner as well as a small chunk of DWR land and BLM land near Echo reservoir. The only portion of the Henefer/Echo WMA that can be hunted on this unit is south of I-80. While there is a high ratio of bucks there is also a higher ratio of deer on private land compared to public land. This hunt is mostly private lands. Be aware of property boundaries. Make sure you secure permission before hunting on private lands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell phone coverage is spotty. Hunters are encouraged to use a "spot tracker" device in areas without good cell coverage. Road conditions may be difficult in remote areas. Hunters should prepare for muddy roads and occasional snowdrifts which will make travel difficult.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions can be unpredictable and hunters should prepare accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is comprised primarily of private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to applying for the hunt if they wish to hunt private property. This is a limited entry hunt on a general season unit and is not managed for trophy bucks. You will lose your bonus points if you draw out on this hunt. This hunt is intended to provide hunters with an opportunity to hunt later in the season as deer begin to enter the rut. Although the unit is managed for opportunity, there are several CWMUs and parcels of private land throughout the unit, which manage for better buck quality than general season units typically offer. This can result in better buck quality and higher buck numbers on the public land. Please be respectful of private property and do not trespass.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Please note: the winter of 2022/2023 had record snowfall and extremely cold temperatures, which resulted in a significant reduction in the deer population on this unit. Adult doe survival for deer that wintered on the Wasatch Back was approximately 14% and survival for deer that wintered on the Wasatch Front was approximately 50%. Survival on an average year is typically around 85%. The Wildlife Board approved a 40% cut in permits in 2023 and will remain similar for 2024, so expect to continue to see very few hunters and less crowding than historically on the unit. Although a large percent of deer were lost in 2022/23, climatic conditions over the last year have been excellent with lots of moisture and a warmer than average winter, which will result in more available bucks to hunt this Fall. Buck:Doe ratios have also remained high (above the objective) on the unit. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding early in the mornings and late in the evenings. The deer will likely not be in the same place during the late season muzzleloader hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Use quality binoculars or a spotting scope to locate animals. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Migration: Deer migrate from higher elevations to lower elevations in early to late fall. During most years, deer will begin migrating before or during the late season muzzleloader hunt. If fall conditions remain warm, deer will remain at higher elevations and can be found in Aspen stands, open meadows or bedded in conifer stands. This hunt can be challenging if weather conditions are dry and warm. Most years, the area will receive snow before or during the hunt, and deer will begin migrating to lower elevations into oak stands on the Wasatch Front and Sagebrush stands on the Wasatch Back. Rut: Deer typically begin rutting early to mid-November depending on weather conditions. Cold and snowy conditions will be beneficial for hunters during this hunt. Recommended areas for the hunt: For motorized access, the B in Bountiful is a good access point for the Wasatch National Forest Land that extends between North Salt Lake and I-84. This area primarily holds yearling bucks, but getting off road and into thicker vegetation and rugged terrain can lend success in finding mature bucks to harvest. Highway 65 has several access points from Little Dell Reservoir to Big Mountain Pass where deer can be found. If conditions are warm, hunt the higher elevation areas. If conditions are snowy, hunt the lower elevation areas. Please be mindful of the archery only zone and avoid Emigration Canyon. East Canyon WMA also has many deer later in the season. Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) has been detected on this unit. It is recommended that hunters have deer harvested on this unit tested for CWD. To do so, call the Ogden Division Office.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Despite being close to the Wasatch Front, service is spotty on this unit. Most ridgetops have service, while many lower elevation areas do not. Much of the terrain is steep, so be cautious while hiking, especially when conditions are wet or snowy. Always let someone know where you are going and when you will return home. Be sure to keep campsites clean, and keep food and garbage inaccessible to bears. Store any items with an odor in a vehicle, hung in a tree at least 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches, or in a bear proof container. Coolers are not bear proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Most years, the snow will melt off within a few days throughout the hunting season. This unit usually receives some snow during October and/or November. Consider bringing multiple layers of clothing to keep comfortable as conditions can change drastically throughout the day.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Please note: the winter of 2022/2023 had record snowfall and extremely cold temperatures, which resulted in a significant reduction in the deer population on this unit. Although a large percent of deer were lost in 2022/23, climatic conditions over the last year have been excellent, with lots of moisture and a warmer than average winter, which will result in more available bucks to hunt this Fall. Use quality binoculars or a spotting scope to locate animals. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. If fall conditions remain warm, deer will remain at higher elevations and can be found in Aspen stands, open meadows or bedded in conifer stands. Most years, the area will receive a snowstorm before or during the hunt, and deer will begin migrating to lower elevations into oak and sagebrush stands. Rut: Deer typically begin rutting early to mid-November depending on weather conditions. Cold and snowy conditions will be beneficial for hunters during this hunt. Recommended areas for the hunt: The Henefer Echo WMA has several access points and holds many young bucks year round. An early cold snap can result in more mature bucks moving onto the WMA during the hunt. The US Forest Service land near Causey Reservoir can also be excellent hunting if conditions stay relatively warm. In colder temperatures, deer will be found on south slopes in sagebrush stands. In warmer weather, deer will be found in aspen or conifer stands near the reservoir. Additionally, South of Monte Cristo Peak has a good number of deer in the summer and fall. If weather remains relatively warm, hunters can find deer throughout the US Forest Service land but the deer may begin migrating to lower elevations during the hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Thousand Lakes unit is now a limited entry hunt unit and is also part of a study being conducted on primitive weapons hunts. The unit has some good deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years the unit has experienced an increase in the deer population and an increase in the buck/doe ratio. Deer hunting has been good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters have been noticing an increasing number of mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit, however the highest density of deer tend to be on the central part of the unit. The southern portion of the unit is drier and has fewer deer. Plan to spend time scouting this unit before hunting it. During the Archery season most of the deer tend to be in the higher elevations near water. Hunter densities can be high unless you move away from roads and ATV trails . Remember that Capitol Reef National Park is on the eastern portion of this unit and the park is closed to hunting and ATV travel.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the Archery season deer are scattered over the entire unit. Much of the buck movement is dictated by weather conditions. Bucks tend to remain higher in elevation than does. The Table Top is above 11,000 ft elevation and generally most deer move off the top by late September. Most of the deer tend to be at the intersection of the conifer/aspen habitats and the aspen/mountain brush/sage habitats. If you choose to hunt near agricultural areas be sensitive to trespassing on private lands. You must have written permission on your person to hunt on private property. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some very remote areas on this unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Monsoonal rains can occur during this hunt. Be prepared for muddy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Little Rockies are located southeast of the Henry Mountains, they are extremely rugged and steep. The unit features mesas and deep canyons that are difficult to access and navigate. Utilizing watercraft on Lake Powell may offer an easier route to the lower elevation canyons. Given the limited access, you should be prepared for long days and cold nights in this desert environment. This is a desert unit and deer are not plentiful. It is also desert bighorn habitat. While some deer migrate from the Henry Mountains to the Little Rockies, this typically occurs late in the season, usually in December. Most deer present during the hunt are resident rather than migratory. Success on this hunt will likely require significant experience, time, and effort, because it is an extremely low-density desert buck hunt. This hunt was established by the Mule Deer Committee to offer a new opportunity; however, it is not designed for harvesting Henry Mountain deer. Although the Little Rockies are located within the Henry Mountains deer unit-which is why it is named Henry Mtn's, Little Rockies -harvesting a deer similar in size to those found on the Henry Mountains is not assured.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The 2025 harvest rate for this hunt was 40%, with an average of 12 days spent hunting. Hunter satisfaction was rated 1.2 out of 5, and the mean antler width/points were 14" with 3 points. There are many hunters interested in this hunt and asking if it would be worth burning their points on. There are not a lot of deer on the unit, seriously, very few deer! It is a desert unit, and has no similarities to the Henry Mountain hunt. I strongly recommend scouting the area for a year to determine if this hunt aligns with your expectations before using your points. A successful hunt will likely require a significant time commitment, knowledge of buck behavior, and high level of physical fitness. Familiarity with the area will be a bonus. Good luck in your decision!

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is an opportunity to use a primitive weapon type during the mule deer rut in desert and canyon terrain. Deer densities are extremely low and hunters should expect a challenging hunt. This is not a guaranteed hunt; hunters may not harvest a deer-let alone see one.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This is a challenging hunt. Deer densities are extremely low. Time spent before the hunt scouting and getting to know the area will be critical to increasing chances of success. The unit is very dry, so finding sources of water and looking for tracks can be an effective strategy to find if deer are in the area.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Much of this unit is very remote and has very limited cell service. Please inform others where you plan to hunt before leaving. Expect rough roads and rugged terrain. Some roads become effectively impassable when muddy. Do not push your comfort levels navigating this terrain, it is easy to get yourself into a bad situation.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Be prepared for muddy road conditions. Although unlikely during this hunt, be aware of flash flood potential.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt was created to target potential transmission of Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) out of the Moab/ Spanish Valley area during the rut. CWD prevalence has been increasing in this area, so this hunt is to try to minimize spread of CWD outside of this area. This is a limited-entry hunt because of the season dates, not because of the trophy potential. The boundary occurs within a general-season unit, so hunters should expect the quality of bucks to reflect this. Please consider this before putting in for this hunt. Although this is an Any Legal Weapon hunt, there are areas within this hunt boundary that have weapon restrictions (i.e. Matheson Wetland Preserve), so hunters should be familiar with these before going afield. There is also no hunting within city limits. There is a lot of private property encompassed in this hunt boundary, hunters must obtain written permission if they wish to hunt on private property. If you harvest a buck on this hunt, there is a chance it will test positive for CWD. It is recommended that hunters do not consume meat from CWD positive animals. If your deer comes back positive, you can surrender the meat to UDWR for proper disposal. You will not be reissued another tag if you harvest a CWD positive animal. To find out more about CWD, visit our website: https://wildlife.utah.gov/chronic-wasting-disease.html
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There is an abundant resident deer population in the Moab and Spanish Valley bottoms, but deer will migrate out of the higher elevations of the La Sals and close to town during the rut. Preseason scouting may give hunters an idea of the quality of bucks on the unit, but deer migrate from various areas across the La Sal unit to this hunt boundary so deer will move into this area as the season progresses.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: There is rugged terrain included within this hunt boundary, be conscious not to put yourself into a spot you can't get out of. There are residential areas within this hunt boundary, please be aware of people and structures near and beyond your target. Be considerate of other people, their property, and pets during your hunt.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather during this season can be highly variable. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind, and heat.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Except for about 750 hectares around the town of Alton, Utah; the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) surrounds the town. To the northeast of Alton (7500 feet), mountains rise from 8500 to 9000 feet. These mountains slope down toward the Sevier River at an elevation of around 7200 feet on the north. On the the south, these mountains slope down to the Kanab River which parts the Alton CWMU on the southeast. The most common elevation is 7400 feet but ranges from 6400 feet to 9000 feet with an elevation difference of 2600 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7300 feet and 8200 feet an elevation difference of 900 feet. Lower elevations on the Unit are around 6800 feet. Towards the southwest of the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWM), there are extensive areas of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36). A co-dominant land cover type is Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). This Shrubland occurs throughout the Unit except for the extreme north. In the extreme north and towards the middle of the Unit are large areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). There are also large patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). The Alton CWMU also has large patches of Rocky Mountain Ponderosa Pine Woodland (34) and Agriculture (114) is scattered throughout the Unit. One of the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ALTON (420086), is about 1.0 km from the middle of the CWMU. ALTON has eighty-three (83) years of records, 1915 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 4.14 inches, but it can be as high as 11.35 inches or as low as 0.36 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 9 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch of perciptiation. Total FALL snowfall averages 7.6 inches but can be as high as 41.7 inches. FALL temperature at ALTON averages 47.3 degrees F. but can be as high as 91.0 degrees F. or as low as -5.0 degrees F. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Except for about 750 hectares around the town of Alton, Utah; the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) surrounds the town. To the northeast of Alton (7500 feet), mountains rise from 8500 to 9000 feet. These mountains slope down toward the Sevier River at an elevation of around 7200 feet on the north. On the the south, these mountains slope down to the Kanab River which parts the Alton CWMU on the southeast. The most common elevation is 7400 feet but ranges from 6400 feet to 9000 feet with an elevation difference of 2600 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7300 feet and 8200 feet an elevation difference of 900 feet. Lower elevations on the Unit are around 6800 feet. Towards the southwest of the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWM), there are extensive areas of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36). A co-dominant land cover type is Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). This Shrubland occurs throughout the Unit except for the extreme north. In the extreme north and towards the middle of the Unit are large areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). There are also large patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). The Alton CWMU also has large patches of Rocky Mountain Ponderosa Pine Woodland (34) and Agriculture (114) is scattered throughout the Unit. One of the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ALTON (420086), is about 1.0 km from the middle of the CWMU. ALTON has eighty-three (83) years of records, 1915 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 4.14 inches, but it can be as high as 11.35 inches or as low as 0.36 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 9 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch of perciptiation. Total FALL snowfall averages 7.6 inches but can be as high as 41.7 inches. FALL temperature at ALTON averages 47.3 degrees F. but can be as high as 91.0 degrees F. or as low as -5.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 44 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Antelope Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is in the southeast part of Duchesne County, about 10.5 km from Duchesne, Utah. Higher elevations are in the southwest corner of the unit (6300 feet). Antelope Creek that cuts the CWMU ranges from 5300 feet to 5800 feet. Pleasant Valley in the east ranges from 5300 feet to 5800 feet. The most common elevation is 5500 feet but ranges from 5300 feet to 6300 feet with an elevation difference of 1000 feet. Fifty (50%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5600 feet and 6100 feet an elevation difference of 500 feet. About thirty-six perecent (36%) of the Antelope Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Colorado Plateau Mixed Low Sagebrush Shrubland (50), located on the westside of the unit. Another thirty-four percent (34%) is Inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58), located mostly on the eastside of the unit. Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (66), Inter-Mountain Basins Greasewood Flat (82), and Inter-Mountain Basins Semi-Desert Grassland (76) also figure into the mix. One of the Antelope Creek Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, DUCHESNE (422253), is about 6.0 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. DUCHESNE has eighty-three (92) years of records, 1906 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.57inches, but it can be as high as 6.21 inches or as low as 0.25 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 3.1 inches but can be as high as 17.1 inches. FALL temperature at DUCHESNE averages 46.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 93.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 49 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Avintaquin Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located southeast of Duchesne, Utah about 30 km. The major feature of the CWMU is the Avintaquin Canyon and Avintaquin River. The Avintaquin River ranges from 6400 feet to 6800 feet on the unit. At 6800 feet the river splits into the West Fork Avintaquin River (6900 feet to 6800 feet) and the South Fork Avintaquin River (7100 feet to 6800 feet). Minnie Creek is another major drainage on the CWMU. Minnie Creek flows from the west to the east entering at 7100 feet and merging with the West Fork Avintaquin River at 6800 feet. On the Avintaquin Canyon CWMU 7300 feet is the most common elevation. However, elevation ranges from 6400 feet to 8400 feet, a difference of 2000 feet. Fifty-five percent (55%) of the unit's elevation ranges from 6400 feet to 7300 feet, a difference of 900 feet. The Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) is the most common cover type, nearly 50%. The only other cover type that takes up much area is the Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Most of this cover type is on the west side of the unit. Together the pinyon-juniper woodland and the sagebrush steppe account for 70% of the cover. One of the Avintaquin Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, SOLDIER SUMMIT (427959), is about 39.0 km from the edge of the CWMU in a southwest direction. SOLDIER SUMMIT has one hundred nine (109) years of records, 1893 - 2002. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.09 inches, but it can be as high as 7.56 inches or as low as 1.27 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 16 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 14.3 inches but can be as high as 33.3inches. FALL temperature at SOLDIER SUMMIT averages 40.5degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -20.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 71 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Bally Watts Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is divided into north and south by Cottonwood Creek. Cottonwood Creek enters the Unit at about 5400 feet elevation and exits the unit at 5200 feet. In the north part Bally Watts Creek starts around 6800 feet and exits about 5400 feet, flowing in northwest direction. On the north part Elk Mountain at 7400 feet is the highest point and sloping in a northwest direction to 5400 feet. In the south, Big Mohagany Mountain at 7700 feet and Little Mohagany Mountain at 7200 feet are the highest points. The lowest is about 5000 feet along the Weber River. The most common elevation is 6000 feet but ranges from 5000 feet to 8700 feet with an elevation difference of 3700 feet. Fifty-four percent (54%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5900 feet and 7600 feet an elevation difference of 1700 feet. The Bally Watts Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is dominated by Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Patches of Rocky Mountain Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) area scattered throughout the Unit. In the middle and north part of the Unit are large areas of Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23). There are also large patches of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) scattered throughout the Unit. Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) adds to the Forest and Woodland character of the Unit. Invasive Perennial Garssland (119) and Southern Rocky Mountain Montane- Subalpine Grassland (71) adds to the Grassland character of the Unit. Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Steppe (66) and Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48) add to the shrubland character of the Unit. One of the Bally Watts Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY (424135), is about 4.4 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY has thirty-one (31) years of records, 1976 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 5.74 inches, but it can be as high as 12.30 inches or as low as 1.36 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of percipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 10.2 inches but can be as high as 31.0 inches. FALL temperature at HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY averages 46.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -16.0 degrees F. On the westside, besides the Sagebrush Steppe, there are intermixed patches of Inter- Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). In the middle of the Unit there are some large patches of Rocky Mountain Ponderosa Pine Woodland (34). hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Just southeast of Mount Pleasant, Utah is the Bear Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) ranging from 10000 feet to about 6200 feet. The west part of the Unit is a series of moderate sloping benches and rapidly climbing slopes. On the east at the higher elevations, Bear Mountain CWMU, is cut by the Straight Fork of Pleasant Creek, Dry Pole Creek, and the North and South Forks of Coral Fork. The most common elevation is 7300 feet but ranges from 6200 feet to 10000 feet with an elevation difference of 3800 feet. Fifty (50%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7300 feet and 9100 feet an elevation difference of 1800 feet. Much of the Bear Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit is covered with Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). At the higher elevations there are substantial areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). At lower elevations there is some Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36). At the higher elevation besides the Aspen Forest and Woodland, there is a mixture of Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (28), Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), and Inter-Mountain West Aspen-Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland Complex (38). There are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) scattered from the lowest elevation to the highest. One of the Bear Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ELECTRIC LAKE (422424), is about 13.0 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. ELECTRIC LAKE has twenty-seven (27) years of records, 1980 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 6.31 inches, but it can be as high as 10.05 inches or as low as 1.73 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 26 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 18 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 4 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There is no reliable snowfall data for ELECTRIC LAKE. FALL temperature at ELECTRIC LAKE averages 36.6 degrees F. but can be as high as 81.0 degrees F. or as low as -22.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 71 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is cut east-west by Dry Creek and north-south by State Road 68. Dry Creek starts at about 7200 feet and flows east and then south and exits the Unit at about 4400 feet. The higher elevations are on the west below Snow Basin Ski Resort. Then with a moderate slope the terrian slopes to the southeast and drops down into the Dry Creek cut before exiting the Unit. The most common elevation is 5800 feet but ranges from 5000 feet to 8500 feet with an elevation difference of 3500 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5700 feet and 7600 feet an elevation difference of 1900 feet. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is the dominant land cover type on the Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). There are many large patches of Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23) dispersed among the Gambel Oak, as are smaller patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). There are patches of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) on the west side, more in the middle of the Unit are patches of Rocky Mountain Lower Montane Riparian Shrubland (79), and scattered about are patches of Recently Burned (116) areas. There are some minor areas of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) scattered about. One of the Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, PINE VIEW DAM (422424), is about 3.6 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. PINE VIEW DAM has twenty-seven (72) years of records, 1935 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 7.33 inches, but it can be as high as 16.43 inches or as low as 1.52 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 15 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There is also 2 days with precipitation greater than or equal to 1.00 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 13.7 inches but can be as high as 49.5 inches. FALL temperature at PINE VIEW DAM averages 46.2 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 48 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Blubell Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is about 3.25 miles north of Liberty, Utah on the border of Cache and Weber Counties, mostly in Cache County. In the south are the headwaters of Cache Valley Creek and Broadmouth Canyon. In the northwest is the South Fork of the Little Bear River and the headwaters of Birch Creek. In the northeast are the headwaters of Fish Creek. Elevation ranges from 5600 feet to 9300 feet, a difference of 3700 feet. The most common elevation is 6500 feet. Sevety-three percent (73%) of the unitís elevation ranges between 5600 feet and 7200 feet, a difference of 1600 feet. On the Bluebell CWMU the most dominant land cover is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). About one fourth of the unit is this sagebrush steppe. Almost 20% of the unit is Rocky Mountain Aspen forest and Woodland (22). Rocky Mountain Sualpine Mesic Meadow (70) and southern Rocky Mountain Montane-Subalpine Grassland (71) accounts for another 20% of the unit. An additional eight ecological system and 90% of the unit is covered. One of the Bluebell Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY (424135), is about 17.7 km southeast from the southeast edge of the CWMU. HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY has thirty-one (31) years of records, 1976 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average percipitation is 5.74 inches, but it can be as high as 12.30 inches or as low as 1.36 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of percipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of percipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 10.2 inches but can be as high as 31.0 inches. FALL temperature at HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY averages 46.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -16.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 56 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The westside of the Boobe Hole Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located at 7200 feet in the Plateau Valley. Towards the east the Unit rises to over 10,000 feet on Boobe Hole Mountain. Continuing southwest the Unit slopes down from Boobe Hole Mountain to Otter Creek, 9400 feet in the north and 8400 feet in the south. Finally, the elevation climbs up towards Hightop Plateau to about 9400 feet. The most common elevation is 7100 feet but ranges from 7000 feet to 10000 feet with an elevation difference of 3000 feet. Forty-nine percent (49%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 8000 feet and 9700 feet an elevation difference of 1700 feet. On the Boobe Hole Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) the land cover is distributed in three (3) bands. On the the eastside of the Unit, and taking the most area, is a band of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Moving towards the west, there is a narrow band of Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). Next, there is a wider band of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper (36). Not quite a band, but the extreme west is covered with Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). Back in the Aspen Forest and Woodland are large patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). At the interface between Aspen Forest and Woodland and Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland, are some large areas of Inter-Mountain West Aspen-Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland Complex (38). One of the Boobe Hole Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, KOOSHAREM (424764), is about 14.9 km southwest from the southwest edge of the CWMU. KOOSHAREM has one hundred fourteen (114) years of records, 1893 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.44 inches, but it can be as high as 5.28 inches or as low as 0.58 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 4.7 inches but can be as high as 23.3 inches. FALL temperature at KOOSHAREM averages 45.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 92.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 60 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Buckhorn Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located northwest of the Fruitland, Utah about five to six miles up Current Creek. Water Hollow nearly cuts the CWMU in half. Water Hollows flows from west to east, entering the unit at 7600 feet and leaving the unit at 6900 feet. Another important drainage is Dry Hollow north of Water Hollow. Like Water Hollow, Dry Hollow flows from west to east, entering the unit at 8400 feet and exiting the unit at about 6900 feet. The most common elevation is 7600 feet, but ranges from 6800 feet to 9200 feet, a difference of 2400 feet. Sixty-three percent (63%) of the CWMU elevations ranges between 7700 feet and 9200 feet an elevation difference of 1500 feet. The cover type most common on the Buckhorn Ranch CWMU is Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). This cover type is distributed over much of the unit. Almost as common as the Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland, is the Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) cover type. It too, is distributed over much of the unit. Add Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22), Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), and Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) and over ninety percent (91%) of the CWMU is covered. One of the Buckhorn Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, FRUITLAND (423056), is about 9.0 km southeast from the southeast edge of the CWMU. FRUITLAND has fifty-six (56) years of records, 1910 - 1966. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.92 inches, but it can be as high as 7.89 inches or as low as 1.55 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inches of precipitation, 11 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inches, or 2 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inches of precipitation. There is also 1 day with greater than or equal to 1.00 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 7.9 inches but can be as high as 19.0inches. FALL temperature at FRUITLAND averages 43.9 degrees F. but can be as high as 86.0 degrees F. or as low as -8.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 56 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Coldwater Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is part of the Bear River Range south of Blacksmith Fork. The South Cottonwood Canyon divides the Unit almost into a west and east half. This canyon ranges from about 6400 feet to 7200 feet in elevation. To the east the elevation doesn't rise much and the area flattens out before dropping down to 5600 feet on the northeast boundary. On the west half the elevation rises rapidly to around 8000 feet, then drops quickly to 6400 feet in the north and 7400 feet in the south. The most common elevation is 7100 feet but ranges from 5100 feet to 8200 feet with an elevation difference of 3100 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6300 feet and 7200 feet an elevation difference of 900 feet. The eastern two-thirds of the Coldwater Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU)is composed of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). In conjunction with this Sagebrush Steppe are large patches of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Towards the middle of the unit these large patches of Aspen Forest and Woodland coalesce into a sizable stand of Aspen Forest and Woodland. Much of the rest of the unit is composed of patches of Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23), Rocky Mountain Montane Dry-Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (30), Inter-Mountain Basins Mountain Mahogany Woodland and Shrubland (44), Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Meadow (70), Inter-Mountain West Aspen-Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland Complex (38), and Rocky Mountain Subalpine-Montane Riparian Shrubland (77). One of the Clearwater Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HARDWARE RANCH(423671), is about 0.5 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. HARDWARE RANCH has thirty-five (35) years of records, 1956 - 1991. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.47 inches, but it can be as high as (not available) inches or as low as (not available) inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 12 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 7 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages (not available) inches but can be as high as (not available) inches. FALL temperature at HARDWARE RANCH averages (not available) degrees F. but can be as high as 94.0 degrees F. or as low as -5.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 36 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of December.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) takes up parts of Weber, Morgan and Rich counties, with Rich county having the most area. The higher points on the Deseret CWMU are along Horse Ridge (8500 feet). On the west the Unit drops away to about 6400 feet in the south and 8000 feet in the north. On the eastside of Horse Ridge the Unit makes a less steep drop, dropping down to around 6400 feet in the north and 6800 feet in the south along the Utah - Wyoming state border. The most common elevation is 6400 feet but ranges from 6000 feet to 8700 feet with an elevation difference of 2700 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6800 feet and 7800 feet an elevation difference of 1000 feet. The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is much larger than other CWMUs in Utah, therefore land cover is more diversified. About half (50%) of the land cover on the Deseret CWMU is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Towards the northeast and at lower elevation, there are large areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Steppe (66). Thet higher elevations on the west of the Unit, mixed with Sagebrush Steppe are extensive areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). At lower elevations towards the northeast are several patches of Agriculture (114) land. At minor extents are Southern Rocky Mountain Montane-Subalpine Grassland (71), Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48), and Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane shrubland (41). One of the Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, WOODRUFF (429595), is about 10.5 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. WOODRUFF has one hundred eleven (111) years of records, 1897 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.64 inches, but it can be as high as 5.18 inches or as low as 0.64 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 8.7 inches but can be as high as 29.2 inches. FALL temperature at WOODRUFF averages 40.8 degrees F. but can be as high as 111.0 degrees F. or as low as -26.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 73 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 6 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Double R Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is southeast of Strawberry Reservoir and south of the Strawberry River. The high point of the Unit is more in the middle of the Unit at over 9000 feet, the north extension of the Willow Creek Ridge. This high point drops away to 8200 feet on the west and 8000 feet on the south. Willow Creek cuts the Unit on the west (8000 to 7300 feet), and Bear Canyon cuts the unit on the east (8600 feet to 7400 feet). The most common elevation is 8800 feet but ranges from 7500 feet to 9500 feet with an elevation difference of 2000 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 8200 feet and 8900 feet an elevation difference of 700 feet. About forty percent (40%) of the Double R Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). This Sagebrush Steppe has large patches of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) scattered throughout it. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Durst Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located north of Morgan, Utah and Interstate Highway 84. Cottonwood Creek/Canyon is generally the northern border. Durst Mountain is the high point of the Unit. It is over 9200 feet in elevation. Because Durst Mountain is near the Unit's west boundary elevation only drops to 8700 feet in the west. To the south it drops down to 5200 feet, and to the east and north it decreases to 7600 feet. The entire Unit is quite mountainous. The most common elevation is 7300 feet but ranges from 5100 feet to 9200 feet with an elevation difference of 4100 feet. Forty-nine percent (49%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5900 feet and 8400 feet an elevation difference of 2500 feet. The Durst Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is covered with a mixture of three (3) land cover types, Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41), Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62), and Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Other Forest and Woodland types are Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23), Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), Rocky Mountain Montane Dry-Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (30), and Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (28). There are also patches of Invasive Perennial Grassland (119). One of the Durst Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, MORGAN (425826), is about 10.5 km south from the south edge of the CWMU. MORGAN has one hundred five (105) years of records, 1903 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.80 inches, but it can be as high as 7.28 inches or as low as 0.46 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 18 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 11 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 7.3 inches but can be as high as 25.3 inches. FALL temperature at MORGAN averages 46.9 degrees F. but can be as high as 98.0 degrees F. or as low as -12.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 53 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The East Fork Chalk Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is east of Coalville, Utah up Chalk Creek. Humpy Peak at greater than 10,800 feet is the high point of the Unit. The elevation along the East Fork of Chalk Creek decreases to 6700 feet. Both the East Fork and Middle Fork of Chalk Creek are part of the unit. The East Fork decreases from 9600 feet and the Middle Fork from 7700 feet to where the combine at 7200 feet. Except for the abrupt extension of Humpy Peak the relief on the eastside of the Unit is not as steep as that on the west side. The most common elevation is 9700 feet but ranges from 6700 feet to 10800 feet with an elevation difference of 4100 feet. Fifty-three percent (53%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7800 feet and 9700 feet an elevation difference of 1900 feet. The East Fork Chalk Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) land cover is a combination of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) and Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). The Aspen Forest and Woodland is in the middle of the unit. The Sagebrush Steppe is scattered from the northwest through the middle and into the the southeast part of the Unit. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41)and Rocky Mountain Subalpine Dry-Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (26) also add to the land cover on certain parts of the Unit. One of the East Fork Chalk Creek Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, COALVILLE (421590), is about 3.0 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. COALVILLE has thirty-four (34) years of records, 1974 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.71 inches, but it can be as high as 7.09 inches or as low as 1.68 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 19 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 14.8 inches but can be as high as 32.0 inches. FALL temperature at COALVILLE averages 43.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 87.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 61 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.
