hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of December.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Iron Spring Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located west of Cedar City between the Swett Hills and Three Peaks. It is one block of land that ranges from 5400 feet to 5700 feet. The vegetation ranges from a Pinion Juniper Shrubland on the east of the unit to a Desert Grassland on the west. Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. There may be a few resident deer in the area around the agricultural pivot earlier in the season. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. So it usually does not affect this hunt. On years with cooler weather some of the larger bucks will start into some pre rut behavior in the last week of October. Recommended areas to hunt: The majority of the deer will be found adjacent to the agricultural field that is included in this unit. The unit is managed as a limited entry unit but does not guarantee success. CWMUs are managed separately from the larger units of which they are a part, but management objectives are the same. Specific information related to this CWMU should be directed to the CWMU operator before applying for the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The 5S Land & Livestock Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located in the East Canyon Wildlife Management Unit near the town of Morgan, Utah. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Except for about 750 hectares around the town of Alton, Utah; the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) surrounds the town. To the northeast of Alton (7500 feet), mountains rise from 8500 to 9000 feet. These mountains slope down toward the Sevier River at an elevation of around 7200 feet on the north. On the the south, these mountains slope down to the Kanab River which parts the Alton CWMU on the southeast. The most common elevation is 7400 feet but ranges from 6400 feet to 9000 feet with an elevation difference of 2600 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7300 feet and 8200 feet an elevation difference of 900 feet. Lower elevations on the Unit are around 6800 feet. Towards the southwest of the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWM), there are extensive areas of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36). A co-dominant land cover type is Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). This Shrubland occurs throughout the Unit except for the extreme north. In the extreme north and towards the middle of the Unit are large areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). There are also large patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). The Alton CWMU also has large patches of Rocky Mountain Ponderosa Pine Woodland (34) and Agriculture (114) is scattered throughout the Unit. One of the Alton Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ALTON (420086), is about 1.0 km from the middle of the CWMU. ALTON has eighty-three (83) years of records, 1915 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 4.14 inches, but it can be as high as 11.35 inches or as low as 0.36 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 9 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch of perciptiation. Total FALL snowfall averages 7.6 inches but can be as high as 41.7 inches. FALL temperature at ALTON averages 47.3 degrees F. but can be as high as 91.0 degrees F. or as low as -5.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 44 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This CWMU occurs on the Nine Mile deer unit in southern Carbon County and northern Emery County. It is a new CWMU beginning in 2022. Most of this property was formerly part of the Patmos Ridge CWMU. Elevation on the CWMU ranges from about 7,000 to 9,000 feet. Although there are some resident deer, this CWMU is likely transitional habitat for deer in the fall and spring. Deer densities are likely not very high. Pinyon-Juniper forest predominates at lower elevations with Douglas-fir more prevalent at higher elevations. This area is extremely steep and rugged with very limited road access. Significant water and habitat improvement projects are planned and are underway on this property. In general, buck:doe ratios tend to be high on the surrounding Nine Mile unit due to the predominance of private land.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This CWMU is part of a General Season hunt unit that is managed for a post-season buck to doe ratio of 15-17 bucks per 100 does. The unit is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. CWMUs are managed separately from the larger Unit 1, but management objectives are the same. Specific information related to this CWMU should be directed to the CWMU operator before applying for the unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Services are located in Tremonton, Snowville, and Grouse Creek. Specific rules to maintain safe conditions while on the CWMU are part of the management plan. Hunters should contact the CWMU operator prior to applying for the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of December.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 99% of land where hunters can expect to see deer in the eastern half of the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure. Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Most higher elevation Raft River Mountains deer will remain high on the range until snow depths push them down into the sagebrush flats. Access to higher elevations is through One Mile Canyon, George Creek Canyon, Johnson Canyon, and Wildcat Canyon. Deer are plentiful and hunting opportunities exist up every canyon. Deer along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range can be found up Kimbell Creek, Red Banks, and Keg Springs along the west side and near Devil's Playground and Rocky Pass on the east side. Mule deer in the higher elevations do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the Raft River Mountains to the southeast end of the Grouse Creek Mountains for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats from Kelton to Devil's Playground. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a very productive unit with one of the largest deer herds in the state. Archery hunters will find most success hunting on summer habitats at 7,500 feet and above. In some years hunting on water sources can be productive but water is generally not limiting on the Manti portion of this unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This is a very productive unit with one of the largest deer herds in the state. Archery hunters will find most success hunting on summer habitats at 7,500 feet and above. In some years hunting on water sources can be productive but water is generally not limiting on the Manti portion of this unit. Migration Patterns: There is very little deer migration during the archery hunt. Deer remain on summer ranges typically at 7,500 feet and above. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches east of SR-89 on the west and the sagebrush benches west of SR-6 and SR-10 on the east side of the mountain. There is very little seasonal movement of deer on the San Rafael portion of the unit. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: Upper Fish Creek and it's tributaries. The tributaries include Gooseberry Creek, Silver Creek, C Canyon, and the Straight Fork. This is a roadless area on the north end of the unit. This area has had some prescribed fires recently that has improved deer habitat. It can be accessed from North Skyline Drive on the west or from Scofield Reservoir on the east. The bottom two miles of Upper Fish Creek is privately owned and in a CWMU Bear Ridge and Fish Creek Ridge These ridges have roads going down them. They are northwest of Scofield Reservoir. The bottom 2 miles of these ridges are privately owned. This is excellent habitat in the Pondtown Creek drainage on the north end of the unit. It is best accessed from North Skyline Drive. Trough Spring Ridge This is accessed off of SR-264 southwest of the town of Scofield. It is just above the Skyline Coal Mine. This is the ridge on the east side of Electric Lake. There are some small pockets of private land that are posted well but the majority of the acreage is Forest Service. Much of this ridge burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 which has improved the deer habitat in this area. Gentry Mountain. This is accessed from SR-10 just north of the town of Huntington at Huntington Reservoir. Part of this mountain is privately owned and part of it burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 West of Skyline Drive All the small towns along the west face of the Central Mountains Manti Unit has a canyon road to connect to Skyline Drive. Some roads are fairly rough going with the better access up from Fairview, Ephraim and Mayfield. Concentrate on side roads and trails from the main canyon roads to get to the more likely areas to find deer. The higher elevations in aspen and sagebrush meadows with water in close proximity will hold some of the mature bucks. Down low in the agricultural valleys many younger bucks will use the alfalfa fields in the evenings and early morning. Much of the adjacent property along the agriculture is either Forest Service or State lands and there will be a good opportunities there. East of Skyline Drive and South of Huntington Canyon There is a considerable amount of access along Skyline Drive, high elevation ridge tops, and lower canyons and valleys. There are also many areas where you can hike to get away from roads, much of it very steep, but where nice bucks hold up. Some preliminary scouting with maps is a great way to familiarize yourself with the unit. One of the
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in August and September are generally pretty mild with warm days and cold nights. There is rarely snow on the ground during the archery hunt and most deer are still found on high elevation summer ranges. Roads are generally in good shape. Be prepared for cold nights and occasional rainstorms which can make the roads muddy. August is the wettest month of the year in the Price area as monsoon rainstorms in the afternoon are quite common. This can disrupt hunting and deer behavior as well as the ability to hunt on a water source.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Nebo unit has some very rough terrain. I tell hunters that "the Nebo is either straight up or straight down" so be prepared for some very hard work. ATV use is not allowed on the north Nebo and horses or mules are recommended. At the very least hunters should be in very good physical condition.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: In the past the harvest has been distributed throughout the entire portion of the Nebo. The higher elevations can be good places to start looking for more mature bucks but the younger bucks can be found at lower elevations, especially associated with agriculture areas. Don't limit yourself to a few areas. They can be found anywhere on the mountains. Some of the areas to concentrate on are Nebo Creek, Page Fork, Hop Creek, and Mahogany Knoll. Other good places are off the Nebo Loop Road around Payson Lakes and the Summit Trail. The south Nebo (Sanpitch Mts.), that portion of the Nebo Unit that is south of SR 132, may be more accessible since ATV use is allowed by the USFS. However there is private property further south as well as a CWMU deer unit. Water sources are good places to find deer. Most archery hunters have the most success early in the hunt sitting at remote water holes and canyons with perennial water. Migration Patterns: There is very little deer migration during the archery and muzzleloader hunt. Deer remain on summer ranges typically at 7,500 feet and above. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches which is usually after the rifle hunt. However, heavy snow fall during the hunt may cause deer to migrate to lower elevations early. Scouting Tips: Good hunters will scout and find their own "honey hole". A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting deer in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of deer. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Depending on the season be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road and trail conditions. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat especially during the archery season so in anticipation of hot weather plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fillmore unit has great deer habitat and has had an increase in the buck/doe ratio over the last few years. Although the hunt boundary extends onto the west side of I-15, the Pahvant Mountain Range (east side of I-15) receives most of the hunting pressure.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Deer: Deer can be found across the entire unit, on both the east and west sides, with most of the deer being found at higher elevations. It is common to see bucks off of the main roads which results in those roads receiving a high amount of hunting pressure. Walking out ridges and away from roads can be a great strategy in finding deer and seeing fewer hunters. Water: The Pahvant is relatively dry. There are creeks in the bottoms of some of the canyons and a few springs and stock ponds on top. Water sources can be productive areas for finding deer during the archery hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The main access roads and the road along the top see a lot of traffic during the hunting season from both hunters and recreationists. Be cautious of others on the road. There is not a lot of water on top so be prepared with plenty of water. After heavy rain storms, many places along the road on top get very slick and it can become very easy to slide off the road. There are many steep and rugged areas with no cell coverage. Cell coverage is good on top of the mountain, depending on carrier, but is spotty in the canyons. The bear population is not large but has been increasing. It is always a good idea to keep a clean camp and keep food inaccessible for bears.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Temperatures are high during the archery hunt and you may experience rain and thunderstorms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are no CWMUs on this unit. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. Hunters are reminded that bears often frequent the area. Campers and hikers should maintain a bear-safe campsite and dispose of trash properly. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Meat and garbage should stored inside a vehicle or hung in a tree at least 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most deer are scattered throughout higher elevations, in remote areas away from major roads and ATV trails. Archery hunters are encouraged to do their pre-season scouting on the unit. Weather conditions will heavily influence where deer are found.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal Mountains unit is one of the most beautiful places that you will ever encounter. The unit has high alpine peaks, above 12,000 ft. and goes down to low desert valleys around 4,000 ft. This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit however, every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is good road access throughout the unit, however there are also many places that hunters can hike into and get away from the crowds. Hunters should be aware of the CWMU's and private lands on the unit and learn the boundaries. There are 2 CWMUs on this unit and a list is available on the UDWR webpage: http://wildlife.utah.gov/maps/public/list_cwmus.php
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the La Sals typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Using quality binoculars or spotting scopes will be very valuable to you. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas for the archery hunt: For the archery hunt, focus on mid to high elevations throughout the unit. These areas consist of large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding. Some bucks will be above timberline in very remote areas.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is extremely limited throughout most of the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sals. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms. Dirt roads on this unit can become extremely muddy, very quick. Be attentive and use caution when traveling during stormy weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years the unit has experienced a decrease in the deer population and decrease in the buck/doe ratio. Deer hunting has been good. Typically hunters experience a high success rate. Deer populate the entire Monroe unit, however the highest density of deer tend to be on central and northern parts of the unit. The southern portion of the unit is narrower, drier, as has fewer deer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the past couple of years the Monroe unit has experienced reduced fawn production and survival, primarily due to both drought and harsh winter conditions. This has caused a reduction in the overall deer population and decreased buck/doe ratios. Hunting is still good, but buck permits have been reduced to reflect the current population status. During the archery season most of the deer are concentrated above 8,000 feet in elevation. Several peaks on the unit are above 11,000 ft elevation but most of the unit consists of moderate elevation hunt areas. There are deer on the highest peaks however most of the deer tend to be at the intersection of the conifer/aspen habitats and the aspen/mountain brush/sage habitats. Archers on the Monroe generally enjoy a good hunt with good success rates. There are deer spread across the entire Monroe unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want. Great deer range exists in the Northern part of the unit, productive areas include above the towns of Glenwood and Annabella including the Hunter's Flat, Thompson Basin, and Big Lake areas. On the East side of the unit deer hunting can be good in the Mormon Mountain area (much of this is private) and in the hills above Burrville. Good road access and prime deer habitat are located in the following areas: Box Creeks, Indian Peak, Monroe Peak, Greenwich Creeks, and the Dairies areas. There is some private property in these areas so make sure you know where you are. Most of these areas are aspen and mountain brush habitats. On the West side of the unit good places to find deer include Poverty Flat, the canyons surrounding Marysvale peak, and the area around Barney Lake. The South end of the unit contains deer in the Forshea Mtn, Langdon Peak areas. The sage flats West of Angle have some deer during the rifle season.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has seen good deer numbers over recent years. Hunters have reported seeing more bucks and more mature bucks have been harvested in the last couple years. This unit has several areas that have no vehicle access. Hunters that hike into some of these areas, or use horses have good success at harvesting deer. Before snow falls on the unit you can access the top of the mountain from Antimony, or Cottonwood Creek in Johns Valley. Deer in the summer can be found across the unit in higher and lower elevations. There is good access on most of the BLM lands across the unit, but a lot of the forest service has limited access. There is good access on the south end of the unit in the Hunt Creeks, and often holds deer year round. There was a large fire that burned on the unit in 2002. This made it very good for glassing long distances. There is a lot of pinon and juniper in the lower elevations with Aspen, and mixed conifer stands at higher elevations. During summer months find water and hunt areas around it.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This unit is predominantly roadless so prepare for backcountry hunting conditions
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: During summer months the days are warm, and afternoon thunderstorms are usually present.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This unit is has a high buck/doe ratio primarily due to an abundance of private land where hunting pressure is generally light. This is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The key to this unit is finding public lands. Most of the public lands are at the fringes of the good summer and fall deer habitat as most of the high elevation acreage is privately owned. Migration Patterns: Most deer on the Tavaputs Plateau migrate to the east toward the Green River to spend the winter months. This includes the lower ends of Ceder, Cottonwood, and Flat Iron Ridges as well as the area near Prickly Pear Canyon. Deer on the western part of the unit tend to migrate to the southwest to the foothills just north and east of Price near the Price Airport, Coal Creek, and Soldier Creek. Generally there is no migration during the archery hunt and most deer are on top of the mountain. Mule Deer Rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Cold Springs WMA provides good public land access on high elevation summer habitat and transitional fall habitat near Bruin Point. There is a county road through the middle of the WMA with over 2500 acres of public lands available. Much of the property is walk-in only to maintain quality deer hunting in the area. This area can be accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside or if the weather is bad from Nine Mile Canyon and up Cottonwood Canyon. There is an abundance of wild horses on this part of the mountain. Upper Patmos Ridge/Range Creek - There are 5 sections of BLM land that are surrounded by private lands just south of Bruin Point and North of the Preston Nutter Ranch gate. This provides good deer habitat at high elevations on steep timber covered terrain with ample water. This is accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside. Harmon Canyon/Prickly Pear Canyon - This is good transitional habitat especially if there has been some snow. It is accessed via Nine Mile Canyon then you can drive up the Harmon Canyon road which is about 30 miles east of Wellington Utah. These are sagebrush/PJ habitats at about 7500 feet in elevation. Cottonwood/Ceder Ridge. This is good transitional habitat in sagebrush at elevations of 6500 to 8000 feet. There are private lands to the west but plenty of public lands as you go down the ridges. These areas are accessed via Nine Mile Canyon and then Cottonwood Canyon 45 miles east of Wellington. Anthro Subunit Recommended areas to hunt: The Anthro subunit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer. Because the density is so low, if you do find any bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. There is a lot of area East of Antelope Canyon all the way to the Green River, with even lower deer densities, while hunting these areas your best chance is finding water. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Nutter's Ridge - USFS higher elevation, a few large aspen stands, very accessible Jeep Trail Ridge - USFS just East of Nutter's Ridge, large canyons with a few aspens, several water sources Wire Fence Ridge - USFS rough road, biggest aspen stands on Anthro, good burned side hills Alkaline/Choke Cherry - USFS very open country, few deer, East of Jeep Trail Wells Draw - BLM lands, low elevation pinyon/juniper, low density Cottonwood Ridge - USFS difficult access, higher elevation, many timbered hill sides
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in August and September are generally pretty mild with warm days and cold nights. There is rarely snow on the ground during the archery hunt and most deer are still found on high elevation summer ranges. Roads are generally in good shape. Be prepared for cold nights and occasional rainstorms which can make the roads muddy. August is the wettest month of the year in the Price area as monsoon rainstorms in the afternoon are quite common. This can disrupt hunting and deer behavior as well as the ability to hunt on a water source.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is a migration study underway to look at timing and routes of migration for North Slope deer. We ask that collared deer are not killed. If one is, DO NOT CUT THE COLLAR; remove the collar by loosening the lock nuts and call the number on the collar or the local biologist. This unit encompasses lodgepole pine, open sagebrush, and desert scrub. Hunters should expect to see other deer and elk hunters and other public land users.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer in the High Uintas do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the west side of the North Slope to the east end of the North Slope for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats all along the North Slope. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is after this hunt ends so it does not affect the hunt. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November-mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the North Slope: Deer are found throughout much of the unit. During the archery hunt, deer will be higher in elevation, although there are some that stay year-round in the sagebrush habitat on Dowd Mountain, Death Valley, and Red Creek Flat. Depending on weather conditions, most of the deer on the Summit portion get pushed down into Wyoming before the Any Weapon hunt begins. Also, high country deer are typically pushed down out of the High Country by mid-October if any early season snow storms hit. The majority of the deer in the 3 Corners portion of the unit stay up high on Bear Mountain, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, and Bender Mountain until later in October/early November when deer start showing up in Browns Park for the winter. This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure, especially in Browns Park, Goslin Mountain, South Valley, Dowd Mountain, and along Hwy 44. Areas with highest harvest success include Greendale Junction (along Highway 44 and 191), Sheep Creek Lake, Long Park, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, and 3 Corners. Hunters that receive written permission from private landowners in Manila also do well. Recommended areas include along Highway 44 and 191, Sheep Creep Lake, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, 3 Corners, Henry's Fork, Bridger Lake and along the North Slope Road.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Typically the weather is rather warm during the archery hunt. Be prepared for rain, lightning, wind, heat, and potentially snow in the higher elevations. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. There usually is not snow during the archery hunt, but occasionally early season snowstorms can hit the higher elevations, but they don't usually impact the lower elevations.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Deer habitat includes a lot of public land but there is substantial habitat on private lands throughout the unit. Hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Panguitch Lake unit has a healthy deer population. Expect to see several bucks each day, with the majority probably being young deer. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. During the archery hunt most deer are on summer range with some deer in year round range that may be at lower elevations. Good numbers of deer exist on USFS lands and areas close to Brian Head and Cedar Breaks National Monument will generally see the heaviest hunting pressure. Some good areas to hunt include areas near Cedar Breaks National Monument, Red Desert, Sidney Valley, Asay Bench, Horse Valley, and Little Valleys. Migration Patterns: The migratory segments of this population may begin their fall movements in late September and October. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars can be helpful if you are unfamiliar with the area. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety beyond a cellphone. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, wind, and heat. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Pine Valley Unit is 90% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Deer on the Archery hunt are spread out across their summer ranges deer densities are higher in some areas than they are in other. Some high deer density areas also have higher numbers of hunters and can result in some hunter crowding. Please be aware of other hunters and be courteous. Day time temperatures during the archery hunt can still reach into the low 90's. On years with good monsoonal moisture the deer may be spread out more across their range.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Migration should not be a factor on this hunt. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. So it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Pine Valley Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several livestock tanks, springs and guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Bull Valley Mountains - Forest Service and small tracts of private land South and West of Enterprise. This area is very accessible by vehicles. Deer densities decrease as you move further west towards the Nevada state line. Hunting is best in oak brush and service berry near water sources. Bumblebee Mtn. - BLM, USFS, and SITLA SW of Cedar City. The higher elevation areas in the oak brush best for locating deer. Access is limited to a few main roads and ATV trails. Hunters will do better if they get out and do some hiking and spotting deer. Paradise and Pine Valley Wilderness - Forest Service land from Pace Draw NW of New Harmony to the south face of the Pine Valley Mtn. This area is remote and has little to no vehicle access. There are several foot and horse trails into the area. Some access points are the Anderson and Comanche trail head in the New Harmony area, The Grants Ranch trail head between New Harmony and Pinto, The Paradise trail head near Pinto, The Mill Canyon and Water Canyon trail heads south of the Town of Pine Valley in Grass Valley, The Whipple and Forsyth trail heads in Pine Valley. The further you are willing to hike in the better the hunting may become. Atchison and Harrison Peak - Forest Service land Between Mountain Meadow and Grass Valley. Mostly sagebrush and serviceberry habitat with some scattered pinion and juniper. This area has limited access and with a few ATV trails. Hiking in a ½ mile plus from the roads will increase success in finding the bucks.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: It can be very hot during this season. Please be prepared with plenty of water. Make sure friends and family know where you area going and when you will return. Be aware of rattle snakes!
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder/Kaiparowits unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit has some excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years the unit has experienced an increase in the deer population and an increase in the buck/doe ratio. Deer hunting has been good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters have been noticing an increasing number of mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit, however the highest density of deer tend to be on the Boulder part of the unit. The southern portion of the unit, the Kaiporowits, is drier and has fewer deer. During the Archery season most of the deer tend to be in the higher elevations near water. Hunter densities are not high.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the Archery season deer are scattered over the entire unit. Much of the buck movement is dictated by weather conditions. Bucks tend to remain higher in elevation than does. The Boulder Top is above 11,000 ft elevation and generally most deer move off the top by late September. Most of the deer tend to be at the intersection of the conifer/aspen habitats and the aspen/mountain brush/sage habitats. Hunters who want to hunt the Kaiparowits portion of the unit need to be prepared to see few deer and experience very difficult hunting conditions. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some very remote areas on this unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms often occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. However, deer hunting has been fair/good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters still have reasonable opportunity to find mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer. Archery Season: During the Archery Season most of the deer will be above 8,000 ft. The heaviest populations tend to be in the aspen/oak habitats. There are some deer and some good mature bucks that use the highest elevations. These deer are spooked easily and when disturbed may drop down into more secure cover. Scouting before the season is key in finding where bucks are hanging out. Heavy hunting pressure will be near the good camping areas and roads. Muzzleloader Season: During the Muzzleloader season most of the deer still tend to be in the mid to higher elevations though some have began to move down a little. This season is a great time to hunt the Fish Lake, hunter densities are not high and the weather is often pleasant. Deer will be spread out across the unit. Any Weapon Season: In late October the deer on the Monroe unit tend to be very spread out. On much of the unit, some of the deer have moved onto or near their winter range. Snow levels permitting, there are also some deer on the highest peaks. Hunters should use scouting just prior to the season to locate deer concentrations. Hunters often concentrate in areas where deer are easily seen near agricultural areas. Migration Patterns: Some of the deer on Fish Lake unit begin to migrate to or closer to their winter range in mid-October. By the time the rifle hunt arrives a sizable portion of the herd is often in the transitional ranges between their winter and summer ranges. However many deer also stay as high as they can until heavy snows push them lower. Most of the migration is rather simple, the deer just move up or down in elevation. However there are some deer that move from their summering areas on the North and Central parts of the unit to the Southern, Eastern, and Western parts of the unit closer to their winter range. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it generally does not affect the general deer hunts. Recommended areas to hunt on the Fish Lake unit: There are deer spread across the entire Fish Lake unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather Conditions: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions. During the archery season hunters should be prepared to cool harvested game quickly due to warm temperatures.

hunt_bio_general_information: General Considerations: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit however, every year a few nice bucks are taken. The unit population has been increasing over the past few years, along with the buck to doe ratio. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are 3 CWMUs on this unit, which general season permits are not permitted. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Abajos typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Once the rut starts, bucks will be found with and around does. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect these hunts. Recommended areas for the San Juan, Abajo subunit: Abajo Mountain - For the archery hunt, focus on mid to high elevations throughout the unit. These areas consist of large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the Abajos. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The Uintah Mountain range can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also less deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. Road access on much of the unit is limited to mostly canyon bottoms due to the steepness of the terrain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and tend to stay on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. During this hunt it is not uncommon to find bulls right at timberline. Deer rut: The deer on this unit usually rut mid to late November, and it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Vernal: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. There is a variety of habitat to hunt during the archery hunt. There is pinyon/juniper, sage brush savanna, thick lodge pole pine, and areas above timber line. The larger openings on the forest are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and lots of rocky terrain. During the hunts most of the deer on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. I would recommend trying to locate remote watering holes, feeding and bedding areas. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit: Whiterocks Canyon - Whiterocks River is the western unit boundary, steep terrain. Paradise Park-Higher forest terrain, steep forested canyons. Mosby Mountain-High aspen forest, with large sagebrush bowls, excellent habitat. Red Cloud Loop Rd-Long road that starts in Dry Fork Canyon (west of Vernal). It takes you all the way through the Vernal unit, and comes out on Hwy 191. Charlie's Park-large sagebrush flats. Taylor Mountain-Great vantage points. Excellent area to glass and locate animals from far distances. Colton Ranger Station-Aspen/conifer mix forest. Lime Stone, Little V, and Range Study-These areas are east of Hwy 191 and border a limited entry deer and elk unit. Diamond Mountain.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on tribal lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The unit includes the High Uintas Wilderness area. The wilderness can provide a remote hunt with few hunters, but there are also fewer deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine with little understory. Road access on much of the unit is limited to mostly canyon bottoms due to the steepness of the terrain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit move down in elevation for the winter and they winter primarily on Ute tribal Lands and on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. The deer also move down towards the tribal land boundary as soon as they get much hunting pressure. There is very little hunting pressure on the tribal lands so some deer have learned to go there as soon as hunting pressure starts. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Yellowstone: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. The wilderness area can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also fewer deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine with little understory. Deer in the wilderness are generally found above tree line or in small pockets of openings in the lodge pole cover. The larger openings are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and lots of rocks. During the hunts most of the deer on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. That zone across the South Slope is the most productive for deer. Every canyon across the South Slope, Yellowstone has deer and they are of similar quality. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit: Soapstone area - high elevation, but more road access, closer to the Wasatch Front North Fork of the Duchesne- limited road access Blind Stream - limited road access, tribal land down low, popular area Log Hollow- must cross tribal Lands to access, rough roads Rock Creek - paved road access, steep areas Pigeon Water - popular area but hunters must be aware of tribal boundary Bear Wallow - hunters must be aware of tribal boundary, steep terrain Lake Fork/Moon Lake- paved road access, some private property along the paved road. Yellowstone - rough roads, need to be aware of tribal boundary 77 Flat/Burnt Mill- gravel roads, a little flatter area, be aware of tribal boundary Dry Gulch- very rough road, steep terrain, be aware of tribal boundary on the east Uinta Canyon- tribal lands down low, steep terrain Elk Horn Loop - gravel roads that go almost to the summit of the Uinta Mountains, lots of opportunity to scatter out Whiterocks Canyon - Whiterocks River is the eastern unit boundary
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot, dry, or rainy, lightening, and windy conditions. Early snow storms can occur, but are fairly rare during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so during this hunt. Be prepared for dry or muddy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation towards the end of October and first part of November. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Southwest Desert unit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer because the density is so low. When you do find bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some small private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. The higher elevation areas above the thick pinion and juniper are the best for locating deer. South Wah Wah Range- BLM and SITLA lands from Rose Spring Canyon to Highway 21 on Wah Wah summit. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Mountain Home Range- BLM and SITLA lands from the Loper's Reseed area to Mt Home Pass. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Black Hills -BLM and SITLA lands located southwest of Minersville. Baboon Peak, Dry Willow Peak and Little Horse Valley areas. This area is closer to human population centers and may have higher hunter densities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are many CWMUs on this unit and a list of these can be found on the UDWR webpage
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and typically from West to East, with most of the deer wintering on or near Tabby WMA. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: There are numerous areas to hunt on this unit. The areas surrounding Strawberry Reservoir and Currant Creek Reservoir are excellent for deer hunting. They are easy to access with many roads and trails and camping areas. This of course leads to many people hunting these areas. There are very few areas on this unit without a road in the general area. There is far less hunting pressure on the Avintaquin unit, but that is because the overall deer density is much lower and the terrain is more rugged. This unit has very large aspen stands that hold a lot of deer in the early fall. Many of the best bucks taken each year come from these aspen stands. In the summer there are deer in the more open higher areas, but once they get pressured by hunters they will move into the lower, thicker aspen stands. These areas are difficult to hunt, because of the leaves on the trees and fewer open areas to glass with optics. There are also many lower areas with several different browse species, including; oak brush, service berry, mountain mahogany, bitter brush, snow berry, sage brush, etc. These areas also have deer in them during the hunt, but at a lower density. Some areas to hunt include the following: Currant Creek Reservoir Area- high elevation, large aspen stands, very accessible, high deer density for the unit. Low Pass Creek- near Currant Creek Reservoir, rough road, great for ATV's, great for glassing up high. West Fork of the Duchesne- limited ATV access, but open to trucks. Chicken Creek/Race Track- popular area, but holds a lot of deer and bucks CO-OP Creek- Very Popular area, near Highway 40, great camping, large aspen stands Trout Creek- many bucks taken here opening weekend Wildcat WMA- good access, flat on top, a lot of pressure, many yearling bucks taken here. North Fork of Deep Creek- borders private land, limited access by road, great horse area Tabby Mountain- great for ATV's, better after snow storms, mostly public land. Coleman Basin/Red Creek Mtn- SITLA land, some areas without roads, rough roads Reservation Ridge- fewer deer, but fewer people Strawberry Peak- High elevation, large areas near by with no road access, Cow Hollow, Slab Canyon, low deer density Timber Canyon/Long Ridge- low deer density, rough terrain, better after storms, rough roads. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.

hunt_bio_general_information: Land Ownership: Public, Private. The public lands are primarily US Forest Service lands managed by the Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forest and Wildlife Management Areas managed by the UDWR. There is a large amount of private property on the unit as well, including many CWMU's. Campground information: All Campgrounds on this unit are managed by the US National Forest Service. Camping outside of official campgrounds is also permitted on most of the Forest. Please direct all questions regarding campground availability and other camping questions to the US Forest Service. Maps and camping regulations are available on their websites. Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forest website: http://www.fs.usda.gov/uwcnf ATV and Vehicle Access: All roads and ATV trails on this unit are managed by the US Forest Service and are covered on their Travel Management Plans. Please direct all questions regarding which roads and trails ATVs can be operated on to the US Forest Service. Maps can also be purchased online at: http://www.fs.usda.gov/uwcnf Private lands: There are many CWMU's on this unit. General Season Deer Permits are not valid on CWMU's. All other private land requires written permission before hunting.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. There are many CWMUs on this unit and a list of these can be found on the UDWR webpage. Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and typically from East to West, with most of the deer wintering on Wallsburg WMA, Sheep Creek and Diamond Fork canyons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: There are numerous areas to hunt on this unit. The areas surrounding Strawberry Reservoir, Sheep Creek, Diamond Fork, Hobble Creek, American Fork canyons, Mt. Timpanogos are excellent for deer hunting. They are easy to access with many roads and trails and camping areas. This of course leads to many people hunting these areas. There are very few areas on this unit without a road in the general area. This unit has very large aspen stands, oak brush can hold a lot of deer in the early fall. In the summer there are deer in the more open higher areas, but once they get pressured by hunters they will move into the lower, thicker tree stands. These areas are difficult to hunt, because of the leaves on the trees and fewer open areas to glass with optics. There are also many lower areas with several different browse species, including; oak brush, service berry, mountain mahogany, bitter brush, snow berry, sage brush, etc. These areas also have deer in them during the hunt, but at a lower density. All ways look for areas that deer are watering in. Some areas to hunt include the following: Strawberry Reservoir area- Try Indian canyon, Clyde Creek, Mud Creek, Squaw Creek, Horse Creek, Main canyon and Strawberry ridge. Sheep Creek area- Try any of the waters ( First to Sixth) along Ray's Valley road. Diamond Fork- Diamond Fork is a mixture of public and private. Hobble Creek- Right Hand fork is mostly public land, Left Hand Fork is mostly private land. American Fork Canyon/Mt. Timpanogos-This area is steep and rugged. Timp WMA-This area is real brushy but can be good hunting. Wallsburg WMA-This WMA is mostly open sagebrush. Hunting can be good in October.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: ATTENTION-The US Forest is planning on a few prescribed burns this fall that might interfere with some hunt areas. Please be aware. The Heber-Kamas Ranger District is proposing to treat 3,300 acres with active fire in three operational areas occurring in Summit and Wasatch Counties. These areas are in the Provo watershed 10 miles east of Kamas and in the West Fork watershed 20 miles southeast of Heber City. Operations are planned to begin August 21, 2023, and will continue as conditions allow. The operation will require some area and road closure for public safety, active fire management will occur primarily during the daytime but also could occur at night to increase resource objectives. The Forest Service has established a Wildfire Crisis Strategy for dramatically increasing fuels and forest health treatments. The 10-year Wildfire Crisis Strategy (WCS) is built around the scale of the problem, which estimates that 50 million acres in addition to what we currently treat on an annual basis need fuels and forest health treatment to address the growing wildfire crisis. The goal of the project is to reduce wildfire risks to communities and natural resources by restoring and maintaining healthy, resilient fire-adapted forests. Approximately 382,000 acres (44%) of the Wasatch landscape is classified as high or very high fire hazard, posing a considerable threat to the function of vital watersheds, plant and wildlife habitat, recreational opportunities, and private property. The Forest has been actively managing across the forest to meet resource objectives through vegetation treatments and prescribed fire management. The Forest will continue to use all available tools to continue managing the resources meet the goals in the WCS. We understand there will be so Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Fifty percent of the deer habitat is public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Large blocks of the best deer habitat on this unit are private lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. On years with cooler weather some of the larger bucks will start into some pre rut behavior. Recommended areas to hunt: The Zion Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. During the archery hunt most deer are still in their summer habitat. Most deer will be at the middle to higher elevations from oak brush to the aspen and mixed conifer zone. About 59% of deer summer habitat on the Zion unit is on private lands. The northern portions of the unit south of Highway 14 are the best places for public access onto Forest Service land. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Webster's Flat and Deep Creek - Forest Service land From Woods Ranch area in Cedar Canyon to just east of the Zion Overlook. The Deep Creek area is a USFS roadless area. Access can be found at the trail head a short distance above the turn off to Webster's Flat on Highway 14. Midway - USFS land from the turn off to Cedar Breaks east to Navajo Lake. The old clear cut logging areas and meadows in the Deer Valley area usually have a fair amount of deer use. Strawberry Ridge and Harris Flat- USFS land between Strawberry Cabins area and east to Stout Canyon. This is a ponderosa pine are that has a good understory of bitterbrush. There is good access in to this area with several OHV trails and old logging roads. This area has several wildlife and livestock water catch ponds. This area has several cabin communities and hunters should be careful of private lands and how close they hunt to cabins. Stout Canyon and School Wash - USFS land with some larger blocks of private land. This is a ponderosa pine habitat with a good understory of bitterbrush. There are a few OHV trails and logging roads that cut through this area. Private land - Some of the best deer habitat on the Zion unit is on private lands. This unit is unusual for Southern Utah because of its large parcels of private lands that have several different land owners. Obtaining permission to hunt these areas can be difficult, but is not impossible.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 99% of land where hunters can expect to see deer in the eastern half of the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure. Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Most higher elevation Raft River Mountains deer will remain high on the range until snow depths push them down into the sagebrush flats. Access to higher elevations is through One Mile Canyon, George Creek Canyon, Johnson Canyon, and Wildcat Canyon. Deer are plentiful and hunting opportunities exist up every canyon. Deer along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range can be found up Kimbell Creek, Red Banks, and Keg Springs along the west side and near Devil's Playground and Rocky Pass on the east side. Mule deer in the higher elevations do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the Raft River Mountains to the southeast end of the Grouse Creek Mountains for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats from Kelton to Devil's Playground. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.
