hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is has a high buck/doe ratio primarily due to an abundance of private land where hunting pressure is generally light. This is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The key to this unit is finding public lands. Most of the public lands are at the fringes of the good summer and fall deer habitat as most of the high elevation acreage is privately owned.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most deer on the Tavaputs Plateau migrate to the east toward the Green River to spend the winter months. This includes the lower ends of Ceder, Cottonwood, and Flat Iron Ridges as well as the area near Prickly Pear Canyon. Deer on the western part of the unit tend to migrate to the southwest to the foothills just north and east of Price near the Price Airport, Coal Creek, and Soldier Creek. Hunting is much better if the weather is bad and generally poor if we have had mild weather. Generally there has been very little migration during the muzzleloader hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Cold Springs WMA provides good public land access on high elevation summer habitat and transitional fall habitat near Bruin Point. There is a county road through the middle of the WMA with over 2500 acres of public lands available. Much of the property is walk-in only to maintain quality deer hunting in the area. This area can be accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside or if the weather is bad from Nine Mile Canyon and up Cottonwood Canyon. Lots of wild horses on this part of the mountain. Upper Patmos Ridge/Range Creek There are 5 sections of BLM land that are surrounded by private lands just south of Bruin Point and North of the Preston Nutter Ranch gate. This provides good deer habitat at high elevations on steep timber covered terrain with ample water. This is accessed from Bruin Point near Sunnyside. Harmon Canyon/Prickly Pear Canyon This is good transitional habitat especially if there has been some snow. It is accessed via Nine Mile Canyon then you can drive up the Harmon Canyon road which is about 30 miles east of Wellington Utah. These are sagebrush/PJ habitats at about 7500 feet in elevation. Cottonwood/Ceder Ridge This is good transitional habitat in sagebrush at elevations of 6500 to 8000 feet. There are private lands to the west but plenty of public lands as you go down the ridges. These areas are accessed via Nine Mile Canyon and then Cottonwood Canyon 45 miles east of Wellington. Anthro Subunit Recommended areas to hunt: The Anthro subunit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer. Because the density is so low, if you do find any bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. There is a lot of area East of Antelope Canyon all the way to the Green River, with even lower deer densities, while hunting these areas your best chance is finding water. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Nutter's Ridge - USFS higher elevation, a few large aspen stands, very accessible Jeep Trail Ridge - USFS just East of Nutter's Ridge, large canyons with a few aspens, several water sources Wire Fence Ridge - USFS rough road, biggest aspen stands on Anthro, good burned side hills Alkaline/Choke Cherry - USFS very open country, few deer, East of Jeep Trail Wells Draw - BLM lands, low elevation pinyon/juniper, low density Cottonwood Ridge - USFS difficult access, higher elevation, many timbered hill sides
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in late September and early October are generally pretty mild with warm days and cold nights. There is rarely snow on the ground during the muzzleloader hunt and most deer are still found on high elevation summer ranges. Roads are generally in good shape. Be prepared for cold nights and occasional rainstorms which can make the roads muddy.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is a migration study underway to look at timing and routes of migration for North Slope deer. We ask that collared deer are not killed. If one is, DO NOT CUT THE COLLAR; remove the collar by loosening the lock nuts and call the number on the collar or the local biologist. This unit encompasses lodgepole pine, open sagebrush, and desert scrub. Hunters should expect to see other deer and elk hunters and other public land users. There is a muzzleloader doe hunt that coincides with this hunt on a portion of the unit near Manila.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer in the High Uintas do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the west side of the North Slope to the east end of the North Slope for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats all along the North Slope. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after this hunt ends so it does not affect the hunt. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November-mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the North Slope: Deer are found throughout much of the unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts, deer will be higher in elevation, although there are some that stay year-round in the sagebrush habitat on Dowd Mountain, Death Valley, and Red Creek Flat. Depending on weather conditions, most of the deer on the Summit portion get pushed down into Wyoming before the Any Weapon hunt begins. Also, high country deer are typically pushed down out of the High Country by mid-October if any early season snow storms hit. The majority of the deer in the 3 Corners portion of the unit stay up high on Bear Mountain, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, and Bender Mountain until later in October/early November when deer start showing up in Browns Park for the winter. This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure, especially in Browns Park, Goslin Mountain, South Valley, Dowd Mountain, and along Hwy 44. Areas with highest harvest success include Greendale Junction (along Highway 44 and 191), Sheep Creek Lake, Long Park, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, and 3 Corners. Hunters that receive written permission from private landowners in Manila also do well. Recommended areas include along Highway 44 and 191, Sheep Creep Lake, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, 3 Corners, Henry's Fork, Bridger Lake and along the North Slope Road.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Pine Valley Unit is 90% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Deer on the Muzzleloader hunt are spread out across their summer ranges deer densities are higher in some areas than they are in other. Some high deer density areas also have higher numbers of hunters and can result in some hunter crowding. Please be aware of other hunters and be courteous. Day time temperatures during the Muzzleloader hunt can still reach into the mid 80's. On years with good monsoonal moisture the deer may be spread out more across their range.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Migration should not be a factor on this hunt. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Pine Valley Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several livestock tanks, springs and guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Bull Valley Mtns - Forest Service and small tracts of private land South and West of Enterprise. This area is very accessible by vehicles. Deer densities decrease as you move further west towards the Nevada state line. Hunting is best in oak brush and service berry near water sources. Bumblebee Mtn. - BLM, USFS, and SITLA SW of Cedar City. The higher elevation areas in the oak brush best for locating deer. Access is limited to a few main roads and ATV trails. Hunters will do better if they get out and do some hiking and spotting deer. Paradise and Pine Valley Wilderness - Forest Service land from Pace Draw NW of New Harmony to the south face of the Pine Valley Mtn. This area is remote and has little to no vehicle access. There are several foot and horse trails into the area. Some access points are the Anderson and Comanche trail head in the New Harmony area, The Grants Ranch trail head between New Harmony and Pinto, The Paradise trail head near Pinto, The Mill Canyon and Water Canyon trail heads south of the Town of Pine Valley in Grass Valley, The Whipple and Forsyth trail heads in Pine Valley. The further you are willing to hike in the better the hunting may become. Atchison and Harrison Peak - Forest Service land Between Mountain Meadow and Grass Valley. Mostly sagebrush and serviceberry habitat with some scattered pinion and juniper. This area has limited access and with a few ATV trails. Hiking in a ½ mile plus from the roads will increase success in finding the bucks.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: It can be very hot during this season. Please be prepared with plenty of water. Make sure friends and family know where you area going and when you will return. Be aware of rattle snakes!
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. However, deer hunting has been fair/good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters still have reasonable opportunity to find mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. However, deer hunting has been fair/good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters still have reasonable opportunity to find mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer. Muzzleloader Season: During the Muzzleloader season most of the deer still tend to be in the mid to higher elevations though some have began to move down a little. This season is a great time to hunt the Fish Lake, hunter densities are not high and the weather is often pleasant. Deer will be spread out across the unit. Migration Patterns: Some of the deer on Fish Lake unit begin to migrate to or closer to their winter range in mid-October. By the time the rifle hunt arrives a sizable portion of the herd is often in the transitional ranges between their winter and summer ranges. However many deer also stay as high as they can until heavy snows push them lower. Most of the migration is rather simple, the deer just move up or down in elevation. However there are some deer that move from their summering areas on the North and Central parts of the unit to the Southern, Eastern, and Western parts of the unit closer to their winter range. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it generally does not affect the general deer hunts. Recommended areas to hunt on the Fish Lake unit: There are deer spread across the entire Fish Lake unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a large area and cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions. During the archery season hunters should be prepared to cool harvested game quickly due to warm temperatures.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the Abajos typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Once the rut starts, bucks will be found with and around does. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect these hunts. Recommended areas for the San Juan, Abajo subunit: Abajo Mountain - Muzzleloader hunters may find bucks in the high country, but should also focus on mid elevations. Look for oak-brush stands or sagebrush parks, surrounded by pinyon/juniper communities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the Abajos. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The Uintah Mountain range can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also less deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. Road access is allowed on the majority of the unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and tend to stay on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Vernal: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. There is a variety of habitat to hunt during the muzzleloader hunt. There is pinyon/juniper, sage brush savanna, thick lodge pole pine, and above timber line. The larger openings on the forest are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and rocky terrain. During the hunts most of the deer on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. That zone across the South Slope is the most productive for deer. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit: Whiterocks Canyon - Whiterocks River is the western unit boundary, steep terrain. Paradise Park-Higher forest terrain, steep forested canyons. Mosby Mountain-High aspen forest, with large sagebrush bowls, excellent habitat. Red Cloud Loop Rd-Long road that starts in Dry Fork Canyon (west of Vernal). It takes you all the way through the Vernal unit, and comes out on Hwy 191.. Taylor Mountain-Great vantage points. Excellent area to glass and locate animals from far distances. Colton Ranger Station-Aspen/conifer mix forest. Lime Stone, Little V, and Range Study-These areas are east of Hwy 191 and border a limited entry deer and elk unit. Diamond Mountain.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

Hunters should be aware of the Ute tribal lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on tribal lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The unit includes the High Uintas Wilderness area. The wilderness can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also fewer deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine with little understory. Road access on much of the unit is limited to mostly canyon bottoms due to the steepness of the terrain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit move down in elevation for the winter and they winter primarily on Ute Tribal Lands and on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. The deer move down towards the tribal land boundary as soon as they get much hunting pressure. There is very little hunting pressure on the tribal lands so some deer have learned to go there as soon as hunting pressure starts. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Yellowstone: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. The Wilderness Area can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but there are also fewer deer. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for deer. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine with little understory. Deer in the Wilderness are generally found above tree line or in small pockets of openings in the lodge pole cover. The larger openings are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and lots of rocks. During the hunts most of the deer on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. That zone across the South Slope is the most productive for deer. Every canyon across the South Slope, Yellowstone has deer and they are of similar quality. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation towards the end of October and first part of November. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Southwest Desert unit has very low deer densities. It can be a very difficult hunt. You may go several days without seeing a deer because the density is so low. When you do find bucks, there is a good chance of it being a mature buck. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few deer. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some small private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. The higher elevation areas above the thick pinion and juniper are the best for locating deer. South Wah Wah Range - BLM and SITLA lands from Rose Spring Canyon to Highway 21 on Wah Wah summit. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Mountain Home Range - BLM and SITLA lands from the Loper's Reseed area to Mt Home Pass. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Black Hills -BLM and SITLA lands located southwest of Minersville. Baboon Peak, Dry Willow Peak and Little Horse Valley areas. This area is closer to human population centers and may have higher hunter densities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are many CWMUs on this unit and a list of these can be found on the UDWR webpage.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Deer on this unit migrate down in elevation for the winter and typically from West to East, with most of the deer wintering on or near Tabby WMA. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: There are numerous areas to hunt on this unit. The areas surrounding Strawberry Reservoir and Currant Creek Reservoir are excellent for deer hunting. They are easy to access with many roads and trails and camping areas. This of course leads to many people hunting these areas. There are very few areas on this unit without a road in the general area. There is far less hunting pressure on the Avintaquin unit, but that is because the overall deer density is much lower and the terrain is more rugged. This unit has very large aspen stands that hold a lot of deer in the early fall. Many of the best bucks taken each year come from these aspen stands. In the summer there are deer in the more open higher areas, but once they get pressured by hunters they will move into the lower, thicker aspen stands. These areas are difficult to hunt, because of the leaves on the trees and fewer open areas to glass with optics. There are also many lower areas with several different browse species, including; oak brush, service berry, mountain mahogany, bitter brush, snow berry, sage brush, etc. These areas also have deer in them during the hunt, but at a lower density. Some areas to hunt include the following: Currant Creek Reservoir Area - high elevation, large aspen stands, very accessible, high deer density for the unit. Low Pass Creek- near Currant Creek Reservoir, rough road, great for ATV's, great for glassing up high. West Fork of the Duchesne- limited ATV access, but open to trucks. Chicken Creek/Race Track- popular area, but holds a lot of deer and bucks CO-OP Creek -Very Popular area, near Highway 40, great camping, large aspen stands Trout Creek- many bucks taken here opening weekend Wildcat WMA - good access, flat on top, a lot of pressure, many yearling bucks taken here. North Fork of Deep Creek - borders private land, limited access by road, great horse area Tabby Mountain - great for ATV's, better after snow storms, mostly public land. Coleman Basin/Red Creek Mtn- SITLA land, some areas without roads, rough roads Reservation Ridge -fewer deer, but fewer people Strawberry Peak- High elevation, large areas near by with no road access, Cow Hollow, Slab Canyon, low deer density Timber Canyon/Long Ridge- low deer density, rough terrain, better after storms, rough roads. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Fifty percent of the deer habitat is public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Large Blocks of the best deer habitat on this unit are private lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. On years with cooler weather some of the larger bucks will start into some pre rut behavior. Recommended areas to hunt: The Zion Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. During the archery hunt most deer are still in their summer habitat. Most deer will be at the middle to higher elevations from oak brush to the aspen and mixed conifer zone. About 59% of deer summer habitat on the Zion unit is on private lands. The northern portions of the unit south of Highway 14 are the best places for public access onto Forest Service land. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Webster's Flat and Deep Creek - Forest Service land From Woods Ranch area in Cedar Canyon to just east of the Zion Overlook. The Deep Creek area is a USFS roadless area. Access can be found at the trail head a short distance above the turn off to Webster's Flat on Highway 14. Midway - USFS land from the turn off to Cedar Breaks east to Navajo Lake. The old clear cut logging areas and meadows in the Deer Valley area usually have a fair amount of deer use. Strawberry Ridge and Harris Flat - USFS land between Strawberry Cabins area and east to Stout Canyon. This is a ponderosa pine are that has a good understory of bitterbrush. There is good access in to this area with several OHV trails and old logging roads. This area has several wildlife and livestock water catch ponds. This area has several cabin communities and hunters should be careful of private lands and how close they hunt to cabins. Stout Canyon and School Wash - USFS land with some larger blocks of private land. This is a ponderosa pine habitat with a good understory of bitterbrush. There are a few OHV trails and logging roads that cut through this area. Private land - Some of the best deer habitat on the Zion unit is on private lands. This unit is unusual for Southern Utah because of its large parcels of private lands that have several different land owners. Obtaining permission to hunt these areas can be difficult, but is not impossible.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is an early rifle hunt that takes place during part of the spike elk hunt. Although the hunt boundary extends onto the west side of I-15, the Pahvant Mountain Range (east side of I-15) receives most of the hunting pressure.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The main access roads and the road along the top see a lot of traffic during the hunting season from both hunters and recreationists. Be cautious of others on the road. There is not a lot of water on top so be prepared with plenty of water. After heavy rain storms, many places along the road on top get very slick and it can become very easy to slide off the road. There are many steep and rugged areas with no cell coverage. Cell coverage is good on top of the mountain, depending on carrier, but is spotty in the canyons. The bear population is not large but has been increasing. It is always a good idea to keep a clean camp and keep food inaccessible for bears.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather can change quickly and you may see early snowstorms during this hunt. Temperatures over the last few years have generally been mild during this time.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hunting buck deer in the middle of October is a relatively new thing in Utah. We are accustomed to hunting deer the last week of October when deer are often beginning to rut, and transitioning from summer to winter habitats. During mid October, deer are more likely to be remaining on summer habitats at high elevations. I would focus my efforts on public lands above 7,000 feet in elevation. On the Range Creek subunit, these areas are usually small parcels of public land surrounded by vast areas of private land. Areas to look at would be the small portion of Patmos Ridge that is public land, Cold Springs Ridge, and Cottonwood Ridge. Public land areas occur on Anthro Mountain but deer densities are generally much lower. The Range Creek subunit is also a general season Any Bull unit so expect to see other hunters afield during your deer hunt although elk hunter numbers tend to drop dramatically after the opening weekend. This unit has a high buck/doe ratio. This is due in large part to the large amounts of private land where harvest is conservative.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: A good portion of this hunt unit is in fairly remote country with very little cell coverage. Steep canyons are prone to flash flooding during thunderstorms. Several access roads reach elevations near 10,000 feet where snow can come early in the season
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Fall in Utah. You can expect rain, occasional early fall snowstorms, or warm dry conditions

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is one of two any weapon hunts that take place on this unit. This hunt holds the opportunity to hunt some of the deer on the southern portion of the unit before they migrate to winter ranges, and in some cases off of the unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt was added during the 2019 hunting season as a new hunt. This hunt offers the opportunity to hunt some of the deer on the unit before they migrate from the unit to winter range. Most of the deer on the southern 1/3 of the unit migrate from higher elevation summer ranges to winter ranges, with a good portion of these leaving the unit. Depending on the year the deer may be tricky to find as migration could be occurring during this hunt depending on where you are hunting. If you don't find as many deer as you like, check either higher or lower elevations. You may also want to hunt some of the mid range where migration could be occurring. For the northern 2/3 of the unit slight migration occurs, but it is mainly from higher elevations to mid range, and mountain valleys where ag land and winter range is abundant. There was a significant wildland fire that occurred in the unit in June of 2017. This fire was reseeded, and has taken well as well as a lot of aspen regeneration is occurring. Hunting these burnt areas can now prove to be a good strategy as the feed in these areas is good.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cell service is generally good on most of the unit, however their are some dead spots in canyons.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Generally warm temperatures occur during this hunt during the day, but night temperatures could drop into the 30's. There have been many instances over the years that during this week our first snow fall of the year occurs. Check the weather before the hunt, and prepare accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. The Pine Valley Unit is 90% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Deer on the rifle hunt are beginning to congregate onto their winter ranges so hunters can be expected to be following which will result in some hunter crowding. Please be aware of other hunters and be courteous. Day time temperatures during the rifle hunt can still reach into the low 80's. On years with good monsoonal moisture the deer may be spread out more across their range.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas to hunt: The Pine Valley Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. There are several livestock tanks, springs and guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: North end of Beaver Dam Mtns - BLM and SITLA lands west of St. George. This area is very accessible with some small private properties. Deer movement into this area can vary from year to year depending on migration. Tobin Bench to Motaqua - BLM and SITLA with some small private lands in the Motaqua area. Deer migration is more reliable in this area with increasing numbers on the second weekend of the hunt. Above Dameron and Diamond Valley- BLM, Forest Service and SITLA lands at higher elevations above Dameron and Diamond Valley. Enterprise North Hills and New Castle- BLM, Forest Service, Private and SITLA lands. Deer begin moving into these areas about the second week of October. Most deer will be in the agricultural fields at night and then available on Public Lands during the day. Bumblebee and Sweat Hills -BLM, Forest Service and SITLA lands West and South of Cedar City. Some deer may remain high on Bumblebee Mtn. until heavier snow storms drive them down.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunter crowding can be a spot in localized areas. Make sure you where your hunter orange and know what is beyond your target before shooting.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. However, deer hunting has been fair/good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters still have reasonable opportunity to find mature bucks. This hunt is overlapped by the general season, spike elk season. Deer hunters should expect to run into many elk hunters. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: The Fish Lake unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit is excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years, due to drought and a harsh winter this unit experienced lower than normal fawn production and survival resulting in a decline in population and buck/doe ratios. Buck permit numbers have been reduced to compensate. Deer populate the entire unit and can move in response to hunting pressure and weather. Elevations range from 5,000 ft valleys to peaks over 11,000 ft. Vegetation communities range from sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, to aspen/conifer. Any Weapon Early Season: In early October the deer on the Fish Lake unit tend to be very spread out. During this season there could be deer near 11,000 ft elevation or as low as the valley floors. Hunter pressure will be high due to the high number of spike elk hunters who's hunt overlaps this hunt. Deer hunters may be able to get way from elk hunting pressured areas by hunting where there tends to be fewer elk. Many of the bucks will still be in Bachelor groups, as the rut is still several weeks away. Migration Patterns: Some of the deer on Fish Lake unit begin to migrate to or closer to their winter range in mid-October. By the time the rifle hunt arrives a sizable portion of the herd is often in the transitional ranges between their winter and summer ranges. However many deer also stay as high as they can until heavy snows push them lower. Most of the migration is rather simple, the deer just move up or down in elevation. However there are some deer that move from their summering areas on the North and Central parts of the unit to the Southern, Eastern, and Western parts of the unit closer to their winter range. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it generally does not affect the general deer hunts. Recommended areas to hunt on the Fish Lake unit: There are deer spread across the entire Fish Lake unit. During the archery and muzzleloader hunts concentrate in areas above 8,000 ft. During the any-weapon hunt the deer are spread from the top of the mountain to the valley floors. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather Conditions: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms sometimes occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions. During the archery season hunters should be prepared to cool harvested game quickly due to warm temperatures.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few really nice bucks are taken. Fifty percent of the deer habitat is public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Large Blocks of the best deer habitat on this unit are private lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Many of the deer on this unit migrate down in elevation beginning in the second or third week of October. Dry or wet conditions will dictate where you can find deer during the hunting seasons. Mule Deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect this hunt. On years with cooler weather some of the larger bucks will start into some pre rut behavior in the last week of October. Recommended areas to hunt: The Zion Unit has a healthy deer population. Deer densities are high in good deer habitat. Expect to see several bucks each day. To increase your chances of seeing deer it is best to find water in good deer habitat. During the rifle hunt most deer are in transition to their wintering habitat. Some deer will still be higher on Forest Service and Private lands, but most will be on the lower elevation BLM and private lands. There are several livestock tanks, springs and a few guzzlers in this semi-desert area. Some good areas to hunt are the following: East Zion - BLM and SITLA land East of Zion National Park from Orderville south to the state line. The Sands, Elephant Cove, Poverty Flat are all good areas to find deer in their migration. Be aware of smaller parcels of private land. Kolob Terrace - BLM, SITLA and Private land between the town of Virgin and Kolob Reservoir. This area has some larger blocks of private land. The migration pattern in this area is less consistent than the migration on the eastern portions of the unit. Larger numbers of deer sometimes do not move to the lower elevations until after the hunt is over. Toquerville Falls - BLM and SITLA lands north of Toquerville. This is a lower deer density area, but some good deer are spotted in this area each year. The migration pattern is similar to the Kolob Terrace area. Kanarraville North Hills - BLM, SITLA and Private land between Cedar City and Kanarraville. It usually takes some cooler weather or snow to move very many deer off the private land of Cedar and Kanarraville Mt. into this area, but when they do you can expect to find some nice bucks. Private land - Some of the best deer habitat on the Zion unit is on private lands. This unit is unusual for Southern Utah because of its large parcels of private lands that have several different land owners. Obtaining permission to hunt these areas can be difficult, but is not impossible.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is a migration study underway to look at timing and routes of migration for North Slope deer. We ask that collared deer are not killed. If one is, DO NOT CUT THE COLLAR; remove the collar by loosening the lock nuts and call the number on the collar or the local biologist. This unit encompasses lodgepole pine, open sagebrush, and desert scrub. Hunters should expect to see other deer and elk hunters and other public land users.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Mule deer in the High Uintas do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the west side of the North Slope to the east end of the North Slope for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats all along the North Slope. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid-November-mid-December so it does not affect this hunt. Recommended areas in the North Slope: Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Depending on weather conditions, most of the deer on the Summit portion get pushed down into lower elevations after this hunt begins. Also, high country deer aren't typically pushed down out of the High Country until mid to late October if any early season snow storms hit. The majority of the deer in the 3 Corners portion of the unit stay up high on Bear Mountain, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, and Bender Mountain until later in October/early November when deer start showing up in Browns Park for the winter. This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure, especially in Browns Park, Goslin Mountain, South Valley, Dowd Mountain, and along Hwy 44. Areas with highest harvest success include Greendale Junction (along Highway 44 and 191), Sheep Creek Lake, Long Park, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, and 3 Corners. Hunters that receive written permission from private landowners in Manila also do well. Recommended areas include along Highway 44 and 191, Sheep Creep Lake, Hoop Lake, Goslin Mountain, 3 Corners, Henry's Fork, Bridger Lake and along the North Slope Road.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is comprised primarily of private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to applying for the hunt if they wish to hunt private property. This is a general season unit intended to maximize hunting opportunities and is not managed for trophy bucks. The public land receives a lot of hunting pressure, and hunters accessing public lands on this unit should expect to see other hunters during the hunting season. Although the unit is managed for opportunity, there are a several CWMUs and parcels of private land throughout the unit, which manage for better buck quality than general season units typically offer. This can result in better buck quality and higher buck numbers on the public land. Please be respectful of private property and do not trespass.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Please note: the winter of 2022/2023 had record snowfall and extremely cold temperatures, which resulted in a significant reduction in the deer population on this unit. Adult doe survival for deer that wintered on the Wasatch Back was approximately 14% and survival for deer that wintered on the Wasatch Front was approximately 56%. The Wildlife Board approved a 40% cut in permits in 2023 and will remain similar for 2024, so expect to continue to see very few hunters and less crowding than the unit has historically had. Although a large percent of deer were lost in 2022/23, climatic conditions over the last year have been excellent with lots of moisture and a warmer than average winter, which will result in more available bucks to hunt this Fall. Buck:Doe ratios have also remained high (above the objective) on the unit. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding early in the mornings and late in the evenings. The deer will likely not be in the same place during the general season hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Use quality binoculars or a spotting scope to locate animals. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Migration: Deer migrate from higher elevations to lower elevations in early to late fall. Depending on weather, deer may begin migrating before or during, or after the general season hunt. If fall conditions remain warm, deer will remain at higher elevations and can be found in Aspen stands, open meadows or bedded in conifer stands. This hunt can be challenging if weather conditions are dry and warm. Most years, the area will receive snow before or during the hunt. Recommended areas for the hunt: The B in Bountiful is a good motorized vehicle access point for the Wasatch National Forest Land that extends between North Salt Lake and I-84. This area primarily holds yearling bucks, but getting off road and into thicker vegetation and rugged terrain can lend success in finding mature bucks to harvest. Highway 65 has several access points from Little Dell Reservoir to Big Mountain Pass where deer can be found. If conditions are warm, hunt the higher elevation areas. If conditions are snowy, hunt the lower elevation areas. Please be mindful of the archery only zone and avoid Emigration Canyon. East Canyon WMA also can hold many deer. Use the ridgelines to search for deer on the WMA. Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) was recently detected on this unit. It is recommended that hunters have their animals tested for CWD. This can be done at any check station during opening weekend or by calling the Ogden Division Office.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Despite being close to the Wasatch Front, service is spotty on this unit. Most ridgetops have service, while many lower elevation areas do not. Much of the terrain is steep, so be cautious while hiking, especially when conditions are wet or snowy. Always let someone know where you are going and when you will return home. Be sure to keep campsites clean, and keep food and garbage inaccessible to bears. Store any items with an odor in a vehicle, hung in a tree at least 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches, or in a bear proof container. Coolers are not bear proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Most years, the snow will melt off within a few days throughout the hunting season. This unit usually receives some snow during October and/or November. Consider bringing multiple layers of clothing to keep comfortable as conditions can change drastically throughout the day.

Be sure to keep campsites clean, and keep food and garbage inaccessible to bears. Store any items with an odor in a vehicle, hung in a tree at least 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches, or in a bear proof container. Coolers are not bear proof. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is comprised primarily of private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to applying for the hunt if they wish to hunt private property. Approximately 86% of the unit is private property with approximately 68,000 acres available for public access. This is a general season unit intended to maximize hunting opportunities and is not managed for trophy bucks. The public land receives a lot of hunting pressure, and hunters accessing public lands on this unit should expect to see other hunters during the any legal weapon season. Although the unit is managed for opportunity, there are a large number of CWMUs throughout the unit, which manage for better buck quality than general season units typically offer. This can result in better buck quality and higher buck numbers on the public land. Please be respectful of private property and do not trespass.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Please note: the winter of 2022/2023 had record snowfall and extremely cold temperatures, which resulted in a significant reduction in the deer population on this unit. Adult doe survival for deer that wintered in Morgan County was approximately 14% and survival for deer that wintered in Rich County was approximately 55%. Survival on an average year is typically around 85%. The majority of deer that remain on the unit during the hunts winter on the Morgan county side of the unit. The Wildlife Board approved a 40% cut in permits in 2023 and will remain similar for 2024, so expect to continue to see very few hunters and less crowding than historically on the unit. Although a large percent of deer were lost in 2022/23, climatic conditions over the last year have been excellent, with lots of moisture and a warmer than average winter, which will result in more available bucks to hunt this Fall. Buck:Doe ratios have also remained high (above the objective) on the unit. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July or early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding early in the mornings and late in the evenings. The deer may not be in the same place during the muzzleloader hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Use quality binoculars or a spotting scope to locate animals. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Migration: Deer migrate from higher elevations to lower elevations in early to late Fall. Depending on weather, deer typically begin migrating after the muzzleloader hunt. If Fall conditions remain warm, deer will remain at higher elevations and can be found in Aspen stands, open meadows or bedded in conifer stands. Recommended areas for the muzzleloader hunt: The Henefer Echo WMA has several access points and holds many young bucks year round. Additionally, some mature bucks can be found on the WMA, especially in the thick oak. The number of mature bucks increases from summer to winter. An early cold snap can result in more mature bucks moving onto the WMA during the hunt. The US Forest Service land near Causey Reservoir can also be excellent hunting. In colder temperatures, deer will be found on south slopes in sagebrush stands. In warmer weather, deer will be found in aspen or conifer stands near the reservoir. Additionally, South of Monte Cristo Peak has a good number of deer in the summer and fall. If weather remains relatively warm, deer can be found throughout the US Forest Service land.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Service is spotty on this unit. Most ridgetops have service, while many lower elevation areas do not. Always let someone know where you are going and when you will return home. Be sure to keep campsites clean, and keep food and garbage inaccessible to bears. Store any items with an odor in a vehicle, hung in a tree at least 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches, or in a bear proof container. Coolers are not bear proof.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Most years, the snow will melt off within a few days throughout the hunting season. This unit usually receives some snow during October and/or November. Consider bringing multiple layers of clothing to keep comfortable as conditions can change drastically throughout the day.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder/Kaiparowits unit is a general season hunt unit and is managed to provide deer hunting opportunity. The unit has some excellent deer habitat and is a popular place to hunt. In recent years the unit has experienced an increase in the deer population and an increase in the buck/doe ratio. Deer hunting has been good. Though not managed as a trophy unit, hunters have been noticing an increasing number of mature bucks. Deer populate the entire unit, however the highest density of deer tend to be on the Boulder part of the unit. The southern portion of the unit, the Kaiporowits, is drier and has fewer deer. During the general season most of the deer tend to be in the higher elevations near water.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the general season deer are scattered over the entire unit. Much of the buck movement is dictated by weather conditions. Bucks tend to remain higher in elevation than does. The Boulder Top is above 11,000 ft elevation and generally most deer move off the top by late September. Most of the deer tend to be at the intersection of the conifer/aspen habitats and the aspen/mountain brush/sage habitats. Hunters who want to hunt the Kaiparowits portion of the unit need to be prepared to see few deer and experience very difficult hunting conditions. Every year a few older age class bucks are taken. There is no single area that produces more than others. The key is to scout your areas before the hunt to look for the deer you want.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some very remote areas on this unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms often occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 99% of land where hunters can expect to see deer in the eastern half of the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property. Most roads and ATV trails on this unit are managed by Box Elder County, the US Forest Service, or BLM and are covered on their Travel Management Plans. Please direct all questions regarding which roads and trails ATVs can be operated on to the US Forest Service. BLM: http://www.blm.gov/ut/st/en/fo/salt_lake.html Sawtooth National Forest: http://www.fs.usda.gov/sawtooth/ Box Elder County: http://www.boxeldercounty.org/box-elder-county-web-map.htm All Campgrounds on this unit are managed by the US Forest Service and BLM. Camping outside of official campgrounds is also permitted on most of the public lands. Please direct all questions regarding campground availability and other camping questions to the US Forest Service. Maps and camping regulations are available on their websites. The boundary of this hunt unit does include small portions of Tribal Trust Lands and much private land. 99% of land where hunters can expect to see deer in the eastern half of the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property. Military property also is within the Unit 1 hunt boundary. No access is allowed on military property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit is a general season unit and receives heavy hunting pressure. Deer are found throughout much of the unit. Most higher elevation Raft River Mountains deer will remain high on the range until snow depths push them down into the sagebrush flats. Access to higher elevations is through One Mile Canyon, George Creek Canyon, Johnson Canyon, and Wildcat Canyon. Deer are plentiful and hunting opportunities exist up every canyon. Deer along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range can be found up Kimbell Creek, Red Banks, and Keg Springs along the west side and near Devil's Playground and Rocky Pass on the east side. Mule deer in the higher elevations do migrate down in elevation for the winter. There are some deer that move from the Raft River Mountains to the southeast end of the Grouse Creek Mountains for the winter. During the winter deer can be found down low in sagebrush flats from Kelton to Devil's Playground. Most of these animals move back to higher elevations for the summer and fall, although there are some that stay in these low sagebrush flats year round. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally affect the hunt, unless an early snow storm pushes deer down out of the high country.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Nebo unit has some very rough terrain. I tell hunters that "the Nebo is either strait up or strait down" so be prepared for some very hard work. ATV use is not allowed on the north Nebo and horses or mules are recommended. At the very least hunters should be in very good physical condition.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: In the past the harvest has been distributed throughout the entire portion of the Nebo. The higher elevations can be good places to start looking for more mature bucks but the younger bucks can be found at lower elevations, especially associated with agriculture areas. Don't limit yourself to a few areas. They can be found anywhere on the mountains. Some of the areas to concentrate on are Nebo Creek, Page Fork, Hop Creek, and Mahogany Knoll. Other good places are off the Nebo Loop Road around Payson Lakes and the Summit Trail. The south Nebo (Sanpitch Mts.), that portion of the Nebo Unit that is south of SR 132, may be more accessible since ATV use is allowed by the USFS. However there is private property further south as well as a CWMU deer unit. Water sources are good places to find deer. Most archery hunters have the most success early in the hunt sitting at remote water holes and canyons with perennial water. Migration Patterns: There is very little deer migration during the archery and muzzleloader hunt. Deer remain on summer ranges typically at 7,500 feet and above. When migration begins (typically in mid October to mid-December) deer move down in elevation to the sagebrush benches which is usually after the rifle hunt. However, heavy snow fall during the hunt may cause deer to migrate to lower elevations early. Scouting Tips: Good hunters will scout and find their own "honey hole". A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting deer in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of deer. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Depending on the season be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road and trail conditions. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat especially during the archery season so in anticipation of hot weather plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit but every year a few nice bucks are taken. There are no CWMUs on this unit. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. Hunters are reminded that bears often frequent the area. Campers and hikers should maintain a bear-safe campsite and dispose of trash properly. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Meat and garbage should stored inside a vehicle or hung in a tree at least 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Written permission is required to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most deer are scattered throughout higher elevations, in remote areas away from major roads and ATV trails. Hunters are encouraged to do their pre-season scouting on the unit. Weather conditions will heavily influence where deer will be located during this hunt.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area.

hunt_bio_general_information: The La Sal Mountains unit is one of the most beautiful places that you will ever encounter. The unit has high alpine peaks, above 12,000 ft. and goes down to low desert valleys around 4,000 ft. This unit is a General Season hunt unit and is not managed to be a trophy unit however, every year a few nice bucks are taken. There is good road access throughout the unit, however there are also many places that hunters can hike into and get away from the crowds. Hunters should be aware of the CWMU's and private lands on the unit and learn the boundaries. There are 2 CWMUs on this unit and a list is available on the UDWR webpage: http://wildlife.utah.gov/maps/public/list_cwmus.php
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The Mule deer on the La Sals typically leave the higher elevations during mid to late fall and head for the winter range at lower elevations. Winter range occurs in all directions from the mountain range. In mid to late spring, the deer tend to follow the green-up of grasses/forbs and head back to higher elevations. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late July early August, most deer will be up high and typically seen feeding in large meadows early in the mornings and just before dark. The deer may not be in the same place during the any weapon hunt, but early scouting will give you an idea of what kind of bucks are on the unit. Using quality binoculars or spotting scopes will be very valuable to you. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Typically, bucks will be in bachelor groups from early to late summer. Once the rut starts, bucks will be found with and around does. Yearling bucks can be found year-round with does, or in bachelor groups. Mule deer rut: The mule deer rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not affect these hunts. Recommended areas for the La Sal Mountains unit: La Sal Mountain - For the archery hunt, focus on mid to high elevations throughout the unit. These areas consist of large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding. Some bucks will be above timberline in very remote areas. Muzzleloader hunters may find bucks in the high country, but should also focus on mid elevations. Any weapon hunters should focus on mid to low elevation areas. If any snow accumulates, deer will start heading for lower elevations consisting of oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, intermixed with pinyon/juniper stands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is extremely limited throughout most of the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sals. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms. Dirt roads on this unit can become extremely muddy, very quick. Be attentive and use caution when traveling during stormy weather.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has seen good deer numbers over recent years. Hunters have reported seeing more bucks and more mature bucks have been harvested in the last couple years. This unit has several areas that have no vehicle access. Hunters that hike into some of these areas, or use horses have good success at harvesting deer. Before snow falls on the unit you can access the top of the mountain from Antimony, or Cottonwood Creek in Johns Valley. Deer in the summer can be found across the unit in higher and lower elevations. There is good access on most of the BLM lands across the unit, but a lot of the forest service has limited access. There is good access on the south end of the unit in the Hunt Creeks, and often holds deer year round. There was a large fire that burned on the unit in 2002. This made it very good for glassing long distances. There is a lot of pinon and juniper in the lower elevations with Aspen, and mixed conifer stands at higher elevations. During summer months find water and hunt areas around it.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: A lot of roadless areas on the unit, expect backcountry hunting conditions
