hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is designed to help control elk population numbers.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the East part of the Wasatch Mountains typically migrate from west to east on Currant Creek and Avintaquin subunits and east to west on the Wasatch West subunit. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near Tabby Mountain WMA. On the Wasatch West portion of the unit winter along Heber Valley, Wallsburg WMA, and along the Wasatch front. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many large herds of cows and calves will be up high and in the open. They may not be in the exact same area during the hunt, but they will be in the same general areas. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most spike bulls are with cow and calf herds during the hunts. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. There is a lot of pressure put on these elk during the general season hunts, this will push the elk towards private land or areas with difficult access or terrain. After opening morning spend your time hunting the thick timber canyons or large aspen stands. Road hunting is not a very effective method of hunting during the general season. Wasatch West Subunit: Strawberry Reservoir - All canyons around the reservoir have elk in them. Try Clyde Creek, Squaw Creek, Horse Creek, Indian Canyon, Chipman Creek, Poison Ridge, French Hollow, Buffalo Canyon, and Willow Creek. Strawberry Ridge - The ridge road is rough in some places on ATV have access. This is a great place to glass and listen for elk. Sheep Creek - Try hunting the Waters along the Rays Valley road. Each of the Waters (first through sixth) has a trail head. Try hunting Halls Fork and Yellow Jacket areas. Diamond Fork/Hobble Creek - Try hunting the upper sections, elk will move into the lower sections later in the season. Mt. Timpanogos - There is a herd of around 200 elk in this area. Try looking around Cascade Springs, the top of American Fork Canyon, and the west side above Grove and Battle Creek.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until through the first week on October, after that snow could be permanently on the ground.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Pahvant Ensign Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is divided into two parts, the west part and the east part. The west part is located southwest of Kanosh, Utah, and the east part is more directly south of Kanosh. On the north and west part of the west Unit the boundaries are hard surface roads. The highest elevations on the west part are in the extreme south, 6600 feet. This elevation drops into Dog Valley around 5700 feet. Then the elevation rises again to 6400 feet before dropping down into White Sage Flat, 5000 feet. Another rise in elevation to Six Mile Point (5400 feet) and higher to 5900 feet before dropping down to about 5000 feet just outside of the town of Kanosh. The east part of the Unit is much smaller. The east part is northwest and northeast of Gardner Hollow Reservoir (8300 feet). On the east part the highest elevations are at 9000 feet on the east unit border. These elevation decrease to 8800 feet at Pole Hill and are about 7900 feet on the westside of this part. Skinner Hollow, 8100 feet to 8600 feet; Lewis Hollow. 8500 to 8600 feet; Pole Creek, 7900 feet to 9100 feet; and Skunk Creek, 7300 feet to 7600 feet are major drainages that cut the east part. The most common elevation is 5700 feet but ranges from 5000 feet to 9100 feet with an elevation difference of 4100 feet. Forty-nine percent (49%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5400 feet and 8300 feet an elevation difference of 2900 feet. The Pahvant Ensign Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) has three parts, but the southeast parts are small in comparison and close together. The larger part of the CWMU is dominated by Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36), and though the smaller parts have Pinyon-Juniper, the dominate land cover on these subunits is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). There are localized areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48) on the large area, and localized areas of Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) on the smaller areas. One of the nearest weather stations, KANOSH (424527), is about 2.4 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. KANOSH has one hundred (100) years of records, 1907 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.52 inches, but it can be as high as 8.43 inches or as low as 0.69 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 9 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 12.0 inches but can be as high as 66.0 inches. FALL temperature at KANOSH averages 53.6 degrees F. but can be as high as 99.0 degrees F. or as low as 1.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 27 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 4 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt was established to address overall elk population numbers, and to help landowners experiencing damage to hay fields in the county.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: During the hunting season elk will be found at high elevations where heavy timber is bordered by open faces where they feed. Glassing during early morning and evenings is critical to find these groups of elk. Elk are almost never observed close to roads on this unit. It is imperative that hunters get off the roads either on foot or by horse or mule if they wish to observe cows. Many elk in the area are located on the east slope of the Bear River Range west of Garden City, Round Valley, Randolph and Woodruff. Much of the unit is private property, so be sure to secure permission before accessing these properties. Many of the landowners will allow access but will charge a trespass fee.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Elk are usually not found near roads. Be prepared to hike or ride to observe elk. Make sure you are in good physical condition, harvesting and processing an elk can be physically demanding.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is variable, so check the local forecast and be prepared for likely conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: Unit is currently over population objective. The goal of this hunt is to reduce elk numbers throughout the unit and decrease depredation issues and landowner conflict.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk can be found throughout the entire unit depending on weather conditions and hunter pressure. Often times deep snow and cold temps will push the elk to lower elevations near the Utah/Wyoming state line. Scouting prior to the start of the hunt is critical to hunter success.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Hunters should be prepared for extreme weather conditions of all variety. This area often times has snow and cold temps anytime after October 1.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt has been set up to address concerns about elk doing damage to fields and haystacks in the Richmond foothills.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk can be found across the unit, but the largest groups of cows are found east of Richmond in the foothills and main drainages like High Creek, Cherry Creek and Smithfield Canyon. Many elk are using both forest service land and private land in the area depending on conditions and weather. Secure written permission from private landowners for access to their property before entering. In some years, elk can be found in the Wellsville area that cross the highway from Mount Sterling.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared to spend time away from roads and get harvested elk out over long distances on foot or by horseback.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather can vary, be prepared for all conditions.

Nephi Canyon, Salt Creek, Spencer Fork, Nebo Creek, Payson Canyon, and Dry Mountain are popular areas. Use your optics to glass for elk and elk trails/tracks. Waiting for snowy conditions may help bring elk to lower elevation but may also hinder access.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Snowy conditions are likely.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a new hunt on a general season elk unit. Currently the elk herd is over objective.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The elk population on this unit has been growing. This is a general season elk unit. During this hunt, the majority of the elk can be found on the northern half of the unit. Good areas to look include Leamington Pass road, Wild Horse Canyon, and Wide Canyon. There are some large tracts of private land on the north end. Please get written permission before accessing private land. However, there is plenty of public land as well that can hold elk.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This mountain range is rugged and steep. Cell coverage can be spotty as you get into canyons and away from main roads.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt will be cold and likely snowy.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is typically a low success hunt. Success is higher with early snow storms to get the elk migrating to this unit from surrounding areas.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the Avintaquin unit will typically migrate from West to East. This migration will start in early October and will continue throughout the winter depending on the amount of snow. Many of the elk that will winter on the Avintaquin unit will spend their summers in the Strawberry Valley. Scouting Tips : Start scouting in late June early July many large herds of cows and calves will be up high and in the open. They may not be in the exact same area during the hunt, but they will be in the same general areas for the October hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most spike bulls are with cow and calf herds during the hunts. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. There is a lot of pressure put on these elk during the general season hunts, this will push the elk towards private land or areas with difficult access or terrain. After opening morning spend your time hunting the thick timber canyons or large aspen stands. Road hunting is not a very effective method of hunting during the general season. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas Avintaquin Subunit: Reservation Ridg e- big area, road on the divide, great area for glassing, not as many elk as Currant Creek Strawberry Peak Area - Highest peak on Avintaquin, great access to roadless areas(Slab Canyon and Cow Hollow), great area for glassing on the October hunt. This area is difficult to access in November. Long Ridge - low density for elk, but can hold some elk, great glassing area, good access to roadless area (Lion Hollow), best on the November hunt, a couple of nice burn areas, steep and rough terrain Lake Canyon, Right Fork of Indian Canyon, Skitzy WMA - not good areas for the early hunts, but can be good areas for the November hunt if there are early snow storms.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Hunt takes place in early October, be prepared for any type of weather. Warm, hot, cold, rain, snow, wind, etc..

hunt_bio_general_information: Access to different areas varies and travel maps are recommended for motorized vehicle access.This hunting area has variable numbers of elk highly impacted by weather patterns. It is not legal to drive a motorized vehicle anywhere you may kill an animal.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Fish Lake unit has a very healthy population of elk. Hunters should be aware of private property and have a good map. The Thousand Lakes portion of this hunt doesn't have many elk in it until it snows a few times. Then elk can be found on the Geyser, around Tubb Flat and east of Lyman. It is unlawful to hunt in the fields near Lyman during this hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Depending on where and when you hunt you could find large amounts of snow, limited access, and roadless areas.Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some remote areas on this unit. It is very easy to become disoriented especially when hiking.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms often occur during this hunt. Usually snow this time of year is here to stay. Snowdrifts are common on roads. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions. ATVs or snowmobiles may be needed for access. The later in the year the higher chances you will have of the snow impacting access to many areas of this hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Book Cliffs offers a challenging landscape. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. Most of the canyons and ridges have roads or ATV trails to provide access. There are plenty of areas to hike and get away from the main roads.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Book Cliffs elk herd has been stagnant for several years, biologists and researchers have been monitoring the populations age structure and pregnancy rates and we have observed alarming results - a very old elk population with extremely low pregnancy rates. This cow hunt was designed to remove some elk, hopefully some of these older cows that are abundant in the population. Older females have been documented to produce fewer calves. We are working to have a healthy and productive elk population on the Book Cliffs. To get better data on the age class of this population all successful applicants will be contacted by the DWR and given instructions to collect and submit teeth for aging harvested animals. It is very important that hunters submit teeth from harvested cows. This is a quality elk hunt that should provide plenty of opportunities to harvest a cow elk, if you are an experienced hunter or even a novice/youth hunter. Many times I see elk during these season dates near main roads and fairly accessible areas. The cows and calves will migrate to lower elevations but most will stay along the Divide Ridge. Once the snow melts elk will be more tied to sustainable water sources. During the summer month's elk congregate to the Divide Ridge. After the calving season you can find large herds of elk. Once the rut begins the bulls begin to herd up smaller herds of cows and the elk seem to spread out through the whole Book Cliffs Range. Some of the main roads/areas to focus your hunting efforts on are: Seep Ridge Road, McCook Ridge, Big Park, Bitter Creek, and the many spur ridges and valleys adjacent to the Book Cliffs Divide Road. Take careful note of the boundary with the Book Cliffs, Little Creek or Roadless area if you proceed west beyond 10 Mile Knoll on the Divide Road, this area is not included in this hunt boundary Some years the temperature starts to fall and causes the ponds and guzzlers to freeze. Springs and creeks will still flow, and can be good areas to hunt. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting elk in this area. There are several recovering burned areas that have produced large amounts of grass that is excellent for elk. Elk spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. There are no service stations for many miles. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, and good tires with extra spares. The Book Cliffs has a high bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or call the local dispatch center (435 789-4222).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and snow. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Book Cliffs elk herd has been stagnant for several years, biologists and researchers have been monitoring the populations age structure and pregnancy rates and we have observed alarming results - a very old elk population with extremely low pregnancy rates. This cow hunt was designed to remove some elk, hopefully some of these older cows that are abundant in the population. Older females have been documented to produce fewer calves. We are working to have a healthy and productive elk population on the Book Cliffs. To get better data on the age class of this population all successful applicants will be contacted by the DWR and given instructions to collect and submit teeth for aging harvested animals. It is very important that hunters submit teeth from harvested cows. This is a quality elk hunt that should provide plenty of opportunities to harvest a cow elk, if you are an experienced hunter or even a novice/youth hunter. Many times I see elk during these season dates near main roads and fairly accessible areas. The cows and calves will migrate to lower elevations but most will stay along the Divide Ridge. Once the snow melts elk will be more tied to sustainable water sources. During the summer month's elk congregate to the Divide Ridge. After the calving season you can find large herds of elk. Once the rut begins the bulls begin to herd up smaller herds of cows and the elk seem to spread out through the whole Book Cliffs Range. Some years the temperature starts to fall and causes the ponds and guzzlers to freeze. Springs and creeks will still flow, and can be good areas to hunt. Some of the main roads/areas to focus your hunting efforts on are: Seep Ridge Road, McCook Ridge, Big Park, Bitter Creek, and the many spur ridges and valleys adjacent to the Book Cliffs Divide Road. Take careful note of the boundary with the Book Cliffs, Little Creek or Roadless area if you proceed west beyond 10 Mile Knoll on the Divide Road, this area is not included in this hunt boundary. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting elk in this area. There are several recovering burned areas that have produced large amounts of grass that is excellent for elk. Elk spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is comprised primarily of private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to applying for the hunt if they wish to hunt private property. Approximately 86% of the unit is private property with approximately 68,000 acres available for public access. The public land receives a lot of hunting pressure, and hunters accessing public lands on this unit should expect to see other hunters during their hunt. Please be respectful of private property and do not trespass.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most elk will begin migrating to winter range late fall or early winter. The Henefer Echo WMA is the primary publicly accessible winter range for elk on this unit. Warm, dry weather will keep elk at higher elevations and potentially on private property during this hunt. As snow accumulates and temperatures drop, elk migrate to lower elevations and are typically easier to harvest. There is very limited access with a motorized vehicle and most successful hunters have the ability to hike fairly long distances on this hunt. Success rates for the hunt are closely tied with climatic conditions. Lots of snow and cold temperatures result in higher success rates, while warm, dry weather will reduce success rates.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Service is spotty on this unit. Most ridgetops have service, while many lower elevation areas do not. Always let someone know where you are going and when you will return home. Be sure to keep campsites clean, and keep food and garbage inaccessible to bears. Store any items with an odor in a vehicle, hung in a tree at least 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches, or in a bear proof container. Coolers are not bear proof.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, snow, wind and heat. Consider bringing multiple layers of clothing to keep comfortable as conditions can change drastically throughout the day.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is comprised primarily of private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to applying for the hunt if they wish to hunt private property. Approximately 86% of the unit is private property with approximately 68,000 acres available for public access. The public land receives a lot of hunting pressure, and hunters accessing public lands on this unit should expect to see other hunters during their hunt. Please be respectful of private property and do not trespass.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most elk will begin migrating to winter range late fall or early winter. The Henefer Echo WMA is the primary publicly accessible winter range for elk on this unit. Warm, dry weather will keep elk at higher elevations and potentially on private property during this hunt. As snow accumulates and temperatures drop, elk migrate to lower elevations and are typically easier to harvest. There is very limited access with a motorized vehicle and most successful hunters have the ability to hike fairly long distances on this hunt. Success rates for the hunt are closely tied with climatic conditions. Lots of snow and cold temperatures result in higher success rates, while warm, dry weather will reduce success rates.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Service is spotty on this unit. Most ridgetops have service, while many lower elevation areas do not. Always let someone know where you are going and when you will return home.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow and wind. Consider bringing multiple layers of clothing to keep comfortable as conditions can change drastically throughout the day.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a very large hunt area. Elk are in small groups throughout the area and move on a regular basis. The habitat is generally mountains with large open valleys between, with grasslands in the bottoms, sagebrush on the benches that transition into juniper woodlands. Access is good. The terrain varies greatly, from flat valley bottoms to steep mountain canyons. Elk are primarily found in juniper woodlands and adjacent grassy areas
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk in this unit are very low density and cryptic. They can be found at high elevation near water sources or in and around agricultural fields in the early portion of the hunt. During the later part, they can be found in low elevation. Focus on habitat chainings and other habitat treatments, especially area with creasted wheatgrass openings in juniper woodlands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a large hunt area with some part being very remote. There is intermittent cell phone coverage. Some areas have great coverage, while other areas have no coverage. Make sure someone knows where you are hunting. Roads can be dangerous and become impassable due to storms.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region. Snow and cold temperatures can be a factor during the later parts of the season.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Avintaquin Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located southeast of Duchesne, Utah about 30 km. The major feature of the CWMU is the Avintaquin Canyon and Avintaquin River. The Avintaquin River ranges from 6400 feet to 6800 feet on the unit. At 6800 feet the river splits into the West Fork Avintaquin River (6900 feet to 6800 feet) and the South Fork Avintaquin River (7100 feet to 6800 feet). Minnie Creek is another major drainage on the CWMU. Minnie Creek flows from the west to the east entering at 7100 feet and merging with the West Fork Avintaquin River at 6800 feet. On the Avintaquin Canyon CWMU 7300 feet is the most common elevation. However, elevation ranges from 6400 feet to 8400 feet, a difference of 2000 feet. Fifty-five percent (55%) of the unit's elevation ranges from 6400 feet to 7300 feet, a difference of 900 feet. The Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) is the most common cover type, nearly 50%. The only other cover type that takes up much area is the Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Most of this cover type is on the west side of the unit. Together the pinyon-juniper woodland and the sagebrush steppe account for 70% of the cover. One of the Avintaquin Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, SOLDIER SUMMIT (427959), is about 39.0 km from the edge of the CWMU in a southwest direction. SOLDIER SUMMIT has one hundred nine (109) years of records, 1893 - 2002. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.09 inches, but it can be as high as 7.56 inches or as low as 1.27 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 16 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 14.3 inches but can be as high as 33.3inches. FALL temperature at SOLDIER SUMMIT averages 40.5degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -20.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 71 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Sharp Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is about 5 km southeast from Porcupine Reservoir in south Cache County. Almost all of the CWMU is in Cache County, but a small section in the southeast is in Weber County. The CWMU's name sake, Sharp Mountain rises to 9100 feet. Porcupine Ridge in the north is 8500 feet and in the south higher elevations are around 8300 feet. Davenport Creek in the south ranges from 6000 feet to 7400 feet on the unit. In the north Porcupine Creek ranges from 7400 feet to 8800 feet on the unit, and in the, east La Plata Canyon ranges from 7000 feet to 7900 feet. Much of the Sharp Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit is covered (32%) with Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). This Sagebrush Steppe is not concentrated in just one area but is spread throughout the CWMU. Similarly, Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) covers 29% of the CWMU and is spread throughout the unit too. Inter-Mountain West Aspen-Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland Complex (38) covers 7% of the unit, and Inter-Mountain Basins Mountain Mahogany Woodland and Shrubland (44) covers 5% of the unit. The Woodland Complex is spread throughout the unit, but the Mahogany Woodland and Shrubland is more concentrated in the southwest part of the unit. One of the Green Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, LOGAN FARM (425194), is about 8.8 km northwest from the northwest edge of the CWMU. LOGAN FARM has thirty-nine (39) years of records, 1989 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 4.28 inches, but it can be as high as 7.98 inches or as low as 0.96 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 21 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 12 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There will also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 5.3 inches but can be as high as 15.5 inches. FALL temperature at LOGAN FARM averages 47.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 94.0 degrees F. or as low as -16.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 47 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: This Unit is primarily private land and hunter success is closely related to weather conditions.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The elk population did not see significant losses due to the 2022/23 winter. Elk are more hardy than deer, and survival was approximately 90%. Some elk movement patterns, however, have altered over the last year, and are likely a result of weather conditions. Most elk will begin migrating to winter range late fall or early winter. Success rates on this hunt are weather dependent. Most elk herds spend significant time on private property throughout the summer and will migrate to lower elevation, public land when temperatures drop and snow accumulates. During light winter, only a few elk may be available on public land and they may be challenging to get to. In average to heavy winters, larger numbers of elk typically move onto public land during this hunt. Hunters should expect to hike to be successful. Areas around Mountain Dell, Mormon Flats, and East Canyon WMA typically have the greatest success.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is focused on the northeast portion of the La Sal unit. Large numbers of elk are typically counted within this hunt boundary during aerial surveys. Weather can really dictate the availability of elk within this hunt boundary. During light snow years, elk may stay high or remain on private property, but roads are still accessible. During years with heavy snow, elk will be pushed to lower elevations and will largely be on public land, but access can be difficult. There are multiple private lands throughout this hunt unit, be sure of your location before hunting. ALL CWMU's are excluded from this hunt. The population estimate of 1900 elk is for the entire La Sal unit; this hunt boundary makes up a small portion of that, though there can be several hundred elk within this boundary. Also note: this hunt occurs on the Manti- La Sal National Forest, this does not occur on the Manti unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the La Sal Mountains typically migrate from West to East. The majority of the elk will winter near the Utah/Colorado border. Elk also migrate off of the high mesa tops, into lower elevation valleys throughout the unit. Scouting Tips: Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. The elk probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see where elk may move into. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. Recommended areas La Sal Mountains, North Subunit: Bar-A Creek- Northeast side of the mountain, large meadows with aspen stands mixed with conifers, great camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. Pine Ridge- This entire area is good for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, great access, camping, nice roads, several different draws or canyons to hunt. Deep Creek- No roads and limited access, great area for pack-in hunts, borders private lands in many spots, great area for elk. Taylor Flat- Large sagebrush clearing surrounded by rolling hills of pine and aspen stands. North Beaver & Polar Mesa- Good access, thick pinyon and juniper stands with some high vantage points for glassing.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Weather can be unpredictable this time of year, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Snow is likely and can keep you from getting to or from your destination. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind, heat, both dry or muddy conditions, as well as flash flooding in canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt and has a considerable amount of hunting pressure. This hunt has many hunters and there are fewer elk compared to limited entry areas. This hunt was established to help during severe winters when elk come lower in the Valley and cause damage to hay stacks. Most of the elk on Taylor Mtn. when pressured flee to the large mine where there is no hunting. There are some areas that the elk will stay in that border the mine. Little Mtn. has a small resident elk herd, and hunters have had success hunting the top of it in the past. Road access is allowed on the majority of the unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There is a federally managed refuge called The Ouray National Wildlife Refuge. It is located south of Vernal and has the potential of holding elk during the winter months. The refuge has their own set of regulations and hunting areas. Contact them to answer any hunting questions http://www.fws.gov/refuge/ouray . There is a significant amount of private land in this hunt boundary. It can be difficult to obtain permission to hunt on these private lands. Please consider this before you apply for this hunt. Migration Patterns: Elk on this unit migrate down in elevation during the winter and tend to stay on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. In harsh conditions the elk will pull off of these faces and come lower onto this hunt unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for adverse weather conditions and limited cell coverage.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a General Season hunt and has a considerable amount of hunting pressure. This hunt has many hunters and there are fewer elk compared to limited entry areas. This hunt was established to help during severe winters when elk come lower in the Valley and cause damage to hay stacks. Most of the elk on Taylor Mtn. when pressured flee to the large mine where there is no hunting. There are some areas that the elk will stay in that border the mine. Little Mtn. has a small resident elk herd, and hunters have had success hunting the top of it in the past. Road access is allowed on the majority of the unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There is a federally managed refuge called The Ouray National Wildlife Refuge. It is located south of Vernal and has the potential of holding elk during the winter months. The refuge has their own set of regulations and hunting areas. Contact them to answer any hunting questions http://www.fws.gov/refuge/ouray . There is a significant amount of private land in this hunt boundary. It can be difficult to obtain permission to hunt on these private lands. Please consider this before you apply for this hunt. Migration Patterns: Elk on this unit migrate down in elevation during the winter and tend to stay on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. In harsh conditions the elk will pull off of these faces and come lower onto this hunt unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for adverse weather conditions and limited cell coverage.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area during this hunt. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two. Be prepared for dry or muddy/snowy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt occurs during the General Season Any Bull elk hunt. This hunt is intended to help reduce this elk herd. This unit is currently over objective by over 2,000 elk because a large number of the elk on this unit move onto the adjacent Ute tribal lands where there is little to no hunting pressure and no public access. The elk that move onto the tribal lands often stay there with no hunting pressure all fall and winter. At least half of the elk on the unit have learned to move onto the tribal lands as soon as hunting pressure starts in Sept. and the rest will trickle down throughout the fall. During this hunt, the majority of the elk on the unit are moving onto Tribal Lands and may stay there unless the weather cooperates and they drift back up onto the Forest Service lands. Hunters should be aware of the Ute tribal lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on tribal lands but hunting near the tribal boundary are usually the best areas to hunt. There are no CWMUs on this unit. The unit includes the High Uintas Wilderness area, but many of the elk will be moving down out of the wilderness prior to or during this hunt. Road access on the unit is limited to mostly canyon bottoms due to the steepness of the terrain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk on this unit move down in elevation for the winter and they winter primarily on Ute tribal Lands and on south facing slopes at lower elevation on the Forest Service lands. The elk move towards the tribal land boundary as soon as they get much hunting pressure starting in Sept. There is very little hunting pressure on the tribal lands so elk have learned to go there as soon as hunting pressure starts. They will also move into difficult to access areas on the Forest. Locating elk on public land is the real key for this hunt. Remember that you are also able to hunt elk on private land on this unit if you can gain written permission. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Yellowstone: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit and working east): Soapstone Basin and Lightening Ridge- Good road access, but usually fairly popular and the roads are heavily traveled all summer so the elk move away from the areas with roads North Fork of the Duchesne- paved road access in the lower main canyon, tribal lands down low Blind Stream- limited road access, tribal land down low Rock Creek- paved road access, steep areas Pigeon Water- popular area but hunters must be aware of the tribal boundary Lake Fork/Moon Lake- paved road access, some private property along the paved road Yellowstone- need to be aware of tribal boundary 77 Flat/Burnt Mill- a little flatter area, be aware of tribal boundary, hunt along the tribal boundary Dry Gulch- usually has elk this time of year near the tribal boundary Uinta Canyon- tribal lands down low, Lower Pole Creek area has been good in recent years Farm Creek- will likely need to get away from roads to find the elk, has been a good area the last couple years Whiterocks Canyon- Whiterocks River is the eastern unit boundary, steep terrain, usually some elk in the rough canyons north of Farm Creek trail head area Private Lands areas that usually have elk during this hunt: Arcadia, north side of Tabiona, Talmage, Mtn. Home, Altonah, Bluebell, Neola all have elk that come down off of the tribal land and onto private property when there is enough snow. If it snows early there may be land owners willing to let the public hunt elk if they move onto their private lands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for sudden severe weather changes during this hunt.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather can vary during this hunt from hot and dry to cold and snowy. Be prepared for either extreme. Be prepared for muddy roads.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt coincides with the general season any weapon elk hunt. Cow elk hunters should expect to see other hunters. Elk can be found throughout the unit on the Ashley National Forest during this hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move back and forth across Wyoming and Utah state lines. Majority of the elk are up high in elevation during the summer months and will move down in elevation towards Wyoming or Flaming Gorge Reservoir during the winter. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk out of the high country earlier than normal. Scouting Tips: In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Visibility on this unit is low due to dense trees. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October. Where to find elk: Elk are found throughout much of the unit. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources. Recommended areas in the North Slope, West Daggett: Good areas to look for elk include Hwy 44, Deep Creek, Greendale Junction, and along the road to Spirit Lake and Sheep Creek Lake.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically from year to year. Be prepared for rain, snow, wind and cold. Early fall snow storms usually occur in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable or very muddy.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: North end of the Mountain Home Range and the Burbank Hills_ BLM and SITLA lands located east and south of Burbank/Garrison. Elk are using some the private land agriculture fields in the the Burbank and Garrison area. This depredation is the the reason for the this limited area hunt on the the Southwest Desert unit. Elk typically will come to the fields in the evening and return to the foothills during the day. They are usually visible in the open areas on Public Land in that short window of time. Patterning the elk and the route they use will help with success.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "InReach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Pine Valley elk population is very small. The population objective is 50 and it is currently estimated to be around 75. Elk are a rare sight on this unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: A few elk can be found north of Atchison Peak and west of Harrison Peak in the Horse Valley area. The majority of the elk area found in the area west of enterprise along the the state line from Pine Park then north up to the Crest line and the Nephi Spring area. This portion of the population is transient between Utah and Nevada. In recent years a few elk have been found north of Pinto and in the Silver Peak/Antelope Peak areas. When Hunting in the Pine Park and Crestline areas be sure to know where the state line is at all times.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for a variety of weather conditions. Expect wet, snowy, muddy condition's in the later days of the hunt.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather in the early portion of the season is very warm. In the November/December portion of the season day time temps area into the 50-60's and night time temps are below freezing. Expect some rain and snow. Snow does not usually last for for more than a couple of days.

hunt_bio_general_information: During the fall hunts elk begin to migrate out of the Ferron drainage away form hunting pressure towards the southwest side of the town of Ferron where they take up refuge in the foothills. As many as 400 elk will cause damage to fences and agricultural crops and fields below the foothills at the edge of Ferron. Depredation permits have been provided to landowners in the past but this has not reduced the number of elk or reduced much agricultural damage. This hunt provides an increased opportunity to hunt cow elk in order to help reduce herd numbers and consequently reduce damages to private property. Do not assume that this will be an easy hunt. There are few roads and the elk come into the ag fields after dark and leave before daylight so the hunting will not likely be on private property. You may need horses to pack out your elk or a good strong back. Atv's will likely be usefull accessing what few roads are available. There is very limited access through private property, do not expect landowners to give permission to access. During the day the elk are up in the foothills and there are a couple atv roads that can get you some access from the south and the north. U.S. Forest Service roads/trails that makeup the western boundary may have winter closures.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is focused on the northeast portion of the La Sal unit. Large numbers of elk are typically counted within this hunt boundary during aerial surveys. Weather can really dictate the availability of elk within this hunt boundary. During light snow years, elk may stay high or remain on private property, but roads are still accessible. During years with heavy snow, elk will be pushed to lower elevations and will largely be on public land, but access can be difficult. There are multiple private lands throughout this hunt unit, be sure of your location before hunting. ALL CWMU's are excluded from this hunt. The population estimate of 1900 elk is for the entire La Sal unit; this hunt boundary makes up a small portion of that, though there can be several hundred elk within this boundary. Also note: this hunt occurs on the Manti- La Sal National Forest, this does not occur on the Manti unit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the La Sal Mountains typically migrate from West to East. The majority of the elk will winter near the Utah/Colorado border. Elk also migrate off of the high mesa tops, into lower elevation valleys throughout the unit. Scouting Tips: Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. The elk probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see where elk may move into. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. Recommended areas La Sal Mountains, North Subunit: Bar-A Creek- Northeast side of the mountain, large meadows with aspen stands mixed with conifers, great camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. Pine Ridge- This entire area is good for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, great access, camping, nice roads, several different draws or canyons to hunt. Deep Creek- No roads and limited access, great area for pack-in hunts, borders private lands in many spots, great area for elk. Taylor Flat- Large sagebrush clearing surrounded by rolling hills of pine and aspen stands. North Beaver & Polar Mesa- Good access, thick pinyon and juniper stands with some high vantage points for glassing.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Weather can be unpredictable this time of year, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Snow is likely and can keep you from getting to or from your destination. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind, heat, both dry or muddy conditions, as well as flash flooding in canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Division wants to provide more hunting opportunities on units where it is difficult to harvest antlerless elk. To provide this opportunity, the Division issues antlerless elk-control permits. You may only obtain an antlerless elk-control permit if you have a buck, bull or once-in-a-lifetime permit for areas that overlap antlerless elk-control hunting units. If you obtained a permit (including general season) to harvest a buck, bull or once-in-a-lifetime species on any of the above units ( CWMU permits are no longer included ), you have the option of purchasing an antlerless elk-control permit. The antlerless elk-control permit allows you to harvest an antlerless elk in the same unit where you'll already be hunting an antlered big game animal. Antlerless elk-control permits are not valid statewide. Please verify all hunt boundaries before heading into the field. You may hunt the antlerless elk only during the season dates-and with the same weapon-listed on your buck, bull or once-in-a-lifetime permit. Example 1: If you have a permit to hunt buck deer on the Pine Valley unit, you may purchase an antlerless elk-control permit and harvest an antlerless elk on the Pine Valley unit during your deer hunt. Example 2: If you have an any bull elk permit and you're hunting on the Morgan, South Rich unit, you can obtain an antlerless elk-control permit. You can harvest a bull elk anywhere on the unit, but you may only harvest an antlerless elk within the Morgan, South Rich elk-control unit. NOTE: If you harvest with your buck, bull or OILT permit before harvesting with your antlerless control permit, your antlerless control permit remains valid for the remainder of the season listed on your qualifying buck, bull or OILT permit.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is currently over the population objective. Land Ownership on the unit is 89% Private Property-11% Public Land -Mostly US Forest Service. Written permission is required to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Most elk are scattered throughout higher elevations, in remote areas away from major roads and ATV trails. Hunters are encouraged to do their pre-season scouting on the unit and get written permission from private landowners prior to applying for the hunt. The Whitney Reservoir area contains most of the public land on this unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters are reminded that bears often frequent the area. Campers and hikers should maintain a bear-safe campsite and dispose of trash properly. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Meat and garbage should be stored inside a vehicle or hung in a tree at least 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area, making many of the roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: This Hunt is entirely on Private Property and agricultural lands. Written permission is required to hunt on Private Property. Obtain permission before attempting to hunt this hunt. Due to legal privacy issues the DWR does not provide a list of landowners that allow access to hunters. Hunters need to identify and have written permission from landowners before they attempt to hunt this area.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk in this unit move back and forth across Wyoming and Utah state lines. Majority of the elk are up high in elevation during the summer months and will move down in elevation towards Wyoming or Flaming Gorge Reservoir during the winter. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk out of the high country earlier than normal and during some mild winters, very few elk will move down onto the private property.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is generally good on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.

hunt_bio_general_information: Private Lands Only. This Hunt is entirely on Private Property. Written permission is required to hunt on Private Property. Obtain permission before purchasing this permit. Due to legal privacy issues the DWR does not provide a list of landowners that allow access to hunters. Hunters need to identify and have written permission from landowners before they purchase this permit. Elk are very smart animals. They respond quickly to hunting pressure. They learn quickly where they are pursued and where they are not. There is a significant portion of the elk in the state that have learned to "hide out" on private property and tribal lands during the fall hunting seasons where they are inaccessible to the public. The purpose of the Private Lands Only antlerless elk hunt is to provide hunting pressure to elk on private property to encourage them to move onto public lands where they are more beneficial to the hunting public and to reduce depredation on private property. There are numerous areas where elk have become year round residents of low elevation agricultural areas on this unit. This unit is over the management objective by over 2000 elk. This elk herd is very productive and produces a large number of calves each year. Additional antlerless elk harvest is needed just to maintain this elk herd at it current size. This will be a difficult hunt for those that are unfamiliar with the area and individual property owners. The intent is for sportsmen that are able to get permission to hunt these private lands to put pressure on those elk that have become habituated to private property. The reason for the large number of permits for this hunt is to ensure that those sportsmen who can acquire access can then purchase a permit over the counter and hunt these elk as hard as possible while they are on private property. The intent is to not sell out of permits in case a need arises in late winter where additional hunting pressure on private lands becomes necessary to address depredation situations.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hunters need to be aware of all Ute Tribal Lands as they are closed to all non-tribal members. A memory chip showing landownership for GPS units is strongly recommended for this hunt if you are unfamiliar with the property boundaries. Elk are found on private property in numerous areas across this hunt area depending on the weather. At times during this hunt elk can be found on private property almost anywhere along the tribal boundary which runs along the north boundary of the hunt area from Hanna to the Whiterocks river. Elk are also consistently found in the following areas during this hunt: Arcadia, Bridgeland, Myton, Upalco, Cedar View, Randeltt, Montez Creek, Lower Uinta River drainage, etc... Hunters may be able to identify individual landowners to ask for permission by using the Duchesne and Uintah County Parcel Viewer websites that are available through the Counties online. Hunters should be respectful of private landowners and their property & livestock.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunter should be aware that this hunt overlaps much of the Uinta Basin Extended Archery hunt so be certain of your target as some archers may not be wearing hunter orange.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt can vary dramatically during the long hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Snow storms occur often during later half of this hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: Most of the private lands on this unit are on the North, West and South sides of the mountain range. Be sure to get permission to hunt private lands (excluding CWMU's) before hunting.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the La Sal Mountains typically migrate from West to East. Many bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near the Circle E CWMU, or near the Utah/Colorado border. Elk also migrate off of the high mesa tops, into lower elevation valleys throughout the unit. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the elk will be up high and in the open and in large groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see how many elk you can expect on your hunt. The unit is large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas La Sal Mountains Subunit: Bar-A Creek- Northeast side of the mountain, large meadows with aspen stands mixed with conifers, great camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. Pine Ridge- This entire area is good for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, great access, camping, nice roads, several different draws or canyons to hunt. Deep Creek- No roads and limited access, great area for pack-in hunts, borders private lands in many spots, great area for elk. Dark Canyon- Higher elevation, borders some private lands, one good main road with several two-track roads splitting off, great camping, good place to glass for elk on the early season hunts. La Sal Pass- Lots of places to glass for elk, rolling meadows with timbered North facing slopes and large aspen stands, not a lot of cows, but does hold a good number of bulls. North/South/Polar Mesas- These mesas are typically best for the late hunts, great for ATV's, good place for late season hunts.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sal unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Late summer and early fall monsoon storms occur regularly in this area. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions, as well as flash flooding in canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: There are several areas of private land on this unit, including 3 CWMU's (Spring Creek Dodge, Deer Haven and Summit Point). Hunters must receive written permission before hunting private lands. Private Lands Only elk permits are not valid on elk CWMU's or Native American lands.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the San Juan limited entry unit typically migrate from West to East. Many of the elk will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near Dry Mesa, Salt Creek Mesa and Bridger Jack Mesa. Elk also migrate onto private property areas East of Monticello. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July. The elk probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the number of elk you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points and property owners. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sal unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Late summer and early fall monsoon storms occur regularly in this area. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions, as well as flash flooding in canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: Private Lands Only. This Hunt is entirely on Private Property. Written permission is required to hunt on Private Property. Obtain permission before purchasing this permit. Due to legal privacy issues the DWR does not provide a list of landowners that allow access to hunters. Hunters need to identify and have written permission from landowners before they purchase this permit. Elk are very smart animals. They respond quickly to hunting pressure. They learn quickly where they are pursued and where they are not. There is a significant portion of the elk in the state that have learned to "hide out" on private property and tribal lands during the fall hunting seasons where they are inaccessible to the public. The purpose of the Private Lands Only antlerless elk hunt is to provide hunting pressure to elk on private property to encourage them to move onto public lands where they are more beneficial to the hunting public and to reduce depredation on private property. There are areas where elk have become year round residents of private lands on this unit. This unit is over the management objective by over 1000 elk. This elk herd is very productive and produces a large number of calves each year. Additional antlerless elk harvest is needed just to maintain this elk herd at it current size. This will be a difficult hunt for those that are unfamiliar with the area and individual property owners. The intent is for sportsmen that are able to get permission to hunt these private lands to put pressure on those elk that have become habituated to private property. The reason for the large number of permits for this hunt is to ensure that those sportsmen who can acquire access can then purchase a permit over the counter and hunt these elk as hard as possible while they are on private property. The intent is to not sell out of permits in case a need arises in late winter where additional hunting pressure on private lands becomes necessary to address depredation situations.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt can vary dramatically during the long hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Snow storms occur often during later half of this hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: Private Lands Only. This Hunt is entirely on Private Property. Written permission is required to hunt on Private Property. Obtain permission before purchasing this permit. Due to legal privacy issues the DWR does not provide a list of landowners that allow access to hunters. Hunters need to identify and have written permission from landowners before they purchase this permit. Elk are very smart animals. They respond quickly to hunting pressure. They learn quickly where they are pursued and where they are not. There is a significant portion of the elk in the state that have learned to "hide out" on private property and tribal lands during the fall hunting seasons where they are inaccessible to the public. The purpose of the Private Lands Only antlerless elk hunt is to provide hunting pressure to elk on private property to encourage them to move onto public lands where they are more beneficial to the hunting public and to reduce depredation on private property. This elk herd is very productive and produces a large number of calves each year. Antlerless elk harvest is needed just to maintain this elk herd at it current size. This will be a difficult hunt for those that are unfamiliar with the area and individual property owners. The intent is for sportsmen that are able to get permission to hunt these private lands to put pressure on those elk that have become habituated to private property. The reason for the large number of permits for this hunt is to ensure that those sportsmen who can acquire access can then purchase a permit over the counter and hunt these elk as hard as possible while they are on private property. The intent is to not sell out of permits in case a need arises in late winter where additional hunting pressure on private lands becomes necessary to address depredation situations.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt can vary dramatically during the long hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Snow storms occur often during later half of this hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a private lands only permit. Permit holders will only be allow to hunt on private land within the Unit boundaries. It is advised to obtain permission before obtaining a permit. This is a very large hunt area. Elk are in small groups throughout the area and move around on a regular basis. The habitat is generally mountains with large open valleys between, with grasslands in the bottoms, sagebrush on the benches that transition into juniper woodlands. Access is good. The terrain varies greatly, from flat valley bottoms to steep mountain canyons. Elk are primarily found in juniper woodlands and adjacent grassy areas.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk in this unit are very low density and cryptic. They can be found at high elevation near water sources or in and around agricultural fields in the early portion of the hunt. During the later part, they can be found in low elevation. Focus on habitat chainings and other habitat treatments, especially area with creasted wheatgrass openings in juniper woodlands.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a large hunt area with some part being very remote. There is intermittent cell phone coverage. Some areas have great coverage, while other areas have no coverage. Make sure someone knows where you are hunting. Roads can be dangerous and become impassable due to storms.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunderstorms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region. Snow and cold temperatures can be a factor during the later parts of the season.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a private land hunt only. Please make sure you have written permission to hunt on private land on the Zion hunt unit before purchasing this permit. This hunt has a long season August 1 through January 31st. Elk are on higher elevation properties (7500'-9000') early on in the season and move down to lower elevations (6000'-7500') in December and January.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This elk population is over objective and elk spend most of their time on private lands. This hunt is a tool that will help us reach the population objective.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunts that do not requiter hunter orange overlap this hunt. Even though you will be hunting on private land be sure to know where other hunters are when you are shooting. They may not be wearing hunter orange if their hunt does not require it.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Mud and snow may be a factor in the later part of the season. Access may be limited.

hunt_bio_general_information: New hunt on a new general season any bull unit
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This will be a difficult hunt, but a great opportunity to try to harvest a cow while also hunting bulls. The elk are spread all across the unit. Many of the elk will rut in the low elevation desert areas. The unit has a lot of roads on most ridges and canyon bottoms. Try to find areas away from the heavily traveled roads. 30% of the unit is Ute Tribal Lands, make sure to stay on public access roads. Roads with public access through Ute Tribal Lands are the following from West to East: Sowers Canyon, Nutters Ridge, Jeep Trail, Right Fork of Antelope Canyon, Left Fork of Antelope Canyon, and Gilsonite Ridge.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a new antlerless elk hunt intended to provide archery hunters the opportunity to harvest antlerless elk while hunting for bulls during the General Season Archery hunt. Hunters should be aware of the Ute Tribal Lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on Tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. Note- The Division will be conducting helicopter surveys for Mtn Goats across the Uintas the week of Aug. 28th-Sept. 2nd. The helicopter activity may impact elk behavior that week. The unit includes much of the High Uintas Wilderness area. The Wilderness can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but elk can be hard to locate. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for elk. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. In the Wilderness elk are usually found either above tree line in or in the "parks" or meadows in the conifer belt or along the base of the "bollies" where there is usually a strip of green grass and water. Road access on the remainder of the unit is limited to mostly canyon bottoms due to the steepness of the terrain. Most of the elk during this hunt are found outside the wilderness boundary.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: During this hunt it is not uncommon to find elk scattered from the Forest boundary to above timberline. Elk on this unit move down in elevation for the winter and they winter primarily on Ute Tribal lands or lower elevation Forest Service lands. The elk usually start to move towards the Tribal Land as soon as they get much hunting pressure. There is very little hunting pressure on the Tribal Lands so elk have learned to go there as soon as hunting pressure starts. Hunting near the Tribal boundary can be productive in a lot of areas. Elk rut: The elk rut on this unit usually peaks around mid to late Sept.. This hunt runs into the rut. The later into this hunt you go, the more rutty the elk will likely become. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Yellowstone: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. The Wilderness Area can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but is a very tough area to hunt and it can be hard to locate elk. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed for elk. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine without much of an understory. Elk in the Wilderness are generally found above tree line or in small pockets of openings in the lodge pole cover. The larger openings are called parks and can be found on most maps but the smaller openings are scattered across the high country. As stated above, often elk can be found in the high country along the base of the "bollies" where the rocky cliffs meet the timber. There is usually a narrow strip of grass and often water springs along this strip and elk utilize those areas. If you choose to hunt the high country, be prepared for unpredictable weather and lots of rocks. During the hunts most of the deer & elk on the unit are found in the habitat belt where aspen mixes with sagebrush and conifer. That zone across the South Slope is the most productive for big game. Every canyon across the South Slope, Yellowstone has elk, finding them is the hard part. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit): Soapstone area - high elevation, but more road access, closer to the Wasatch Front. North Fork of the Duchesne- limited road access Blind Stream - limited road access, tribal land down low, popular area Log Hollow- must cross Tribal Lands to access, rough roads Rock Creek - paved road access, steep areas Pigeon Water - popular area but hunters must be aware of tribal boundary Bear Wallow - hunters must be aware of tribal boundary, steep terrain Lake Fork/Moon Lake- paved road access, some private property along the paved road Yellowstone - rough roads, need to be aware of Tribal boundary 77 Flat/Burnt Mill- gravel roads, a little flatter area, be aware of Tribal boundary Dry Gulch- very rough road, steep terrain, be aware of Tribal boundary on the east Uinta Canyon- Tribal lands down low, steep Terrain Elk Horn Loop - gravel roads that go almost to the summit of the Uintas, lots of opportunity to scatter out Whiterocks Canyon - Whiterocks river is the eastern subunit boundary, steep terrain
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage can be spotty in some parts of this hunt unit. Satellite phones or an "InReach" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Early snow storms often occur towards the end of this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Wasatch unit is one of the largest in the state and holds a large population of elk. Most of the unit is at or over the current population objective. This hunt will help the population to get back to objective and not put on as much pressure on the elk as the muzzleloader and any weapon hunts do. The elk live across the entire unit with the greatest concentrations in the Strawberry Valley area and Currant Creek drainage. The many large stands of aspen trees on the unit are excellent habitat for elk.
