[{"BOUNDARY_ID":12,"ACREAGE":0,"LAND_OWNERSHIP":"The majority of land is managed by SITLA and DWR. There is a large DWR Wildlife Management Area (WMA) known as the Little Creek WMA. This area is managed for wildlife and the DWR encourages hunting on all WMA’s.
","WMA_IN_UNIT":"Little Creek.","CAMPGRND_INFO":"Suggested Maps: BLM: Vernal, West Water, and they have a general map that labels most of the main roads. DWR WMA’S: UDWR WMAs is limited to 14 days at one location. There are no established campgrounds in this unit, it is a first-come first-served basis. Some hunters prefer to camp at the trailheads. There are DWR cabins in this unit that are not for public use. There is no camping allowed within a quarter mile of a DWR cabin. The trails are seasonally maintained by the DWR, and sportsmen. ","PRIM_ACCESS_PTS":"There are two trailheads for the roadless area, a north and a south. The north access is called the Ten Mile Knoll trailhead. If you take Utah State Road 88, it is located between Vernal and Roosevelt. Follow SR 88 south and it turns into the Seep Ridge Road. The Seep Ridge Rd splits and becomes the Divide Rd. If you take the Divide Rd west the trail head is at the start of Steer Ridge. There is a sign at the parking area. It is a large parking area but it can fill up in a hurry with trucks and horse trailers. The Hay Canyon Rd is the main access road on the south side of the Book Cliffs. You can access it from I-70. It is a hard packed dirt/gravel road. The Steer Ridge Rd can be very dangerous if it has been snowing or raining but it can dry out quickly.
The second access point, on the south side, is located at the top of Sego Canyon. Access to the Little Creek herd unit via the Sego Canyon trailhead crosses Ute Tribal Trust lands north of the parking area. Historically, access for sportsmen across the Ute Tribe was granted as part of a cooperative agreement between the Division of Wildlife Resources and the Ute Tribe. This agreement was terminated by the Ute Tribe in January of 2024.
The DWR is working with the Ute Tribe to enter into a new agreement. DWR is hopeful that the new agreement will once again grant access across tribal trust lands near the Sego Canyon trailhead. All hunters will need to find alternative access points to the Little Creek unit until a new agreement can be reached. It is uncertain when a new agreement may be reached, as such, hunters should plan accordingly before applying for hunts in the Little Creek unit. Access remains available from the Tenmile Knoll trail. ","SUGGESTED_MAPS":"BLM: Vernal, West Water, and they have a general map that labels most of the main roads. The Book Cliffs offers a challenging landscape. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. Most of the canyons and ridges have roads or ATV trails to provide access. There are plenty of areas to hike and get away from the main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend.

There are two roads that allow you to drive across the majority of the Book Cliffs. The Kings Well Rd starts at the Seep Ridge Rd on the west side, and it can take you all the way to the Dragon Rd on the east side. The Indian Ridge Road starts at the Seep Ridge Rd and goes through the bottom of Sweet Water, top of McCook Ridge, Bitter Creek, and to Big Park. It is a great road to locate wildlife during this time of year.

Interstate 70 will provide access to most of the drainages on the south side of the Book Cliffs. Wildlife are found often found in these canyons. Major canyons and access points include Thompson/Sego Canyon, Nash Wash, Cottonwood Canyon, Hay/Middle/East Canyons, and Bryson Canyon. There are roads that will take you to the top of the Book Cliffs only in Sego Canyon, Hay Canyon, East Canyon, and Bitter Creek. The remainder of the roads dead end a short way up the canyons. hunt_bio_general_information: "Any bull" units are managed to provide over-the-counter hunting opportunity. As such, they are not managed for older age class bulls, but every year many great bulls are harvested on "any bull" units. Removing excess bulls from the population can maximize calf production because cows have less competition for available resources. High calf production maximizes both cow and bull hunting opportunities because more animals are added to the population each year. Many of the "any bull" units in Utah are comprised of wilderness areas or private lands, and we encourage hunters to abide by all trespass laws. If you purchase an "any bull" permit you may hunt on any of the "any bull" units in the state during the corresponding season.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Generally speaking, "any bull" units receive above average hunting pressure. Going the extra mile and getting away from roads and other hunters is a good way to increase your odds of success. At the beginning of this hunt, elk are at the tail end of the rut. Bulls may still be grouped up with cows and can still be fairly vocal. However, as the rut winds down and the hunt progresses, bulls will leave cow groups and seek areas of sanctuary to recover from the rut and prepare for winter. Young bulls may remain with cow groups. Finding a good vantage point and using your optics is a good strategy this time of year, but keep in mind elk may be in thick cover especially if they are experiencing heavy hunting pressure.

Pronghorn: Private lands make up a small portion of pronghorn habitat, but pronghorn tend to use irrigated hayfields in late summer which are privately owned. These areas can be avoided. Some landowners provide access to hunters. Please secure permission prior to hunting. Pockets of private lands can be found in lower Coal Creek near Wellington, and portions of Icelander Wash southwest of Sunnyside.

Mule Deer and elk: the vast majority of the high elevation summer and fall habitat is on private land. There are a few small pockets of public land that can be found on the Cold Springs WMA east of Sunnyside, Cottonwood Ridge, and Harmon Canyon. Make sure you have a map or GPS depicting land ownership as there is an abundance of private land and it is essential that you know where you are.

Bison: A large part of the area where bison reside in Range Creek is managed by the Natural History Museum of Utah. hunt_bio_general_information: "Any bull" units are managed to provide over-the-counter hunting opportunity. As such, they are not managed for older age class bulls, but every year many great bulls are harvested on "any bull" units. Removing excess bulls from the population can maximize calf production because cows have less competition for available resources. High calf production maximizes both cow and bull hunting opportunities because more animals are added to the population each year. Many of the "any bull" units in Utah are comprised of wilderness areas or private lands, and we encourage hunters to abide by all trespass laws. If you purchase an "any bull" permit you may hunt on any of the "any bull" units in the state during the corresponding season.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Generally speaking, "any bull" units receive above average hunting pressure. Going the extra mile and getting away from roads and other hunters is a good way to increase your odds of success. This is a late season hunt. Elk distribution during this time of year can vary dramatically depending on weather. Elk will usually remain at high elevations until deep snow and cold temperatures force them to migrate to winter ranges at lower elevations. Keep in mind that elk have been hunted since August and know how to avoid roads and pressure. Look for spikes with cow groups and older bulls in small bachelor groups. With snow on the ground, let your optics do your walking for you. Wind swept ridges and south facing slopes are good places to start looking.

Elk: The major access points for elk hunting will be the Bruin Point road which is accessed via SR-123 through the town of Sunnyside, the Argyle Canyon road near the top of the summit of US-191 between Price and Duchesne, and the Nine Mile Canyon road out of the town of Wellington.

Pronghorn: Private lands make up a small portion of pronghorn habitat, but pronghorn tend to use irrigated hayfields in late summer which are privately owned. These areas can be avoided. Some landowners provide access to hunters. Please secure permission prior to hunting. Pockets of private lands can be found in lower Coal Creek near Wellington, and portions of Icelander Wash southwest of Sunnyside.

Mule Deer and elk: the vast majority of the high elevation summer and fall habitat is on private land. There are a few small pockets of public land that can be found on the Cold Springs WMA east of Sunnyside, Cottonwood Ridge, and Harmon Canyon. Make sure you have a map or GPS depicting land ownership as there is an abundance of private land and it is essential that you know where you are.

Bison: A large part of the area where bison reside in Range Creek is managed by the Natural History Museum of Utah. hunt_bio_general_information: A spike bull is a bull elk which has at least one antler beam with no branching above the ears. Branched means a projection on an antler longer than one inch, measured from its base to its tip. Spike bull hunts take place on most Limited Entry elk units. These units have healthy populations of elk and are managed for older age class bulls. The purpose of spike bull hunts is to provide hunting opportunity while removing excess bulls from the population. Removing spikes can maximize calf production because cows have less competition for available resources. High calf production maximizes both cow and bull hunting opportunities because more animals are added to the population each year. If you purchase a "spike bull" permit you may hunt on any of the "spike bull" units with a corresponding weapon type and season. See the big game guidebook for weapon type exceptions on "spike bull" units.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Generally speaking, "spike bull" hunts coincide with cow hunts and can receive a lot of hunting pressure. Going the extra mile and getting away from roads and other hunters is a good way to increase your odds of success. At the beginning of this hunt, elk are at the tail end of the rut. Bulls may still be grouped up with cows and can still be fairly vocal which helps in locating elk. During the rut, spikes will typically be driven away from herds by larger bulls but will remain close by and follow herds as they move, while remaining in the periphery. However, as the rut winds down and the hunt progresses, older bulls will leave cow groups and seek areas of sanctuary to recover from the rut and prepare for winter. Spikes and other young bulls may remain with cow groups or form their own bachelor groups. Finding a good vantage point and using your optics to locate cow herds is a good strategy this time of year. Generally, if you find large groups of elk you will find spike bulls.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers

The work on Segment 2 and 3 consists of roadway bench widening, paving, drainage improvements, and safety improvements. dwr_harvest_reporting_text: REQUIRED : click here or call your local DWR office to report your harvest. You must report your harvest, even if you did not take an animal, by the Harvest Survey Due Date below (30 days from the end date of the season printed on your permit - or by February 15 for hunts ending January 16 or later); failure to do so will make you ineligible to apply in next year's Big Game and Antlerless applications - unless you pay a late fee. Submitting teeth or other biological samples from your animal, or having your animal checked by a DWR representative or CWMU operator does NOT fulfill your mandatory harvest reporting requirement.

hunt_bio_general_information: A spike bull is a bull elk which has at least one antler beam with no branching above the ears. Branched means a projection on an antler longer than one inch, measured from its base to its tip. Spike bull hunts take place on most Limited Entry elk units. These units have healthy populations of elk and are managed for older age class bulls. The purpose of spike bull hunts is to provide hunting opportunity while removing excess bulls from the population. Removing spikes can maximize calf production because cows have less competition for available resources. High calf production maximizes both cow and bull hunting opportunities because more animals are added to the population each year. If you purchase a "spike bull" permit you may hunt on any of the "spike bull" units with a corresponding weapon type and season. See the big game guidebook for weapon type exceptions on "spike bull" units.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This is a late season hunt. Elk distribution during this time of year can vary dramatically depending on weather. Elk will usually remain at high elevations until deep snow and cold temperatures force them to migrate to winter ranges at lower elevations. Keep in mind that elk have been hunted since August and know how to avoid roads and pressure. Look for spikes with cow groups and older bulls in small bachelor groups. With snow on the ground, let your optics do your walking for you. Wind swept ridges and south facing slopes are good places to start looking.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. I suggests handheld radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs roadless area has a high bear population. I recommend keeping a clean camp and putting your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeast Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or local the local dispatch center (435 789-4222). The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. The trails are very steep and challenging. Every year sportsmen have horses and mules die in the roadless area. I would suggest bringing horses that are in good physical condition.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region. It is not uncommon to have thunderstorms, flash floods and have trails wash out. Tire chains can come in very handy.

hunt_bio_general_information: If you obtain a general-season archery elk permit, you may use archery equipment to take only one of the following animals: •One elk of either sex on a general-season any bull elk unit •An antlerless elk or a spike bull elk on a general-season spike bull elk unit •Only a spike bull on the Book Cliffs unit •One elk of either sex on the extended archery elk areas A spike bull is a bull elk which has at least one antler beam with no branching above the ears. Branched means a projection on an antler longer than one inch, measured from its base to its tip.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This is an early season hunt. Elk key in on water during this time of year, but priorities will shift towards breeding as the season progresses. Towards the end of the hunt the rut will be starting up, and elk may be vocal, making them easier to locate. Look for spikes with cow groups and older bulls in small bachelor groups until the rut when they will join cow groups. Going the extra mile and getting away from roads and other hunters is a good way to increase your odds of success on this hunt. Finding a good vantage point and glassing early and late is a good strategy this time of year. At the beginning of this hunt, temperatures are high, forcing elk to bed in cover for most of the day. Sitting on water holes is also an effective hunt strategy.

Historically, access for sportsmen across the Ute Tribe was granted as part of a cooperative agreement between the Division of Wildlife Resources and the Ute Tribe. This agreement was terminated by the Ute Tribe in January of 2024.
The DWR is working with the Ute Tribe to enter into a new agreement. DWR is hopeful that the new agreement will once again grant access across tribal trust lands near the Sego Canyon trailhead. All hunters will need to find alternative access points to the Little Creek unit until a new agreement can be reached. The northeast portion of the mountain near Scofield Reservoir has a high percentage of private land on good elk habitat. Most of these lands are managed under the CWMU program and can not provide hunter access as your permit will not be valid on those properties. Other private properties require prior written permission before hunting. Small pockets of private lands at high elevations can be found surrounding Electric Lake and on East Mountain. Late Season any weapon hunters may encounter private lands in the Spring Canyon area west of Helper as well as upper Gordon Creek. Weather Conditions: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until the first week of October.

The work on Segment 2 and 3 consists of roadway bench widening, paving, drainage improvements, and safety improvements. Elk: The major access points for elk hunting will be the Bruin Point road which is accessed via SR-123 through the town of Sunnyside, the Argyle Canyon road near the top of the summit of US-191 between Price and Duchesne, and the Nine Mile Canyon road out of the town of Wellington.

Some private lands near Sunnyside and Horse Canyon.

Pronghorn: Private lands make up a small portion of pronghorn habitat, but pronghorn tend to use irrigated hayfields in late summer which are privately owned. These areas can be avoided. Some landowners provide access to hunters. Please secure permission prior to hunting. Pockets of private lands can be found in lower Coal Creek near Wellington, and portions of Icelander Wash southwest of Sunnyside.

Mule Deer and elk: the vast majority of the high elevation summer and fall habitat is on private land. There are a few small pockets of public land that can be found on the Cold Springs WMA east of Sunnyside, Cottonwood Ridge, and Harmon Canyon. Make sure you have a map or GPS depicting land ownership as there is an abundance of private land and it is essential that you know where you are.

Bison: A large part of the area where bison reside in Range Creek is managed by the Natural History Museum of Utah. hunt_bio_general_information: "Draw-only youth any bull/hunter's choice elk" hunts are managed to provide youth 12-17 years old the opportunity to hunt during or close to the rut. This permit allows hunters to harvest a mature bull, spike bull, or an antlerless elk during this hunt. These hunts are held on the General Season Any Bull elk units. As such, they are not managed for trophy class bulls, but every year many great bulls are harvested on "any bull" units. Removing excess bulls from the population can reduce wounding loss from bulls fighting with each other as well as maximize calf production because cows have less competition for available resources. High calf production maximizes both cow and bull hunting opportunities because more animals are added to the population each year. Many of the "any bull" units in Utah have large portions that are wilderness areas or private lands. We encourage hunters to abide by all trespass laws and wilderness regulations. Youth may only obtain one Draw-only youth any bull/hunter's choice elk permit in their lifetime, and preference points do not apply to this hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The elk rut usually peaks around mid to late Sept. during this hunt. The later into the hunt you go, the more rutty the elk usually become. Some hunters are successful in locating bulls by bugling during this hunt but many bulls are harvested simply by spot and stalk type hunting. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's often more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Generally speaking, elk are usually in their late summer range during this hunt and may be found at higher elevations than during the regular Any Weapon hunt in October. Going the extra mile and getting away from roads and other hunters is a good way to increase your odds of success. Bulls will likely be grouped up with cows which can make sneaking in on them difficult, but they can be fairly vocal which helps in locating elk. During the peak of rut, spikes & other young bulls will typically be driven away from herds by larger bulls but will remain close by and follow herds as they move, while remaining in the periphery.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers

This will access the top of the Beckwith Plateau but will require an ATV. Be careful crossing the Price River especially if it has rained recently. This road is found along SR-6 about 35 miles south of Price. An additional access is the Horse Canyon Road on SR-6 about 25 miles south of Price. This will provide access to the cliffs above Horse Canyon and Lila Canyon. Some hunters will drive the Hastings Road on the east side of the Green River in the town of Green River. From this road you can glass across the river to the cliffs on the west side of the river. You will obviously need some sort of boat to cross the river.

Pronghorn:Major access points include the following roads (all are accessed via SR-6); the Coal Creek Road in Wellington, the Soldier Creek Road in Wellington, the Clark Valley Road, SR-123 near Sunnyside, the Horse Canyon Road, and the Lila Canyon Road.

Mule Deer: Major access points include the Nine Mile Canyon road found at the east end of Wellington and the Bruin Point Road which is accessed via SR-123 going through the town of Sunnyside. These two roads will access much of the public lands on the West Tavaputs Plateau.

Elk: The major access points for elk hunting will be the Bruin Point road which is accessed via SR-123 through the town of Sunnyside, the Argyle Canyon road near the top of the summit of US-191 between Price and Duchesne, and the Nine Mile Canyon road out of the town of Wellington.

Bison: The Horse Canyon Road is found 25 miles south of Price on SR-6. This accesses the Range Creek area via Horse Canyon or Turtle Canyon. Some private lands near Sunnyside and Horse Canyon.

Pronghorn: Private lands make up a small portion of pronghorn habitat, but pronghorn tend to use irrigated hayfields in late summer which are privately owned. These areas can be avoided. Some landowners provide access to hunters. Please secure permission prior to hunting. Pockets of private lands can be found in lower Coal Creek near Wellington, and portions of Icelander Wash southwest of Sunnyside.

Mule Deer and elk: the vast majority of the high elevation summer and fall habitat is on private land. There are a few small pockets of public land that can be found on the Cold Springs WMA east of Sunnyside, Cottonwood Ridge, and Harmon Canyon. Make sure you have a map or GPS depicting land ownership as there is an abundance of private land and it is essential that you know where you are.

Bison: A large part of the area where bison reside in Range Creek is managed by the Natural History Museum of Utah. You must have an access permit to be on this property and it is walk in or horseback only. Please visit https://nhmu.utah.edu/range-creek/visitor-permits to get an access permit. hunt_bio_general_information: A spike bull is a bull elk which has at least one antler beam with no branching above the ears. Branched means a projection on an antler longer than one inch, measured from its base to its tip. Spike bull hunts take place on most Limited Entry elk units. These units have healthy populations of elk and are managed for older age class bulls. The purpose of spike bull hunts is to provide hunting opportunity while removing excess bulls from the population. Removing spikes can maximize calf production because cows have less competition for available resources. High calf production maximizes both cow and bull hunting opportunities because more animals are added to the population each year. If you purchase a "spike bull" permit you may hunt on any of the "spike bull" units with a corresponding weapon type and season. See the big game guidebook for weapon type exceptions on "spike bull" units.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Generally speaking, "spike bull" hunts coincide with cow hunts and can receive a lot of hunting pressure. Going the extra mile and getting away from roads and other hunters is a good way to increase your odds of success. At the beginning of this hunt, elk are at the tail end of the rut. Bulls may still be grouped up with cows and can still be fairly vocal which helps in locating elk. During the rut, spikes will typically be driven away from herds by larger bulls but will remain close by and follow herds as they move, while remaining in the periphery. However, as the rut winds down and the hunt progresses, older bulls will leave cow groups and seek areas of sanctuary to recover from the rut and prepare for winter. Spikes and other young bulls may remain with cow groups or form their own bachelor groups. Finding a good vantage point and using your optics to locate cow herds is a good strategy this time of year. Generally, if you find large groups of elk you will find spike bulls.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers

","PRIM_ACCESS_PTS":"There are two trailheads for the roadless area, a north and a south. The north access is called the Ten Mile Knoll trailhead. If you take Utah State Road 88, it is located between Vernal and Roosevelt. Follow SR 88 south and it turns into the Seep Ridge Road. The Seep Ridge Rd splits and becomes the Divide Rd. If you take the Divide Rd west the trail head is at the start of Steer Ridge. There is a sign at the parking area. It is a large parking area but it can fill up in a hurry with trucks and horse trailers. The Hay Canyon Rd is the main access road on the south side of the Book Cliffs. You can access it from I-70. It is a hard packed dirt/gravel road. The Steer Ridge Rd can be very dangerous if it has been snowing or raining but it can dry out quickly.
The second access point, on the south side, is located at the top of Sego Canyon. Access to the Little Creek herd unit via the Sego Canyon trailhead crosses Ute Tribal Trust lands north of the parking area. Historically, access for sportsmen across the Ute Tribe was granted as part of a cooperative agreement between the Division of Wildlife Resources and the Ute Tribe. This agreement was terminated by the Ute Tribe in January of 2024.
The DWR is working with the Ute Tribe to enter into a new agreement. DWR is hopeful that the new agreement will once again grant access across tribal trust lands near the Sego Canyon trailhead. All hunters will need to find alternative access points to the Little Creek unit until a new agreement can be reached. It is uncertain when a new agreement may be reached, as such, hunters should plan accordingly before applying for hunts in the Little Creek unit. Elk: The major access points for elk hunting will be the Bruin Point road which is accessed via SR-123 through the town of Sunnyside, the Argyle Canyon road near the top of the summit of US-191 between Price and Duchesne, and the Nine Mile Canyon road out of the town of Wellington.

Pronghorn: Private lands make up a small portion of pronghorn habitat, but pronghorn tend to use irrigated hayfields in late summer which are privately owned. These areas can be avoided. Some landowners provide access to hunters. Please secure permission prior to hunting. Pockets of private lands can be found in lower Coal Creek near Wellington, and portions of Icelander Wash southwest of Sunnyside.

Mule Deer and elk: the vast majority of the high elevation summer and fall habitat is on private land. There are a few small pockets of public land that can be found on the Cold Springs WMA east of Sunnyside, Cottonwood Ridge, and Harmon Canyon. Make sure you have a map or GPS depicting land ownership as there is an abundance of private land and it is essential that you know where you are.

Bison: A large part of the area where bison reside in Range Creek is managed by the Natural History Museum of Utah. ","WMA_IN_UNIT":"Little Creek.","CAMPGRND_INFO":"Suggested Maps: BLM: Vernal, West Water, and they have a general map that labels most of the main roads. ","PRIM_ACCESS_PTS":"There are two trailheads for the roadless area, a north and a south. The north access is called the Ten Mile Knoll trailhead. If you take Utah State Road 88, it is located between Vernal and Roosevelt. Follow SR 88 south and it turns into the Seep Ridge Road. The Seep Ridge Rd splits and becomes the Divide Rd. If you take the Divide Rd west the trail head is at the start of Steer Ridge. There is a sign at the parking area. It is a large parking area but it can fill up in a hurry with trucks and horse trailers. The Hay Canyon Rd is the main access road on the south side of the Book Cliffs. You can access it from I-70. It is a hard packed dirt/gravel road. The Steer Ridge Rd can be very dangerous if it has been snowing or raining but it can dry out quickly.
The second access point, on the south side, is located at the top of Sego Canyon. Access to the Little Creek herd unit via the Sego Canyon trailhead crosses Ute Tribal Trust lands north of the parking area. Historically, access for sportsmen across the Ute Tribe was granted as part of a cooperative agreement between the Division of Wildlife Resources and the Ute Tribe. This agreement was terminated by the Ute Tribe in January of 2024.
The DWR is working with the Ute Tribe to enter into a new agreement. DWR is hopeful that the new agreement will once again grant access across tribal trust lands near the Sego Canyon trailhead. All hunters will need to find alternative access points to the Little Creek unit until a new agreement can be reached. It is uncertain when a new agreement may be reached, as such, hunters should plan accordingly before applying for hunts in the Little Creek unit. Access remains available from the Tenmile Knoll trail. ","SUGGESTED_MAPS":"BLM: Vernal, West Water, and they have a general map that labels most of the main roads. Late Season any weapon hunters may encounter private lands in the Spring Canyon area west of Helper as well as upper Gordon Creek. Pronghorn: Private lands make up a small portion of pronghorn habitat, but pronghorn tend to use irrigated hayfields in late summer which are privately owned. These areas can be avoided. Some landowners provide access to hunters. Please secure permission prior to hunting. Pockets of private lands can be found in lower Coal Creek near Wellington, and portions of Icelander Wash southwest of Sunnyside.

Mule Deer and elk: the vast majority of the high elevation summer and fall habitat is on private land. There are a few small pockets of public land that can be found on the Cold Springs WMA east of Sunnyside, Cottonwood Ridge, and Harmon Canyon. Make sure you have a map or GPS depicting land ownership as there is an abundance of private land and it is essential that you know where you are.

Bison: A large part of the area where bison reside in Range Creek is managed by the Natural History Museum of Utah. hunt_bio_general_information: The Beaver offers a challenging landscape. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. A lot of the canyons and ridges have roads or ATV trails to provide access. There are plenty of areas to hike and get away from the main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of hunters choose to hunt the higher elevation areas during the archery hunt. The areas around Big Johns flat and Big Flat hold large amounts of elk. There are canyons and areas surrounding those areas where you can get out and hike to get away from people. There is plenty of water on the mountain for the elk. However as you hike you can find several unmarked springs. The northern areas of the unit have recently been through an extensive burn. As the burned area reestablishes vegetation it attracts large amounts of elk. Migration Patterns: You will find elk from one end of the Beaver to the other. The elk will start feeling pressured toward the end of the archery hunt with increased rifle hunters scouting for their upcoming hunt. During the winter months the bulls prefer to stay in the highest elevations. They will locate wind swept south slopes and wait out the winter. The cows and calves will migrate to lower elevations. After the calving season you can find large herds of elk at higher elevation in grassy meadows. Once the rut begins the bulls begin to herd up smaller herds of cows and the elk seem to spread out through the whole Beaver Range. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting elk in this area. Scouting is most effective late-summer to early fall. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of the bulls. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are several recovering burned areas that have produced large amounts of grass that is excellent for elk. Elk spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs. Scouting during the summer is effective for learning the areas where you want to hunt. I would not expect to see the same elk on the same ridge during the summer and also in the fall. The elk do tend to move before the rut. I would focus scouting efforts during the first of September. Behavior: The elk seem to prefer bedding down in the dark conifer timber during the day. Towards the evening the elk will start to work their way onto the burned faces and points of the ridges. Once the bulls shed their velvet they will start to break up from their winter and summer bachelor herds. They will usually water at least two times a day. It is not unusual for elk to graze through the night. As the hunt progresses and if colder weather moves in, the elk will start to come into the rut. Before they start to herd the cows up the bulls are very susceptible to cow elk calls. I have had success calling bulls in from far distances in the unit with the use of a cow call in early September. As elk get closer to the rut they will become more vocal and will start to round up small herds of cows. The larger bulls will usually try to keep their cows away from contending bulls. It is normal to have one herd bull and other bulls surrounding the cows at a distance. During this hunt it is effective to hunt water holes early on the hunt. Later in the hunt it is more efficient to call and locate the bulls and try to get them to come to cow calls.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Beaver Mountains has a moderate bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Southern Regional Office as soon as possible (435-865-6100).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and high temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: Most hunters plan on spending five days hunting in this remote area. There are plenty of water sources so don't plan on bringing much water in with you. Some hunters who do not have much horse experience camp at the trail heads and hike in and out every day. There are several guides and outfitters who work in this area. I would plan on a very challenging and rewarding hunt. Not many hunters can say they have killed a trophy bull in the true back country like this unit can provide. Currently there is no cattle grazing in this area, to allow stream bank restoration, and let the landscape heal after the massive fire. There are native Colorado cutthroat trout in most of the streams. There are 30-40 wild horses in this area. I have seen anywhere from 30-70 bison on this unit. It is not uncommon to see black bears in this area. There is usually plenty of feed for horses, most sportsman hobble their horses; for a few hours a day. This area is patrolled quite frequently by DWR personnel. Keep this in mind when you are transporting your game. Try to make it easy to access the permit and tag on the animal.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The roadless area has four main drainages: West Willow Creek, She Creek, Little Creek, and East Willow Creek. All of these drainages are good for camping. The ridges that separate the drainages are: Went Ridge, and Little Creek Ridge. There is a spring on Little Creek Ridge called Three Springs that has good drinking water. This is a popular elk hunting area. Other popular areas to find elk are: Santio Knolls, One Eye Canyon, Rivoguts Canyon, Fish Creek, and Dry Fork Canyon. The elk are found more on the tops of the ridges and come down on the faces and in the canyons to feed and drink. Most archery hunters have the most success early in the hunt sitting remote water holes. As the hunt progress the elk start to rut and become easier to spot and stalk. Migration Patterns: During the archery hunt I would expect to see large herds of cows, calves, and spike bulls. The bulls will start breaking up from their bachelor herds. If there isn't much pressure in the bottom of the canyons I would expect to see elk coming out in the evenings to drink from the creeks. You will find elk from one end of the roadless area to the other. The elk will start feeling pressured towards the end of the hunt with increased rifle hunters scouting for their upcoming hunt. Little Creek Ridge consistently holds a lot of elk. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting elk in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of the bulls. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are several recovering burned areas that have produced large amounts of grass that is excellent for elk. Elk spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs. There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area. Behavior: Once the bulls shed their velvet they will start to break up from their winter and summer bachelor herds. They will usually water at least two times a day. It is not unusual for elk to graze through the night. As the hunt progresses and if colder weather moves in, the elk will start to come into the rut, or breeding season. Before they start to herd the cows up the bulls are very susceptible to cow elk calls. I have had success calling bulls in from far distances in the unit with the use of a cow call in early September. As elk get closer to the rut they will become more vocal and will start to round up small herds of cows. The larger bulls will usually try to keep their cows away from contending bulls. It is normal to have one herd bull and other bulls surrounding the cows at a distance.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The Biologist suggests handheld radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs roadless area has a high bear population. I recommend keeping a clean camp and putting your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeast Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or local the local dispatch center (435 789-4222). The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. The trails are very steep and challenging. Every year sportsmen kill horses and mules in the roadless area. I would suggest bringing horses that are in good physical condition. It is not uncommon to have thunderstorms, flash floods and have trails wash out. If it rains hard it makes it difficult to navigate the trails, and the access roads. Tire chains can come in very handy.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat. I would plan on hot weather and plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Manti is the largest elk herd in the state.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: For the most part the elk will not show any migratory behavior during the archery, muzzleloader, and early rifle hunts. These elk will remain on summer ranges at elevations generally above 8,000 feet. Bulls will begin to migrate by the Late Season Any Weapon Hunt. Most bulls tend to move down in elevation on to steep ridges predominated by mountain mahogany shrubs. About 90% of the elk move east to winter and spend the winter months on the ridges west of SR-10 Scouting Tips: You can not go terribly wrong on this unit. There is excellent access to most of the unit. A popular route to learn the unit is Skyline Drive. Skyline Drive runs along the spine of the mountain range and provides access to most of the high elevation habitat on the entire unit. Learn country! There are over 12,000 elk on this mountain so there are small groups of elk with bulls in nearly every canyon with good habitat on the mountain. Listen for bugling activity and cow calls to locate elk. Also listen for domestic sheep. There are an abundance of sheep that will still be on the mountain during the September hunts. If you can hear sheep in the canyon below you, it is best to move to the next canyon as elk and sheep are rarely found in the same vicinity it seems. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Glass the open south facing slopes where elk like to feed or small meadows near the canyon bottoms. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended Areas to look on the Central Mountains Manti Unit Upper Fish Creek and it's tributaries. The tributaries include Gooseberry Creek, Silver Creek, C Canyon, and the Straight Fork. This is a roadless area on the north end of the unit. This area typically holds a lot of elk and had some prescribed fires recently that has improved elk habitat. It can be accessed from North Skyline Drive on the west or from Scofield Reservoir on the east. The bottom two miles of Upper Fish Creek is privately owned and in a CWMU Bear Ridge and Fish Creek Ridge These ridges have roads going down them. They are northwest of Scofield Reservoir. The bottom 2 miles of these ridges are privately owned. This is excellent habitat in the Pondtown Creek drainage on the north end of the unit. It is best accessed from North Skyline Drive. Trough Spring Ridge This is accessed off of SR-264 southwest of the town of Scofield. It is just above the Skyline Coal Mine. This is the ridge on the east side of Electric Lake. There are some small pockets of private land that are posted well but the majority of the acreage is Forest Service. Much of this ridge burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 which has improved the elk habitat in this area. Gentry Mountain. This is accessed from SR-10 just north of the town of Huntington at Huntington Reservoir. Part of this mountain is privately owned and part of it burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 Ford Ridge (Late Rifle Hunters Only) This area is the top of a steep canyon overlooking Spring Canyon west of Helper. It holds bachelor groups of bulls in the fall and winter. There are numerous private lands around so be very careful of where you are. There is ample public lands also. West of Skylin
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until the first week of October.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Pahvant has many steep and rugged areas. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. There is a main road across the top of the mountain with few ATV trails. Most of the ATV trails will be found on the southern half of the unit. There are some ATV trails that start in low elevation areas and go part way up several canyons. Many of the canyons have hiking trails that can help in accessing areas away from main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This is a great unit to hunt elk. There are many really nice bulls harvested off this mountain every year. This hunt takes in the beginning of the rut in September and can be a great time to locate and hunt elk. Water is limited on the mountain and finding water sources away from main roads can be a productive for finding elk. Elk can be found across the entire unit. Get out on ridges and glass into some of the deep canyons. Many canyons north of Chalk Creek are great places to locate bulls.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The main access roads and the road along the top see a lot of traffic during the hunting season from both hunters and recreationists. Be cautious of others on the road. There is not a lot of water on top so be prepared with plenty of water. After heavy rain storms, many places along the road on top get very slick and it can become very easy to slide off the road. There are many steep and rugged areas with no cell coverage. Cell coverage is good on top of the mountain, depending on carrier, but is spotty in the canyons. The bear population is not large but has been increasing. It is always a good idea to keep a clean camp and keep food inaccessible for bears.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather can change quickly and you may see some light rainstorms during this time. The temperatures during this hunt are warm and can be in the 80's.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a great unit for the opportunity to harvest a bull elk . Typical harvested bulls on the unit score around 310" to 330", but a few bigger bulls are taken each year. Make sure that you are in good physical condition and spend plenty of time scouting prior to your hunt. Portions of the unit are extremely steep. Cow calling or bugling can prove to be very valuable in locating bulls during the early season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk migration on the La Sal Mountains varies, depending on weather conditions. Elk will typically migrate off of the high mountain and mesa tops, into lower elevations throughout the unit. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open and in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas La Sal Mountains Subunit: Bar-A Creek - Northeast side of the mountain, large meadows with aspen stands mixed with conifers, great camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. Pine Ridge - This entire area is good for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, great access, camping, nice roads, several different draws or canyons to hunt. Deep Creek - No roads and limited access, great area for pack-in hunts, borders private lands in many spots, great area for elk. Dark Canyon - Higher elevation, borders some private lands, one good main road with several two-track roads splitting off, great camping, good place to glass for elk on the early season hunts. La Sal Pass - Lots of places to glass for elk, rolling meadows with timbered North facing slopes and large aspen stands, not a lot of cows, but does hold a good number of bulls. North/South/Polar Mesas - These mesas are typically best for the late hunts, great for ATV's, good place for late season hunts.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sal unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe unit has long been considered a great unit to hunt elk. Good numbers of Mature bulls, beautiful scenery, and good access makes it a popular place to hunt. The unit is managed for an average age of harvested bulls of to be 6.5-7 yrs.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: The Monroe unit has long been considered a great unit to hunt elk. Good numbers of Mature bulls, beautiful scenery, and good access makes it a popular place to hunt. Archery Season: Elk use the entire Monroe unit. However, during the Archery season they tend to be more concentrated near the aspen/conifer habitats above 8,000 ft. In mid and late August when the hunt generally begins the bulls will often be segregated from the cows in bachelor groups. Preseason scouting is important for this hunt as the elk will not be vocal. Bulls will be near water sources in cooler canyons. As the season progresses and the rut approaches bulls will begin to follow the cow herds and will become more vocal which will aid in bull location. Good areas to hunt: The central part of the unit is the most popular place for elk hunters for several reasons: There is really good camping and access, the terrain is mild, and the largest part of the elk herd resides there during the archery hunt. Elk can be found across the entire central part of the unit. Just about every meadow and canyon may have elk in them. Many people hunt this large area consisting of gentle terrain between the Dry Creek ranger station and the Koosharem ranger station. Hunters should not overlook the many side canyons that lead from the top of the plateau down to the foothills. Elk use these because of the good feed and also they get less pressure as there are fewer roads. Hunters should also not overlook elk that are using agriculture fields near Koosharem and Greenwich. Good numbers of elk also use the north end of the mountain. Elk can be found near Hunter's Flat, Big Lake, Magleby pass, and Monument peak. There are several sections of private ground in this area so be sure to know where you are. There are some elk that use the south end of the unit during the archery hunt, though not as many as the central or northern areas. Elk will be on the Forshea Mountain area where the thick aspen stands are. There are also small groups of elk stretching from the Forshea to the Langdon mountain area. Migration Patterns: Very little migration occurs during the archery hunt, though the bulls will often move to join the cow herds as the rut approaches Scouting Tips: Start scouting in June. The elk are less wary and there will be less people on the mountain. Elk will still be growing their antlers but will be easier to locate. The elk may move some before the archery hunt begins but you will have an idea of what is in the area. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for effective and efficient scouting in this area. Focus on the large meadows and recently logged or burned areas. Other Information: Hunters enjoy a high harvest rate on the Monroe unit. Hunters are usually able to locate quite a few mature bulls during scouting and hunting trips.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, lightning, cold and high temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: Elk numbers during summer months aren't as high as they are during the winter months on this unit. Alot of the elk migrate off of the unit for the summer months and return during the fall and winter months. This can be a tough hunt, but mature bulls are harvested on it every year.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has several areas that have no vehicle access. Hunters that hike into some of these areas, or use horses have good success at harvesting elk. Before snow falls on the unit you can access the top of the mountain from Antimony, or Cottonwood Creek in Johns Valley. Elk in the summer can be found across the unit in higher and lower elevations. There is good access on most of the BLM lands across the unit, but a lot of the forest service has limited access. There is good access on the south end of the unit in the Hunt Creeks, and often holds elk year round. There was a large fire that burned on the unit in 2002. This made it very good for glassing long distances. There is a lot of pinon and juniper in the lower elevations with Aspen, and mixed conifer stands at higher elevations. During summer months find water and hunt areas around it. A lot of the elk can be found at higher elevations during this hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: A lot of roadless areas on the unit expect backcountry hunting conditions.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Summer months are generally warm, but afternoon thunderstorms can be present most days in the afternoon.

hunt_bio_general_information: This elk herd has seen a reduction in cow numbers the past several years. This unit is currently below objective for bull ages. This is a very tough hunt and 330+ size bulls are rare; success is very low for this hunt. This hunt coincides with the general season archery buck deer hunt, so elk hunters should expect to see deer hunters. This unit also sees a lot of tourism due to the Green River and Flaming Gorge Reservoir. There is a Landowner Association in this unit and the majority of the private property is towards Colorado and Wyoming state lines. There was a fire this summer on the north and east sides of Goslin Mountain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move back and forth across state lines quite regularly. Cow elk are sensitive to hunting pressure. Success rates on this unit vary widely by year depending on where the elk are. Scouting Tips: In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot. Visibility on this unit is high due to the lack of trees. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Behavior: Like other wildlife, elk are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. If it's a dry year, they will be more concentrated around water sources, and these can sometimes be hunted successfully. On average precipitation or wet years, elk won't be as concentrated around water. Elk can move long distances in short periods of time, especially if they are disturbed by vehicles or people. Elk can be called in close for a shot during the rut. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October. In some years, the elk are starting to rut towards the end of the archery season. Where to find elk: Elk are found throughout much of the unit. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, guzzlers, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources. Recommended areas in the North Slope, Three Corners: Good areas to look for elk include Bare Top, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, Bender Mountain, and Dutch John Mountain.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Typically, the weather is warm throughout the archery hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Panguitch Lake elk herd is currently managed for 1300 wintering elk across the unit. Recent surveys and estimates suggest the population is approximately 1200. Substantial summer range exists on the Markagunt Plateau which is heavily forested. There are also several mid-elevation areas across the unit that bull elk will use as summer range. Elk occupy most all suitable habitat throughout the unit. The unit had a significant burned in 2017 and has opened alot of new habitat for ELK, look for elk in the burn.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Nursery groups of cow elk can be observed generally very early in the morning or right before sunset. During warmer times of the day, elk will be staying cool in the forested areas and will be more difficult to observe. Focus on areas with high densities of aspen near water sources. Look for elk in the burn. Migration Patterns: All elk in this hunt boundary will migrate but these movements are generally not observed until late October and November. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars will be helpful. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points and hiking trails. Behavior: Elk will be on summer range and will begin to rut in September with cooler weather patterns.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Panguitch Lake unit offers substantial truck and ATV access. Cellular phone coverage within this hunt boundary is generally good but there are areas within the hunt boundary with little or no coverage. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, as well as warm weather conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake/Thousand Lake unit is a very popular hunting area. Elevation ranges from some peaks above 11,600 feet to some valley floors near 5,000 feet. There are all types of vegetation and terrain. The good scenery, camping, fishing, and hunting draws many people to the area every fall. The Fish Lake unit has a large herd of 5,600 elk. It is manages for a 5.5 to 6 year average age of harvest. In 2015, the average bull harvested was just under 6 years old. This unit can produce a few really large bulls, but in general you can expect to see a fair number of medium sized, mature bulls with a chance at some larger ones. On the earlier hunts, many elk can find refuge on private property which can be frustrating.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Fish Lake/Thousand Lake unit is a very popular hunting area. Elevation ranges from some peaks above 11,600 feet to some valley floors near 5,000 feet. There are all types of vegetation and terrain. The good scenery, camping, fishing, and hunting draws many people to the area every fall. CWMU's and Private property The Fish Lake Unit contains several large tracts of private property, several of which are CWMU's that require a special permit in order to hunt. These ranches are prime elk habitat and many elk find refuge on them during the earlier hunts. This can be frustrating to hunters. Hunters are reminded that trespassing and hunting on these properties can result in large fines and loss of hunting privileges. To avoid problems have a good map and hunt well away from private property. Hunting areas and seasons: Concentrations of elk and bulls can change depending on the season you are hunting. Archery Elk are generally concentrated in the higher elevations during the archery hunt (above 8,000 ft.). The bulk of the herd tends to be in the higher elevations in the north/central part of the unit. Some good places to look are High Top Plateau, Mtn. Terrel, Mtn. Marvine, Mtn. Hilgard, Gooseberry area, Niotche, and UM Plateau. There are some elk on the Thousand Lake portion of the unit but not a large number until the late hunt. They will generally be in the higher elevations for this hunt. Elk will be easier to see in June and July as the bulls spend a lot of time grazing in the open meadows and hillsides. As the Archery season progresses the bulls will begin to split up and concentrate on the cow herds. There will be a lot of hunting/camping traffic along the main access roads. To find pressured elk you will need to get on foot and get to the more remote areas. Though the bulk of the elk will be in the aspen/conifer habitat, some elk will frequent the oak/pinyon country as long as there is water nearby. Sitting on water holes and wallows is often a good strategy in the lower and dryer country. Bulls are generally quiet for the first half of the season. As the rut approaches in early September the bulls will begin to bugle and locating them may become easier.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a large area and cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Fish Lake unit has a healthy bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting seasons. Be prepared for snow, rain, lightning, and both hot and cold temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions. The Archery and early rifle season can be very warm. Be prepared to get meat to a locker quickly or be prepared to cool meat as fast as possible to avoid spoilage.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is one of the best bull elk limited entry units in the state. The unit is managed for a 7.5 to 8 yr. old bull, which is what is being harvested, so we have an older age class of bulls in the population, although it can be a tough hunt. Make sure that you are in good physical condition and spend plenty of time scouting prior to your hunt. The Elk Ridge portion of the unit is flat and thick with vegetative cover and visual opportunities are limited. Cow calling or bugling can prove to be very valuable in locating bulls during the early season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk migration on the San Juan unit varies, depending on weather conditions. Typical migration goes from high elevations in the summer and early fall to low elevations in the winter and early spring. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near Dry Mesa, Salt Creek Mesa, Bridger Jack Mesa, Milk Ranch Pnt., Peter's Point and Devil's Cyn. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads, access points and watering holes. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas for the San Juan limited entry subunit: Abajo Mountain - Higher elevations include large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding, lower elevations contain oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, good camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. North Elk Ridge - A good area for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, limited clearings for glassing, camping, nice roads, several different draws, canyons and mesa tops to hunt. South Elk Ridge - Good roads on mesa tops, limited access to rugged canyons, great area for pack-in hunts (Dark Canyon).
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the San Juan unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The elk on this unit are doing well, with nice bulls being harvested the past several years. Habitat on Diamond Mountain consists of sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, pine, aspen, and lower elevation desert scrub. This unit contains a Landowner Association and consists of about 35% private property. The private property is posted and a GPS showing private/public property boundaries is recommended. Even though the unit has private property, there is still 65% public land that is huntable. Public hunters should not expect to be allowed to hunt the private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move up and down in elevation throughout the year. During normal winters, elk will move down off the rim to the north and south. Bull elk will typically stay up higher in elevation in more inaccessible places. In dry years, elk will stay on the top of Diamond through the winter. Scouting Tips: In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Behavior: Like other wildlife, elk are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. If it's a dry year, they will be more concentrated around water sources, and these can sometimes be hunted successfully. On average precipitation or wet years, elk won't be as concentrated around water. Elk can move long distances in short periods of time, especially if they are disturbed by vehicles or people. Elk can be called in close for a shot during the rut. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October. In some years, the rut starts towards the end of the archery hunt. Where to find elk: Elk are usually found in the higher elevations of the unit during the hunting season. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, guzzlers, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Diamond Mtn Unit: Good areas to look for elk include Wild Mountain, Top of Crouse Canyon, Marshall Draw, Warren Draw, and Mail Draw. Most of the ridges on this unit are public land and are accessible through public lands, although not always easily.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Typically, the weather is warm during the archery hunt.
