hunt_bio_general_information: Elk will spread out through all areas of the mountain during the duration of this hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hunt Success and Average Age of bulls harvested tends to be highest during the early hunts during the rut, especially the early rifle and muzzleloader. Hunter densities are lowest during the archery and late season rifle hunts. This permit allows you to have the best of both worlds. See descriptions for the other Central Mountains, Manti bull elk hunts for descriptions on where to find elk. Generally speaking during September most elk will be at high elevations above 8500 feet near Skyline Drive. Skyline Drive transverses the entire mountain range is an excellent way to look at a lot of country. Bulls during these early hunts will be in small groups mixed in with cows and calves. During the late hunts, many bulls move down in elevation on to mahogany slopes at around 8000 feet. This hunt can be very weather dependent. With mild weather elk may still be on summer habitats near the top of the mountain, however, with some significant snow, bulls will often migrate to winter ranges early in the season. Good late season hunt locations to look are Horn Mountain, Trail Mountain, Ford Ridge, and Gentry Mountain.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Some of the season dates on this multi-season hunt overlap general season. Be aware of other hunting parties while on the mountain.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect varying weather. Ranging from summer monsoon to late season snow conditions. See specific hunt forecast for a more accurate description.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a great unit for the opportunity to harvest a bull elk . Typical harvested bulls on the unit score around 310" to 330", but a few bigger bulls are taken each year. Make sure that you are in good physical condition and spend plenty of time scouting prior to your hunt. Portions of the unit are extremely steep. Cow calling or bugling can prove to be very valuable in locating bulls during the early season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk migration on the La Sal Mountains varies, depending on weather conditions. Elk will typically migrate off of the high mountain and mesa tops, into lower elevations throughout the unit. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open and in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas La Sal Mountains Subunit: Bar-A Creek - Northeast side of the mountain, large meadows with aspen stands mixed with conifers, great camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. Pine Ridge - This entire area is good for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, great access, camping, nice roads, several different draws or canyons to hunt. Deep Creek - No roads and limited access, great area for pack-in hunts, borders private lands in many spots, great area for elk. Dark Canyon - Higher elevation, borders some private lands, one good main road with several two-track roads splitting off, great camping, good place to glass for elk on the early season hunts. La Sal Pass - Lots of places to glass for elk, rolling meadows with timbered North facing slopes and large aspen stands, not a lot of cows, but does hold a good number of bulls. North/South/Polar Mesas - These mesas are typically best for the late hunts, great for ATV's, good place for late season hunts.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sal unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe is a popular unit for hunting and outdoor recreation. There is ample public land with good road/trail access. Valley floors start between 5,000 - 6,000 feet with some of the peaks reaching near 11,000 ft in elevation. Habitat types include sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and aspen/conifer. This unit is managed for an average age of harvest bulls of 6.5-7 yrs.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Archery, Muzzleloader, and Early Any Weapon: The central part of the unit is the most popular place for elk hunters for several reasons: There is really good camping and access, the terrain is mild, and the largest part of the elk herd resides there during the archery and early any weapon, and Muzzleloader seasons. Elk can be found across the entire central part of the unit. Just about every meadow and canyon may have elk in them. Many people hunt this large area consisting of gentle terrain between the Dry Creek ranger station and the Koosharem ranger station. There are several large tracts of private property here. Consult maps to avoid conflicts with Private ground. Hunters should not overlook the many side canyons that lead from the top of the plateau down to the foothills. Elk use these because of the good feed and also they get less pressure as there are fewer roads. During these seasons there are generally significant numbers of elk using the agricultural fields near Koosharem, Greenwich, and Monroe. If you ask, many of these landowners may grant permission to hunt on their property or at least pass through. Generally the elk move onto public ground during daylight hours so they are accessible. Good numbers of elk also use the north end of the mountain. Elk can be found near Hunter's Flat, Big Lake, Magleby pass, and Monument peak. There are several sections of private ground in this area so be sure to know where you are. Make sure to check the mid-elevation areas. There are some elk on the south end of the unit. Elk will be on the Forshea Mountain area where the thick aspen stands are. There are also small groups of elk stretching from the Forshea to the Langdon mountain area. Elk numbers on the south end grow as the seasons progress. Many elk move to the south end and then some even jump over to the Mt. Dutton unit. Late Season: Elk use the entire Monroe unit. During the Late Any Weapon season generally the bulls have separated from the cow herds. Though bulls may occasionally bugle they are generally quiet. Long range glassing is important for finding the bulls on this hunt. Many of the bulls spend this season high on ridges far from roads. A fair number of elk have left the unit by migrating south to Mt. Dutton. The bulls will be spread out across the entire unit in small bachelor groups. If snows are deep most of the elk will be forced off of the flatter terrain on the top of the unit and will be on south facing slopes. If snows are light they could be anywhere. Generally there are no other hunts during this season. As a result, hunters enjoy a quality hunt with little pressure from other hunters. The Monroe unit is a long mountain unit running north and south with the top being a plateau with more gentle terrain. Many of the bulls in November live along the rim and the side canyons of the plateau. Bulls really tend to like ridges with thick mahogany. North end - Hunter's Flat, The Circle, Bear Valley, and Little Creek. East side - Drainages west of Burrville and Koosharem, including: Blue Peak, Indian Peak, upper Box Creek. Also check the steep canyons south of Greenwich between Brown's canyon and Pine canyon. South End - This end will have bulls on the edges of the Forshea. There is a lot of pinyon/juniper on the extreme south end that holds a few bulls. Also, the country between Dry Creek and Twin Peaks will hold bulls. West side - Good places to find groups of bulls include Marysvale Peak area, Hunts lake, and the roadless drainages east of the town of Monroe. Migration Patterns: Though most of the elk that spend the summer on Monroe also stay there for the winter. A significant number also migrate south to the Mt. Dutton unit. This movement usually begins in September and elk trickle south through November. Because of this, do not count on bulls being is the same place you may have scouted them in during the summer. Also, many elk now use the mid-elevation areas that have fewer roads and less pressure. Though there are plenty of bulls on the unit this time of year, realize that there are not as many as there were in earlier seasons. Scouting Tips: Bulls in the later seasons may not be where you found them in the summer or early fall. The best way to scout for the late hunt is the several days just before the hunt. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for effective and efficient scouting in this area. Other Information: Hunters enjoy a high harvest rate on the Monroe unit. Hunters are usually able to locate quite a few mature bulls during scouting and hunting trips. This unit typically produces good mature bulls though not as many really large bulls as some nearby units that have more difficult terrain and access.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting seasons. Be prepared for snow, rain, and cold temperatures. Storms can cause muddy or snow-packed road conditions. In early seasons also be prepared for very warm temperatures.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a good hunt to draw for this unit. Good elk numbers are found during this hunt, with good success of harvest. Elk are usually rutting during first any weapon season, and muzzleloader seasons. The late any weapon hunt can also be great because this is when the most elk are seen on the unit. The Mt Dutton winters elk from neighboring units which all have higher age objectives. Killing an older age class bull is better on the late any weapon hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has several areas that have no vehicle access. Hunters that hike into some of these areas, or use horses have good success at harvesting elk. Before snow falls on the unit you can access the top of the mountain from Antimony, or Cottonwood Creek in Johns Valley. Elk in the summer can be found across the unit in higher and lower elevations. There is good access on most of the BLM lands across the unit, but a lot of the forest service has limited access. There is good access on the south end of the unit in the Hunt Creeks, and often holds elk year round. There was a large fire that burned on the unit in 2002. This made it very good for glassing long distances. There is a lot of pinon and juniper in the lower elevations with Aspen, and mixed conifer stands at higher elevations.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: A lot of roadless areas are located on the unit, expect backcountry conditions.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Earlier hunt are generally warmer, with thunderstorms present. Snow is very prevalent during later months.

hunt_bio_general_information: This elk herd has seen a reduction in cow numbers the past several years. Average age of bulls has decreased and is currently below objective. This is a tough hunt; elk move back and forth across state lines. 330+ size bulls are rare. Elk hunters should expect to see deer hunters. This unit also sees a lot of tourism due to the Green River and Flaming Gorge Reservoir. There is a Landowner Association in this unit and the majority of the private property is towards Colorado and Wyoming state lines. There was a fire this summer on the north and east sides of Goslin Mountain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move back and forth across state lines quite regularly. Cow elk are sensitive to hunting pressure. Success rates on this unit vary widely by year depending on where the elk are. Scouting Tips: In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot. Visibility on this unit is high due to the lack of trees. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Behavior: Like other wildlife, elk are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. If it's a dry year, they will be more concentrated around water sources, and these can sometimes be hunted successfully. On average precipitation or wet years, elk won't be as concentrated around water. Elk can move long distances in short periods of time, especially if they are disturbed by vehicles or people. Elk can be called in close for a shot during the rut. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October. Where to find elk: Elk are found throughout much of the unit. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, guzzlers, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources. Recommended areas in the North Slope, Three Corners: Good areas to look for elk include Bare Top, Goslin Mountain, Home Mountain, Bender Mountain, and Dutch John Mountain.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable or very muddy.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Panguitch Lake elk herd is currently managed for 1300 wintering elk across the unit. Recent surveys and estimates suggest the population is approximately 1200. Substantial summer range exists on the Markagunt Plateau which is heavily forested. There are also several mid-elevation areas across the unit that bull elk will use as summer range. Elk occupy most all suitable habitat throughout the unit. The unit had a significant burned in 2017 and has opened alot of new habitat for ELK, look for elk in the burn.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Nursery groups of cow elk can be observed generally very early in the morning or right before sunset. During warmer times of the day, elk will be staying cool in the forested areas and will be more difficult to observe. Focus on areas with high densities of aspen near water sources. Look for elk in the burn. Migration Patterns: All elk in this hunt boundary will migrate but these movements are generally not observed until late October and November. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars will be helpful. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points and hiking trails. Behavior: Elk will be on summer range and will begin to rut in September with cooler weather patterns.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Panguitch Lake unit offers substantial truck and ATV access. Cellular phone coverage within this hunt boundary is generally good but there are areas within the hunt boundary with little or no coverage. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, as well as warm weather conditions. Winter storms are also likely. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake/Thousand Lake unit is a very popular hunting area. Elevation ranges from some peaks above 11,600 feet to some valley floors near 5,000 feet. There are all types of vegetation and terrain. The good scenery, camping, fishing, and hunting draws many people to the area every fall. The Fish Lake unit has a large herd of 5,600 elk. It is manages for a 5.5 to 6 year average age of harvest. In 2015 the average bull was just under 6 years old. This unit can produce a few really large bulls, but in general you can expect to see a fair number of medium sized, mature bulls with a chance at some larger ones. On the earlier hunts many elk can find refuge on private property which can be frustrating.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hunting areas and seasons: Concentrations of elk and bulls can change depending on the season you are hunting. Archery Elk are generally concentrated in the higher elevations during the archery hunt (above 8,000 ft.). The bulk of the herd tends to be in the higher elevations in the north/central part of the unit. Some good places to look are High Top Plateau, Mtn. Terrel, Mtn. Marvine, Mtn. Hilgard, Gooseberry area, Niotche, and UM Plateau. There are some elk on the Thousand Lake portion of the unit but not a large number until the late hunt. They will generally be in the higher elevations for this hunt. Elk will be easier to see in June and July as the bulls spend a lot of time grazing in the open meadows and hillsides. As the Archery season progresses the bulls will begin to split up and concentrate on the cow herds. There will be a lot of hunting/camping traffic along the main access roads. To find pressured elk you will need to get on foot and get to the more remote areas. Though the bulk of the elk will be in the aspen/conifer habitat, some elk will frequent the oak/pinyon country as long as there is water nearby. Sitting on water holes and wallows is often a good strategy in the lower and dryer country. Bulls are generally quiet for the first half of the season. As the rut approaches in early September the bulls will begin to bugle and locating them may become easier. Early Rifle Elk are generally concentrated in the higher elevations during the early rifle hunt (above 8,000 ft.). The bulk of the herd tends to be in the higher elevations in the north/central part of the unit. Some good places to look are High Top Plateau, Mtn. Terrel, Mtn. Marvine, Mtn. Hilgard, Gooseberry area, Niotche, and UM Plateau. There are some elk on the Thousand Lake portion of the unit but they can be difficult to find. The elk will not be as easy to find as they were earlier in the year. During this hunt the rut is in full swing. Locating bulls by their bugles early and late in the day and even at night is a good strategy. These elk hear a lot of bugles and can be difficult to call in. A few more elk may have moved down into the oak brush habitats during this hunt, so don't overlook it. Muzzleloader This hunt also occurs during the elk rut. Bulls are still vocal but a little more wary as they have already been hunted. Try locating bulls with bugles or cow calls but don't expect many to come into the calls. After locating the elk try stalking to get into range. The majority of the elk will still be in the areas they used during the early season, though some movement may have occurred. The elk will be sticking close to the trees or not even leaving cover if ample feed exists under the trees. This hunt overlaps with the muzzleloader buck deer hunt, so there will be other hunters in the field. Late Rifle This hunt occurs in mid-November and many of the elk have moved to different areas. A large number of elk move to the eastern portion of the unit, some even crossing hwy 72 onto the Thousand Lake part of the unit. Good areas to look for bulls in this part of the unit include: Red Creek, Clear Creek, Last Chance, Tidwell Slopes, Danish Meadows, and Hen's Hole Peak and Geyser Peak on the Thousand Lake. On the south end good places to look for bulls include the Mytogi, Pole, Splatter, and Ivey Canyons. On the east side of the unit bulls can be in the upper reaches of the Praetor Slopes and Skougaard canyon, Daniels Canyon, Rose Meadow, Rex's Reservoir, and the east face above Fish Lake (if there is little snow). The north end contains a few bulls in Gooseberry, Cedar Mountain, and The Rocks. Bulls could be anywhere, but they are generally in small bachelor groups away from the cow herds. The bulls often will be on the high ridges away from the roads. Glassing is key to finding these bulls. Check carefully on high mahogany ridges. Migration Patterns: From late October to early November many of the elk on the unit move to lower elevations. A large number of the elk head east to their wintering grounds on Mytogi, Last Chance, Red and Clear Creeks, Tidwell Slopes and Thousand Lake. Some elk will move south off of the unit onto the Parker Plateau. On the rest of the unit the elk drop down to lower elevations all around the unit. Scouting Tips: To see a lot of bulls, late June and July are great times to scout while elk are using the open meadows and hillsides. Many of these bulls will have moved by the time the hunting seasons arrive but you will get a good idea of what caliber of bulls are in the area. Good binoculars and spotting scope help you cover a lot of ground. One last trip just before your hunt will let you know where the elk are. For the early hunts concentrate on the conifer/aspen habitats and for the later hunt hit the oak brush/pinyon, mahogany areas.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a Large area and cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Fish Lake unit has a healthy bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting seasons. Be prepared for snow, rain, lightning, and both hot and cold temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions. The Archery and early rifle season can be very warm. Be prepared to get meat to a locker quickly or be prepared to meat as fast as possible to avoid spoilage.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is one of the best bull elk limited entry units in the state. The unit is managed for a 7.5 to 8 yr. old bull, which is what is being harvested, so we have an older age class of bulls in the population, although it can be a tough hunt. Make sure that you are in good physical condition and spend plenty of time scouting prior to your hunt. The Elk Ridge portion of the unit is flat and thick with vegetative cover and visual opportunities are limited. Cow calling or bugling can prove to be very valuable in locating bulls during the early season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk migration on the San Juan unit varies, depending on weather conditions. Typical migration goes from high elevations in the summer and early fall to low elevations in the winter and early spring. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near Dry Mesa, Salt Creek Mesa, Bridger Jack Mesa, Milk Ranch Pnt., Peter's Point and Devil's Cyn. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads, access points and watering holes. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas for the San Juan limited entry subunit: Abajo Mountain - Higher elevations include large alpine meadows with aspen/conifer stands surrounding, lower elevations contain oak stands with large sagebrush clearings, good camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. North Elk Ridge - A good area for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, limited clearings for glassing, camping, nice roads, several different draws, canyons and mesa tops to hunt. South Elk Ridge - Good roads on mesa tops, limited access to rugged canyons, great area for pack-in hunts (Dark Canyon).
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the San Juan unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The elk on this unit are doing well, with nice bulls being harvested the past several years. Habitat on Diamond Mountain consists of sagebrush, pinyon/juniper, pine, aspen, and lower elevation desert scrub. This unit contains a Landowner Association and consists of about 35% private property. The private property is posted and a GPS showing private/public property boundaries is recommended. Even though the unit has private property, there is still 65% public land that is huntable. Public hunters should not expect to be allowed to hunt the private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Elk in this unit move up and down in elevation throughout the year. During normal winters, elk will move down off the rim to the north and south. Bull elk will typically stay up higher in elevation in more inaccessible places. In dry years, elk will stay on the top of Diamond through the winter. Scouting Tips: In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Behavior: Like other wildlife, elk are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. If it's a dry year, they will be more concentrated around water sources, and these can sometimes be hunted successfully. On average precipitation or wet years, elk won't be as concentrated around water. Elk can move long distances in short periods of time, especially if they are disturbed by vehicles or people. Elk can be called in close for a shot during the rut. Elk rut: The elk rut usually runs from mid-September to early October. Where to find elk: Elk are usually found in the higher elevations of the unit during the hunting season. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, guzzlers, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Diamond Mtn Unit: Good areas to look for elk include Wild Mountain, Top of Crouse Canyon, Marshall Draw, Warren Draw, and Mail Draw. Most of the ridges on this unit are public land and are accessible through public lands, although not always easily.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Typically, the weather is warm during the archery hunt but roads can become muddy and impassable later in the season.

hunt_bio_general_information: Land Ownership: Salt Lake county east of I-15 is archery only for buck deer and bull elk. NO rifle or muzzleloader hunting aloud. 75%-85% of summer and fall elk habitat is public land.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the East part of the Wasatch Mountains typically migrate from west to east. On the Wasatch West portion the elk migrate east to west. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near Tabby Mountain WMA. On the Wasatch West portion of the unit winter along Heber Valley, Wallsburg WMA, and along the Wasatch front. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open and in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut : There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas Currant Creek Subunit: CO-OP Creek - Just North of Strawberry Reservoir, large aspen stands, great camping, nice road, a lot of elk. Currant Creek Drainage - This entire area is great for elk, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands, great access, camping, nice road, several different draws or canyons to hunt(Layout Canyon, Big Dry Hollow, Low Pass Creek, Race Track), can hold large herds of elk North Fork Deep Creek/Water Hollow - very few roads, great area for horseback hunts, land managed by UDWR, borders private land in many spots, great area for elk. Wildcat WMA - UDWR land, borders private, lots of roads, not as many elk, West Fork Duchesne - Big area, road access, limited ATV access, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands. Tabby Mountain WMA - the North slope is best, the entire WMA great spot for the late season hunts, UDWR land, great for ATV's Recommended areas Avintaquin Subunit: Reservation Ridge - big area, road on the divide, great area for glassing(especially on the late season hunts), not as many elk as Currant Creek Strawberry Peak Area - Highest peak on Avintaquin, great access to roadless areas(Slab Canyon and Cow Hollow), great area for glassing Long Ridge - low density for elk, but can hold some elk, great glassing area, good access to roadless area (Lion Hollow), best on the late season hunts, a couple of nice burn areas, steep and rough terrain Lake Canyon, Right Fork of Indian Canyon, Skitzy WMA - not good areas for the early hunts, good areas for the late season hunts, not a lot of cows, but does hold a lot of bulls Recommended area on Wasatch West subunit: Strawberry Reservoir -All canyons around the reservoir have elk in them. Try Clyde Creek, Squaw Creek, Horse Creek, Indian Canyon, Chipman Creek, Poison Ridge, French Hollow, Buffalo Canyon, and Willow Creek. Strawberry Ridge - The ridge road is rough, in some places on ATV have access. This is a great place to glass and listen for elk. Sheep Creek - Try hunting the Waters along the Rays Valley road. Each of the Waters (first through sixth) has a trail head. Try hunting Halls Fork and Yellow Jacket areas. Diamond Fork/Hobble Creek - Try hunting the upper sections, elk will move into the lower sections later in the season. Mt. Timpanogos - There is a herd of around 200 elk in this area. Try looking around Cascade Springs, the top of American Fork Canyon, and the west side above Grove and Battle Creek. In late season bull elk move onto the face of the Wasatch front. Try Hunting the Timp WMA. Spanish Fork Canyon - In the late season bull elk will move from their summer range into Spanish Fork Canyon where they winter. Any side canyon should have bull elk in them such as Tie Fork. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: ATTENTION-The US Forest is planning on a few prescribed burns this fall that might interfere with some hunt areas. Please be aware. The Heber-Kamas Ranger District is proposing to treat 3,300 acres with active fire in three operational areas occurring in Summit and Wasatch Counties. These areas are in the Provo watershed 10 miles east of Kamas and in the West Fork watershed 20 miles southeast of Heber City. Operations are planned to begin August 21, 2023, and will continue as conditions allow. The operation will require some area and road closure for public safety, active fire management will occur primarily during the daytime but also could occur at night to increase resource objectives. The Forest Service has established a Wildfire Crisis Strategy for dramatically increasing fuels and forest health treatments. The 10-year Wildfire Crisis Strategy (WCS) is built around the scale of the problem, which estimates that 50 million acres in addition to what we currently treat on an annual basis need fuels and forest health treatment to address the growing wildfire crisis. The goal of the project is to reduce wildfire risks to communities and natural resources by restoring and maintaining healthy, resilient fire-adapted forests. Approximately 382,000 acres (44%) of the Wasatch landscape is classified as high or very high fire hazard, posing a considerable threat to the function of vital watersheds, plant and wildlife habitat, recreational opportunities, and private property. The Forest has been actively managing across the forest to meet resource objectives through vegetation treatments and prescribed fire management. The Forest will continue to use all available tools to continue managing the resources meet the goals in the WCS. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This is a new hunt. There will be lots of people afield during this hunt as it occurs during the general season spike and cow hunts. This can be to your advantage as there will be plenty of "spotters" for you. On some years, elk are still bugling and can easily be located, although they may not respond to a call as well as they have been hunted for several weeks and the rut will be ending very soon. Elk are typically at high elevations during this hunt as deep snows typically do not occur until November. Hunt the high stuff between 8000 and 10000 feet. Just about every drainage at that elevation will be holding some elk. Hunting along Skyline Drive will provide good access to these habitats. This road goes along the spine of the entire mountain range from SR6 to Interstate 70. If you hear domestic sheep in a canyon, avoid the canyon. The elk typically aren't there while the sheep are there.

hunt_bio_general_information: ATTENTION HUNTERS: Salt Lake county east of I-15 is archery only for buck deer and bull elk. NO rifle or muzzleloader hunting aloud.This is a new hunt for 2017 season. This hunt is at the same time as the general season spike elk hunt. Hunters should be aware and expect to encounter spike elk hunters. This hunt was designed to relieve hunting pressure from the early and late season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk on the East part of the Wasatch Mountains typically migrate from west to east on Currant Creek and Avintaquin subunits and east to west on the Wasatch West subunit. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. The majority of the elk will winter on or near Tabby Mountain WMA. On the Wasatch West portion of the unit winter along Heber Valley, Wallsburg WMA, and along the Wasatch front. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many large herds of cows and calves will be up high and in the open. They may not be in the exact same area during the hunt, but they will be in the same general areas. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most spike bulls are with cow and calf herds during the hunts. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. There is a lot of pressure put on these elk during the general season hunts, this will push the elk towards private land or areas with difficult access or terrain. After opening morning spend your time hunting the thick timber canyons or large aspen stands. Road hunting is not a very effective method of hunting during the general season. Elk rut: The peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September.There will typically be a little rutting activity during the first weeks in October. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas Currant Creek Subunit: CO-OP Creek- Just North of Strawberry Reservoir, large aspen stands, great camping, nice road, a lot of elk. Currant Creek Drainage- This entire area is great for elk, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands, great access, camping, nice road, several different draws or canyons to hunt(Layout Canyon, Big Dry Hollow, Low Pass Creek, Race Track), can hold large herds of elk North Fork Deep Creek/Water Hollow- very few roads, great area for horseback hunts, land managed by UDWR, borders private land in many spots, great area for elk. Wildcat WMA- UDWR land, borders private, lots of roads, not as many elk, West Fork Duchesne- Big area, road access, limited ATV access, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands. Tabby Mountain WMA- the North slope is best, the entire WMA great spot for the muzzleloader hunt, UDWR land, great for ATV's Recommended areas Avintaquin Subunit: Reservation Ridge- big area, road on the divide, great area for glassing(especially on the muzzleloader hunt), not as many elk as Currant Creek Strawberry Peak Area- Highest peak on Avintaquin, great access to roadless areas(Slab Canyon and Cow Hollow), great area for glassing Long Ridge- low density for elk, but can hold some elk, great glassing area, good access to roadless area (Lion Hollow), best on the muzzleloader hunt, a couple of nice burn areas, steep and rough terrain Lake Canyon, Right Fork of Indian Canyon, Skitzy WMA- not good areas for the early hunts, good areas for the muzzleloader hunt, not a lot of cows, but does hold a lot of bulls Recommended area on Wasatch West subunit: Strawberry Reservoir-All canyons around the reservoir have elk in them. Try Clyde Creek, Squaw Creek, Horse Creek, Indian Canyon, Chipman Creek, Poison Ridge, French Hollow, Buffalo Canyon, Trout Creek and Willow Creek. Strawberry Ridge- The ridge road is rough, in some places on ATV have access. This is a great place to glass and listen for elk. Sheep Creek- Try hunting the Waters along the Rays Valley road. Each of the Waters (first through sixth) has a trail head. Try hunting Halls Fork and Yellow Jacket areas. Diamond Fork/Hobble Creek- Try hunting the upper sections, elk will move into the lower sections later in the season. Mt. Timpanogos- There is a herd of around 200 elk in this area. Try looking around Cascade Springs, the top of American Fork Canyon, and the west side above Grove and Battle Creek. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: ATTENTION-The US Forest is planning on a few prescribed burns this fall that might interfere with some hunt areas. Please be aware. The Heber-Kamas Ranger District is proposing to treat 3,300 acres with active fire in three operational areas occurring in Summit and Wasatch Counties. These areas are in the Provo watershed 10 miles east of Kamas and in the West Fork watershed 20 miles southeast of Heber City. Operations are planned to begin August 21, 2023, and will continue as conditions allow. The operation will require some area and road closure for public safety, active fire management will occur primarily during the daytime but also could occur at night to increase resource objectives. The Forest Service has established a Wildfire Crisis Strategy for dramatically increasing fuels and forest health treatments. The 10-year Wildfire Crisis Strategy (WCS) is built around the scale of the problem, which estimates that 50 million acres in addition to what we currently treat on an annual basis need fuels and forest health treatment to address the growing wildfire crisis. The goal of the project is to reduce wildfire risks to communities and natural resources by restoring and maintaining healthy, resilient fire-adapted forests. Approximately 382,000 acres (44%) of the Wasatch landscape is classified as high or very high fire hazard, posing a considerable threat to the function of vital watersheds, plant and wildlife habitat, recreational opportunities, and private property. The Forest has been actively managing across the forest to meet resource objectives through vegetation treatments and prescribed fire management. The Forest will continue to use all available tools to continue managing the resources meet the goals in the WCS. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a Limited Entry hunt unit and is managed for the harvest of 4.5-5.0 year old bulls. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 60% of land where hunters can expect to see elk in the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk in this unit move back and forth across Nevada, Idaho, and Utah state lines. The majority of the elk are near agricultural fields during the summer months and will move west into Nevada during the winter. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk out of the country earlier than normal. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Visibility on this unit is variable due to dense trees and open rolling sagebrush hills. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Elk are found throughout much of the unit, but are concentrated on the Grouse Creek Mountain Range. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources and irrigated agricultural fields. Good areas to look for elk include west of Hwy 30 along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range, Lynn Narrows, West of Grouse Creek, and from Keg Springs to Rocky Pass. Be aware that a portion of this unit was removed in 2021 to create the Box Elder, Sawtooth unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada; Wendover, Utah/Nevada; or Oakley, Idaho.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a Limited Entry hunt unit and is managed for the harvest of 4.5-5.0 year old bulls. There are no elk CWMUs on this unit, but there is a Landowner Association. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. Hunters can expect to see elk on private land within the unit. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property. This unit is part of a cooperative interstate hunt agreement and allows hunters to hunt on the Nevada portion of the unit. Likewise, Nevada hunters can hunt on the Utah side.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk in this unit move back and forth across the Nevada and Utah state lines, but an interstate hunt agreement exists allowing Utah hunters to hunt Nevada's unit 091. The majority of the elk are near agricultural fields during the summer months and will move west into Nevada during the winter. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk out of the country earlier than normal. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there is usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Visibility on this unit is variable due to dense trees and open rolling sagebrush hills. Elk will use the irrigated agricultural fields at the base of the east side of the mountain. Elk are found throughout much of the unit, but are concentrated up Bettridge Canyon, Patterson Pass, Governor's Spring, and TL Bar Ranch.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Services are available in Grouse Creek, Montello, Nevada, or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: Elk use all habitats from the bottom of the valleys to the top of the mountains. The Southwest Desert, North Unit is 96+% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Please be respectful of private lands and other hunters.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bulls can be found throughout the unit. Elk can be found from the bottoms of the valleys in the open sagebrush to the top of the mountain in the Pinions and Mahogany. The unit is a very large unit. It can be a difficult hunt. You may have days without seeing an elk because the density is low. To increase your chances of seeing elk it is best to find water in good elk habitat. There are several guzzlers and and few springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few elk. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Wah Wah Range- BLM and SITLA lands from Wah Wah summit to Crystal Peak. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. There are no springs in this area. All water sources are artificial (Guzzlers). Frisco Range- BLM and SITLA lands from Frisco Summit to Black Rock Pass. There are a few perennial springs and a some guzzlers in this area. Crickets -BLM and SITLA lands east of Sevier dry lake. Most water sources in this area are guzzlers and livestock tanks. Burbank Hills - BLM and SITLA lands east of Garrison near the Utah/Nevada stateline. There are several guzzlers and a few livestock tanks in this area. Elk will cross highway 21 and off the unit to use the Ag fields in the Burbank and Garrison areas.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "InReach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The majority of the elk are on the Deep Creek Mountains. These mountains are a classic Basin and Range mountain, with steep and rocky terrain. They look like a mountain sprouting out of the desert. The Deep Creeks have sagebrush benches that transition into juniper woodlands, with aspen and conifer at the highest elevations. Water is limited and very critical for these elk. Please be aware of private land, review your maps frequently to avoid trespass issues especially on the Goshute Tribal Lands. Foot hunters who plan to hunt in the upper elevations should plan on staying up there for several days. It is just too far to come down every day. Hunting with horses is possible with some difficulty from the steep terrain and limited grass and water, scout the area before taking horses in. Review your maps frequently to avoid trespass issues on the Goshutes. This area is patrolled quite frequently by DWR and BLM personnel. Keep this in mind when you are transporting your game and driving an ATV. Try to make it easy to access the permit and tag on the animal.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Most of the harvest is from the bench above Ibapah. In recent years elk behavior has changed a little bit. Some of the elk have moved out to the flats west of Ibapah. Caution should be taken when hunting west of Ibapah. The Goshute Reservation Lands are not open to hunting and all fence lines look alike. Consult the the Goshutes for the latest map. Elk are found top to bottom. Most archery hunters have the most success early in the hunt sitting on remote water holes. As the hunt progress the elk start to rut and become easier to spot and stalk. Migration Patterns: During the archery hunt I would expect to see herds of cows, calves, and spike bulls. The bulls will start breaking up from their bachelor herds. If there isn't much pressure in the bottom of the canyons I would expect to see elk coming out in the evenings to drink from the creeks and springs. You may find elk centralized from Cold Springs to the Delle. Scouting Tips: If you never have seen the Deep Creeks you better go look before you apply and definitely before your hunt. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting elk in this area. Scouting is most effective mid-summer. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of the bulls along with everyone else. This is a popular unit to put cameras out. In the hot early fall temperatures I would expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset)unless pressured. Elk can start feeling pressure early with people scouting or recreating on ATV's and may be hiding deeper in the trees. They are known to start moving after dark and go into the trees before light. Upper elevations elk spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. Consult with the Goshute Reservation for info on the reservation boundaries. The reservation expanded a few years ago and the public maps are not up to date. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with limited access. There are few water sources so plan on bringing extra water in with you. Cellular phones will not work. Digital cell phones may show a bar but will not connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The Biologist suggests handheld radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Bring an extra spare tire, water and gas. There are not facilities. Wendover is the closest (60 miles). It is not uncommon to have thunderstorms, flash floods and have trails wash out. If it rains hard it makes it difficult to navigate the trails.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat. I would plan on hot weather and plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: Elk use all habitats from the bottom of the valleys to the top of the mountains. The Southwest Desert, North Unit is 96+% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Please be respectful of private lands and other hunters.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bulls can be found throughout the unit. Elk can be found from the bottoms of the valleys in the open sagebrush to the top of the mountain in the Pinions and Mahogany. The unit is a very large unit. It can be a difficult hunt. You may have days without seeing an elk because the density is low. To increase your chances of seeing elk it is best to find water in good elk habitat. There are several guzzlers and and few springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few elk. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Wah Wah Range- BLM and SITLA lands from Wah Wah summit to Crystal Peak. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. There are no springs in this area. All water sources are artificial (Guzzlers). Frisco Range- BLM and SITLA lands from Frisco Summit to Black Rock Pass. There are a few perennial springs and a some guzzlers in this area. Crickets -BLM and SITLA lands east of Sevier dry lake. Most water sources in this area are guzzlers and livestock tanks. Burbank Hills - BLM and SITLA lands east of Garrison near the Utah/Nevada stateline. There are several guzzlers and a few livestock tanks in this area. Elk will cross highway 21 and off the unit to use the Ag fields in the Burbank and Garrison areas.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "InReach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

The Biologist suggests handheld radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Bring an extra spare tire, water and gas. There are not facilities. Wendover is the closest (60 miles). It is not uncommon to have thunderstorms, flash floods and have trails wash out. If it rains hard it makes it difficult to navigate the trails.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat. I would plan on hot weather and plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder is one of the best units in the state but one of the most difficult to hunt. The area is very large and some places are very remote. Pre-season scouting is crucial to finding the elk you want to pursue.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bulls will be found in every habitat type during this hunt. They also move a lot this time of year. Do not be surprised to see a group of bulls in a place all summer then suddenly vanish the day you show up to hunt. Weather and temperature play a huge role in how vocal bulls are during the rut. If you want a chance to hunt the rut come towards the end of the season. Because this unit is large and rugged, it's often a better strategy to select a few areas to learn and hunt than attempt to hunt the entire unit. It's better to get to know one or two areas well rather than guess the right place to be due to trying to cover too much country during scouting trips. This is a difficult unit to glass due to large areas of thick timber.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Depending on where and when you hunt you may find limited access and roadless areas. Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some remote areas on this unit. It is very easy to become disoriented especially when hiking.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms occasionally occur during this hunt. Monsoon rains sometimes bring moisture every afternoon. Be prepared for muddy road conditions. ATVs may be needed for access.

hunt_bio_general_information: Elk are found on all mountain ranges except for the Black Hills between Cedar City and Minersville. Elk use all habitats from the bottom of the valleys to the top of the mountains. The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Please be respectful of private lands and other hunters.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bulls can be found throughout the unit. More elk reside in the central portions of the unit on and surrounding the Indian Peaks Range. Elk can be found from the bottoms of the valleys in the open sagebrush to the top of the mountain in the Pinions and Mahogany. The Southwest Desert unit is a very large unit. It can be a difficult hunt. You may have days without seeing an elk because the density is low. To increase your chances of seeing elk it is best to find water in good elk habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few elk. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline/Hamlin Valley - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some larger blocks of private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. This area also has a few larger blocks of private land. South Wah Wah Range- BLM and SITLA lands from Rose Spring Canyon to Highway 21 on Wah Wah summit. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Mountain Home Range- BLM and SITLA lands from the Loper's Reseed area to Mt Home Pass. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Jockeys and Shaunties -BLM and SITLA lands located west of Minersville SW of Milford. This area is closer to human population centers and may have higher hunter densities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "InReach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a Limited Entry hunt unit and is managed for the harvest of 4.5-5.0 year old bulls. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 60% of land where hunters can expect to see elk in the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk in this unit move back and forth across Nevada, Idaho, and Utah state lines. The majority of the elk are near agricultural fields during the summer months and will move west into Nevada during the winter. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk out of the country earlier than normal. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Visibility on this unit is variable due to dense trees and open rolling sagebrush hills. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Elk are found throughout much of the unit, but are concentrated on the Grouse Creek Mountain Range. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources and irrigated agricultural fields. Good areas to look for elk include west of Hwy 30 along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range, Lynn Narrows, West of Grouse Creek, and from Keg Springs to Rocky Pass. Be aware that a portion of this unit was removed in 2021 to create the Box Elder, Sawtooth unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada; Wendover, Utah/Nevada; or Oakley, Idaho.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: Elk are found on all mountain ranges except for the Black Hills between Cedar City and Minersville. Elk use all habitats from the bottom of the valleys to the top of the mountains. The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Please be respectful of private lands and other hunters.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bulls can be found throughout the unit. More elk reside in the central portions of the unit on and surrounding the Indian Peaks Range. Elk can be found from the bottoms of the valleys in the open sagebrush to the top of the mountain in the Pinions and Mahogany. The Southwest Desert unit is a very large unit. It can be a difficult hunt. You may have days without seeing an elk because the density is low. To increase your chances of seeing elk it is best to find water in good elk habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few elk. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline/Hamlin Valley - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some larger blocks of private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. This area also has a few larger blocks of private land. South Wah Wah Range- BLM and SITLA lands from Rose Spring Canyon to Highway 21 on Wah Wah summit. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Mountain Home Range- BLM and SITLA lands from the Loper's Reseed area to Mt Home Pass. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Jockeys and Shaunties -BLM and SITLA lands located west of Minersville SW of Milford. This area is closer to human population centers and may have higher hunter densities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "InReach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.
