hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a Limited Entry hunt unit and is managed for the harvest of 4.5-5.0 year old bulls. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 60% of land where hunters can expect to see elk in the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk in this unit move back and forth across Nevada, Idaho, and Utah state lines. The majority of the elk are near agricultural fields during the summer months and will move west into Nevada during the winter. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk out of the country earlier than normal. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Visibility on this unit is variable due to dense trees and open rolling sagebrush hills. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Elk are found throughout much of the unit, but are concentrated on the Grouse Creek Mountain Range. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources and irrigated agricultural fields. Good areas to look for elk include west of Hwy 30 along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range, Lynn Narrows, West of Grouse Creek, and from Keg Springs to Rocky Pass. Be aware that a portion of this unit was removed in 2021 to create the Box Elder, Sawtooth unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada; Wendover, Utah/Nevada; or Oakley, Idaho.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Boulder is one of the best units in the state but one of the most difficult to hunt. The area is very large and some places are very remote. Pre-season scouting is crucial to finding the elk you want to pursue.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The difficulty or ease of this hunt is highly contingent on weather conditions. If temperatures are warm, bulls can be found in every habitat type during this hunt and will often remain higher in the timber. If snow flies or colder temperatures hit, bulls will begin to move toward wintering areas during or before this hunt. Because this unit is large and rugged, it's often a better strategy to select a few areas to learn and hunt than attempt to hunt the entire unit. It's better to get to know one or two areas well rather than guess the right place to be due to trying to cover too much country during scouting trips. This is a difficult unit to glass due to large areas of thick timber.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Depending on where and when you hunt you could find limited access and roadless areas. Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some remote areas on this unit. It is very easy to become disoriented especially when hiking.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms occasionally occur during this hunt. Be prepared for snowy road conditions. ATVs may be needed for access.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is a Limited Entry hunt unit and is managed for the harvest of 4.5-5.0 year old bulls. There are several CWMUs on this unit and access to those properties will only be allowed with the appropriate permit issued for the specific CWMU. This unit encompasses aspen, open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and desert scrub. 60% of land where hunters can expect to see elk in the unit is private land. Hunters should receive written permission from private landowners prior to the start of the hunts if they wish to hunt private property.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Elk in this unit move back and forth across Nevada, Idaho, and Utah state lines. The majority of the elk are near agricultural fields during the summer months and will move west into Nevada during the winter. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk out of the country earlier than normal. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Visibility on this unit is variable due to dense trees and open rolling sagebrush hills. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts. Elk are found throughout much of the unit, but are concentrated on the Grouse Creek Mountain Range. There are water sources across the unit in the form of stock ponds, creeks, and springs. In warm and dry weather, elk can be found close to these water sources and irrigated agricultural fields. Good areas to look for elk include west of Hwy 30 along the Grouse Creek Mountain Range, Lynn Narrows, West of Grouse Creek, and from Keg Springs to Rocky Pass. Be aware that a portion of this unit was removed in 2021 to create the Box Elder, Sawtooth unit.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada; Wendover, Utah/Nevada; or Oakley, Idaho.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bulls will be found in every habitat type during this hunt unless snow has driven them from the higher elevations. Early snow and cold temps may cause bulls to move toward their wintering ranges during this hunt. Because this unit is large and rugged, it's often a better strategy to select a few areas to learn and hunt than attempt to hunt the entire unit. It's better to get to know one or two areas well rather than guess the right place to be due to trying to cover too much country during scouting trips. This is a difficult unit to glass due to large areas of thick timber. One advantage of this hunt is bulls wanting to spend the afternoon laying in the sunshine.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Depending on where and when you hunt you could find limited access and roadless areas. Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms occasionally occur during this hunt. Monsoon rains sometimes bring moisture every afternoon. Be prepared for muddy road conditions. ATVs may be needed for access.

hunt_bio_general_information: Elk are found on all mountain ranges except for the Black Hills between Cedar City and Minersville. Elk use all habitats from the bottom of the valleys to the top of the mountains. The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Please be respectful of private lands and other hunters.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bulls can be found throughout the unit. More elk reside in the central portions of the unit on and surrounding the Indian Peaks Range. Elk can be found from the bottoms of the valleys in the open sagebrush to the top of the mountain in the Pinions and Mahogany. The Southwest Desert unit is a very large unit. It can be a difficult hunt. You may have days without seeing an elk because the density is low. To increase your chances of seeing elk it is best to find water in good elk habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few elk. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline/Hamlin Valley - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some larger blocks of private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. This area also has a few larger blocks of private land. South Wah Wah Range- BLM and SITLA lands from Rose Spring Canyon to Highway 21 on Wah Wah summit. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Mountain Home Range- BLM and SITLA lands from the Loper's Reseed area to Mt Home Pass. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Jockeys and Shaunties -BLM and SITLA lands located west of Minersville SW of Milford. This area is closer to human population centers and may have higher hunter densities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "InReach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "InReach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: Late season archery
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt is intended to be difficult. Bulls will be solitary or in small groups and difficult to find. Stalking conditions will likely not be ideal and may include loud, crusty snow. Bulls will most likely be on South facing slopes between 6,500 and 9,000 feet depending on snow depths. Pay attention to patches of mahogany and other shrubs that provide nutrition and protection for elk during the winter. Bulls can be found almost anywhere around the unit including both the East and West sides of the range. Good places to start might include Pine creek, Wildcat, Indian creek on the Beaver side, and Sargent Mtn and Ten mile on the East side.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Beaver has a fair amount of difficult, remote country. Be prepared for intense hiking and know your physical limitations.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect and prepare for cold weather and snow. Depending on the year there may be anywhere from 2 inches to 3 feet of snow at 7,000 ft of elevation.

hunt_bio_general_information: Mid-season any legal weapon hunt
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Rut activity typically will have slowed down and mature bulls may be more solitary and difficult to find during this hunt. You'll still see some rut activity, but it's typically smaller bulls trying to breed smaller groups of cows. There is overlap with the general season spike elk hunt so expect to see other hunters while in the field. The Northern half of the unit has a fair amount of difficult, remote country that has burned in recent history. The elk will use those burn scars and take advantage of the new aspen and other plants growing there. Good places to start can be the Pine creek, South fork of North creek, Bullion canyon, and Iant creek.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Beaver has a fair amount of difficult, remote country. Be prepared for intense hiking and know your physical limitations.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: It's not uncommon to get snow on top during mid October. Depending on the year, the weather can vary wildly during the fall. Be prepared for temperatures anywhere from 20-80 degrees.

","WMA_IN_UNIT":"Little Creek.","CAMPGRND_INFO":"Suggested Maps: BLM: Vernal, West Water, and they have a general map that labels most of the main roads. DWR WMA’S: UDWR WMAs is limited to 14 days at one location. There are no established campgrounds in this unit, it is a first-come first-served basis. Some hunters prefer to camp at the trailheads. There are DWR cabins in this unit that are not for public use. There is no camping allowed within a quarter mile of a DWR cabin. The trails are seasonally maintained by the DWR, and sportsmen. ","PRIM_ACCESS_PTS":"There are two trailheads for the roadless area, a north and a south. The north access is called the Ten Mile Knoll trailhead. If you take Utah State Road 88, it is located between Vernal and Roosevelt. Follow SR 88 south and it turns into the Seep Ridge Road. The Seep Ridge Rd splits and becomes the Divide Rd. If you take the Divide Rd west the trail head is at the start of Steer Ridge. There is a sign at the parking area. It is a large parking area but it can fill up in a hurry with trucks and horse trailers. The Hay Canyon Rd is the main access road on the south side of the Book Cliffs. You can access it from I-70. It is a hard packed dirt/gravel road. The Steer Ridge Rd can be very dangerous if it has been snowing or raining but it can dry out quickly.
The second access point, on the south side, is located at the top of Sego Canyon. Access to the Little Creek herd unit via the Sego Canyon trailhead crosses Ute Tribal Trust lands north of the parking area. Historically, access for sportsmen across the Ute Tribe was granted as part of a cooperative agreement between the Division of Wildlife Resources and the Ute Tribe. This agreement was terminated by the Ute Tribe in January of 2024.
The DWR is working with the Ute Tribe to enter into a new agreement. DWR is hopeful that the new agreement will once again grant access across tribal trust lands near the Sego Canyon trailhead. All hunters will need to find alternative access points to the Little Creek unit until a new agreement can be reached. It is uncertain when a new agreement may be reached, as such, hunters should plan accordingly before applying for hunts in the Little Creek unit. Access remains available from the Tenmile Knoll trail. ","SUGGESTED_MAPS":"BLM: Vernal, West Water, and they have a general map that labels most of the main roads. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt is intended to be difficult. Bulls will likely be solitary or in small groups and difficult to find. Stalking conditions will likely be difficult in steep terrain and likely in snowy conditions. The large majority of the bulls will be wintering on the West on mostly private property. Plan to spend a lot of time glassing and using optics. Bulls will most likely be on south facing slopes between 6,500 and 8,500 feet depending on snow depths.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: With this hunt being a late season hunt, be prepared for extreme weather conditions which could include heavy snow and cold temperatures. It will be a good idea to notify others of your daily locations in case something happens.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Be prepared for extreme winter conditions. Some years there could be several inches of snow and others there could be several feet.

The Cache, Meadowville is mostly made up of private property; you should plan to spend a lot of time behind optics.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for all kinds of conditions and a physically demanding hunt.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather this time of year can be unpredictable. It could go from cold and snowy to hot and sunny. Be prepared for all conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Manti is the largest elk herd in the state.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: For the most part the elk will not show any migratory behavior during the archery, muzzleloader, and early rifle hunts. These elk will remain on summer ranges at elevations generally above 8,000 feet. Bulls will begin to migrate by the Late Season Any Weapon Hunt. Most bulls tend to move down in elevation on to steep ridges predominated by mountain mahogany shrubs. About 90% of the elk move east to winter and spend the winter months on the ridges west of SR-10 Scouting Tips: You can not go terribly wrong on this unit. There is excellent access to most of the unit. A popular route to learn the unit is Skyline Drive. Skyline Drive runs along the spine of the mountain range and provides access to most of the high elevation habitat on the entire unit. Learn country! There are over 12,000 elk on this mountain so there are small groups of elk with bulls in nearly every canyon with good habitat on the mountain. Listen for bugling activity and cow calls to locate elk. Also listen for domestic sheep. There are an abundance of sheep that will still be on the mountain during the September hunts. If you can hear sheep in the canyon below you, it is best to move to the next canyon as elk and sheep are rarely found in the same vicinity it seems. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Glass the open south facing slopes where elk like to feed or small meadows near the canyon bottoms. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended Areas to look on the Central Mountains Manti Unit Upper Fish Creek and it's tributaries. The tributaries include Gooseberry Creek, Silver Creek, C Canyon, and the Straight Fork. This is a roadless area on the north end of the unit. This area typically holds a lot of elk and had some prescribed fires recently that has improved elk habitat. It can be accessed from North Skyline Drive on the west or from Scofield Reservoir on the east. The bottom two miles of Upper Fish Creek is privately owned and in a CWMU Bear Ridge and Fish Creek Ridge These ridges have roads going down them. They are northwest of Scofield Reservoir. The bottom 2 miles of these ridges are privately owned. This is excellent habitat in the Pondtown Creek drainage on the north end of the unit. It is best accessed from North Skyline Drive. Trough Spring Ridge This is accessed off of SR-264 southwest of the town of Scofield. It is just above the Skyline Coal Mine. This is the ridge on the east side of Electric Lake. There are some small pockets of private land that are posted well but the majority of the acreage is Forest Service. Much of this ridge burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 which has improved the elk habitat in this area. Gentry Mountain. This is accessed from SR-10 just north of the town of Huntington at Huntington Reservoir. Part of this mountain is privately owned and part of it burned in the Seeley Wildfire in 2012 Ford Ridge (Late Rifle Hunters Only) This area is the top of a steep canyon overlooking Spring Canyon west of Helper. It holds bachelor groups of bulls in the fall and winter. There are numerous private lands around so be very careful of where you are. There is ample public lands also. West of Skyline
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until the first week of October.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Nebo unit has pretty tough terrain in many locations where you find elk. Hunters are either faced with straight up or straight down hikes so good physical condition for hunters is a must. As already noted, the north portion of the Nebo unit is restricted from ATV use so hunters with horses or mules will have the advantage.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The majority of hunters choose to hunt the higher elevation areas during the early rifle hunt. The areas around the Nebo Loop Road being most popular is an excellent place to start. Elk can be seen from a distance by glassing the ridges and canyons from the overlooks on the Loop Road. Since ATV use is not permitted on the north Nebo (that portion of the Nebo that is north of SR 132) there are canyons and trails where you can get out and hike to get away from people. There is plenty of water on the mountain for the elk. However as you hike you can find several unmarked springs. Wildfires have affected the habitat on both the east and west sides of the unit As the burned area reestablishes vegetation it attracts large amounts of elk. Migration Patterns: You will find elk from one end of the Nebo to the other. The north portion of the Nebo has the greater percentage of the elk population. The south portion of the Nebo unit (that portion that is south of SR 132) has much fewer elk but do not count that out as an opportunity to find a nice bull. The elk will start feeling pressured toward the end of the archery hunt with increased rifle hunters scouting for their upcoming hunt. During the archery season migration is not an issue but elk will move in response to hunter pressure. Generally bulls prefer to stay in the highest elevations and begin to spread out a little in preparation to the rut. After the calving season you can find large herds of elk at higher elevation in grassy meadows. Once the rut begins, which can be beginning toward the later half of the archery season, the bulls begin to herd up smaller herds of cows and the elk seem to spread out. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting elk in this area. Scouting is most effective late-summer to early fall. If you are able to place trail cameras on the remote springs and water holes you will be able to pattern the movements of the bulls. In the hot early fall temperatures expect to see the most animals at prime time (1/2 hour before dawn and an hour before sunset). There are several recovering burned areas that have produced large amounts of grass that is excellent for elk. Elk spend a lot of time in the aspen patches where there is a good understory of grass and forbs. Scouting during the summer is effective for learning the areas where you want to hunt but don't expect to see the same elk on the same ridge during the summer and also in the fall. The elk do tend to move before the rut so focus scouting efforts during the first of September. Behavior: The elk seem to prefer bedding in the dark conifer timber during the day. Towards the evening the elk will start to work their way onto the burned faces and points of the ridges. Once the bulls shed their velvet they will start to break up from their winter and summer bachelor herds. They will usually water at least two times a day. It is not unusual for elk to graze through the night. As the hunt progresses and if colder weather moves in, the elk will start to come into the rut. Before they start to herd the cows up the bulls are very susceptible to cow elk calls. As elk get closer to the rut they will become more vocal and will start to round up small herds of cows. The larger bulls will usually try to keep their cows away from contending bulls. It is normal to have one herd bull and other bulls surrounding the cows at a distance. During this hunt it is effective to hunt water holes early on the hunt. Later in the hunt it is more efficient to call and locate the bulls and try to get them to come to cow calls.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is fair over most this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The Biologist suggests handheld radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Depending on the season be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Thunder storms can cause muddy road and trail conditions. Most hunters struggle with meat spoiling in the heat especially during the archery season so in anticipation of hot weather plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: Late season archery hunt
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt is intended to be difficult. Bulls will be solitary or in small groups and difficult to find. Stalking conditions will likely not be ideal and may include loud, crusty snow. The large majority of the bulls will be wintering on the West side of the Pahvant range (the Fillmore side). Bulls can be found all the way from Ebbs canyon on the North end to Dog valley and Three creeks on the South end. Plan to spend a lot of time glassing and using optics. The pahvant is steep and the topography lends itself to finding animals with optics. Bulls will most likely be on South facing slopes between 6,500 and 9,000 feet depending on snow depths. Pay attention to patches of mahogany and other shrubs that provide nutrition and protection for elk during the winter.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The pahvant is steep; especially where you're going to find the elk. Be physically prepared for intense hiking and know your own physical limitations.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect and prepare for cold weather and snow. Depending on the year there may be anywhere from 2 inches to 3 feet of snow at 7,000 ft of elevation.

hunt_bio_general_information: Mid-Season any legal weapon hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Rut activity typically will have slowed down and mature bulls may be more solitary and difficult to find during this hunt. You'll still see some rut activity, but it's typically smaller bulls trying to breed smaller groups of cows. The central and southern portions of the unit currently hold the majority of the elk. Good starting points to look can be in the North and South forks of Chalk creek, Meadow creek, and the South side of the Corn creek drainage. There is overlap with the general season spike elk hunt so expect to see other hunters while in the field. The pahvant has decent access and is a very glassable unit; you should plan to spend a lot of time behind optics.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The pahvant is steep; especially where you're going to find the elk. Be physically prepared for intense hiking and know your own physical limitations.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: It's not uncommon to get snow on top during mid October. Depending on the year, the weather can vary wildly during the fall. Be prepared for temperatures anywhere from 20-80 degrees.

Some of the areas that bulls will spend time in are cliffy or thick with vegetation so glassing can be difficult. Suggested Hunting Areas: Fischer Mesa on north end of La Sals Pole Canyon/ Black Ridge in west side Carpenter Basin/ Carpenter Ridge on south end Polar Mesa on northeast end
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Bulls will likely be in rough or thick terrain. Know your limits.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a great unit for the opportunity to harvest a bull elk . Typical harvested bulls on the unit score around 310" to 330", but a few bigger bulls are taken each year. Make sure that you are in good physical condition and spend plenty of time scouting prior to your hunt. Portions of the unit are extremely steep. Cow calling or bugling can prove to be very valuable in locating bulls during the early season hunts.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: The elk migration on the La Sal Mountains varies, depending on weather conditions. Elk will typically migrate off of the high mountain and mesa tops, into lower elevations throughout the unit. Many of the bulls will start this migration after the rut ends in early October. Scouting Tips: Start scouting in late June early July many of the bulls will be up high and in the open and in large bachelor groups. They probably won't be in the exact same area during the hunt, but it will give you a chance to see the type of bulls you can expect on your hunt. The unit is very large with elk scattered across most of it. Spend some time before your hunt to learn the roads and access points Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find elk. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Most bulls are only with cows during the rut. Before the rut they are in bachelor groups and then immediately after the rut they form their bachelor groups again. Keep this in mind as you plan your hunt. The archery, any weapon (early), and muzzleloader hunters will want to find cows. The any weapon (late) hunters should look for pockets of bachelor bulls. Typically only smaller bulls will be with cows during the late hunt. Elk rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting the first part of September, with the peak of the rut being September 15th-the end of September. There will still be some rutting activity in October, but it will be winding down by then. Recommended areas La Sal Mountains Subunit: Bar-A Creek - Northeast side of the mountain, large meadows with aspen stands mixed with conifers, great camping, nice roads, holds a good number of elk. Pine Ridge - This entire area is good for elk, timbered North slopes, aspen stands, great access, camping, nice roads, several different draws or canyons to hunt. Deep Creek - No roads and limited access, great area for pack-in hunts, borders private lands in many spots, great area for elk. Dark Canyon - Higher elevation, borders some private lands, one good main road with several two-track roads splitting off, great camping, good place to glass for elk on the early season hunts. La Sal Pass - Lots of places to glass for elk, rolling meadows with timbered North facing slopes and large aspen stands, not a lot of cows, but does hold a good number of bulls. North & South/ Beaver/Polar Mesas - These mesas are typically best for the late hunts, great for ATV's, good place for late season hunts. Slaughter Flat & Pole Cyn. - West side of the mountain. Good places to look for bulls on the late season hunt. Upper Castle Crk. - North side of the mountain. Good place to look during the late season hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Flash floods and lightning strikes are very likely during inclement weather, make sure to watch the sky and plan accordingly. Always let somebody know where you'll be, and when you expect to be back. Cell phone service is somewhat limited throughout the unit. Black bears are regularly seen on the La Sal unit. Keep a clean camp and make sure to place all food and garbage in locations that bears cannot get into.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges and flash floods in the canyon bottoms.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe is a popular unit for hunting and outdoor recreation. There is ample public land with good road/trail access. Valley floors start between 5,000 - 6,000 feet with some of the peaks reaching near 11,000 ft in elevation. Habitat types include sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: The Monroe unit has long been considered a great unit to hunt elk. Good numbers of Mature bulls, beautiful scenery, and good access makes it a popular place to hunt. It is managed for an average age of harvested bull of 6-6.5 yrs. Elk use the entire Monroe unit. During this Late archery season generally the bulls have separated from the cow herds. Though bulls may occasionally bugle they are generally quiet. Long range glassing is important for finding the bulls on this hunt. Many of the bulls spend this season high on ridges far from roads. A fair number of elk have left the unit by migrating south to Mt. Dutton. The bulls will be spread out across the entire unit in small bachelor groups. If snows are deep most of the elk will be forced off of the flatter terrain on the top of the unit and will be along the ridges between 6,500 - 9,000 feet elevation. If snows are light, they could be anywhere. Generally there are few other hunts during this season. As a result, hunters enjoy a quality hunt with little pressure from other hunters. Good areas to hunt: The Monroe unit is a long mountain unit running north and south with the top being a plateau with more gentle terrain. Many of the bulls in December live along the rim and the side canyons of the plateau. Bulls really tend to like ridges with thick mahogany. North end - Hunter's Flat, The Circle, Bear Valley, and Little Creek. East side - Drainages west of Burrville and Koosharem, including: Blue Peak, Indian Peak, upper Box Creek. Also check the steep canyons south of Greenwich between Brown's canyon and Pine canyon. South End - This end will have bulls on the edges of the Forshea. There is a lot of pinyon/juniper on the extreme south end that holds a few bulls. Also, the country between Dry Creek and Twin Peaks will hold bulls. West side - Good places to find groups of bulls include Marysvale Peak area, Dry creek, Hunts lake, and the roadless drainages east of the town of Monroe. Migration Patterns: Though most of the elk that spend the summer on Monroe also stay there for the winter. A significant number also migrate south to the Mt. Dutton unit. This movement usually begins in September and elk trickle south through November. Because of this, do not count on bulls being is the same place you may have scouted them in during the summer. Also, many elk now use the mid-elevation areas that have fewer roads and less pressure. Though there are plenty of bulls on the unit this time of year, realize that there are not as many as there were in earlier seasons. Scouting Tips: Bulls will likely not be where you found them in the summer or early fall. The best way to scout for this hunt is the several days just before the hunt. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for effective and efficient scouting in this area. Other Information: Hunters enjoy a high harvest rate on the Monroe unit. Hunters are usually able to locate quite a few mature bulls during scouting and hunting trips. This unit typically produces good mature bulls though not as many really large bulls as some nearby units that have more difficult terrain and access. Monroe is managed for an average age of harvest of 6 to 6.5 yrs.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, and cold temperatures. Storms can cause muddy or snow-packed road conditions. Deep snow may limit access to higher elevations.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Monroe is a popular unit for hunting and outdoor recreation. There is ample public land with good road/trail access. Valley floors start between 5,000 - 6,000 feet with some of the peaks reaching near 11,000 ft in elevation. Habitat types include sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and aspen/conifer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: General Considerations: The Monroe unit has long been considered a great unit to hunt elk. Good numbers of Mature bulls, beautiful scenery, and good access makes it a popular place to hunt. It is managed for an average age of harvested bull of 6.5-7yrs. Elk use the entire Monroe unit. During this October season the rut is winding down. Hunter should keep in mind that this season overlaps with the general spike elk hunt so there will be significant hunters on the unit. By this time, due to the rut and hunting pressure, some of the elk have started using the mid elevation oak and pinyon/juniper habitats. Most of the bulls are with or at least near the cow herds. A good number of elk have also began to move south on the unit. The southern part of the unit will have increased numbers of elk during this season. Hunting pressure may cause elk to vacate the easily accesiable areas and seek refuge far from roads. Good areas to hunt: The central part of the unit is the most popular place for elk hunters for several reasons: There is really good camping and access, the terrain is mild, and the largest part of the elk herd resides there during the earlier hunts. Elk can be found across the entire central part of the unit. Just about every meadow and canyon may have elk in them. Many people hunt this large area consisting of gentle terrain between the Dry Creek ranger station and the Koosharem ranger station. There are several large tracts of private property here. Consult maps to avoid conflicts with Private ground. Hunters should not overlook the many side canyons that lead from the top of the plateau down to the foothills. Elk use these because of the good feed and they get less pressure as there are fewer roads. During this season there are generally significant numbers of elk using the agricultural fields near Koosharem, Greenwich, and Monroe. If you ask, many of these landowners may grant permission to hunt on their property or at least pass through. Generally the elk move onto public ground during daylight hours so they are accessible. Good numbers of elk also use the north end of the mountain. Elk can be found near Hunter's Flat, Big Lake, Magleby pass, and Monument peak. There are several sections of private ground in this area so be sure to know where you are. Make sure to check the mid-elevation areas. A few elk have now moved down to the south end of the unit during this hunt. Elk will be on the Forshea Mountain area where the thick aspen stands are. There are also small groups of elk stretching from the Forshea to the Langdon mountain area. Migration Patterns: Though most of the elk that spend the summer on Monroe also stay there for the winter. A significant number also migrate south to the Mt. Dutton unit. This movement usually begins in September and elk trickle south through November. Because of this, do not count on bulls being is the same place you may have scouted them in during the summer. Also, many elk now use the mid-elevation areas that have fewer roads and less pressure. Scouting Tips: June and July are great times to begin scouting, as elk are less wary and there will be less people on the mountain. Elk will still be growing their antlers but will be easier to locate. The elk may move before this hunt but you will have an idea of what is in the area. A scouting trip just before the season opens will tell you what areas the bulls and cow herds are using. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for effective and efficient scouting in this area. Other Information: Hunters enjoy a high harvest rate on the Monroe unit. Hunters are usually able to locate quite a few mature bulls during scouting and hunting trips. This unit typically produces good mature bulls though not as many really large bulls as some nearby units that have more difficult terrain and access.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for snow, rain, lightning, cold and high temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions. During some seasons very warm temperatures may occur. Hunters should be prepared to cool meat quickly to avoid wasting meat.

hunt_bio_general_information: Elk numbers during summer months aren't as high as they are during the winter months on this unit. Alot of the elk migrate off of the unit for the summer months and return during the fall and winter months. This can be a tough hunt, but mature bulls are harvested on it every year.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has several areas that have no vehicle access. Hunters that hike into some of these areas, or use horses have good success at harvesting elk. Before snow falls on the unit you can access the top of the mountain from Antimony, or Cottonwood Creek in Johns Valley. Elk in the summer can be found across the unit in higher and lower elevations. There is good access on most of the BLM lands across the unit, but a lot of the forest service has limited access. There is good access on the south end of the unit in the Hunt Creeks, and often holds elk year round. There was a large fire that burned on the unit in 2002. This made it very good for glassing long distances. There is a lot of pinon and juniper in the lower elevations with Aspen, and mixed conifer stands at higher elevations. During summer months find water and hunt areas around it. A lot of the elk can be found at higher elevations during this hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: A lot of roadless areas on the unit expect backcountry hunting conditions.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Summer months are generally warm, but afternoon thunderstorms can be present most days in the afternoon.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Panguitch Lake elk herd is currently managed for 1300 wintering elk across the unit. Recent surveys and estimates suggest the population is approximately 1200. Substantial summer range exists on the Markagunt Plateau which is heavily forested. There are also several mid-elevation areas across the unit that bull elk will use as summer range. Elk occupy most all suitable habitat throughout the unit. The unit had a significant burned in 2017 and has opened alot of new habitat for ELK, look for elk in the burn.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Nursery groups of cow elk can be observed generally very early in the morning or right before sunset. During warmer times of the day, elk will be staying cool in the forested areas and will be more difficult to observe. Focus on areas with high densities of aspen near water sources. Look for elk in the burn. Migration Patterns: All elk in this hunt boundary will migrate but these movements are generally not observed until late October and November. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars will be helpful. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate public lands and access points and hiking trails. Behavior: Elk will be on summer range and will begin to rut in September with cooler weather patterns.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Panguitch Lake unit offers substantial truck and ATV access. Cellular phone coverage within this hunt boundary is generally good but there are areas within the hunt boundary with little or no coverage. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, as well as warm weather conditions. Winter storms are also likely. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Fish Lake/Thousand Lake unit is a very popular hunting area. Elevation ranges from some peaks above 11,600 feet to some valley floors near 5,000 feet. There are all types of vegetation and terrain. The good scenery, camping, fishing, and hunting draws many people to the area every fall. The Fish Lake unit has a large herd of over 5,000 elk. It is managed for a 5.5 to 6 year average age of harvest. In recent years the average bull harvested has been over 6 years old. This unit can produce a few really large bulls, but in general you can expect to see a fair number of medium sized, mature bulls with a chance at some larger ones. On the earlier hunts, many elk can find refuge on private property which can be frustrating
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Fish Lake/Thousand Lake unit is a very popular hunting area. Elevation ranges from some peaks above 11,600 feet to some valley floors near 5,000 feet. There are all types of vegetation and terrain. The good scenery, camping, fishing, and hunting draws many people to the area every fall. CWMU's and Private property: The Fish Lake Unit contains several large tracts of private property, several of which are CWMU's that require a special permit in order to hunt. These ranches are prime elk habitat and many elk find refuge on them during the earlier hunts. This can be frustrating to hunters. Hunters are reminded that trespassing and hunting on these properties can result in large fines and loss of hunting privileges. To avoid problems have a good map and hunt well away from private property. Hunting areas and seasons: Concentrations of elk and bulls can change depending on the season you are hunting. Early Rifle: Elk are generally concentrated in the higher elevations during the early rifle hunt (above 8,000 ft.). The bulk of the herd tends to be in the higher elevations in the north/central part of the unit. Some good places to look are High Top Plateau, Mtn. Terrel, Mtn. Marvine, Mtn. Hilgard, Gooseberry area, Niotche, and UM Plateau. There are some elk on the Thousand Lake portion of the unit but they can be difficult to find. Late Rifle and Late Archery: These hunts occur in Mid-November and Early December and many of the elk have moved to different areas. A large number of elk move to the eastern portion of the unit, some crossing hwy 72 onto the Thousand Lake part of the unit. Good areas to look for bulls in this part of the unit include: Red Creek, Clear Creek, Last Chance, Tidwell Slopes, Danish Meadows, and Hen's Hole Peak and Geyser Peak on the Thousand Lake. On the south end, good places to look for bulls include the Mytogi, Pole, Splatter, and Ivey Canyons. On the east side of the unit bulls can be in the upper reaches of the Praetor Slopes and Skougaard canyon, Daniels Canyon, Rose Meadow, Rex's Reservoir, and the east face above Fish Lake (if there is little snow). The north end contains a few bulls in Gooseberry, Cedar Mountain, and The Rocks. Bulls could be anywhere, but they are generally in small bachelor groups away from the cow herds. The bulls often will be on the high ridges away from the roads. Glassing is key to finding these bulls. Check carefully on high mahogany ridges. Migration Patterns: From late October to early December many of the elk on the unit move to mid and lower elevations. A large number of the elk head east to their wintering grounds on Mytogi, Last Chance, Red and Clear Creeks, Tidwell Slopes and Thousand Lake. Some elk will move south off of the unit onto the Parker Plateau. On the rest of the unit the elk drop down to lower elevations all around the unit. Scouting Tips: To see a lot of bulls, late June and July are great times to scout while elk are using the open meadows and hillsides. Many of these bulls will have moved by the time the hunting seasons arrive but you will get a good idea of what caliber of bulls are in the area. Good binoculars and spotting scope help you cover a lot of ground. One last trip just before your hunt will let you know where the elk are. For the early hunts concentrate on the conifer/aspen habitats and for the later hunt hit the oak brush/pinyon, mahogany areas.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a large area and cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Fish Lake unit has a healthy bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting seasons. Be prepared for snow, rain, lightning, and both hot and cold temperatures. Storms can cause muddy road conditions. The Archery and early rifle season can be very warm. Be prepared to get meat to a locker quickly or be prepared to cool meat as fast as possible to avoid spoilage.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt is intended to be difficult. Bulls will be solitary or in small groups and difficult to find. Stalking conditions will likely not be ideal and may include loud, crusty snow. Bulls will be in rough terrain come this hunt, where access can be difficult. Some of the areas that bulls will spend time in are cliffy or thick with vegetation so glassing can be difficult. Suggested Hunting Areas: Chippean Ridge Dry Mesa Dark Canyon Shay Mesa Peters Point
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Bulls will likely be in rough or thick terrain. Know your limits.

hunt_bio_general_information: Elk are found on all mountain ranges except for the Black Hills between Cedar City and Minersville. Elk use all habitats from the bottom of the valleys to the top of the mountains. The Southwest Desert Unit is 96% public land, but hunters should be aware of the private lands and learn the boundaries. Please be respectful of private lands and other hunters.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bulls can be found throughout the unit. More elk reside in the central portions of the unit on and surrounding the Indian Peaks Range. Elk can be found from the bottoms of the valleys in the open sagebrush to the top of the mountain in the Pinions and Mahogany. The Southwest Desert unit is a very large unit. It can be a difficult hunt. You may have days without seeing an elk because the density is low. To increase your chances of seeing elk it is best to find water in good elk habitat. There are several guzzlers and springs in this desert area, but even around these water sources there are very few elk. Some good areas to hunt are the following: Stateline/Hamlin Valley - BLM and SITLA lands along the Utah/Nevada border from the Paradise to White Rocks areas. This area is very accessible with some larger blocks of private properties. Indian Peaks Range - BLM, SITLA and DWR lands from Arrowhead Pass to Vance Pass. This area also has a few larger blocks of private land. South Wah Wah Range- BLM and SITLA lands from Rose Spring Canyon to Highway 21 on Wah Wah summit. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Mountain Home Range- BLM and SITLA lands from the Loper's Reseed area to Mt Home Pass. This area is covered heavily with pinion and juniper. Hunting near perennial water sources will greatly increase your success. Jockeys and Shaunties -BLM and SITLA lands located west of Minersville SW of Milford. This area is closer to human population centers and may have higher hunter densities.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "InReach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has opened private land for public use to help compensate the public for having public land in the CWMU. Here is a link to a map showing "trade lands" in CWMUs https://wildlife.utah.gov/cwmu.html . The Bar J Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located southeast of Salina, Utah. The elevation ranges from a low of about 6800 feet to a high of 8800 feet. A No named drainage cuts the Unit, and there is an undulating slope from highest point in the east to the lowest in the west. The most common elevation is 7500 feet but ranges from 6700 feet to 9100 feet with an elevation difference of 2400 feet. Forty-nine percent (49%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7500 feet and 8400 feet an elevation difference of 900 feet. Down the middle of the Bar J Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is the dominant land cover type, Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). Towards the west are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Towards the east is almost a solid patch of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Land fingers in the north are covered with Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36). On the westside, besides the Sagebrush Steppe, there are intermixed patches of Inter- Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). In the middle of the Unit there are some large patches of Rocky Mountain Ponderosa Pine Woodland (34). One of the Bar J Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, SALINA (427557), is about 16.6 km northwest from the northwest edge of the CWMU. SALINA has seventy- four (74) years of records, 1923 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.48 inches, but it can be as high as 6.67 inches or as low as 0.43 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 12 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 2.8 inches but can be as high as 18.0 inches. FALL temperature at SALINA averages 49.9 degrees F. but can be as high as 102.0 degrees F. or as low as -8.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 48 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 4 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Just southeast of Mount Pleasant, Utah is the Bear Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) ranging from 10000 feet to about 6200 feet. The west part of the Unit is a series of moderate sloping benches and rapidly climbing slopes. On the east at the higher elevations, Bear Mountain CWMU, is cut by the Straight Fork of Pleasant Creek, Dry Pole Creek, and the North and South Forks of Coral Fork. The most common elevation is 7300 feet but ranges from 6200 feet to 10000 feet with an elevation difference of 3800 feet. Fifty (50%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7300 feet and 9100 feet an elevation difference of 1800 feet. Much of the Bear Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit is covered with Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). At the higher elevations there are substantial areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). At lower elevations there is some Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36). At the higher elevation besides the Aspen Forest and Woodland, there is a mixture of Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (28), Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), and Inter-Mountain West Aspen-Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland Complex (38). There are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) scattered from the lowest elevation to the highest. One of the Bear Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ELECTRIC LAKE (422424), is about 13.0 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. ELECTRIC LAKE has twenty-seven (27) years of records, 1980 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 6.31 inches, but it can be as high as 10.05 inches or as low as 1.73 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 26 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 18 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 4 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There is no reliable snowfall data for ELECTRIC LAKE. FALL temperature at ELECTRIC LAKE averages 36.6 degrees F. but can be as high as 81.0 degrees F. or as low as -22.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 71 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is cut east-west by Dry Creek and north-south by State Road 68. Dry Creek starts at about 7200 feet and flows east and then south and exits the Unit at about 4400 feet. The higher elevations are on the west below Snow Basin Ski Resort. Then with a moderate slope the terrian slopes to the southeast and drops down into the Dry Creek cut before exiting the Unit. The most common elevation is 5800 feet but ranges from 5000 feet to 8500 feet with an elevation difference of 3500 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5700 feet and 7600 feet an elevation difference of 1900 feet. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is the dominant land cover type on the Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). There are many large patches of Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23) dispersed among the Gambel Oak, as are smaller patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). There are patches of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) on the west side, more in the middle of the Unit are patches of Rocky Mountain Lower Montane Riparian Shrubland (79), and scattered about are patches of Recently Burned (116) areas. There are some minor areas of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) scattered about. One of the Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, PINE VIEW DAM (422424), is about 3.6 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. PINE VIEW DAM has twenty-seven (72) years of records, 1935 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 7.33 inches, but it can be as high as 16.43 inches or as low as 1.52 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 15 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There is also 2 days with precipitation greater than or equal to 1.00 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 13.7 inches but can be as high as 49.5 inches. FALL temperature at PINE VIEW DAM averages 46.2 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 48 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The westside of the Boobe Hole Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located at 7200 feet in the Plateau Valley. Towards the east the Unit rises to over 10,000 feet on Boobe Hole Mountain. Continuing southwest the Unit slopes down from Boobe Hole Mountain to Otter Creek, 9400 feet in the north and 8400 feet in the south. Finally, the elevation climbs up towards Hightop Plateau to about 9400 feet. The most common elevation is 7100 feet but ranges from 7000 feet to 10000 feet with an elevation difference of 3000 feet. Forty-nine percent (49%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 8000 feet and 9700 feet an elevation difference of 1700 feet. On the Boobe Hole Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) the land cover is distributed in three (3) bands. On the the eastside of the Unit, and taking the most area, is a band of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Moving towards the west, there is a narrow band of Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). Next, there is a wider band of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper (36). Not quite a band, but the extreme west is covered with Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). Back in the Aspen Forest and Woodland are large patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). At the interface between Aspen Forest and Woodland and Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland, are some large areas of Inter-Mountain West Aspen-Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland Complex (38). One of the Boobe Hole Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, KOOSHAREM (424764), is about 14.9 km southwest from the southwest edge of the CWMU. KOOSHAREM has one hundred fourteen (114) years of records, 1893 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.44 inches, but it can be as high as 5.28 inches or as low as 0.58 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 4.7 inches but can be as high as 23.3 inches. FALL temperature at KOOSHAREM averages 45.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 92.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 60 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has opened private land for public use to help compensate the public for having public land in the CWMU. Here is a link to a map showing "trade lands" in CWMUs https://wildlife.utah.gov/cwmu.html . The Bastian Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is west and north of Causey Reservoir. Beaver Creek and State Highway 39 forms the west boundary and Elk Ridge forms the east boundary. The Unit consists of a main ridge which is about 8000 feet in the north dropping to 6700 feet in the south before it drops into Water Hollow. From this main ridge the Unit drops into Beaver Creek (5600 feet to 6600 feet). On the eastside the unit drops in to Dry Bread Hollow (6000 feet to 7200 feet) before rising up to Elk Ridge (7600 feet to 7900 feet). The most common elevation is 6800 feet but ranges from 5500 feet to 7900 feet with an elevation difference of 2400 feet. Fifty-four percent (54%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6000 feet and 7300 feet an elevation difference of 1300 feet. There are three (3) main land cover types and one (1) land cover type that dominates the Bastian Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). First, there is the Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Then there are the Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) and Rocky Mountain Gamble Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) in about equal amounts. In lesser amounts is Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland(23). One of the Bastian Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY (424135), is about 11.0 km southwest from the southwest edge of the CWMU. HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY has thirty-one (31) years of records, 1976 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 5.74 inches, but it can be as high as 12.30 inches or as low as 1.36 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 10.2 inches but can be as high as 31.0 inches. FALL temperature at HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY averages 46.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -16.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 56 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Coldwater Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is part of the Bear River Range south of Blacksmith Fork. The South Cottonwood Canyon divides the Unit almost into a west and east half. This canyon ranges from about 6400 feet to 7200 feet in elevation. To the east the elevation doesn't rise much and the area flattens out before dropping down to 5600 feet on the northeast boundary. On the west half the elevation rises rapidly to around 8000 feet, then drops quickly to 6400 feet in the north and 7400 feet in the south. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is located northeast of Grouse Creek. Habitat types include open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, and irrigated and non-irrigated agricultural fields.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The majority of the elk will use higher elevations of the CWMU through the summer months and move lower into irrigated agricultural fields towards the end of summer. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the elk out of the country earlier than normal. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for elk and then working to get close for a shot or stalking elk through the trees. Visibility on this unit is variable due to dense trees and open rolling sagebrush hills. Elk are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) takes up parts of Weber, Morgan and Rich counties, with Rich county having the most area. The higher points on the Deseret CWMU are along Horse Ridge (8500 feet). On the west the Unit drops away to about 6400 feet in the south and 8000 feet in the north. On the eastside of Horse Ridge the Unit makes a less steep drop, dropping down to around 6400 feet in the north and 6800 feet in the south along the Utah - Wyoming state border. The most common elevation is 6400 feet but ranges from 6000 feet to 8700 feet with an elevation difference of 2700 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6800 feet and 7800 feet an elevation difference of 1000 feet. The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is much larger than other CWMUs in Utah, therefore land cover is more diversified. About half (50%) of the land cover on the Deseret CWMU is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Towards the northeast and at lower elevation, there are large areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Steppe (66). Thet higher elevations on the west of the Unit, mixed with Sagebrush Steppe are extensive areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). At lower elevations towards the northeast are several patches of Agriculture (114) land. At minor extents are Southern Rocky Mountain Montane-Subalpine Grassland (71), Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48), and Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane shrubland (41). One of the Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, WOODRUFF (429595), is about 10.5 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. WOODRUFF has one hundred eleven (111) years of records, 1897 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.64 inches, but it can be as high as 5.18 inches or as low as 0.64 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 8.7 inches but can be as high as 29.2 inches. FALL temperature at WOODRUFF averages 40.8 degrees F. but can be as high as 111.0 degrees F. or as low as -26.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 73 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 6 days above 90 degrees F.

There are also patches of Invasive Perennial Grassland (119). hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The East Fork Chalk Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is east of Coalville, Utah up Chalk Creek. Humpy Peak at greater than 10,800 feet is the high point of the Unit. The elevation along the East Fork of Chalk Creek decreases to 6700 feet. Both the East Fork and Middle Fork of Chalk Creek are part of the unit. The East Fork decreases from 9600 feet and the Middle Fork from 7700 feet to where the combine at 7200 feet. Except for the abrupt extension of Humpy Peak the relief on the eastside of the Unit is not as steep as that on the west side. The most common elevation is 9700 feet but ranges from 6700 feet to 10800 feet with an elevation difference of 4100 feet. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Folley Ridge Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is northwest of Croydon, Utah. This CWMU is in two distinct areas. The south area follows the Folley Ridge which ranges between 7000 feet in the south to 8300 feet in the north. The north border of the south area is around 8100 feet, to the east about 7200 feet, to the south 5400 feet and to the west 6800 feet. The north area is northeast of the south area. The north area highest point is Guilder Peak at around 8300 feet. To the north the area is 8100 feet, to the east 8000 feet, to the south also 8000 feet, and to the west 8300 feet like Guilder Peak. The most common elevation is 8200 feet but ranges from 5400 feet to 8400 feet with an elevation difference of 3000 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6100 feet and 7700 feet an elevation difference of 1600 feet. Most of the Folley Ridge Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is covered by Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). The next most common land cover type is Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). This Forest and Woodland is more prominent on the north section of the Unit. Another prominent land cover type particularly on the south section is Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). Although in a minor role Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23) is present on both the north and south sections. One of the Folley Ridge Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, MORGAN (425826), is about 9.8 km southwest from the southwest edge of the CWMU. MORGAN has one hundred five (105) years of records, 1903 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.80 inches, but it can be as high as 7.28 inches or as low as 0.46 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 18 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 11 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 7.3 inches but can be as high as 25.3 inches. FALL temperature at MORGAN averages 46.9 degrees F. but can be as high as 98.0 degrees F. or as low as -12.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 53 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Grass Valley - Clark Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) lies east of Echo Reservoir. Although it is continuous, Chalk Creek cuts the Unit into a west and east sub-unit. On the west area the high point is around 7600 feet. The ridge line drops in a southwest direction too the shore of Echo Reservoir at about 5600 feet. To the north the Unit drops down into Echo Canyon, about 5800 feet before rising again to 7200 feet. Grass Valley Canyon cuts this west area and ranges from 5600 feet to 6400 feet. Then rises up to 7800 feet above Chappell Lake before dropping down again to Chalk Creek at 6000 feet. The east area is quite long and narrow with a high point around 7600 feet in the north and 7700 feet in the south. The most common elevation is 6300 feet but ranges from 5300 feet to 8000 feet with an elevation difference of 2700 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6300 feet and 7100 feet an elevation difference of 800 feet. Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) is the dominant land cover on the GrassValley - Clark Canyon-Moose Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). Closely behind and almost equal with the Sagebrush Steppe is Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). There are a number of areas particularly in the north part of the Unit that have areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). To a lesser extent there are patches of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) and Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). There are also a number of large patches of Agriculture (114) closer to riparian areas. One of the Grass Valley - Clark Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ECHO DAM (422385), is about 1.2 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. ECHO DAM has sixty-seven (67) years of records, 1940 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.88 inches, but it can be as high as 10.59 inches or as low as 0.47 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 21 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 11 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 12.1 inches but can be as high as 41.5 inches. FALL temperature at ECHO DAM averages 46.5 degrees F. but can be as high as 97.0 degrees F. or as low as -21.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 54 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 3 days above 90 degrees F.

The Hardscrabble Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is east of East Canyon Reservoir and southwest of Porterville, Utah. The Unit highpoint is around 8000 feet. This highpoint is in the southeast part of the unit. The elevation in the north decreases to 6000 feet, in the south it decreases to 7600 feet, in the west 6600 feet and in the east 5800 feet. Hardscrabble Creek divides this Unit starting at 7600 feet in the south, then exiting the Unit in the northeast corner at 5400 feet. The most common elevation is 6600 feet but ranges from 5400 feet to 9300 feet with an elevation difference of 3900 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6700 feet and 8100 feet an elevation difference of 1400 feet. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is the dominant land cover type on the Hardscrabble Cooperative Wildlife Management Units (CWMU). This Shrubland is more dominant in the central and north parts of the Unit, than in the south. Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) is also a prominent feature of the Unit scattered through the shrubland. There are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) scattered on the Unit. Rocky Mountain Montane Dry-Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (30), Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), and Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23) add to the Forest and Woodland character of the Unit. One of the Hardscrabble Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, CITY CREEK (421446), is about 6.2 km southwest from the southwest edge of the CWMU. CITY CREEK has fifty-three (53) years of records, 1955 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 6.94 inches, but it can be as high as 10.80 inches or as low as 2.38 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 24 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 5 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There is also 1 day where the precipitation and be greater than or equal to 1.00 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 18.6 inches but can be as high as 56.0 inches. FALL temperature at CITY CREEK averages 49.9 degrees F. but can be as high as 92.0 degrees F. or as low as 2.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 34 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.
