hunt_bio_general_information: The purpose of Utah's extended archery seasons are to apply hunting pressure to deer and elk adjacent to urban and agricultural areas while providing additional hunting opportunities for archers. Participating in Utah's extended archery seasons: If you obtain a general or limited entry archery deer or elk permit and haven't taken a deer or elk by the end of the archery season printed on your permit-and you complete the required archery ethics course-you may hunt in the extended archery deer or elk areas during their respective seasons. The online archery ethics course is an annual requirement for all archers who want to hunt the extended areas and seasons. Additional information and a link to the training course can be found here: https://wildlife.utah.gov/extendedarchery.html After you successfully complete the course, print your completion certificate and keep it with you while hunting. The following can participate in extended archery seasons: -General archery deer permit holders who completed the extended archery ethics course -Limited Entry archery deer permit holders who completed the extended archery ethics course -Premium Limited Entry archery deer permit holders who completed the extended archery ethics course -General archery elk permit holders who completed the extended archery ethics course -Limited Entry archery elk permit holders who completed the extended archery ethics course
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This Hunt is almost entirely on Private Property and agricultural lands. Written permission is required to hunt on Private Property. Obtain permission before attempting to hunt this hunt. Due to legal privacy issues the DWR does not provide a list of landowners that allow access to hunters. Hunters need to identify and have written permission from landowners before they attempt to hunt this area. Hunters need to be aware of all Ute Tribal Lands as they are closed to all non-tribal members. Elk are found in numerous areas depending on the weather. At times during this hunt elk can be found almost anywhere along the tribal boundary which runs along the north boundary of the west portion of the hunt area. Elk are also consistently found in the following areas during this hunt: Arcadia, Bridgeland, Myton, Upalco, Randeltt, Ouray, Lower Uinta River drainage, etc... Hunters may be able to identify individual landowners to ask for permission by using the Duchesne and Uintah County Parcel Viewer websites that are available through the Counties online.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be aware that on much of this hunt area Any Weapon Private Lands Only antlerless elk permits overlap the hunt dates of this hunt. Archery Hunters should contact Landowners immediately prior to hunting to know if Any Weapon antlerless elk hunters may be hunting the property at the same time to know if they need to wear hunter orange.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt can vary dramatically during the long hunting season. Be prepared for hot & dry, or rainy, lightening, windy or even snowy conditions. Snow storms occur often during later half of this hunt.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit has a population estimate of ~160 mountain goats. This is a difficult and physically demanding hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Most of the mountain goats in this unit can be found near Loafer Peak, Bald Mountain, and Mount Nebo above or near 11,000 feet. Scouting trips are highly recommended. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Mountain goat hunting requires a lot of glassing in cliff faces and "Bollies." Mountain goats do move during the year, so where you find them in the winter and summer may not be where they are in the fall. Some areas they stay fairly consistently all year while others they move quite far. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Goats do have areas they like and stay in the same general area but they can simply walk over the ridge and be gone for a day or two. What they can hike in minutes can take you all day. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in the cliffs or on rocky ridge tops, etc... occasionally move down into the trees so don't overlook those areas too. Mature Billies often like to hang out in very steep, rocky, cliffs by themselves or in small groups of two and threes. Nannies with kids prefer areas that are a little less steep are open and green where they find better feed. Nannies and kids are usually in larger groups of five to fifty. Billy vs. Nanny: It is very difficult to tell the difference between a billy and a nanny mountain goat from a distance. Please review the Rocky Mountain Goat Hunt Orientation packet to learn how to properly identify mountain goats https://dwrapps.utah.gov/wex/examBorder.jsp?content=loginForm.jsp&formstat=0 . There are also other informational resources including this video produced by the Rocky Mountain Goat Alliance https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J8gUaMx8G7I While permits are either sex permits, hunters are encouraged to take billies and avoid harvesting a nanny with a kid.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Mountain goat habitat on this unit is very remote and hard to access. Appropriate precautions should be taken. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Mountain goats live in very steep, cliffy, treacherous terrain. Do not shoot a mountain goat in an area where you cannot safely retrieve it. You may need to wait until it moves to a safer spot before you can harvest the animal.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind, and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges where mountain goats live. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until through the first week on October. It is recommended that hunters do not wait until the very end of the hunt to go out hunting. At high elevations, there is a very real chance of a snowstorm that will not melt out until spring after the first week of October.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a difficult hunt with very limited motorized vehicle access. Mtn. goat habitat on this unit is very remote and hard to access. Appropriate precautions should be taken. Mtn. goats live in very steep, treacherous terrain. Do not shoot a mtn. goat in an area where you cannot safely retrieve it. You may need to wait until it moves to a safer spot before you can harvest the animal. Wasting of wildlife is not excusable simply because you chose to shoot it in a location you couldn't safely get to.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: When it comes to mtn. goats, most hunters consider the beautiful white cape to be the main trophy and they're concerned about the hair quality of the goats. I've heard from numerous taxidermists that the hair quality of Uinta Mountain mtn. goats is as good at the opening of the hunt as most other mtn. goat units have at the end of the hunt. The Uinta Mountains goats hair up quite quickly after shedding their winter coats. Billies shed first in the summer and also hair back up first in the fall. I recommend against waiting until the very end of the hunt to have good hair for the cape. I would suggest the end of September and first few days of October to be a great time to hunt the Uintas for a good cape on a goat. Mountain Scouting trips are highly recommended and good quality binoculars and spotting scopes are essential. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Goats do have areas they like and stay in the same general area but they can simply walk over the ridge and be gone for a day or two. What they can hike in minutes can take you all day. Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most often they are in found in the cliffs or on rocky ridge tops. Mountain goats on this unit occasionally move down into the trees so don't overlook those areas. Mature Billies often like to hang out in very steep, rocky, cliffs. Nannies with kids prefer areas that are a little less steep and with rubble rock or green patches in rock where they find better feed. You can often guess whether it's a billy or a nanny just by the habitat it's in. Goats on the Chalk Creek/Kamas unit migrate very little during the winter. Goats can be found at or above 9000' in elevation throughout most of the year on this unit. Mountain goats can be found throughout the hunt on Bald Mountain, Notch Mountain and Haystack, as well as the Whiskey Lake area.

Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The Biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges where Mtn. Goats live. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until through the first week on October. hunt_bio_general_information: 100% of the mountain goat habitat in this hunt unit is within the High Uintas Wilderness Area where motor vehicles are prohibited and access is difficult and remote. Mtn. goats live in very steep, cliffy, treacherous terrain. Do not shoot a mtn. goat in an area where you cannot safely retrieve it. You may need to wait until it moves to a safer spot before you can harvest the animal. Wasting of wildlife is not excusable simply because you chose to shoot it in a location you couldn't safely get to. Where to find mountain goats: Access to almost all of the mountain goat habitat is by foot or horseback only and is very remote. Mountain goat hunting is very physically demanding. Mountain goats live in steep cliffy areas, usually above tree line. Hunting can be very difficult, particularly in this hunt unit. Mountain goats are usually found in small groups or by themselves scattered across the cliff faces and the "bollies" between drainages and across the summit of the Uintas. Goats are well distributed in cliffy habitat across the entire unit. Goats are found in every drainage. Mountain goat rut:The mtn. goat rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not really affect the hunt. Recommended areas in the High Uintas Central:Goats are found across the spine of the Uintas. Billies in particular seems to prefer the spine of the Unitas. The Red Castle Peak area is probably the most popular area to hunt on this unit because there are almost always goats in the area. To the east of Red Castle, Flat Top Mtn also always has good numbers of goats along both sides up in the cliffs. On the South Slope, there are always mtn goats on the east side of the Lake Fork drainage but those areas can be difficult to access due to lack of trails on the Lake Fork side. There are goats from Swasey's Hole to Garfield Basin too. Another popular area is Swift Creek area and Yellowstone Canyon. Further east in the Uinta Canyon drainage, the Krebs Creek area has been popular, and up high on the sides of Mt. Emmons and above the Chain Lakes Basin.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: 2024 update- mtn goats numbers across the Uintas are currently down due to high harvest of nannies and high winter mortality due to recent harsh winter conditions. Be advised that permit numbers will be reduced by about half in 2024 to reduce nanny harvest and let the herd recover. Coat Condition: When it comes to mtn. goats, most hunters consider the beautiful white cape to be the main trophy and they're concerned about the hair quality of the goats. I've heard from numerous taxidermists that the hair quality of Uinta Mountain mtn. goats is as good at the opening of the hunt as most other mtn. goat units have at the end of the hunt. The Uinta Mountains goats hair up quite quickly after shedding their winter coats. Billies shed first in the summer and also hair back up first in the fall. I recommend against waiting until the very end of the season to have good hair for the cape. There is very little difference in hair quality in one or even two weeks. I would suggest the end of Sept. and first few days of October to be a great time to hunt the Uintas for a good cape on a mtn goat. Location of harvest: Mtn. goats are famous for being able to take a bullet and still be able to get up and run. Wounded goats will often run towards cliffs to escape and then fall and damage or destroy much of meat, horns and cape. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your goat. If you cannot safely retrieve the goat, do not shoot. Migration Patterns: Some of the mtn. goats on the High Uintas Central unit do migrate down in elevation for the winter. During the winter mtn. goats can be found down low in every drainage across the South Slope. Most of these animals move back to the north for the summer and fall. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally effect the hunt. Some of the goats do not migrate down in elevation and can be found all winter near the top of the Uintas. We found a radio collared nanny that spent the winter near Kings Peak at almost 13,000' all winter and she survived. They often move to south facing ridges or windblown faces for the winter. Scouting Tips: In the Uintas locating mtn. goats is the hardest part of the hunt. Scouting trips are highly recommended. Take your fishing pole along and enjoy the High Uintas. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Lots of glassing of cliff faces and "Bollies." Mtn. goats do move during the year, so where you find them in the winter and summer may not be where they are in the fall. Some areas they stay fairly consistently all year while others they move quite far. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Goats do have areas they like and stay in the same general area but they can simply walk over the ridge and be gone for a day or two. What they can hike in minutes can take you all day. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in the cliffs or on rocky ridge tops, etc... but they occasionally move down into the trees so don't overlook those areas too. Mature billies often like to hang out in very steep, rocky, cliffs. Nannies with kids prefer areas that are a little less steep and with rubble rock or green patches in rock where they find better feed. You can often guess whether it's a billy or a nanny just by the habitat it's in. Billy vs Nanny: It is very difficult to tell the difference between a billy and a nanny mtn. goat from a distance. Please review the Rocky Mountain Goat Hunt Orientation packet to learn how to properly identify mtn. goats https://dwrapps.utah.gov/wex/dbconnection.jsp?examnbr=510923 There are also other orientation slide shows available on various state fish and game websites:http://www.adfg.alaska.gov/static/hunting/goathunting/pdfs/goat_long_quiz_for_web.pdf<brhttp://fwp.mt.gov/hunting/planahunt/huntingGuides/msg/mountainGoatGuideBrochure.html While permits are either sex permits, hunters are encouraged to take billies and make sure you do not harvest a nanny with a kid.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a wilderness hunt. Mtn. goat habitat on this unit is very remote and hard to access. Appropriate precautions should be taken. Due to the Wilderness Area restrictions and the remoteness of mtn. goat habitat on this unit cellular phone coverage is very spotty at best in the high country on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents but bear incidents in the Wilderness area have been rare in the past.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges where Mtn. Goats live. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until after the first week on October. It is recommended that hunters do not wait until the very end of the season to go out hunting. At high elevations, there is a very real chance of a snowstorm that will not melt out until spring after the first week of October.

hunt_bio_general_information: Mountain goat rut: The mtn. goat rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not really affect the hunt. Where to find mountain goats: This hunt unit does not include any of the High Uintas Wilderness Area. There are gravel roads that will get you close to mtn goat country but all most access to the mountain goat habitat is by foot or horseback only and can be very remote. Mountain goat hunting is very physically demanding. Mountain goats live in steep cliffy areas, usually above tree line. Hunting can be very difficult, particularly in this hunt unit. Mountain goats are usually found in small groups or by themselves scattered across the cliff faces and the "bollies" between drainages and across the summit of the Uintas. Goats are well distributed in cliffy habitat across the entire unit. Goats are found in every drainage. Recommended areas in the High Uintas East: Goats are found across the spine of the Uintas. Billies in particular seems to prefer the spine of the Unitas. On this unit there are some mtn goats that hang out lower in some of the canyons than other parts of the Uintas year round. Goats can be found in lower Whiterocks Canyon and in Paradise Park Creek canyon. Marsh Peak is always a good area to hunt for goats and Leidy Peak can also be good. There are also good numbers of goats all along the bollie ridge between Blanchet Park and the upper Whiterocks river. Good billies are also taken in the basins above Pollen Lake on the North Slope.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: 2024 update- mtn goats numbers across the Uintas are currently down due to high harvest of nannies and harsh winter conditions in 2023. Be advised that permit numbers will be reduced by half in 2024 to reduce nanny harvest and let the herd recover. Coat Condition: When it comes to mtn. goats, most hunters consider the beautiful white cape to be the main trophy and they're concerned about the hair quality of the goats. I've heard from numerous taxidermists that the hair quality of Uinta Mountain mtn. goats is as good at the opening of the hunt as most other mtn. goat units have at the end of the hunt. The Uinta Mountains goats hair up quite quickly after shedding their winter coats. Billies shed first in the summer and also hair back up first in the fall. I recommend against waiting until the very end of the season to have good hair for the cape. There is very little difference in hair quality in one or even two weeks. I would suggest the end of Sept. and first few days of October to be a great time to hunt the Uintas for a good cape on a mtn goat. Location of harvest: Mtn. goats are famous for being able to take a bullet and still be able to get up and run. Wounded goats will often run towards cliffs to escape and then fall and damage or destroy much of meat, horns and cape. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your goat. If you cannot safely retrieve the goat, do not shoot. Migration Patterns: Some of the mtn. goats on the High Uintas Leidy Peak unit do migrate down in elevation for the winter but many do not. During the winter mtn. goats can be found down low in every drainage across the South Slope. Most of these animals move back to the north for the summer and fall. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally effect the hunt. Some of the goats do not migrate down in elevation and can be found all winter near the top of the Uintas. We found a radio collared nanny that spent the winter near Kings Peak at almost 13,000' all winter and she survived. They often move to south facing ridges or windblown faces for the winter. Scouting Tips: In the Uintas locating mtn. goats is the hardest part of the hunt. Scouting trips are highly recommended. Take your fishing pole along and enjoy the High Uintas. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Lots of glassing of cliff faces and "Bollies." Mtn. goats do move during the year, so where you find them in the winter and summer may not be where they are in the fall. Some areas they stay fairly consistently all year while others they move quite far. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Goats do have areas they like and stay in the same general area but they can simply walk over the ridge and be gone for a day or two. What they can hike in minutes can take you all day. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in the cliffs or on rocky ridge tops, etc... but they occasionally move down into the trees so don't overlook those areas too. Mature billies often like to hang out in very steep, rocky, cliffs. Nannies with kids prefer areas that are a little less steep and with rubble rock or green patches in rock where they find better feed. You can often guess whether it's a billy or a nanny just by the habitat it's in. Billy vs Nanny: It is very difficult to tell the difference between a billy and a nanny mtn. goat from a distance. Please review the Rocky Mountain Goat Hunt Orientation packet to learn how to properly identify mtn. goats https://dwrapps.utah.gov/wex/dbconnection.jsp?examnbr=510923 There are also other orientation slide shows available on various state fish and game websites: http://www.adfg.alaska.gov/static/hunting/goathunting/pdfs/goat_long_quiz_for_web.pdf http://fwp.mt.gov/hunting/planahunt/huntingGuides/msg/mountainGoatGuideBrochure.html While permits are either sex permits, hunters are encouraged to take billies and make sure you do not harvest a nanny with a kid.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a high country hunt. Mtn. goat habitat on this unit is very remote and hard to access. Appropriate precautions should be taken. Due to the remoteness on mtn. goat habitat on this unit cellular phone coverage is very spotty at best in the high country on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The Biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Mtn. goats live in very steep, cliffy, treacherous terrain. Do not shoot a mtn. goat in an area where you cannot safely retrieve it. You may need to wait until it moves to a safer spot before you can harvest the animal. Wasting of wildlife is not excusable simply because you chose to shoot it in a location you couldn't safely get to.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges where Mtn. Goats live. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until through the first week on October. It is recommended that hunters do not wait until the very end of the season to go out hunting. At high elevations, there is a very real chance of a snowstorm that will not melt out until spring after the first week of October.

hunt_bio_general_information: Mountain goat rut: The mtn. goat rut usually runs from mid Nov.-mid Dec. so it does not really affect the hunt. Where to find mountain goats: 90% of the mountain goat habitat in this hunt unit is in the High Uintas Wilderness Area where motor vehicle access is prohibited. Access to almost all of the mountain goat habitat is by foot or horseback only and is very remote. Mountain goat hunting is very physically demanding. Mountain goats live in steep cliffy areas, usually above tree line. Hunting can be very difficult, particularly in this hunt unit. Goats are well distributed in cliffy habitat across the entire unit. Goats are found in every drainage. Recommended areas in the High Uintas West: There are a couple areas on this unit where goats frequent that are not too far from roads but those areas are very popular with hunters. Those areas include: Murdock Mountain, Hayden Peak, Blindstream Slope overlooking the South Fork of Rock Creek and East Grandaddy Mtn., Iron Mine Creek cliffs, the Grandview trailhead area, and the head of Dry Ridge overlooking Brown Duck Basin. For a more back country hunt it is recommended that hunters look farther into the Wilderness Area on both the North and South Slope. Billies can be found anywhere in good goat habitat across the unit, but during the most recent aerial surveys more billies have been found across the spine of the Uintas and along the ridges on the North Slope on the West unit.

hunt_bio_general_information: Land Ownership: 100% Public Land - US Forest Service lands. Population Objective: There is a population objective for this hunt units is 125. Current Population Estimate: Around 100 Mtn. Goats on the Unit. Goat numbers on this hunt unit have been stable over the last 10 years.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Coat Condition: When it comes to mtn. goats, most hunters consider the beautiful white cape to be the main trophy and they're concerned about the hair quality of the goats. I've heard from numerous taxidermists that the hair quality of Uinta Mountain mtn. goats is as good at the opening of the hunt as most other mtn. goat units have at the end of the hunt. Billies shed first in the summer and also hair back up first in the fall. I recommend against waiting until the very end of the hunt to have good hair for the cape. There is very little difference in hair quality in one or even two weeks. I would suggest the end of Sept. and first few days of October to be a great time to hunt for a good cape on a mtn. goat. Location of harvest: Mtn. goats are famous for being able to take a bullet and still be able to get up and run. Wounded goats will often run towards cliffs to escape and then fall and damage or destroy much of meat, horns and cape. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your goat. If you cannot safely retrieve the goat, do not shoot. Migration Patterns: Some of the mtn. goats do migrate down in elevation for the winter. During the winter months mtn. goats can be found down low in drainage across the Wasatch front. These animals move back to the top of the mountains for the summer and fall. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally interfere with the hunt. Goats most often move to south facing ridges or windblown faces for the winter. Goats can be seen in winter in Provo canyon. Scouting Tips: In locating mtn. goats is the hardest part of the hunt. Scouting trips are highly recommended. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Mtn. Goat hunting requires a lot of glassing in cliff faces and "Bollies." Mtn. goats do move during the year, so where you find them in the winter and summer may not be where they are in the fall. Some areas they stay fairly consistently all year while others they move quite far. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Goats do have areas they like and stay in the same general area but they can simply walk over the ridge and be gone for a day or two. What they can hike in minutes can take you all day. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in the cliffs or on rocky ridge tops, etc... occasionally move down into the trees so don't overlook those areas too. Mature Billies often like to hang out in very steep, rocky, cliffs by themselves or in small groups of two and threes. Nannies with kids prefer areas that are a little less steep are open and green where they find better feed. Nannies and kids are is big group of five to fifty. Avoid hunting in these big nanny groups. You can often guess whether it's a billy or a nanny just by the habitat it's in. Billy vs. Nanny: It is very difficult to tell the difference between a billy and a nanny mtn. goat from a distance. Please review the Rocky Mountain Goat Hunt Orientation packet to learn how to properly identify mtn. goats https://dwrapps.utah.gov/wex/examBorder.jsp?content=loginForm.jsp&formstat=0 . There are also other orientation slide shows available on various state fish and game websites: http://www.adfg.alaska.gov/static/hunting/goathunting/pdfs/goat_long_quiz_for_web.pdf and http://fwp.mt.gov/hunting/planahunt/huntingGuides/msg/mountainGoatGuideBrochure.html While permits are either sex permits, hunters are encouraged to take billies and make sure you do not harvest a nanny with a kid.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Mtn. goat habitat on this unit is very remote and hard to access. Appropriate precautions should be taken. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents but bear incidents. Mtn. goats live in very steep, cliffy, treacherous terrain. Do not shoot a mtn. goat in an area where you cannot safely retrieve it. You may need to wait until it moves to a safer spot before you can harvest the animal. Wasting of wildlife is not excusable simply because you chose to shoot it in a location you couldn't safely get to.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges where Mtn. Goats live. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until through the first week on October. It is recommended that hunters do not wait until the very end of the hunt to go out hunting. At high elevations, there is a very real chance of a snowstorm that will not melt out until spring after the first week of October.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a new hunt starting in 2017. No previous hunt information is available for the unit. Mt Goats were transplanted here in the fall of 2013. A survey was done in the summer of 2016 and good numbers of Mt Goats were found and the population was found to be huntable.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The highest concentrations of goats are found on the west face of the unit from Circleville to Panguitch. I would suggest accessing the top of the mountain and go to Mt. Pearson or Mt. Dutton peaks. From these areas hike and glass from the rim into the steeper rocky points and along the base of these ledges where the trees meet the cliffs. The goats often times work these cliff edges feeding in the mornings and evenings. I would suggest spending a lot of time glassing to locate the goats first them determine if access to them is possible. This is an extremely steep and rugged unit so please keep this in mind when planning on hunting here.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Very steep, remote terrain where these goats live.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Varied weather conditions could be possible. Because of the high elevations these goats are found anything from hot sunny days, extreme thunderstorms, and winter storms could be present.

hunt_bio_general_information: This herd was first hunted in 2018. The herd is comprised of individuals transplanted from the Tushar Mtns in 2013 and 2014. This herd has had good production and survival since introduction.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This has been a high success hunt. Focus your efforts on the north and middle peaks of the La Sal range. Burro Pass/ Manns Peak, Mt. Waas, Miners Basin, and Beaver Basin are all good locations in the north peaks to find goats. Goats can be found throughout the middle peaks (Mt. Peale, Mt. Tukuhnikivatz, Mt. Mellenthin), and will often travel the ridges between them. There is great access in the La Sals, but expect rugged hiking to get to areas the goats are utilizing.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for all types of weather. Most slopes occupied by Mtn. goats are steep and above 10,000' elevation. Rain, lightning and snow can occur during this hunt. Dry hot conditions are also possible, so take plenty of water. If a goat is in dangerous terrain, wait for it to move into a more suitable spot before taking a shot.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Rain, lightning and snow can occur during this hunt. Dry, hot conditions are also possible.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Coat Condition: When it comes to mtn. goats, most hunters consider the beautiful white cape to be the main trophy and they're concerned about the hair quality of the goats. I've heard from numerous taxidermists that the hair quality of Uinta Mountain mtn. goats is as good at the opening of the hunt as most other mtn. goat units have at the end of the hunt. Billies shed first in the summer and also hair back up first in the fall. I recommend against waiting until the very end of the hunt to have good hair for the cape. There is very little difference in hair quality in one or even two weeks. I would suggest the end of Sept. and first few days of October to be a great time to hunt for a good cape on a mtn. goat. Location of harvest: Mtn. goats are famous for being able to take a bullet and still be able to get up and run. Wounded goats will often run towards cliffs to escape and then fall and damage or destroy much of meat, horns and cape. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your goat. If you cannot safely retrieve the goat, do not shoot. Most goats are found on the north side of Superior Peak in the Mill B South Fork drainage. Migration Patterns: Some of the mtn. goats do migrate down in elevation for the winter. During the winter months mtn. goats can be found down low in drainage across the Wasatch front. These animals move back to the top of the mountains for the summer and fall. This migration is usually after the hunt ends so it does not normally interfere with the hunt. Goats most often move to south facing ridges or windblown faces for the winter. Goats can be seen in winter in Provo canyon. Scouting Tips: In locating mtn. goats is the hardest part of the hunt. Mtn. goats do move during the year, so where you find them in the winter and summer may not be where they are in the fall. Some areas they stay fairly consistently all year while others they move quite far. Scouting is most effective the last couple weeks before the hunt opens when they are more likely to stay in the same general area. Most of the time they are in the cliffs or on rocky ridge tops, etc... occasionally move down into the trees so don't overlook those areas too. Mature Billies often like to hang out in very steep, rocky, cliffs by themselves or in small groups of two and threes. Nannies with kids prefer areas that are a little less steep are open and green where they find better feed. Nannies and kids are is big group of five to fifty. hunt_bio_general_information: Late season archery
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt is intended to be difficult. Access on top can vary year to year depending on what kind of storms we've had. Some years you may be able to drive a 4wheeler to the top and hunt goats near Delano, Holly, Copper Belt, etc. Other years, you may be snow-shoeing into country like Mary's Nipple, Cougar canyon, Bullion canyon, etc. Most of the goats seem to pull off the East side once we get heavy snow on top, but some will head off the North and West sides of the range also. Expect to find them on rugged, steep South facing slopes.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Goats can live in treacherous country. Prepare physically and make sure you know your own physical limitations. When planning to harvest a mountain goat you sometimes need to consider where the goat will end up and if you can safely retrieve it.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: There will likely be snow on the ground and depending on the year, it could be a lot of snow. Prepare for cold weather and heavy snow conditions.

","WMA_IN_UNIT":"Gordon Creek, Lower Fish Creek, Starvation, Dairy Fork, Lake Fork, Birdseye, Lasson Draw, White Hill, Black Hill, Bald Mountain, Sixmile, Nine Mile, Twelve Mile, Miller Manti Face, Willow Creek, Desert Lake, Huntington, Upper San Rafael, Lower San Rafael","CAMPGRND_INFO":"All Campgrounds on the Manti part of this unit are managed by the US Forest Service. Maps and camping regulations are available on their websites at http://www.fs.usda.gov/mantilasal. There are also numerous dispersed camping opportunities on the BLM lands on the San Rafael portion of the unit. There are very few developed campgrounds in these desert habitats. For information on BLM Campsites contact the Price BLM office at www.blm.gov/ut/st/en/fo/price.html","SUGGESTED_MAPS":"The 1:100,000 scale maps that cover this unit include; Hanksville, Hite Crossing, San Rafael Desert, Huntington, Price, Nephi, Manti, Salina","COUNTY_ROAD_INFO":"Most roads and ATV trails on the Manti part of the unit are managed by the US Forest Service and are covered on their Travel Management Plans. Please direct all questions regarding which roads and trails ATVs can be operated on to the Price BLM office at www.blm.gov/ut/st/en/fo/price.html ","ATV_VEH_ACCESS":"see above","PRIV_TRIBE_LAND_ISSUES":"There are no Tribal Land issues on this unit. The vast majority of the archery deer summer habitat on the Manti portion of the unit is on public land. A few exceptions include the following areas; The northeast portion of the mountain near Scofield Reservoir has a high percentage of private land on good deer habitat. Most of these lands are managed under the CWMU program and can not provide hunter access as your permit will not be valid on those properties. Other private properties require prior written permission before hunting. Small pockets of private lands at high elevations can be found surrounding Electric Lake and on East Mountain. Anthro Subunit
Public, Private and Tribal Lands. Range Creek Subunit

There is more public land on the northern third of the unit near Anthro Mountain. There is a mix of USFS and BLM lands in this area although wildlife densities tend to be lower in this area.

Public, Private and Tribal Lands. The public lands are primarily US Forest Service lands managed by the Ashley National Forest and The Bureau of Land Management(BLM) managed out of the Vernal Field Office. This unit also includes large tracks of Ute Tribal lands that are closed to non-tribal members. The Tribal lands are mostly on the North end of the unit in the pinyon/juniper belt, with heavy oil field activity. The private land on the unit is primarily North of the Tribal boundary and in the low elevation desert areas and agricultural lands. There are two CWMU's on the unit (Antelope Creek and Cottonwood Ridge).

Range Creek Subunit
Most of the high elevation summer and early fall habitat is privately owned. Much of this private land occurs on 5 CWMU's (Preston Nutter Ranch, Patmos Ridge, Roan Cliffs, Conover-Jensen, and Minnie Maud CWMU's). Public lands occur at mid elevations and on the winter range. The vast majority of Nine Mile Canyon is privately owned. ","WMA_IN_UNIT":"The Cold Springs WMA exists on good habitat near the town of Sunnyside

The Cottonwood WMA exists on the Anthro subunit. ","CAMPGRND_INFO":"There are no known developed campgrounds on the unit. There are ample opportunities for dispersed camping on BLM and SITLA properties. No camping is allowed on the Cold Springs WMA. Please consult the Price BLM office for any camping restrictions at http://www.blm.gov/ut/st/en/fo/price.html

Anthro Subunit
There are no official campgrounds on this unit. Camping outside of official campgrounds is also permitted on most of the Forest. Please direct all questions regarding campground availability and other camping questions to the US Forest Service. Maps and camping regulations are available on their websites. Ashley National Forest website: http://www.fs.usda.gov/ashley ","PRIM_ACCESS_PTS":"The Nine Mile Canyon road is accessed from SR6 in Wellington. [{"BOUNDARY_ID":615,"ACREAGE":0,"LAND_OWNERSHIP":"The vast majority of the habitat from Argyle Canyon south is privately owned. Many of these properties are enrolled in the CWMU program where a separate hunting permit is required for big game on their property and they can not allow access. On this part of the unit there are only small isolated parcels of public lands on summer ranges to hunt. Prior permission must be secured before hunting on private lands. There is more public land on the northern third of the unit near Anthro Mountain. There is a mix of USFS and BLM lands in this area although wildlife densities tend to be lower in this area.

Anthro Subunit
Public, Private and Tribal Lands. The public lands are primarily US Forest Service lands managed by the Ashley National Forest and The Bureau of Land Management(BLM) managed out of the Vernal Field Office. This unit also includes large tracks of Ute Tribal lands that are closed to non-tribal members. The Tribal lands are mostly on the North end of the unit in the pinyon/juniper belt, with heavy oil field activity. The private land on the unit is primarily North of the Tribal boundary and in the low elevation desert areas and agricultural lands. There are two CWMU's on the unit (Antelope Creek and Cottonwood Ridge).

Range Creek Subunit
Most of the high elevation summer and early fall habitat is privately owned. Much of this private land occurs on 5 CWMU's (Preston Nutter Ranch, Patmos Ridge, Roan Cliffs, Conover-Jensen, and Minnie Maud CWMU's). Public lands occur at mid elevations and on the winter range. [{"BOUNDARY_ID":615,"ACREAGE":0,"LAND_OWNERSHIP":"The vast majority of the habitat from Argyle Canyon south is privately owned. Many of these properties are enrolled in the CWMU program where a separate hunting permit is required for big game on their property and they can not allow access. On this part of the unit there are only small isolated parcels of public lands on summer ranges to hunt. Prior permission must be secured before hunting on private lands. There is more public land on the northern third of the unit near Anthro Mountain. There is a mix of USFS and BLM lands in this area although wildlife densities tend to be lower in this area.

Anthro Subunit
Public, Private and Tribal Lands. The public lands are primarily US Forest Service lands managed by the Ashley National Forest and The Bureau of Land Management(BLM) managed out of the Vernal Field Office. This unit also includes large tracks of Ute Tribal lands that are closed to non-tribal members. The Tribal lands are mostly on the North end of the unit in the pinyon/juniper belt, with heavy oil field activity. The private land on the unit is primarily North of the Tribal boundary and in the low elevation desert areas and agricultural lands. There are two CWMU's on the unit (Antelope Creek and Cottonwood Ridge).

Range Creek Subunit
Most of the high elevation summer and early fall habitat is privately owned. Much of this private land occurs on 5 CWMU's (Preston Nutter Ranch, Patmos Ridge, Roan Cliffs, Conover-Jensen, and Minnie Maud CWMU's). Public lands occur at mid elevations and on the winter range. The vast majority of Nine Mile Canyon is privately owned. ","WMA_IN_UNIT":"The Cold Springs WMA exists on good habitat near the town of Sunnyside

The Cottonwood WMA exists on the Anthro subunit. ","CAMPGRND_INFO":"There are no known developed campgrounds on the unit. There are ample opportunities for dispersed camping on BLM and SITLA properties. No camping is allowed on the Cold Springs WMA. Please consult the Price BLM office for any camping restrictions at http://www.blm.gov/ut/st/en/fo/price.html

Anthro Subunit
There are no official campgrounds on this unit. Camping outside of official campgrounds is also permitted on most of the Forest. Please direct all questions regarding campground availability and other camping questions to the US Forest Service. Maps and camping regulations are available on their websites. Ashley National Forest website: http://www.fs.usda.gov/ashley ","PRIM_ACCESS_PTS":"The Nine Mile Canyon road is accessed from SR6 in Wellington. It will provide access to Minnie Maud Canyon, lower Argyle Canyon, Harmon Canyon, as well as Cottonwood and Cedar Ridges. The Bruin Point road is accessed via SR123 in the town of Sunnyside. This road is impassible during the winter months.","SUGGESTED_MAPS":"1:100,000 scale USGS maps include; Price, Huntington, Duchesne, Seep Ridge","COUNTY_ROAD_INFO":"All roads and ATV trails on this unit are managed by the BLM and are covered on their Travel Management Plans. Most major roads are maintained by Carbon, Emery, and Duchesne Counties. The Bruin Point dugway and Cottonwood Canyon dugway are both very steep and should not be attempted if there is a bunch of snow without tire chains. Pulling a camper trailer up the Bruin Point Dugway is possible but difficult. Please direct all questions regarding which roads and trails ATVs can be operated on to the Price BLM office at http://www.blm.gov/ut/st/en/fo/price.html","ATV_VEH_ACCESS":"see above","PRIV_TRIBE_LAND_ISSUES":"The hunt unit does not include Ute Tribal lands as shown on the hunt boundary map on the Division's website. All ATVs are prohibited on Tribal Lands, they must be trailered on access roads across Tribal Lands. This unit has a high percentage of private property on high elevation summer habitat, much of this property is managed as CWMU’s. All private land requires written permission before hunting. A GPS unit is also very handy. hunt_bio_general_information: Land Ownership: Moose habitat is primarily public land. Population Objective: 500 Current Population Estimate: 350
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Most moose are seen near rivers, streams, ponds, or lakes, focus your efforts near these areas. Later in the fall they will move into thick, brushy areas of oak brush and mahogany. Moose are very spread out on these subunits, so it is important to cover a lot of area. It is a great place to camp in the summer to scout and learn the roads and trails. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find moose. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Moose are typically a solitary animals. Recommended areas Wasatch West Subunit: American Fork Canyon- The canyon road takes you from the mouth of AF canyon east to Heber City. This area has a lot of moose. Look around Casacade Springs area. Strawberry Reservoir- Look along all streams feeding into Strawberry Reservoir, such as Strawberry River, Coop Creek, Mud Creek and Indian Creek and Trout Creek. These areas are not a high density area. Salt Lake County- All canyons on the east side of the valley have moose in them, such as Big and Little Cottonwood Canyons, Mill Creek, and Lambs Canyon. You can hunt with any weapon east on I-15 for cow moose. Other canyons to look in- Squaw Peak road, Right Hand Fork of Hobble Creek, Diamond Fork, Sheep Creek and Tie Fork. Not a lot of moose in these areas.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Always be sure of your target. Don't shoot from roads. Do not keep a loaded gun in your vehicle
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightening while hunting on high ridges. Early fall snow storms occur regularly in this area. Most years the snow will melt off, within a day or two until through the first week on October.

hunt_bio_general_information: Nearly 90% of this unit is on private property. Hunters should have written permission to hunt private land prior to applying for this hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Moose are very large animals and difficult to haul long distances. They are often found near or in water. Do not shoot if you cannot retrieve the animal where it may go down, such as in a lake or stream. Choose your shot wisely; you may have to wait for it to move to a better location. Migration Patterns: Moose do not show a definite migration pattern on this unit.. They are not as dependent on water sources during the winter months. Snow depth also does not seem to affect where they are located. Scouting Tips: Scouting trips are highly recommended in order to become familiar with the area. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Plan to spend a lot of time hiking in areas away from human disturbance. Bull Moose can move long distances, especially during the rut when they are in search of cows so you may not see the same moose on different scouting trips. Behavior: Like other wildlife, moose are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. They are often found in mountain riparian areas, near lakes and streams, with willows or aspen. During the rut, bulls and cows will call to attract mates. This can be useful in finding bulls in the thick vegetation. Moose rut: The moose rut usually runs during September and October. Where to find moose: Moose can be found throughout the higher elevations of this unit, mainly on private property. Written permission to hunt private land is recommended prior to applying for this hunt. During the hunt, moose will generally be found along streams and in aspen stands, but they may also be found in conifer stands moving between areas. Recommended areas: High elevation riparian and wet meadow habitat types, away from human disturbance.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past in this unit. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Moose can be unpredictable and dangerous if you encroach into their space. Females can be protective of young and may charge if they perceive you as a threat. Males can be defensive, especially during the rut.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning if you're crossing high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Occasionally a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Kamas moose population has remained stable. Moose are very large animals and difficult to haul long distances. They are often found near or in water. Do not shoot if you cannot retrieve the animal where it may go down, such as in a lake or stream. Choose your shot wisely; you may have to wait for it to move to a better location.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Moose do not show a definite migration pattern on the Kamas unit. They are not as dependent on water sources during the winter months. Snow depth also does not seem to affect where they are located. Scouting Tips: Scouting trips are highly recommended in order to become familiar with the area. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Plan to spend a lot of time hiking in areas away from human disturbance. Bull Moose can move long distances, especially during the rut when they are in search of cows so you may not see the same moose on different scouting trips. Behavior: Like other wildlife, moose are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. They are often found in mountain riparian areas, near lakes and streams, with willows or aspen. During the rut, bulls and cows will call to attract mates. This can be useful in finding bulls in the thick vegetation. Moose rut: The moose rut usually runs during September and October. Where to find moose: Moose can be found throughout the higher elevations of this unit. Highest densities of moose generally occur away from major roads and trails. During the hunt, moose will generally be found along streams and in aspen stands, but they may also be found in conifer stands moving between areas. Recommended areas: Good areas to hunt include Spring Canyon, Upper Setting and above the Washington/Trial Lake trailhead.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past in this unit. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Moose can be unpredictable and dangerous if you encroach into their space. Females can be protective of young and may charge if they perceive you as a threat. Males can be defensive, especially during the rut.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning if you're crossing high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms are frequent in this area. Occasionally a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit encompasses low desert to high mountain terrain. Moose are found on both sides of Flaming Gorge Reservoir, with the majority found in the higher elevations west of Flaming Gorge Reservoir. This unit is a general season deer unit and the West Daggett subunit is a general season elk unit; this area is heavily utilized during these other hunts with many people camping out during the seasons.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Moose are very large animals and difficult to haul long distances. They are often found near or in water. Do not shoot if you cannot retrieve the animal where it may go down, such as in a lake or stream. Choose your shot wisely; you may have to wait for it to move to a better location. If you cannot retrieve the moose, do not shoot; this is not an excuse for wasting game. Migration Patterns: Moose do not show a definite migration pattern on the North Slope. They are not as dependent on water sources during the winter months. Snow depth also does not seem to affect where they are located. Scouting Tips: In the Uintas, locating a bull moose is the hardest part of the hunt. Scouting trips are highly recommended so you become familiar with the unit and know the size of bull you will most likely harvest. Take your fishing pole along and enjoy the mountain lakes and streams. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Bull moose can move long distances, especially during the rut when they are in search of cows so you may not see the same moose on different scouting trips. Moose do move during the year, so where you find them in the winter and summer may not be where they are in the fall. When the rut starts, a bull moose may move many miles in one day so don't count on finding the same bull in an area on consecutive days. Behavior: Like other wildlife, moose are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time, they are found in mountain riparian areas near lakes and streams, most often where there are willows or aspen. During the rut, bulls and cows will call to attract mates. This can be useful in finding bulls in the thick vegetation they are often in. Bulls are sometimes attracted to thrashing willows if they think it's another bull. You may be able to use this trick to lure them into a different area for a better shot. Moose rut: The moose rut usually runs during September and October. Where to find moose: The majority of the moose are found on the West Daggett portion of the unit. It is generally higher in elevation and has more water than the 3 Corners side. During the hunt, moose will generally be found along streams and in aspen stands, but they may also be found in conifer stands moving between areas. Recommended areas in the West Daggett/3 Corners: Good areas to hunt include Carter Creek, Spirit Lake, Sheep Lake, Sheep Creek, and Moose Ponds area. These areas are all on USFS lands. Occasionally a bull can be found in the 3 Corners area and Willow Creek drainage. There is private property in this area so you should receive written permission from landowners if you wish to hunt their property.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past in this unit. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree. Moose can be unpredictable and dangerous if you encroach into their space. Females can be protective of young and may charge if they perceive you as a threat. Males can be defensive, especially during the rut.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning if you're crossing high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a Once in a lifetime hunt. The quality of the bulls on this unit is average. Moose can be found during this hunt anywhere across the unit from the highest elevations in the Wilderness area to the lowest along the Duchesne River corridor. Hunters should be aware of Ute tribal lands and learn the boundaries. Public hunting is not permitted on tribal Lands. There are no CWMUs on this unit. Moose are found primarily along stream corridors and near lakes and ponds. They can also be found in forested areas and brushy areas away from water. This unit includes the South Slope portion of the High Uintas Wilderness Area. The wilderness can provide a remote hunt with very few hunters but moose can be hard to locate. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine with little understory vegetation. Road access on the remainder of the unit is limited to mostly canyon bottoms due to the steepness of the terrain.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Migration Patterns: Moose on this unit can be found almost anywhere during the hunt. This herd generally move down in elevation for the winter. Most of the moose winter on Ute Tribal Lands or on lower elevation slopes on Forest Service lands. They also winter in river bottoms etc... Some moose are found on ridgetops and fairly high elevation during the winter. Moose rut: The moose rut on this unit usually peaks the end of Sept. and early Oct. The rut is usually dropping off by the end of the hunt. Some hunters are successful calling in bulls during this hunt, but most bulls are harvested simply by spot and stalk style hunting. During the rut, bull moose will cover a lot of ground looking for cows that are in heat. Finding a bull in one canyon does not mean he will still be there the next day when they really get rutty. When on the rut and looking for cows, bulls will often make a low grunting noise while they travel. Recommended areas in the South Slope, Yellowstone: There are numerous suggested areas to hunt on this unit. The Wilderness Area can provide a remote hunt with few hunters but is very tough to hunt and it can be hard to locate moose. Much of the habitat in the high country is fairly sterile without much feed. It is generally Lodge Pole Pine with little understory. Moose in the wilderness are generally found near lakes and along the stream corridors. During the hunt, most of the moose are found near water but can be also be found in brushy or timbered areas. The suggested areas to hunt include (starting on the west side of the unit): Mirror Lake Hwy - Hwy 150 is the west boundary of the hunt, closest to the Wasatch front Soapstone/Iron Mine - good road access, closer to the Wasatch Front North Fork of the Duchesne - limited road access Log Hollow - must cross tribal Lands to access, rough roads Rock Creek - paved road access, steep areas, be aware of tribal boundary Bear Wallow - steep terrain, be aware of tribal boundary Lake Fork/Moon Lake - paved road access, some private property to be aware of Yellowstone - rough roads, be aware of tribal boundary 77 Flat/Burnt Mill - gravel roads, a little flatter area, be aware of tribal boundary Dry Gulch - very rough road, steep terrain, be aware of tribal boundary on the east Uinta Canyon - tribal lands down low, steep terrain Painter Basins - wilderness area, very remote Elk Horn Loop - gravel roads that go almost to the summit of the Uinta Mountains, lots of opportunity to scatter out, good access to the high country Whiterocks Canyon - Whiterocks River is the eastern unit boundary, steep terrain

hunt_bio_general_information: Land Ownership: Moose habitat is primarily public land. Population Objective: 500 Current Population Estimate : 350
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Most moose are seen near rivers, streams, ponds, or lakes, focus your efforts near these areas. Later in the fall they will move into thick, brushy areas of oak brush and mahogany. Moose are very spread out on these subunits, so it is important to cover a lot of area. It is a great place to camp in the summer to scout and learn the roads and trails. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find moose. This is when most rutting activity will take place as well. Moose are typically a solitary animal, groups of bulls are uncommon until late fall and winter. Bull moose can, and will travel long distances during the rut in search of cows. This is important to know, because areas where you saw bulls in the summer might not be where they will be in the fall, however areas where you saw cows in the summer may be good places to find bulls during the rut. Moose rut: There will typically be a little rutting activity starting middle of September, with the peak of the rut being the end of September through the middle of October. There should be rutting activity throughout the entire hunting season. Areas to Hunt: Recommended areas Currant Creek Subunit: Currant Creek Drainage - This entire area is great for moose, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands, lots of ponds, creeks, streams, and lakes. Great access, camping, nice road, several different draws or canyons to hunt(Layout Canyon, Big Dry Hollow, Low Pass Creek, Race Track), can hold moose. North Fork Deep Creek/Water Hollow - very few roads, great area for horseback hunts, land managed by UDWR, borders private land in many spots. Wildcat WMA - UDWR land, borders private, lots of roads, highest density of moose on the subunit. West Fork Duchesne - Big area, road access, limited ATV access, timbered North slopes, large aspen stands, lots of water. Tabby Mountain WMA - the North slope is best, ponds on top, UDWR land, great for ATV's. Red Creek Drainage - Great area for moose, some private property, lots of SITLA property that is open for hunting, anywhere along the Red Creek is good for moose. Strawberry River - The entire river corridor East of Strawberry Reservoir. Area is thick and can be difficult to spot moose. Primarily land managed by the UDWR Recommended areas Avintaquin Subunit: Reservation Ridge - Big area, road on the divide, great area for glassing, not as many moose as Currant Creek. Strawberry Peak Area - Highest peak on Avintaquin, great access to roadless areas(Slab Canyon and Cow Hollow), not a lot of moose in these areas. Long Ridge - Great glassing area, areas South of Long Ridge along creeks and near ponds. Not a high density area. Recommended areas Wasatch West Subunit: American Fork Canyon - The canyon road takes you from the mouth of AF canyon east to Heber City. This area has a lot of moose. Look around Casacade Springs area. Strawberry Reservoir - Look along all streams feeding into Strawberry Reservoir, such as Strawberry River, Coop Creek, Mud Creek and Indian Creek and Trout Creek. These areas are not a high density area. Salt Lake County - All canyons on the east side of the valley have moose in them, such as Big and Little Cottonwood Canyons, Mill Creek, and Lambs Canyon. You can hunt with any weapon east on I-15 for OIAL hunts. Other canyons to look in - Squaw Peak road, Right Hand Fork of Hobble Creek, Diamond Fork, Sheep Creek and Tie Fork. Not a lot of moose in these areas, but big bulls have been seen in the past. Dollar Ridge Fire Update - July 2018 In early July 2018 the Dollar Ridge Fire burned approximately 50,000 acres on the Avintaquin and Currant Creek subunits of the Wasatch Mountains unit. The fire started in the Strawberry River Corridor and areas burned include portions of the Strawberry River wildlife management area and the Wildcat wildlife management area. Wildfire can have both negative and positive consequences for habitat and wildlife. In the right circumstances, wildfire can be a very effective tool for improving wildlife habitat. At lower elevation winter ranges fire may be detrimental if it removes important wintering feed sources or opens a niche for invasive weeds. In mid to high elevations fire often removes old, decadent growth and allows for new plants with high nutritional value. Grasses and forbs with high nutritional value are usually the first plant communities to come back after a fire. Regeneration in aspen stands is triggered by fire and mountain browse communities are quick to rebound. This fire mostly occurred in higher summer and transition ranges for big game. Based on current burned locations, we anticipate the effects of the Dollar Ridge Fire to be mostly positive for deer, elk and moose. We have observed that GPS collared moose and elk in the burn temporarily moved to adjacent habitats while the fire was actively burning, then moved back almost immediately after the active fire subsided. If we receive our normal late-summer monsoon weather pattern it is very likely the burned areas will have a flush of new growth or "green-up" prior to the hunting season. Wildfire can change wildlife distribution. Removal of cover may make an area less desirable for wary animals. Conversely, a good fall green-up might actually pull animals out of adjacent areas into the newly burned areas. Don't overlook burned areas when hunting as they can be good places to locate game. In 2017 the Brian Head fire burned 71,000 acres, nearly 25% of the Panguitch unit. At the end of the 2017 hunting season there were very few complaints from hunters and hunter success rates were normal to above normal. The Wasatch is a large unit and there are many locations with good hunting that were not affected by the Dollar Ridge Fire. We anticipate good opportunities for sportsmen this fall despite disturbance from the fire. In the long term we expect wildlife to reap many benefits from this fire.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is cut east-west by Dry Creek and north-south by State Road 68. Dry Creek starts at about 7200 feet and flows east and then south and exits the Unit at about 4400 feet. The higher elevations are on the west below Snow Basin Ski Resort. Then with a moderate slope the terrian slopes to the southeast and drops down into the Dry Creek cut before exiting the Unit. The most common elevation is 5800 feet but ranges from 5000 feet to 8500 feet with an elevation difference of 3500 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5700 feet and 7600 feet an elevation difference of 1900 feet. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is the dominant land cover type on the Bear Springs Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). There are many large patches of Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23) dispersed among the Gambel Oak, as are smaller patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). There are patches of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) on the west side, more in the middle of the Unit are patches of Rocky Mountain Lower Montane Riparian Shrubland (79), and scattered about are patches of Recently Burned (116) areas. There are some minor areas of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) scattered about. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Beaver Hollow Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is just east of the right extension of Lost Creek Reservoir. The CWMU is cut by Francis Canyon from the northeast to the west. The elevation range for Francis Canyon as it enters and exits the Unit is 7000 feet to 6200 feet, east to west. Elevation ranges from 7600 feet to 6100 feet on the Unit. Besides being cut by Francis Canyon, the Beaver Hollow CWMU is cut by the South Fork of Francis Canyon, Beaver Dam, Long Hollow and Red Hollow. The most common elevation is 7200 feet but ranges from 6100 feet to 7700 feet with an elevation difference of 1600 feet. Fifty-seven percent (57%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6500 feet and 7200 feet an elevation difference of 700 feet. The dominate land cover type on the Beaver Hollow Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is the Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Towards the northeast corner are extensive areas of Recently Burned (116) land cover. Distributed among the Sagebrush Steppe are patches of Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) and Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). One of the Beaver Hollow Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ECHO DAM (422385), is about 21.5 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. ECHO DAM has sixty-seven (67) years of records, 1940 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.88 inches, but it can be as high as 10.59 inches or as low as 0.47 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 21 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 11 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 12.1 inches but can be as high as 41.5 inches. FALL temperature at ECHO averages 46.5 degrees F. but can be as high as 97.0 degrees F. or as low as -21.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 54 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 3 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has opened private land for public use to help compensate the public for having public land in the CWMU. Here is a link to a map showing "trade lands" in CWMUs https://wildlife.utah.gov/cwmu.html . The Bastian Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is west and north of Causey Reservoir. Beaver Creek and State Highway 39 forms the west boundary and Elk Ridge forms the east boundary. The Unit consists of a main ridge which is about 8000 feet in the north dropping to 6700 feet in the south before it drops into Water Hollow. From this main ridge the Unit drops into Beaver Creek (5600 feet to 6600 feet). On the eastside the unit drops in to Dry Bread Hollow (6000 feet to 7200 feet) before rising up to Elk Ridge (7600 feet to 7900 feet). The most common elevation is 6800 feet but ranges from 5500 feet to 7900 feet with an elevation difference of 2400 feet. Fifty-four percent (54%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6000 feet and 7300 feet an elevation difference of 1300 feet. There are three (3) main land cover types and one (1) land cover type that dominates the Bastian Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). First, there is the Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Then there are the Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) and Rocky Mountain Gamble Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) in about equal amounts. In lesser amounts is Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland(23). One of the Bastian Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY (424135), is about 11.0 km southwest from the southwest edge of the CWMU. HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY has thirty-one (31) years of records, 1976 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 5.74 inches, but it can be as high as 12.30 inches or as low as 1.36 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 10.2 inches but can be as high as 31.0 inches. FALL temperature at HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY averages 46.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -16.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 56 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.
