hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) takes up parts of Weber, Morgan and Rich counties, with Rich county having the most area. The higher points on the Deseret CWMU are along Horse Ridge (8500 feet). On the west the Unit drops away to about 6400 feet in the south and 8000 feet in the north. On the eastside of Horse Ridge the Unit makes a less steep drop, dropping down to around 6400 feet in the north and 6800 feet in the south along the Utah - Wyoming state border. The most common elevation is 6400 feet but ranges from 6000 feet to 8700 feet with an elevation difference of 2700 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6800 feet and 7800 feet an elevation difference of 1000 feet. The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is much larger than other CWMUs in Utah, therefore land cover is more diversified. About half (50%) of the land cover on the Deseret CWMU is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Towards the northeast and at lower elevation, there are large areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Steppe (66). Thet higher elevations on the west of the Unit, mixed with Sagebrush Steppe are extensive areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). At lower elevations towards the northeast are several patches of Agriculture (114) land. At minor extents are Southern Rocky Mountain Montane-Subalpine Grassland (71), Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48), and Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane shrubland (41). One of the Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, WOODRUFF (429595), is about 10.5 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. WOODRUFF has one hundred eleven (111) years of records, 1897 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.64 inches, but it can be as high as 5.18 inches or as low as 0.64 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 8.7 inches but can be as high as 29.2 inches. FALL temperature at WOODRUFF averages 40.8 degrees F. but can be as high as 111.0 degrees F. or as low as -26.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 73 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 6 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Durst Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located north of Morgan, Utah and Interstate Highway 84. There are also patches of Invasive Perennial Grassland (119). One of the Durst Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, MORGAN (425826), is about 10.5 km south from the south edge of the CWMU. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The East Fork Chalk Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is east of Coalville, Utah up Chalk Creek. Humpy Peak at greater than 10,800 feet is the high point of the Unit. The elevation along the East Fork of Chalk Creek decreases to 6700 feet. Both the East Fork and Middle Fork of Chalk Creek are part of the unit. The East Fork decreases from 9600 feet and the Middle Fork from 7700 feet to where the combine at 7200 feet. Except for the abrupt extension of Humpy Peak the relief on the eastside of the Unit is not as steep as that on the west side. The most common elevation is 9700 feet but ranges from 6700 feet to 10800 feet with an elevation difference of 4100 feet. Fifty-three percent (53%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7800 feet and 9700 feet an elevation difference of 1900 feet. The East Fork Chalk Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) land cover is a combination of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) and Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). The Aspen Forest and Woodland is in the middle of the unit. The Sagebrush Steppe is scattered from the northwest through the middle and into the the southeast part of the Unit. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41)and Rocky Mountain Subalpine Dry-Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (26) also add to the land cover on certain parts of the Unit. One of the East Fork Chalk Creek Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, COALVILLE (421590), is about 3.0 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. COALVILLE has thirty-four (34) years of records, 1974 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.71 inches, but it can be as high as 7.09 inches or as low as 1.68 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 19 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 14.8 inches but can be as high as 32.0 inches. FALL temperature at COALVILLE averages 43.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 87.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 61 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Ensign Ranches Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is up Echo Canyon on both sides of Interstate Highway I-80. The highest point on the Unit is in the southeast at 9200 feet. This drops down to 5900 feet in Echo Canyon. On the other side of I-80 the elevation ranges from 7600 feet to 5900 feet. To the north elevation is around 6800 feet, to the east 7300 feet, to the south 6400 feet, and to the west 7600 feet. There are relatively flat areas in the southeast (7600 feet) with many waterbodies. The terrain on the north side of I-80 is steeper than on the south side. The most common elevation is 6900 feet but ranges from 5900 feet to 9100 feet with an elevation difference of 3200 feet. Fifty-five percent (55%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6900 feet and 8100 feet an elevation difference of 1200 feet. Over fifty percent (50%) of the land cover on the Ensign Ranches Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Towards the southwest are areas of Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). Towards the southeast and some in the northwest area areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). There are areas of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36), and in the north patches of Southern Rocky Mountain Montane-Subalpine Grassland (71). Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Steppe (66) adds to the Shrub-Steppe component, and there are large patches of Recently Burned (116) areas. One of the Ensign Ranches Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, COALVILLE (421590), is about 5.4 km south from the south edge of the CWMU. COALVILLE has thirty-four (34) years of records, 1974 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.71 inches, but it can be as high as 7.09 inches or as low as 1.68 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 19 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 14.8 inches but can be as high as 32.0 inches. FALL temperature at COALVILLE averages 43.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 87.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 61 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Grass Valley - Clark Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) lies east of Echo Reservoir. Although it is continuous, Chalk Creek cuts the Unit into a west and east sub-unit. On the west area the high point is around 7600 feet. The ridge line drops in a southwest direction too the shore of Echo Reservoir at about 5600 feet. To the north the Unit drops down into Echo Canyon, about 5800 feet before rising again to 7200 feet. Grass Valley Canyon cuts this west area and ranges from 5600 feet to 6400 feet. Then rises up to 7800 feet above Chappell Lake before dropping down again to Chalk Creek at 6000 feet. The east area is quite long and narrow with a high point around 7600 feet in the north and 7700 feet in the south. The most common elevation is 6300 feet but ranges from 5300 feet to 8000 feet with an elevation difference of 2700 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6300 feet and 7100 feet an elevation difference of 800 feet. Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) is the dominant land cover on the GrassValley - Clark Canyon-Moose Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). Closely behind and almost equal with the Sagebrush Steppe is Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). There are a number of areas particularly in the north part of the Unit that have areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). To a lesser extent there are patches of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) and Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). There are also a number of large patches of Agriculture (114) closer to riparian areas. One of the Grass Valley - Clark Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ECHO DAM (422385), is about 1.2 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. ECHO DAM has sixty-seven (67) years of records, 1940 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.88 inches, but it can be as high as 10.59 inches or as low as 0.47 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 21 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 11 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 12.1 inches but can be as high as 41.5 inches. FALL temperature at ECHO DAM averages 46.5 degrees F. but can be as high as 97.0 degrees F. or as low as -21.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 54 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 3 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Sharp Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is about 5 km southeast from Porcupine Reservoir in south Cache County. Almost all of the CWMU is in Cache County, but a small section in the southeast is in Weber County. The CWMU's name sake, Sharp Mountain rises to 9100 feet. Porcupine Ridge in the north is 8500 feet and in the south higher elevations are around 8300 feet. Davenport Creek in the south ranges from 6000 feet to 7400 feet on the unit. In the north Porcupine Creek ranges from 7400 feet to 8800 feet on the unit, and in the, east La Plata Canyon ranges from 7000 feet to 7900 feet. Much of the Sharp Mountain Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit is covered (32%) with Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). This Sagebrush Steppe is not concentrated in just one area but is spread throughout the CWMU. Similarly, Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) covers 29% of the CWMU and is spread throughout the unit too. Inter-Mountain West Aspen-Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland Complex (38) covers 7% of the unit, and Inter-Mountain Basins Mountain Mahogany Woodland and Shrubland (44) covers 5% of the unit. The Woodland Complex is spread throughout the unit, but the Mahogany Woodland and Shrubland is more concentrated in the southwest part of the unit. One of the Green Canyon Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, LOGAN FARM (425194), is about 8.8 km northwest from the northwest edge of the CWMU. LOGAN FARM has thirty-nine (39) years of records, 1989 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 4.28 inches, but it can be as high as 7.98 inches or as low as 0.96 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 21 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 12 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There will also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 5.3 inches but can be as high as 15.5 inches. FALL temperature at LOGAN FARM averages 47.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 94.0 degrees F. or as low as -16.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 47 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Skull Crack Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is south of Causey Reservoir. Part of the Weber - Morgan County line forms the boundary of this Unit in the southeast, the Unit overlaps this boundary in the south. Highest elevation is the west is 7700 feet elevation, rising to 8200 feet in the middle of the Unit, then dropping again to 8000 feet elevation. Many small drainages drop off to the north and west. The Pete Nelson Hollow, ranging from 6400 feet to 8000 feet is one of these drainages. Skull Crack (5800 feet to 8000 feet), Mill Hollow (5800 feet to 8000 feet), Mill Canyon (5600 feet to 7300 feet), Magpie Canyon (5400 feet to 7800 feet), Quarry Hollow (5300 feet to 6600 feet), and Sheep Herd Creek (5700 feet to 8000 feet) are other small drainages on the Unit. The most common elevation is 8100 feet but ranges from 5100 feet to 8200 feet with an elevation difference of 3100 feet. Forty-nine percent (49%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6000 feet and 7400 feet an elevation difference of 1400 feet. The Skull Crack Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) has a mixture of two (2) land cover types with strong contribution from a third. Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) is the most common, but Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrsuh Steppe (62) is almost as common. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is also very common. Another common type is Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23). Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32) and Rocky Mountain Montane Dry-Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (30) contribute minor amounts to the Forest and Woodland character of the unit. One of the Skull Crack Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY (424135), is about 1.3 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY has thirty-one (31) years of records, 1976 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 5.74 inches, but it can be as high as 12.30 inches or as low as 1.36 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 22 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 3 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be 1 day of greater than or equal to 1.00 inch precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 10.2 inches but can be as high as 31.0 inches. FALL temperature at HUNTSVILLE MONESTERY averages 46.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 95.0 degrees F. or as low as -16.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 56 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: South Canyon CWMU is south of Avon, Utah and southwest of Porcupine Reservoir. The south shore of Porcupine Reservoir is part of the northern boundary of the Unit. Higher elevation range between 7000 in the west to 8800 feet in the east. The Unit is cut near the middle by two major drainages, South Fork Little Bear River and Davenport Creek. Both of these drainages range from 5100 feet to 5600 feet. Clay Valley is in the west at 6100 feet elevation. The most common elevation is 6000 feet but ranges from 5100 feet to 8800 feet with an elevation difference of 3700 feet. Fifty-seven percent (57%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6000 feet and 7800 feet an elevation difference of 1800 feet. For the Woodland and Shrubland character, Inter-Mountain Basins Mountain Mahogany Woodland and Shrubland (44) and Rocky Mountain Lower Montane Riparian Woodland and Shrubland (79) are representative. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Three C Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is southeast of Heber City. The highest elevation is in the southeast at near 9900 feet. This high elevation decreases to 7200 feet in the northwest. Crooked Creek is one of the drainages that cuts the Unit. It ranges from 6600 feet to 8700 feet. Center Creek is another drainage that cuts the Unit. It ranges from 6400 feet to 8600 feet. The most common elevation is 8000 feet but ranges from 5800 feet to 9900 feet with an elevation difference of 4100 feet. Fifty-three percent (53%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7000 feet and 8700 feet an elevation difference of 1700 feet. The Three C Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is somewhat divided in half. On the west half the land cover is dominated by Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) and Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41). Whereas, the east half is dominated by Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23), Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland (28), and Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) add to the Forest and Woodland character of the Unit. Rocky Mountain Subalpine-Montane Riparian Shrubland (77) and Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland support the Shrubland character. One of the Three C Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HEBER (423809), is 4.6 km northwest of the northwest edge of the CWMU. HEBER has one hundred sixteen (116) years of records, 1892 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.92 inches, but it can be as high as 10.14 inches or as low as 0.50 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 18 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 11 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 8.9 inches but can be as high as 29.5 inches. FALL temperature at HEBER averages 46.6 degrees F. but can be as high as 98.0 degrees F. or as low as -21.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 57 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 1 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Two Bear Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located just south of the Idaho - Utah state-line with State Highway 150 forming much of the east boundary. The high elevation is around 9100 feet. The Hayden Fork (7800 feet to 8400 feet) and the West Fork (7800 feet to 9000 feet) of the Bear River cut the Unit on the east. Two major drainages flowing into the Bear River and its forks are Mill City Creek (8400 feet to 9200 feet) and Deer Creek (8300 feet to 9100 feet). On the west side of the Unit, Yellow Creek, ranging from 7700 feet to 8800 feet, cuts the unit. The most common elevation is 8900 feet but ranges from 7500 feet to 9600 feet with an elevation difference of 2100 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 8100 feet and 8900 feet an elevation difference of 800 feet. The Two Bear Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) land cover is dominated by two (2) types in almost equal proportions, Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) and Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Rocky Mountain Subalpine-Montane Riparian Shrubland (77) is also a prominent land cover type on the Unit. There is also a large patch of Rocky Mountain Lodgepole Pine Forest (29) in the southeast corner that contributes to the land cover mix. One of the Two Bear Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, COALVILLE (421590), is about 14.2 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. COALVILLE has thirty-four (34) years of records, 1974 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.71 inches, but it can be as high as 7.09 inches or as low as 1.68 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 19 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 10 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 14.8 inches but can be as high as 32.0 inches. FALL temperature at COALVILLE averages 43.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 87.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 61 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: NOTE: DIFFICULT HUNT , HORSES ARE RECOMMENDED . The Hardscrabble Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is east of East Canyon Reservoir and southwest of Porterville, Utah. The Unit highpoint is around 8000 feet. This highpoint is in the southeast part of the unit. The elevation in the north decreases to 6000 feet, in the south it decreases to 7600 feet, in the west 6600 feet and in the east 5800 feet. Hardscrabble Creek divides this Unit starting at 7600 feet in the south, then exiting the Unit in the northeast corner at 5400 feet. The most common elevation is 6600 feet but ranges from 5400 feet to 9300 feet with an elevation difference of 3900 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6700 feet and 8100 feet an elevation difference of 1400 feet. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) is the dominant land cover type on the Hardscrabble Cooperative Wildlife Management Units (CWMU). This Shrubland is more dominant in the central and north parts of the Unit, than in the south. Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) is also a prominent feature of the Unit scattered through the shrubland. There are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62) scattered on the Unit. Rocky Mountain Montane Dry-Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (30), Rocky Mountain Montane Mesic Mixed Conifer Forest and Woodland (32), and Rocky Mountain Bigtooth Maple Ravine Woodland (23) add to the Forest and Woodland character of the Unit. One of the Hardscrabble Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, CITY CREEK (421446), is about 6.2 km southwest from the southwest edge of the CWMU. CITY CREEK has fifty-three (53) years of records, 1955 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 6.94 inches, but it can be as high as 10.80 inches or as low as 2.38 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 24 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 14 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 5 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There is also 1 day where the precipitation and be greater than or equal to 1.00 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 18.6 inches but can be as high as 56.0 inches. FALL temperature at CITY CREEK averages 49.9 degrees F. but can be as high as 92.0 degrees F. or as low as 2.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 34 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Woodruff Creek South Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located southwest of Woddruff, Utah. High elevations in the east are 7900 feet and 8400 feet in the west. Woodruff Creek (6800 feet to 7300 feet) forms the north border along with Woodruff Reservoir (6800 feet) and approximates the west Unit border. Meachem Canyon (7000 feet to 7700 feet) forms the south border. One primary drainage, Road Hollow, flowing east to west cuts the Unit, ranging from 7200 feet to 7800 feet. The most common elevation is 7800 feet but ranges from 6900 feet to 8500 feet with an elevation difference of 1600 feet. Fifty-four percent (54%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7400 feet and 8000 feet an elevation difference of 600 feet. Almost seventy-five percent (75%) of the Woodruff Creek South Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). The only other major land cover types is Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). This Aspen Forest and Woodland are in large patches in the middle and towards the west of the Unit. On the westside Rocky Mountain Subalpine Mesic Spruce-Fir Forest and Woodland occur in several large patches. One of the Woodruff Creek South Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, WOODRUFF (429595), is about 14.6 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. WOODRUFF has one hundred eleven (111) years of records, 1897 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.64 inches, but it can be as high as 5.18 inches or as low as 0.64 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 8.7 inches but can be as high as 29.2 inches. FALL temperature at WOODRUFF averages 40.8 degrees F. but can be as high as 111.0 degrees F. or as low as -26.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 73 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 6 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Services are located in Tremonton, Snowville, and Grouse Creek. hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of December.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is located northeast of Grouse Creek near Lynn. Habitat types include open sagebrush, pinyon/juniper woodlands, sub-alpine forest, and irrigated and non-irrigated agricultural fields.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The majority of the moose will use higher elevations of the CWMU through the summer months. Sometimes early season snow storms will push the moose out of the country earlier than normal. In warm weather, hunters do best hunting water sources in mornings and evenings. Later in the season when there's usually more water available, hunters do best either glassing for moose and then working to get close for a shot or stalking moose through the trees. Visibility on this unit is variable due to dense trees and open rolling sagebrush hills. Moose are most active in the early mornings and late afternoons, which are the best times for scouting elk prior to and during the hunts
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Few services exist west of Snowville - the Grouse Creek store is the only public gas station until Montello, Nevada or Wendover, Utah/Nevada.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Some years a big snowstorm will hit the beginning of October and make some roads impassable.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Moon's Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located west of Hanna,Utah. The highest elevation on the east side starts about 8400 feet and increases to 8800 feet before dropping down into several drainages, but it rises again to 8200 feet on the west side of the Unit. In the north, the West Fork of the Duchesne River, ranging from 7200 feet to 7600 feet, cuts the Unit. In the south, Sand Creek, ranging from 6800 feet to 8000 feet, cuts the Unit. On the west side, Little Sand Creek, ranging from 7500 feet to 8000 feet, cuts the unit. The most common elevation is 8000 feet but ranges from 6700feet to 8800 feet with an elevation difference of 2100 feet. Fifty-seven percent (57%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 7500 feet and 8100 feet an elevation difference of 600 feet. Over half of the land cover on the Moon's Ranch CWMU is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). This cover type is generally distributed over the entire unit. Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane Shrubland (41) and Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22) are the next largest contributors. Several hundred hectares each of Colorado Plateau Pinyon-Juniper Woodland (36) and Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland round out most of the land cover types. One of the Moons Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, HANNA (423624), is 0.5 km east of the east edge of the CWMU. HANNA has forty-two (42) years of records, 1952 - 1994. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.35 inches, but it can be as high as 4.43 inches or as low as 2.52 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 10 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inches of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inches, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inches of prercipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 2.2 inches but can be as high as 5.0 inches. FALL temperature at HANNA averages 63.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 78.0 degrees F. or as low as 5.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 23 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and no day above 90 degrees F.

DWR WMA’S: There is a 14 day limit on WMA’s, and there is no camping on the Willow Creek WMA. ","PRIM_ACCESS_PTS":"There are several access points to the Book Cliffs. From the north side there are two main roads that take you to the Book Cliffs. Utah State Road 88 located between Vernal and Roosevelt. As you follow it south it turns into the Seep Ridge Road. Hwy 45 or the Bonanza Hwy is located east of Vernal. It takes you towards the east side of the Book Cliffs. After you cross the White River you come to the Dragon or Duck Rock intersection. The Dragon Rd will take you south to the Book Cliffs. The Hay Canyon Rd is the main access road on the south side of the Book Cliffs. You can access it from I-70. It is a hard packed dirt/gravel road. The roadless area has two access points, a north and a south. The north access is called the Ten Mile Knoll trailhead. It is located at the start of Steer Ridge. There is a parking area, but it can fill up in a hurry with trucks and horse trailers. The south trailhead starts at the top of Sego Canyon. The road starts at Thompson Springs in Grand County and continues up the Sego Canyon Rd; follow it to the end of the road. There is a water trough at the trailhead, but it is not always full of water. This trailhead can also fill up with vehicles, and trailers. There are no bathrooms or other facilities at either of these trailheads, so plan accordingly. The DWR WMA’s are restricted to ATV and vehicle travel on established roads and trails. Suggested Maps: BLM: Vernal, West Water, and they have a general map that labels most of the main roads. There are several county signs and BLM signs to help direct you. The Book Cliffs offers a challenging landscape. There are large ridges with steep canyons dividing them. Most of the canyons and ridges have roads or ATV trails to provide access. There are plenty of areas to hike and get away from the main roads. The hunting pressure will drastically decrease after opening weekend. There are two roads that allow you to drive across the majority of the Book Cliffs. The Kings Well Rd starts at the Seep Ridge Rd on the west side, and it can take you all the way to the Dragon Rd on the east side. The Indian Ridge Road starts at the Seep Ridge Rd and goes through the bottom of Sweet Water, top of McCook Ridge, Bitter Creek, and to Big Park. It is a great road to locate cougars during this time of year. ","PRIV_TRIBE_LAND_ISSUES":"The boundary excludes all of the Tribal Trust Lands. Bighorn Sheep: Most roads and ATV trails on this unit are managed by the BLM and are covered on its Travel Management Plan. There are only a few roads that go on or near bighorn sheep habitat on the unit. The Hastings Road just east of the Green River in the town of Green River will take you along the east side of the Green River for about 15 miles until the road dead-ends near Rattlesnake Canyon. This road will provide the closest access to where most of the sheep live. This road is graded by the county and is generally in good shape. There are some tight spots along the river that you should be wary of if there is snowy or icy conditions. The Tushar Canyon road will go northeast off of the Hastings Road about 9 miles north of the town of Green River. It will access the right and left fork of Tushar Canyon and loop around along the bench to the east and provide access to Coal, Horse, and Floy Canyons. The Coal Canyon Road is the first right hand turn off of the Hastings Road while still in the town of Green River. It will go through a bunch of alfalfa fields and then up on the cliffs. the Horse Canyon and Floy Canyon roads can be access by following the frontage road along I-70 to the east. Despite all of these directions, most of your time will be spent on foot.

Deer: The main areas with the highest concentrations of deer include Nash Wash (Exit 204 off of Interstate 70), Cottonwood Canyon (Exit 214), Hay Canyon (Exit 221), and Bitter Creek (Exit 227)

Pronghorn: Use any exit off of Interstate 70 or drive the frontage road along the Interstate. Major access points include Green River (Exit 164), Floy Wash (Exit 175), Crescent Junction, Thompson, Yellowcat, Nash Wash (Exit 204), Cottonwood (Exit 214), Sulphur Canyon (Exit 221), and Bitter Creek (Exit 227)","PRIV_TRIBE_LAND_ISSUES":"Bighorn Sheep: The northern boundary of this unit adjoins Ute Tribal lands along Coal Creek. This is good bighorn sheep habitat and bighorns have been seen on both sides of the boundary near the mouth of Coal Creek. Take great care not to hunt or trespass on these tribal lands. The upper Tribal Boundary at upper elevations near Sego Canyon generally doesn't have bighorn sheep during November. There are small isolated pieces of private property in the mouths of Coal, Horse, Floy, and Thompson Canyons. County roads go through these properties so it is best to simply travel through them and park on public lands if you do not have written permission to hunt on these private lands. Bighorn sheep generally do not spend a great deal of time on these private lands.

Pronghorn: There is a large block of private land on the alfalfa fields near the town of Green River. Antelope use this area. Please secure written permission prior to hunting these private lands. The remainder of the private lands on this unit either do not occur in Pronghorn habitat or are scattered and unmarked.

Deer: Deer concentrate on private lands at the mouths of Cottonwood, Hay, and Bitter Creek Canyons. Please secure written permission prior to hunting these private lands. They are relatively small parcels so they are easy to avoid but they do concentrate deer. Elk: The major access points for elk hunting will be the Bruin Point road which is accessed via SR-123 through the town of Sunnyside, the Argyle Canyon road near the top of the summit of US-191 between Price and Duchesne, and the Nine Mile Canyon road out of the town of Wellington.

Pockets of private lands can be found in lower Coal Creek near Wellington, and portions of Icelander Wash southwest of Sunnyside.

Mule Deer and elk: the vast majority of the high elevation summer and fall habitat is on private land. There are a few small pockets of public land that can be found on the Cold Springs WMA east of Sunnyside, Cottonwood Ridge, and Harmon Canyon. Make sure you have a map or GPS depicting land ownership as there is an abundance of private land and it is essential that you know where you are.

Bison: A large part of the area where bison reside in Range Creek is managed by the Natural History Museum of Utah. hunt_bio_general_information: ****IMPORTANT NOTICE-PLEASE READ*** On September 12, 2023 a tamarisk removal project will begin in the Willow Creek drainage of the Book Cliffs and run for approximately 10 weeks. Hunters should be advised that work will be conducted with chainsaws and they may be heard for a short distance from the project location. Please plan accordingly and if you have further questions, contact the Vernal UDWR office: (435)781-9453. The Book Cliffs antelope population has been steadily declining since 1998. It could be from a combination of drought, predation, and interspecific competition. It is a still a good place to draw a permit. It is such a large area that hunter competition is really low. I would put a significant effort into pre-season scouting on this unit. Don't be afraid to ask the oil field workers where they have been seeing pronghorn. They drive the roads that go right through prime antelope habitat every day and can be a great resource. I would work on locating water sources, placing trail cameras, and selecting a site for a ground blind. Unless it rains which has been a rare occurrence, antelope have to come to water. It is an extremely fun hunt, and you can see antelope all throughout the day. Spot and stalk techniques are effective as well. The pronghorn are used to vehicle traffic because of all the oil and gas production in the area. They rely on their eye sight and speed to avoid predation. As long as they don't see anything out of the ordinary they are fairly docile, and calm.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of hunters choose to hunt close to the Seep Ridge Road on the north end of the unit. After the road crosses the White River you are on the unit. Once you cross the river and are off of Tribal land I would start focusing your efforts there. There are several wide open flats with folding hills that antelope prefer. The Glen Bench Road is the first major road that takes you back to the east. I wouldn't be deterred from all of the oil field traffic. The oil field workers spend a lot of time driving through prime antelope habitat, and can provide some great scouting tips. On the west side of the unit there is a large open area called Wild Horse Bench. It is a popular place for antelope, elk, wild horses, livestock, and some deer. I have seen antelope in this area, but it is a large area and sometimes they are difficult to locate. I don't think it receives very much hunting pressure. Winter Ridge is an area with sparse antelope, but receives very little hunting pressure. Migration Patterns: The Book Cliffs antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. During the past decade of drought, the poor maintenance condition of many of these artificial water sources limited their effectiveness. Repairs have been made and are continuing. Natural gas and oil production is rapidly increasing on pronghorn range with subsequent vegetative removal limiting both forage availability and habitat effectiveness. Habitat loss and disturbance associated with drilling and other energy extraction activities may be a significant factor affecting pronghorn populations. I have seen antelope shade up during the day under the large tanks on oil well pads. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers in the more arid areas on the northern part of the unit. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope in the Book Cliffs is 12-18 head. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. There are no service stations for many miles. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice. The Book Cliffs has a high bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or call the local dispatch center (435 789-4222).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

The pronghorn population on this unit has fluctuated dramatically over the years depending on drought conditions but has always provided quality buck hunting. This unit, also known as the Cisco unit, has a sizable pronghorn herd with plenty of opportunity. There are only a few archery permits so hunters will have tens of thousands of acres to themselves. Hunting on water generally works best for the archery hunt, however be aware that monsoon storms often begin in early August and disperse pronghorn away from guzzlers or ponds they had been using all summer.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: I find most of the antelope between the Cottonwood drainage and the Colorado border. Although there are pronghorn in lower densities on the western half of the unit as well. Antelope are found in the low desert country between the Interstate and the lowest band of cliffs along the Book Cliffs. They generally don't wander up in to the sagebrush habitats above the first cliff layer. Depending on the year and how much rain we have received, hunting near water sources is generally a good idea. There are numerous ponds as well as guzzlers spread across the unit. Antelope activity tends to be highest in the morning hours extending until mid-morning. They generally lie down during the heat of the day and are more difficult to detect. Evening activity doesn't seem to be as prominent as mornings because temperatures tend to still be quite high. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope in the Book Cliffs is 12-18 head. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for hot weather so bring plenty of water. There are very few reliable sources of water out there. There are gas stations at Thompson, Utah and Fruita Colorado which are approximately 50 miles apart. Make sure your gas tank is full when you leave civilization. Monsoon rains and flash flooding is fairly common in August and September. Many washes become impassible during or after rainstorms causing long detours or waiting for conditions to improve. Cell Service is spotty and best along the freeway.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is primarily characterized by wide desert valleys separated by steep mountain ranges. The valleys are desert shrub and salt flats, with greasewood. The valleys transition into grassy foothills, made up primarily of cheatgrass. The higher benches have bunchgrass and sagebrush. The mid elevations are juniper woodlands. The tallest elevations have junipers and pinyon pines, with pockets of conifers and aspens. This unit primarily consists of three mountain ranges, Lakesides, Grassy and Greyback mountains. Most pronghorn will found in the narrow bench of these mountain ranges and the valleys between them, often within two miles of a water source.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has a low density of pronghorn. A hunter needs to plan to cover many miles to locate groups of pronghorn. During the hunts, bucks will be with groups of does. Most hunters harvest a mature buck with 13" horns. A few bucks will be in the 14 and 15" tall range. A hunter will have to look over many bucks to find one over 13". Plan to cover most of the unit in search of pronghorn, focusing on the grassy benches. Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are a fairly easy animal to locate. Scouting is very important, there are many guzzlers and livestock troughs spread out across the entire unit, these guzzlers and troughs can be an excellent place to set up blinds. Areas where there are pronghorn will more than likely have a guzzler or some water sources nearby. Trail cameras have become very popular over the last several years and they can be a great way to see what type of bucks are coming into water sources. Behavior: The early mornings and evenings are the best times to find pronghorn, but pronghorn can still be fairly easy to find throughout the day, however the mid-day heat waves can make it harder to find them and especially to field judge bucks. Pronghorn rut: There will typically be rutting activity starting in late August, with the peak of the rut being in September. They will be rutting during the any weapon hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "In-reach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. It is a good idea to have lots of drinking water, two spare tires and extra fuel with you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Thunderstorms can cause muddy road conditions and rare flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with keeping their harvest meat cool. Expect hot weather and plan accordingly.

There is a pronghorn CWMU on the southern part of the unit that cannot be hunted on with this permit. There are areas with higher concentrations of pronghorn, however, pronghorn can be found scattered throughout the unit. The any weapon hunt is a great time to hunt pronghorn. The weather is still warm and water can still be a decent place to focus. Some areas have lots of dips that can hide pronghorn and others are flat for a long way. While driving roads can be productive you should also plan to spend time glassing to locate pronghorn.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for hot weather. Watch for snakes. Bring plenty of fuel and water. Roads can get slick after a storm.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is warm during this hunt. Rain and thunderstorms are likely to happen.

hunt_bio_general_information: This herd is doing great, with many bucks available for harvest. With a limited number of archery permits on the unit, hunter competition is low. I would put effort into pre-season scouting on this unit. Don't be afraid to ask the oil field workers where they have been seeing pronghorn. They drive the roads that go right through prime pronghorn habitat every day and can be a great resource. I would work on locating water sources, placing trail cameras, and selecting areas with good vantage points for glassing. Unless it rains, antelope have to come to water. It is an extremely fun hunt, and you can see antelope all throughout the day. Spot and stalk techniques are effective. Antelope rely on their eye sight and speed to avoid predation. As long as they don't see anything out of the ordinary they are fairly docile and calm, so be stealthy.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The South Cisco antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. Natural gas and oil production is increasing on pronghorn range with subsequent vegetative removal limiting both forage availability and habitat effectiveness. Habitat loss and disturbance associated with drilling and other energy extraction activities may be a significant factor affecting pronghorn populations. I would focus on rises that overlook rangelands below. During late summer bucks will be joining small herds of does, preparing for the rut. Glassing these large areas can be very productive. Glassing water sources is also a productive way to locate antelope. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Buck pronghorn are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see a lot of large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope on the South Cisco unit is 10 - 20 head. Antelope are active throughout the day, but like most wildlife species, they are increasingly active just before sunrise and sunset. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp/hunt and when you will return. Flash floods can occur during inclement weather, watch the sky and plan accordingly.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are a fairly easy animal to locate. For archery hunts scouting is important, there are many guzzlers spread out across the entire unit, these guzzlers can be an excellent place to set up blinds. Areas where there are pronghorn will more than likely have a guzzler or some water sources nearby. Trail cameras have become very popular over the last several years and they can be a great way to see what type of bucks are coming into water sources. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find pronghorn, but pronghorn can still be fairly easy to find throughout the whole day. Pronghorn rut: There will typically be rutting activity starting in August, with the peak of the rut being in September. They will be rutting during the any weapon hunt. Recommended areas Anthro Unit from West to East: Anthro Mountain Areas- There are a few groups of pronghorn that live in the higher elevations in the summer and early fall. There are fewer animals in these areas, but it can be a pretty place to hunt. Some areas to try are the following: Wire Fence Ridge, Nutter's Ridge, Jeep Trail, Alkaline Ridge(Best), and Choke Cherry(Good). Wells Draw- Starting just South of Pleasant Valley on BLM property. Lots of pronghorn in this area, there are many roads and well pads. Sand Wash Road- Anywhere along this road and all side roads can hold pronghorn Little Desert- There aren't a lot of pronghorn in this area, there are several guzzlers that should have pronghorn near them. Eight Mile Flat- lots of oil field activity, great area to glass.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt will typically be hot and dry. Be prepared with coolers and ice to cool the meat and cape.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit encompasses low elevation desert and higher mountainous sagebrush terrain, with the pronghorn distributed throughout the unit. Road access is good throughout the unit, with one area-Bare Top-closed to motorized vehicles. There is a migration study occurring to look at winter habitat use; it's asked that collared animals not be harvested if possible.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are fairly habitual and can be found in the same general area from late summer through the hunt. Pronghorn are best scouted from a distance using a spotting scope or binoculars so they don't leave the area. They are most active in the morning and evening when the temperatures are cooler; these are the best times to scout. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time they are in desert scrub/sagebrush flat areas. If the weather is extremely hot, they will often seek shade during the middle part of the day. Pronghorn are herd animals. You will often see groups of does and fawns with only a few bucks mixed in during the fall. During the rut, bucks will separate from other males to find does to mate with. The rest of the year, the bucks are usually with other pronghorn. Buck vs Doe: Hunters can tell bucks from does by several characteristics. Bucks will have larger horns and a black cheek patch. Pronghorn rut: The pronghorn rut usually starts the end of September so it does not really affect the hunt. Where to find pronghorn: 90% of the pronghorn are found on public lands in desert scrub and sagebrush flat areas. They typically stay out of heavily treed and cliffy areas. Pronghorn are found near water sources. Recommended areas in the Three Corners/West Daggett: Good areas to hunt include Clay Basin, Goslin Mountain, Antelope Flat, Bare Top, and Lucerne Valley. Very few pronghorn are found in Browns Park.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October.

hunt_bio_general_information: This pronghorn population is thriving at this time and this can be a very fun hunt. Landownership is 65% private and 35% BLM/SITLA.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn are concentrated on the northern part of this unit in the area north of Antelope Road up to the northern boundary, the Lund Road. Pronghorn can also be found south of the Antelope Road in the area west of Desert Mound out to the Antelope Range. Scout around water sources. Be mindful of private land and respect it. Keep closed gates closed!
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm dry conditions most years. Day time temperatures will be into the 80-90's Be prepared to quarter you animal and get it on ice as soon as possible to ensure you do not waste any meat.

hunt_bio_general_information: Pronghorn are below objective on this unit due to drought but there are numerous roads traversing the area that allow you to see a lot of country to find them. There is opportunity to find antelope throughout the day but like other wildlife they are more active in the morning and evening. There are also many opportunities around cultivated agricultural areas to harvest. This is a great place to hunt having local communities nearby.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Rangeland that borders private agricultural land are good places to hunt especially around the agricultural communities of Wellington, Elmo, and Cleveland. Other hunting areas include, Furniture Draw, Mounds, The Red Ledges area, and south and west of SR6 to Woodside. There are fewer pronghorn to the west of SR6 between Woodside and I-70. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types and into the pinion-juniper zone around the San Rafael Swell and Cedar Mountain. Annual precipitation in this area generally varies from 6 to 12 inches in these vegetation types. Scouting Tips: Binoculars and a good spotting scope are essential companions when hunting. Spend time prior to the hunt getting to know where the pronghorn are. Intensify the scouting efforts leading up to the hunt opening. Pronghorn are most active in the mornings and evenings but can be hunted all day. There are numerous roads on this unit that allow you to see a lot of country. Locating water sources like springs and livestock ponds, setting up blinds or spot and stalk are good hunting strategies; look for tracks and scratch marks where they are marking territories especially on the dirt roads. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same area if water is available unless he is run off or water is scarce. Look for vantage points where you can glass at rangelands below. Bucks are differentiated from does by larger horns and a black cheek patch. They are very curious and sometimes will come closer to you if they cannot figure out what you are. Behavior: San Rafael herds do not migrate long distances, they stay in a general area throughout the year. During the rut larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd depending on food resources. There can be as many as 12-18 in a herd in late summer and fall. As the rut nears mature bucks will separate from one another and look for does. Keep a look out because other bucks may be around the area when a buck is herded up with his does. Later after the rut other bucks join in with some of these smaller herds, which then join together with other herds to make larger wintering herds. There always seems to be solitary bucks and smaller buck herds around throughout all the seasons of the year. Bucks like to make scrapes on dirt roads defending their territory and warn off other competing bucks. They are very fast, and except for fawns they can outrun all their natural predators; their eyes are situated to allow about 300-degrees of visibility, and they can see and detect movement 4 miles away.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Use common sense. Let others know where you will be hunting, camped, etc. Some have been stranded by flat tires, very muddy conditions, flash floods, etc. Carry a survival kit. Most areas have fair cell phone coverage but not all. Consider hand held radios and a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Be prepared for inclement weather, it can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Keep abreast of the weather forecast. Expect and prepare for unfavorable weather conditions such as high temperatures, intense thunder storms, lightning, flash floods, and muddy roads that are difficult to travel even with chains.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit is located in low elevation desert. Much of the unit has been heavily impacted by oil and gas development so there are a lot of roads in the unit where pronghorn can be seen from.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are fairly habitual and can be found in the same general area from late summer through the hunt. Pronghorn are best scouted from a distance using a spotting scope or binoculars so they don't leave the area. They are most active in the morning and evening when the temperatures are cooler. This area has been heavily impacted by energy development. There are a lot of roads from the energy development so hunters should have no problem finding pronghorn. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time they are in desert scrub/sagebrush flat areas. If the weather is extremely hot, they will often seek shade during the middle part of the day. Pronghorn are herd animals. You will often see groups of does and fawns with only a few bucks mixed in during the fall. During the rut, bucks will separate from other males to find does to mate with. The rest of the year, the bucks are usually with other pronghorn. Buck vs Doe: Hunters can tell bucks from does by several characteristics. Bucks will have larger horns and a black cheek patch. Pronghorn rut: The pronghorn rut usually starts the end of September so it does not really affect the hunt. Where to find pronghorn: 90% of the pronghorn are found on public lands in desert scrub and sagebrush flat areas. They typically stay out of heavily treed and cliffy areas. Pronghorn are found near water sources. Pronghorn are not typically found on Diamond Mountain. Recommended areas in the Bonanza/Diamond Mtn: Good areas to hunt include Deadman Bench, Coyote Basin, Glen Bench, and Snake John. Diamond Mountain subunit is not recommended due to either no or very few pronghorn.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is good on this hunt unit. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes.

hunt_bio_general_information: It is such a large area that hunter competition is really low. I would put a significant effort into pre-season scouting on this unit. Don't be afraid to ask the oil field workers where they have been seeing pronghorn. They drive the roads that go right through prime antelope habitat every day and can be a great resource. I would work on locating water sources, placing trail cameras, and selecting a site for a ground blind. Unless it rains which has been a rare occurrence, antelope have to come to water. It is an extremely fun hunt, and you can see antelope all throughout the day. Spot and stalk techniques are effective as well. The pronghorn are used to vehicle traffic because of all the oil and gas production in the area. They rely on their eye sight and speed to avoid predation. As long as they don't see anything out of the ordinary they are fairly docile, and calm.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The Vernal antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. During the past decade of drought, the poor maintenance condition of many of these artificial water sources limited their effectiveness. Repairs have been made and are continuing. Natural gas and oil production is rapidly increasing on pronghorn range with subsequent vegetative removal limiting both forage availability and habitat effectiveness. Habitat loss and disturbance associated with drilling and other energy extraction activities may be a significant factor affecting pronghorn populations. I have seen antelope shade up during the day under the large tanks on oil well pads. I would focus on rangeland that boarder's private agricultural land. During late summer agricultural fields are essential for large herds of antelope. The Ashlee Oil Field holds large groups of antelope. Hwy 88 near the Hwy 40 intersection is a great place to look. North of the Green River there are large salt desert shrub communities. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers in the more arid areas on the northern part of the unit. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope in the Book Cliffs is 12-18 head. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: This pronghorn population has been doing very well over the past few years and is currently on an increasing trend. Pronghorn stick primarily to the open valleys across the unit. In some locations they will use areas with some scattered juniper. This season overlaps with Limited Entry elk seasons and the elk and pronghorn habitats overlap. Expect some overlap with elk hunters in Hamlin and Pine Valley south of Highway 21.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn can be found in all the valleys on this unit. Densities are much higher in areas south of Highway 21. The largest portion of the population can be found in the Escalante Valley area between the Lund Road and the Shauntie Hills. Pronghorn can also be found in Wah wah, Pine, Antelope,Hamilin, Ferguson Desert Sevier Lake valleys and the Cricket Mountains. Pronghorn typically spend most of there time on the benches of the valleys and not in the bottoms. Hunting near water could be the key to success.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is primarily characterized by wide desert valleys separated by steep mountain ranges. The valleys are desert shrub and salt flats, with greasewood. The valleys transition into grassy foothills, made up primarily of cheatgrass. The higher benches have bunchgrass and sagebrush. The mid elevations are juniper woodlands. The tallest elevations have junipers and pinyon pines, with pockets of conifers and aspens. This unit primarily consists of the following mountain ranges - Stansbury, Dugway, Cedar, Keg, Desert, and Simpson. Most pronghorn will found in the narrow bench of these mountain ranges and the valleys, often within two miles of a water source.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has a lot of pronghorn, however they are in low densities. A hunter needs to plan to cover many miles to locate groups of pronghorn. During the hunts, bucks will be with groups of does. Most hunters harvest a mature buck with 13" horns. A few bucks will be in the 14 and 15" tall range. A hunter will have to look over many bucks to find one over 13". Plan to cover most of the unit in search of pronghorn, focusing on the grassy benches. Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are a fairly easy animal to locate. Scouting is very important, there are many guzzlers and livestock troughs spread out across the entire unit, these guzzlers and troughs can be an excellent place to set up blinds. Areas where there are pronghorn will more than likely have a guzzler or some water sources nearby. Trail cameras have become very popular over the last several years and they can be a great way to see what type of bucks are coming into water sources. Behavior: The early mornings and evenings are the best times to find pronghorn, but pronghorn can still be fairly easy to find throughout the day, however the mid-day heat waves can make it harder to find them and especially to field judge bucks. Pronghorn rut: There will typically be rutting activity starting in late August, with the peak of the rut being in September. They will be rutting during the any weapon hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "In-reach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. It is a good idea to have a lot of drinking water, two spare tires and extra fuel with you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Thunderstorms can cause muddy road conditions and rare flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with keeping their harvest meat cool. Expect hot weather and plan accordingly.

Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are a fairly easy animal to locate. For archery hunts scouting is important, there are many guzzlers spread out across the entire unit, these guzzlers can be an excellent place to set up blinds. Areas where there are pronghorn will more than likely have a guzzler or some water sources nearby. Trail cameras have become very popular over the last several years and they can be a great way to see what type of bucks are coming into water sources. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find pronghorn, but pronghorn can still be fairly easy to find throughout the whole day. Pronghorn rut: There will typically be rutting activity starting in August, with the peak of the rut being in September. They will be rutting during the any weapon hunt.

The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "In-reach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. It is a good idea to have lots of drinking water, two spare tires and extra fuel with you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: he weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Thunderstorms can cause muddy road conditions and rare flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with keeping their harvest meat cool. Expect hot weather and plan accordingly.

Pronghorn stick primarily to the open valleys across the unit. In some locations they will use areas with some scattered juniper. This season overlaps with Limited Entry elk seasons and the elk and pronghorn habitats overlap. Expect some overlap with elk hunters in Hamlin and Pine Valley south of Highway 21.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn can be found in all the valleys on this unit. Densities are much higher in areas south of Highway 21. The largest portion of the population can be found in the Escalante Valley area between the Lund Road and the Shauntie Hills. Pronghorn can also be found in Wah wah, Pine, Antelope,Hamilin, Ferguson Desert Sevier Lake valleys and the Cricket Mountains. Pronghorn typically spend most of there time on the benches of the valleys and not in the bottoms. Hunting near water could be the key to success.
