hunt_bio_general_information: The Book Cliffs antelope population has been steadily declining since 1998. It could be from a combination of drought, predation, and interspecific competition. It is a still a good place to draw a permit. It is such a large area that hunter competition is really low. I would put a significant effort into pre-season scouting on this unit. Don't be afraid to ask the oil field workers where they have been seeing pronghorn. They drive the roads that go right through prime antelope habitat every day and can be a great resource. I would work on locating water sources. Unless it rains which has been a rare occurrence, antelope have to come to water. It is an extremely fun hunt, and you can see antelope all throughout the day.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of hunters choose to hunt close to the Seep Ridge Road on the north end of the unit. After the road crosses the White River you are on the unit. Once you cross the river and are off of Tribal land I would start focusing your efforts there. There are several wide open flats with folding hills that antelope prefer. The Glen Bench Road is the first major road that takes you back to the east. I wouldn't be deterred from all of the oil field traffic. The oil field workers spend a lot of time driving through prime antelope habitat, and can provide some great scouting tips. On the west side of the unit there is a large open area called Wild Horse Bench. It is a popular place for antelope, elk, wild horses, livestock, and some deer. I have seen antelope in this area, but it is a large area and sometimes they are difficult to locate. I don't think it receives very much hunting pressure. Winter Ridge is an area with sparse antelope, but receives very little hunting pressure. Migration Patterns: The Book Cliffs antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. During the past decade of drought, the poor maintenance condition of many of these artificial water sources limited their effectiveness. Repairs have been made and are continuing. Natural gas and oil production is rapidly increasing on pronghorn range with subsequent vegetative removal limiting both forage availability and habitat effectiveness. Habitat loss and disturbance associated with drilling and other energy extraction activities may be a significant factor affecting pronghorn populations. I have seen antelope shade up during the day under the large tanks on oil well pads. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers in the more arid areas on the northern part of the unit. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope in the Book Cliffs is 12-18 head. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. The Book Cliffs mountain range is one of the more remote areas in Utah. There are no service stations for many miles. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice. The Book Cliffs has a high bear population. Keep a clean camp and put your garbage in a place that is inaccessible to bears. If you do have problems with bears please report them to the DWR Northeastern Regional Office as soon as possible (435 781-9453), or call the local dispatch center (435 789-4222).
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: I find most of the antelope between the Cottonwood drainage and the Colorado border. Although there are pronghorn in lower densities on the western half of the unit as well. Antelope are found in the low desert country between the Interstate and the lowest band of cliffs along the Book Cliffs. They generally don't wander up in to the sagebrush habitats above the first cliff layer. Depending on the year and how much rain we have received, hunting near water sources is generally a good idea. There are numerous ponds as well as guzzlers spread across the unit. Antelope activity tends to be highest in the morning hours extending until mid-morning. They generally lie down during the heat of the day and are more difficult to detect. Evening activity doesn't seem to be as prominent as mornings because temperatures tend to still be quite high. Migration Patterns: The Book Cliffs antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. During the past decade of drought, the poor maintenance condition of many of these artificial water sources limited their effectiveness. Repairs have been made and are continuing. Natural gas and oil production is rapidly increasing on pronghorn range with subsequent vegetative removal limiting both forage availability and habitat effectiveness. Habitat loss and disturbance associated with drilling and other energy extraction activities may be a significant factor affecting pronghorn populations. I have seen antelope shade up during the day under the large tanks on oil well pads. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope in the Book Cliffs is 12-18 head. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches. General Information: This is a good hunt unit with excellent access. The pronghorn population on this unit has fluctuated dramatically over the years depending on drought conditions but has always provided quality buck hunting.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for hot weather so bring plenty of water. There are very few reliable sources of water out there. There are gas stations at Thompson, Utah and Fruita Colorado which are approximately 50 miles apart. Make sure your gas tank is full when you leave civilization. Monsoon rains and flash flooding is fairly common in August and September. Many washes become impassible during or after rainstorms causing long detours or waiting for conditions to improve. Cell Service is spotty and best along the freeway.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn in this unit are primarily found on private land near cultivated agriculture. Make sure to obtain written permission to hunt on private land before entering. hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Caution should be used when taking aim at pronghorn in this unit to ensure a safe backstop. Long range shots are common when pursuing pronghorn and animals in this unit will be on or near agricultural fields. Cell phone coverage is good in this area but not complete. Ensure that someone else knows where you plan on camping and hunting, and when you will be returning. Nearest services are in Tremonton, Corinne, or Snowville.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until the first week of December.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is primarily characterized by wide desert valleys separated by steep mountain ranges. The valleys are desert shrub and salt flats, with greasewood. The valleys transition into grassy foothills, made up primarily of cheatgrass. The higher benches have bunchgrass and sagebrush. The mid elevations are juniper woodlands. The tallest elevations have junipers and pinyon pines, with pockets of conifers and aspens. This unit primarily consists of three mountain ranges, Lakesides, Grassy and Greyback mountains. Most pronghorn will found in the narrow bench of these mountain ranges and the valleys between them, often within two miles of a water source.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has a low density of pronghorn. A hunter needs to plan to cover many miles to locate groups of pronghorn. During the hunts, bucks will be with groups of does. Most hunters harvest a mature buck with 13" horns. A few bucks will be in the 14 and 15" tall range. A hunter will have to look over many bucks to find one over 13". Plan to cover most of the unit in search of pronghorn, focusing on the grassy benches. Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are a fairly easy animal to locate. Scouting is very important, there are many guzzlers and livestock troughs spread out across the entire unit, these guzzlers and troughs can be an excellent place to set up blinds. Areas where there are pronghorn will more than likely have a guzzler or some water sources nearby. Trail cameras have become very popular over the last several years and they can be a great way to see what type of bucks are coming into water sources. Behavior: The early mornings and evenings are the best times to find pronghorn, but pronghorn can still be fairly easy to find throughout the day, however the mid-day heat waves can make it harder to find them and especially to field judge bucks. Pronghorn rut: There will typically be rutting activity starting in late August, with the peak of the rut being in September. They will be rutting during the any weapon hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "In-reach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. It is a good idea to have lots of drinking water, two spare tires and extra fuel with you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Thunderstorms can cause muddy road conditions and rare flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with keeping their harvest meat cool. Expect hot weather and plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: Approximately 50% of this unit where pronghorn can be found is private property. Hunters should obtain written permission to access private lands before entering. One pronghorn CWMU exists on this unit. No hunting is allowed on CWMUs without the appropriate permit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time they are in desert scrub/sagebrush flat areas. If the weather is extremely hot, they will often seek shade during the middle part of the day. Pronghorn are herd animals. You will often see groups of does and fawns with only a few bucks mixed in during the fall. During the rut, bucks will separate from other males to find does. 50% of the pronghorn are found on public lands in desert scrub and sagebrush flat areas. The other half can be found near irrigated agricultural areas. They typically stay out of heavily treed and cliffy areas. Pronghorn are found near water sources. Good areas to hunt include east Pilot Mtn near TL Bar Ranch, Lucin, Winter Cabin Road, South of Goose Creek, Yost, Rosebud, and Curlew Junction.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Caution should be used when taking aim at pronghorn in this unit to ensure a safe backstop. Long range shots are common when pursuing pronghorn and animals in this unit will be on or near agricultural fields. Cell phone coverage is spotty in this area. Ensure that someone else knows where you plan on camping and hunting, and when you will be returning. Nearest services are in Grouse Creek, Montello, Nevada, Wendover, Utah/Nevada, Oakley, Idaho, or Almo, Idaho.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until the first week of December.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a good unit with decent access in many places. The pronghorn population has been increasing steadily over the last several years.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There are a few groups of pronghorn north of highway 50, though most of those are often on private land. Written permission would need to be obtained before hunting private land. Most of the pronghorn are found south of highway 50. There is a pronghorn CWMU on the southern part of the unit that cannot be hunted on with this permit. There are areas with higher concentrations of pronghorn, however, pronghorn can be found scattered throughout the unit. The any weapon hunt is a great time to hunt pronghorn. The weather is still warm and water can still be a decent place to focus. Some areas have lots of dips that can hide pronghorn and others are flat for a long way. While driving roads can be productive you should also plan to spend time glassing to locate pronghorn.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Roads can get slick after a rain storm. Bring plenty of water and fuel.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather is a little cooler than it was during the archery hunt, though lighting and rain storms are still possible.

hunt_bio_general_information: The pronghorn population on the Kaiparowits exists on the East Clark Bench area near Big Water, UT. This population is limited to the north and east by the cliffs on the Grand Staircase Escalante National Monument. There is a large tract of SITLA lands on the south side of US89 where the population may extend slightly into Arizona. Eastern movements are limited by the Cockscomb but some pronghorn may move west beyond the Paria River onto the Paunsaugunt unit. Overall, this desert population is composed of 50-70 individuals that are usually found in low densities. Arid conditions may cause small groups to form around man-made water sources. Recruitment is generally limited by summer precipitation conditions.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of hunters choose to hunt near Cottonwood Creek east to Wahweap Creek on the north side of US89. Pronghorn densities are lower on the south side of US89 but typically they can be found closer to the AZ border. Be prepared with a GPS to know where the stateline exists. This area is composed mostly of public lands but pronghorn may be found on private lands near Church Wells, UT. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers in the more arid areas of the unit. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of ephemeral pools or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Kaiparowits unit offers substantial truck and ATV access which is highly dependent on weather. Much of this area is inaccessible during wet conditions. A 4WD vehicle is highly recommended. Cellular phone coverage is spotty but many pronghorn areas offer some coverage. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: This herd is doing great, with many bucks available for harvest. With a fairly limited number of permits on the unit, hunter competition is low. I would put effort into pre-season scouting on this unit. Don't be afraid to ask the oil field workers where they have been seeing pronghorn. They drive the roads that go right through prime pronghorn habitat every day and can be a great resource. I would work on locating water sources, placing trail cameras, and selecting areas with good vantage points for glassing. Unless it rains, antelope have to come to water. It is an extremely fun hunt, and you can see antelope all throughout the day. Spot and stalk techniques are effective. Antelope rely on their eye sight and speed to avoid predation. As long as they don't see anything out of the ordinary they are fairly docile and calm, so be stealthy.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The South Cisco antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. Natural gas and oil production is increasing on pronghorn range with subsequent vegetative removal limiting both forage availability and habitat effectiveness. Habitat loss and disturbance associated with drilling and other energy extraction activities may be a significant factor affecting pronghorn populations. I would focus on rises that overlook rangelands below. During late summer bucks will be joining small herds of does, preparing for the rut. Glassing these large areas can be very productive. Glassing water sources is also a productive way to locate antelope. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Buck pronghorn are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see a lot of large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope on the South Cisco unit is 10 - 20 head. Antelope are active throughout the day, but like most wildlife species, they are increasingly active just before sunrise and sunset. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp/hunt and when you will return. Flash floods can occur during inclement weather, watch the sky and plan accordingly.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are a fairly easy animal to locate. For archery hunts scouting is important, there are many guzzlers spread out across the entire unit, these guzzlers can be an excellent place to set up blinds. Areas where there are pronghorn will more than likely have a guzzler or some water sources nearby. Trail cameras have become very popular over the last several years and they can be a great way to see what type of bucks are coming into water sources. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find pronghorn, but pronghorn can still be fairly easy to find throughout the whole day. Pronghorn rut: There will typically be rutting activity starting in August, with the peak of the rut being in September. They will be rutting during the any weapon hunt. Recommended areas Anthro Unit from West to East: Anthro Mountain Areas- There are a few groups of pronghorn that live in the higher elevations in the summer and early fall. There are fewer animals in these areas, but it can be a pretty place to hunt. Some areas to try are the following: Wire Fence Ridge, Nutter's Ridge, Jeep Trail, Alkaline Ridge(Best), and Choke Cherry(Good). Wells Draw- Starting just South of Pleasant Valley on BLM property. Lots of pronghorn in this area, there are many roads and well pads. Sand Wash Road- Anywhere along this road and all side roads can hold pronghorn Little Desert- There aren't a lot of pronghorn in this area, there are several guzzlers that should have pronghorn near them. Eight Mile Flat- lots of oil field activity, great area to glass.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather during this hunt will typically be hot and dry. Be prepared with coolers and ice to cool the meat and cape.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: I find most of the antelope in three areas; Coal Creek near Wellington, Clark's Valley southeast of Wellington, and Icelander Wash south of Sunnyside. Approximately 90% of the antelope we count from the ground or in the plane are found in these areas. There are a few scattered groups of antelope from Lila Canyon south to I-70 but they only represent about 10% of the population and I wouldn't spend a ton of time down there. It is best to get on a high point and glass the basins in each of these drainages for antelope. There are numerous stock ponds and guzzlers that tend to concentrate antelope. Many of the antelope on this unit are associated with the alfalfa fields. Hunting the public lands around these fields is generally pretty productive. Most of the antelope are found in the low desert country between SR-6 and the first band of trees you get to as you approach the cliffs. Antelope generally don't use the sagebrush areas found at upper elevations right below the cliffs on this unit. Antelope activity tends to be highest in the morning hours extending until mid-morning. They generally lie down during the heat of the day and are more difficult to detect. Evening activity doesn't seem to be as prominent as mornings because temperatures tend to still be quite high. Migration Patterns: This antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Look for antelope scat and scrapes in the road to give you an indication of areas where antelope may be using. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope on this unit is 12-18 head. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches. General Information: This is a good hunt with easy quick hunting access close to town. The private land issues are not as significant as you might think because most landowners will allow hunting if you ask first.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Monsoon rains and flash flooding is fairly common in August and September. Many washes become impassible during or after rainstorms causing long detours or waiting for conditions to improve. Cell service is pretty good and you are rarely farther than 5 miles from a paved road and are within 30 minutes of a Price or Green River.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is designed to allow a few hunters the opportunity to harvest a buck pronghorn near the Utah/Wyoming border. It is not a trophy opportunity but occasionally some very nice bucks are harvested.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Hoop Lake, Poison Mountain and Gregory Basin are often times the best areas to scout for these pronghorn. Hunters should plan ample time to locate mature bucks.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit encompasses low elevation desert and higher mountainous sagebrush terrain, with the pronghorn distributed throughout the unit. Road access is good throughout the unit, with one area-Bare Top-closed to motorized vehicles. There is a migration study occurring to look at winter habitat use; it's asked that collared animals not be harvested if possible.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are fairly habitual and can be found in the same general area from late summer through the hunt. Pronghorn are best scouted from a distance using a spotting scope or binoculars so they don't leave the area. They are most active in the morning and evening when the temperatures are cooler; these are the best times to scout. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time they are in desert scrub/sagebrush flat areas. If the weather is extremely hot, they will often seek shade during the middle part of the day. Pronghorn are herd animals. You will often see groups of does and fawns with only a few bucks mixed in during the fall. During the rut, bucks will separate from other males to find does to mate with. The rest of the year, the bucks are usually with other pronghorn. Buck vs Doe: Hunters can tell bucks from does by several characteristics. Bucks will have larger horns and a black cheek patch. Pronghorn rut: The pronghorn rut usually starts the end of September so it does not really affect the hunt. Where to find pronghorn: 90% of the pronghorn are found on public lands in desert scrub and sagebrush flat areas. They typically stay out of heavily treed and cliffy areas. Pronghorn are found near water sources. Recommended areas in the Three Corners/West Daggett: Good areas to hunt include Clay Basin, Goslin Mountain, Antelope Flat, Bare Top, and Lucerne Valley. Very few pronghorn are found in Browns Park.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October.

hunt_bio_general_information: The pronghorn population on the Panguitch Lake has been historically limited by winter range availability from SR20 south to Hatch. The majority of pronghorn winter from Panguitch to Hatch. Recent habitat treatments in the South Canyon area on BLM lands have substantially improved pronghorn wintering areas and year-round range resulting in an increasing trend in recruitment and higher overall population numbers. Summering areas include ponderosa pine habitats along the Mammoth Creek road south to Strawberry Valley on the Zion unit. There are also several pronghorn that summer north and east of Panguitch Lake in the Little Valleys area. Yearlong range can be found in the Sandy Creek / 3 Mile Creek area and Sage Hen Hollow.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The majority of hunters choose to hunt in the Sage Hen Hollow area but pronghorn may also be found closer to summer ranges. This population can frequently be found using forested areas not typically associated with traditional pronghorn life history accounts. Smaller bands of pronghorn may be found in sagebrush communities from SR 20 south to Panguitch. These pronghorn may also be using agricultural fields and permission should be acquired to hunt on private lands. Migration Patterns: The migratory segments of this population may begin their fall movements in late September and October. Migration from summer ranges may be dependent on fall storms and weather conditions. They can often be found in groups of 20 or less at this time. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers in the more arid areas of the unit. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of ephemeral pools or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The Panguitch Lake unit offers substantial truck and ATV access. Cellular phone coverage is spotty but many pronghorn areas offer good coverage. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Plan on bringing plenty of water, fuel, good tires with extra spares, and plenty of ice.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: This pronghorn population is thriving at this time and this can be a very fun hunt. Landownership is 65% private and 35% BLM/SITLA.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn are concentrated on the northern part of this unit in the area north of Antelope Road up to the northern boundary, the Lund Road. Pronghorn can also be found south of the Antelope Road in the area west of Desert Mound out to the Antelope Range. Scout around water sources. Be mindful of private land and respect it. Keep closed gates closed!
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm dry conditions most years. Day time temperatures will be into the 80-90's Be prepared to quarter you animal and get it on ice as soon as possible to ensure you do not waste any meat.

hunt_bio_general_information: In an effort to boost population numbers of this herd, 74 pronghorn were transplanted to the Hatch Point area from the Parker Plateau in 2014. You will more than likely see pronghorn with red collars or ear tags. These markers allow biologists to calculate a sightability index when conducting surveys. This index will help in fine-tuning population estimates. If you should harvest a pronghorn with one of these markers, please notify the Division of Wildlife Resources Southeast Region at 435-613-3700. With a very limited number of permits on the unit, hunter competition is low. I would put effort into pre-season scouting on this unit. Don't be afraid to ask the oil field workers or ranchers where they have been seeing pronghorn. They drive the roads that go right through prime antelope habitat every day and can be a great resource. I would work on locating water sources, placing trail cameras, and selecting areas with good vantage points for glassing. Unless it rains, antelope have to come to water. It is an extremely fun hunt, and you can see antelope all throughout the day. Spot and stalk techniques are effective. Antelope rely on their eye sight and speed to avoid predation. As long as they don't see anything out of the ordinary they are fairly docile and calm, so be stealthy.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The Hatch Point antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. I would focus on rises that overlook rangelands below. During late summer bucks will be joining small herds of does, preparing for the rut. Glassing these large areas can be very productive. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope on the Hatch Point unit is 8 - 12 head. Antelope are active throughout the day, but like most wildlife species, they are increasingly active just before sunrise and sunset. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp/hunt and when you will return. Flash floods can and do occur during inclement weather, watch the sky and plan accordingly.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: The San Rafael Desert pronghorn unit is large combining the South San Rafael and the Henry Mountain units. These units are combined because of small herd sizes distributed over large areas. Drought has impacted population numbers and herd distribution on this unit the past few years, especially east and west of SR24 between I-70 and Hanksville where most hunting has taken place in the past, so plan to expand your hunt area on the unit. There are numerous roads traversing the area allowing access to see a lot of country to find them. The popualtion is estimated at 250 animals and it will take covering a lot of country to find them. You can find antelope throughout the day but like other wildlife they are more active in the morning and evening.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit is located in low elevation desert. Much of the unit has been heavily impacted by oil and gas development so there are a lot of roads in the unit where pronghorn can be seen from.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn rut: The pronghorn rut usually starts the end of September so it does not really affect the hunt. Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are fairly habitual and can be found in the same general area from late summer through the hunt. Pronghorn are best scouted from a distance using a spotting scope or binoculars so they don't leave the area. They are most active in the morning and evening when the temperatures are cooler. This area has been heavily impacted by energy development. There are a lot of roads from the energy development so hunters should have no problem finding pronghorn. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time they are in desert scrub/sagebrush flat areas. If the weather is extremely hot, they will often seek shade during the middle part of the day. Pronghorn are herd animals. You will often see groups of does and fawns with only a few bucks mixed in during the fall. During the rut, bucks will separate from other males to find does to mate with. The rest of the year, the bucks are usually with other pronghorn. Buck vs Doe: Hunters can tell bucks from does by several characteristics. Bucks will have larger horns and a black cheek patch. Where to find pronghorn: 90% of the pronghorn are found on public lands in desert scrub and sagebrush flat areas. They typically stay out of heavily treed and cliffy areas. Pronghorn are found near water sources. Pronghorn are not typically found on Diamond Mountain. Recommended areas in the Bonanza/Diamond Mtn: Good areas to hunt include Deadman Bench, Coyote Basin, Glen Bench, and Snake John. Diamond Mountain subunit is not recommended due to either no or very few pronghorn.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is good on this hunt unit. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes.

hunt_bio_general_information: It is such a large area that hunter competition is really low. I would put a significant effort into pre-season scouting on this unit. Don't be afraid to ask the oil field workers where they have been seeing pronghorn. They drive the roads that go right through prime antelope habitat every day and can be a great resource. I would work on locating water sources, placing trail cameras. Unless it rains which has been a rare occurrence, antelope have to come to water. It is an extremely fun hunt, and you can see antelope all throughout the day. Spot and stalk techniques are effective as well. The pronghorn are used to vehicle traffic because of all the oil and gas production in the area. They rely on their eye sight and speed to avoid predation. As long as they don't see anything out of the ordinary they are fairly docile, and calm.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The Vernal antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. During the past decade of drought, the poor maintenance condition of many of these artificial water sources limited their effectiveness. Repairs have been made and are continuing. Natural gas and oil production is rapidly increasing on pronghorn range with subsequent vegetative removal limiting both forage availability and habitat effectiveness. Habitat loss and disturbance associated with drilling and other energy extraction activities may be a significant factor affecting pronghorn populations. I have seen antelope shade up during the day under the large tanks on oil well pads. I would focus on rangeland that boarder's private agricultural land. During late summer agricultural fields are essential for large herds of antelope. Ouray Valley and the Ashley Oil Field holds large groups of antelope. Hwy 88 near the Hwy 40 intersection is a great place to look. North of the Green River there are large salt desert shrub communities. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers in the more arid areas on the northern part of the unit. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope on the Vernal is 12-18 head. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: This pronghorn population has been doing very well over the past few years and is currently on an increasing trend. Pronghorn stick primarily to the open valleys across the unit. In some locations they will use areas with some scattered juniper. This season overlaps with Limited Entry elk seasons and the elk and pronghorn habitats overlap. Expect some overlap with elk hunters in Hamlin and Pine Valley south of Highway 21.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn can be found in all the valleys on this unit. Densities are much higher in areas south of Highway 21. The largest portion of the population can be found in the Escalante Valley area between the Lund Road and the Shauntie Hills. Pronghorn can also be found in Wah wah, Pine, Antelope,Hamilin, Ferguson Desert Sevier Lake valleys and the Cricket Mountains. Pronghorn typically spend most of there time on the benches of the valleys and not in the bottoms. Hunting near water could be the key to success.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Hunters should be prepared with extra gas and water this unit is remote and there are no services available. This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm and dry conditions though out most seasons on this unit. The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Usually warm temperatures and monsoonal moisture dominate the weather pattern. Be prepared for dry or muddy conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is primarily characterized by wide desert valleys separated by steep mountain ranges. The valleys are desert shrub and salt flats, with greasewood. The valleys transition into grassy foothills, made up primarily of cheatgrass. The higher benches have bunchgrass and sagebrush. The mid elevations are juniper woodlands. The tallest elevations have junipers and pinyon pines, with pockets of conifers and aspens. This unit primarily consists of the following mountain ranges - Stansbury, Dugway, Cedar, Keg, Desert, and Simpson. Most pronghorn will found in the narrow bench of these mountain ranges and the valleys, often within two miles of a water source.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has a lot of pronghorn, however they are in low densities. A hunter needs to plan to cover many miles to locate groups of pronghorn. During the hunts, bucks will be with groups of does. Most hunters harvest a mature buck with 13" horns. A few bucks will be in the 14 and 15" tall range. A hunter will have to look over many bucks to find one over 13". Plan to cover most of the unit in search of pronghorn, focusing on the grassy benches. Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are a fairly easy animal to locate. Scouting is very important, there are many guzzlers and livestock troughs spread out across the entire unit, these guzzlers and troughs can be an excellent place to set up blinds. Areas where there are pronghorn will more than likely have a guzzler or some water sources nearby. Trail cameras have become very popular over the last several years and they can be a great way to see what type of bucks are coming into water sources. Behavior: The early mornings and evenings are the best times to find pronghorn, but pronghorn can still be fairly easy to find throughout the day, however the mid-day heat waves can make it harder to find them and especially to field judge bucks. Pronghorn rut: There will typically be rutting activity starting in late August, with the peak of the rut being in September. They will be rutting during the any weapon hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "In-reach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. It is a good idea to have a lot of drinking water, two spare tires and extra fuel with you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Thunderstorms can cause muddy road conditions and rare flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with keeping their harvest meat cool. Expect hot weather and plan accordingly.

Most pronghorn will found in the narrow bench of these mountain ranges and the valleys, often within two miles of a water source.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has many pronghorn; however, they are in low densities. A hunter needs to plan to cover many miles to locate groups of pronghorn. During the hunts, bucks will be with groups of does. Most hunters harvest a mature buck with 13" horns. A few bucks will be in the 14 and 15" tall range. A hunter will have to look over many bucks to find one over 13". Plan to cover most of the unit in search of pronghorn, focusing on the grassy benches. Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are a fairly easy animal to locate. For archery hunts scouting is important, there are many guzzlers spread out across the entire unit, these guzzlers can be an excellent place to set up blinds. Areas where there are pronghorn will more than likely have a guzzler or some water sources nearby. Trail cameras have become very popular over the last several years and they can be a great way to see what type of bucks are coming into water sources. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find pronghorn, but pronghorn can still be fairly easy to find throughout the whole day. Pronghorn rut: There will typically be rutting activity starting in August, with the peak of the rut being in September. They will be rutting during the any weapon hunt.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" or "In-reach" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. It is a good idea to have lots of drinking water, two spare tires and extra fuel with you.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Thunderstorms can cause muddy road conditions and rare flash floods in this region. Most hunters struggle with keeping their harvest meat cool. Expect hot weather and plan accordingly.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a population of roughly 200 to 300 pronghorn residing on the thin strip of habitat between SR-6 and the Book Cliffs. The area is desert habitat with relatively few trees. Hunter densities are generally pretty low and there is plenty of public land to hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The antelope reside on the desert portion of this unit. Much of the unit boundary is not considered to be antelope habitat. Focus your efforts on area between SR-6 and the cliffs to the east. The vast majority of the antelope will be found in the Coal Creek, Clark's Valley, and Icelander Wash area. Antelope numbers diminish rapidly as you go south of Horse Canyon. Most of the area is public land although there are some private irrigated fields that will have antelope near the town of Wellington. Landowners have been amenable to letting antelope hunters trespass in the past. Please contact them before you go afield. Antelope will be found near water. Water is scarce throughout the summer while you are scouting and then suddenly becomes very abundant during the late summer monsoon season during your hunt. This can be frustrating.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be careful
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: August and September tend to be warm with frequent afternoon thunderstorms. Flash flooding in this desert unit is common during these months. Please plan ahead and be aware of approaching severe weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a new hunt started in 2017 so no harvest information is available from previous years. Pronghorn numbers both overall populations plus buck to doe ratios have increased in recent years this is why the hunt was proposed.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: We manage this unit at a high buck to doe ratio so many of the bucks on the unit are mature bucks. These pronghorn migrate from higher elevation sage flats and ponderosa forests to lower elevation sage hills. Pronghorn are often scattered throughout the unit. Spend a lot of time scouting and finding waterholes, this can be a good way to harvest a buck earlier in the hunt. Toward the end of the hunt bucks will be rutting so locating does, and spot and stalk/decoying could be good methods to harvest a pronghorn.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect hot days with cool mornings, this units elevations ranges from 6000-11000 feet. Often large thunderstorms hit the areas on summer afternoons accompanied by summer monsoons.

hunt_bio_general_information: The San Rafael Desert pronghorn unit is large combining the South San Rafael and the Henry Mountain units. These units are combined because of small herd sizes distributed over large areas. Drought has impacted population numbers and herd distribution on this unit the past few years, especially east and west of SR24 between I-70 and Hanksville where most hunting has taken place in the past, so plan to expand your hunt area on the unit. There are numerous roads traversing the area allowing access to see a lot of country to find them. The popualtion is estimated at 250 animals and it will take covering a lot of country to find them. You can find antelope throughout the day but like other wildlife they are more active in the morning and evening.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The following is not a comprehensive list of areas where you can find pronghorn on this unit. Pronghorn can still be found on both sides of SR24 between the San Rafael River and Fremont/Dirty Devil Rivers and between Goblin Valley, North Pinto Hills, and Factory bench, but it is becoming more difficult to find them. A small number of pronghorn also reside between the San Rafael river and the town of Green River. Also on the west side of the unit south of I-70 to the Last Chance Desert, Mussentuchit Flat, and Rock Springs Bench. And Sinbad areas on the top of the San Rafael Swell off exit 131 on I-70 from Mckay Flat to Jerry's Flat. Areas on the Henry Mountains portion of the unit include the South Pinto Hills, Blue Valley Benches, and the southern portion of the Henry's unit south of Cow Flat, Coal Bed Mesa, Clay Point, Bull Frog Creek, and Eggnog area. Pronghorn seen on the Burr Desert have been few. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types and into the pinion-juniper zone around the San Rafael Swell and Cedar Mountain. Annual precipitation in this area generally varies from 6 to 12 inches in these vegetation types. Scouting Tips: Binoculars and a good spotting scope are essential companions when hunting. Spend time prior to the hunt getting to know where the pronghorn are. along with your pre-season scouting its natural and good to intensify the effort leading up to the hunt opening. Pronghorn are most active in the mornings and evenings but can be hunted all day. There are numerous roads on this unit that allow you to see a lot of country. Locating water sources like springs and livestock ponds, setting up blinds or spot and stalk are good hunting strategies; look for tracks and scratch marks where they are marking territories especially on the dirt roads. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same area if water is available unless he is run off or water is scarce. Look for vantage points where you can glass at rangelands below. Bucks are differentiated from does by larger horns and a black cheek patch. They are very curious and sometimes will come closer to you if they cannot figure out what you are. Behavior: San Rafael herds do not migrate long distances, they stay in a general area throughout the year. During the rut larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd depending on food resources. There can be as many as 12-18 in a herd in late summer and fall. As the rut nears mature bucks will separate from one another and look for does. Keep a look out because other bucks may be around the area when a buck is herded up with his does. Later after the rut other bucks join in with some of these smaller herds, which then join together with other herds to make larger wintering herds. There always seems to be solitary bucks and smaller buck herds around throughout all the seasons of the year. Bucks like to make scrapes on dirt roads defending their territory and warn off other competing bucks. They are very fast, and except for fawns they can outrun all their natural predators; their eyes are situated to allow about 300-degrees of visibility, and they can see and detect movement 4 miles away.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Use common sense. Let others know where you will be hunting, camped, etc. Some have been stranded by flat tires, very muddy conditions, flash floods, etc. Carry a survival kit. Some areas have cell phone coverage but not all. Consider hand held radios and a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety.

hunt_bio_general_information: Pronghorn are below objective on this unit due to drought but there are numerous roads traversing the area that allow you to see a lot of country to find them. There is opportunity to find antelope throughout the day but like other wildlife they are more active in the morning and evening. There are also many opportunities around cultivated agricultural areas to harvest. This is a great place to hunt having local communities nearby.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Rangeland that borders private agricultural land are good places to hunt especially around the agricultural communities of Wellington, Elmo, and Cleveland. Other hunting areas include, Furniture Draw, Mounds, The Red Ledges area, and south and west of SR6 to Woodside. There are fewer pronghorn to the west of SR6 between Woodside and I-70. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types and into the pinion-juniper zone around the San Rafael Swell and Cedar Mountain. Annual precipitation in this area generally varies from 6 to 12 inches in these vegetation types. Scouting Tips: Binoculars and a good spotting scope are essential companions when hunting. Spend time prior to the hunt getting to know where the pronghorn are. Intensify the scouting efforts leading up to the hunt opening. Pronghorn are most active in the mornings and evenings but can be hunted all day. There are numerous roads on this unit that allow you to see a lot of country. Locating water sources like springs and livestock ponds, setting up blinds or spot and stalk are good hunting strategies; look for tracks and scratch marks where they are marking territories especially on the dirt roads. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same area if water is available unless he is run off or water is scarce. Look for vantage points where you can glass at rangelands below. Bucks are differentiated from does by larger horns and a black cheek patch. They are very curious and sometimes will come closer to you if they cannot figure out what you are. Behavior: San Rafael herds do not migrate long distances, they stay in a general area throughout the year. During the rut larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd depending on food resources. There can be as many as 12-18 in a herd in late summer and fall. As the rut nears mature bucks will separate from one another and look for does. Keep a look out because other bucks may be around the area when a buck is herded up with his does. Later after the rut other bucks join in with some of these smaller herds, which then join together with other herds to make larger wintering herds. There always seems to be solitary bucks and smaller buck herds around throughout all the seasons of the year. Bucks like to make scrapes on dirt roads defending their territory and warn off other competing bucks. They are very fast, and except for fawns they can outrun all their natural predators; their eyes are situated to allow about 300-degrees of visibility, and they can see and detect movement 4 miles away.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Use common sense. Let others know where you will be hunting, camped, etc. Some have been stranded by flat tires, very muddy conditions, flash floods, etc. Carry a survival kit. Some areas have cell phone coverage but not all. Consider hand held radios and a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are a fairly easy animal to locate. For archery hunts scouting is important, there are many guzzlers spread out across the entire unit, these guzzlers can be an excellent place to set up blinds. Areas where there are pronghorn will more than likely have a guzzler or some water sources nearby. Trail cameras have become very popular over the last several years and they can be a great way to see what type of bucks are coming into water sources. Behavior: As with most big game animals the early mornings and evenings are the best times to find pronghorn, but pronghorn can still be fairly easy to find throughout the entire day. Pronghorn rut: There will typically be rutting activity starting in August, with the peak of the rut being in September. They will be rutting during the any weapon hunt. During the muzzleloader hunt, rutting activity may slow down, but the dominate bucks will still be with the does. Recommended areas Anthro Unit from West to East: Anthro Mountain Areas- There are a few groups of pronghorn that live in the higher elevations in the summer and early fall. There are fewer animals in these areas, but it can be a pretty place to hunt. Some areas to try are the following: Wire Fence Ridge, Nutter's Ridge, Jeep Trail, Alkaline Ridge(Best), and Choke Cherry(Good). Wells Draw- Starting just South of Pleasant Valley on BLM property. Lots of pronghorn in this area, there are many roads and well pads. Sand Wash Road- Anywhere along this road and all side roads can hold pronghorn Little Desert- There aren't a lot of pronghorn in this area, there are several guzzlers that should have pronghorn near them. Eight Mile Flat- lots of oil field activity, great area to glass.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather for this hunt can range from very hot and dry to cold and wet, especially in the higher elevations.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit is located in low elevation desert. Much of the unit has been heavily impacted by oil and gas development so there are a lot of roads in the unit where pronghorn can be seen from.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn rut: The pronghorn rut usually starts the end of September. Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are fairly habitual and can be found in the same general area from late summer through the hunt. Pronghorn are best scouted from a distance using a spotting scope or binoculars so they don't leave the area. They are most active in the morning and evening when the temperatures are cooler. This area has been heavily impacted by energy development. There are a lot of roads from the energy development so hunters should have no problem finding pronghorn. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time they are in desert scrub/sagebrush flat areas. If the weather is unseasonably warm, they will often seek shade during the middle part of the day. Pronghorn are herd animals. You will often see groups of does and fawns with only a few bucks mixed in during the fall. During the rut, bucks will separate from other males to find does to mate with. The rest of the year, the bucks are usually with other pronghorn. Buck vs Doe: Hunters can tell bucks from does by several characteristics. Bucks will have larger horns and a black cheek patch. Where to find pronghorn: 90% of the pronghorn are found on public lands in desert scrub and sagebrush flat areas. They typically stay out of heavily treed and cliffy areas. Pronghorn are found near water sources. Pronghorn are not typically found on Diamond Mountain. Recommended areas in the Bonanza/Diamond Mtn: Good areas to hunt include Deadman Bench, Coyote Basin, Glen Bench, and Snake John. Diamond Mountain subunit is not recommended due to either no or very few pronghorn.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is good on this hunt unit. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, snow, and wind.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a new hunt started in 2019 so no harvest information is available from previous years. Pronghorn numbers both overall populations plus buck to doe ratios have increased in recent years this is why the hunt was proposed.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: We manage this unit at a high buck to doe ratio so many of the bucks on the unit are mature bucks. These pronghorn migrate from higher elevation sage flats and ponderosa forests to lower elevation sage hills. Pronghorn are often scattered throughout the unit. Spend a lot of time scouting and finding waterholes, this can be a good way to harvest a buck earlier in the hunt. Toward the end of the hunt bucks will be rutting so locating does, and spot and stalk/decoying could be good methods to harvest a pronghorn.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect hot days with cool mornings, this units elevations ranges from 6000-11000 feet. Often large thunderstorms hit the areas on summer afternoons accompanied by summer monsoons.

hunt_bio_general_information: This pronghorn population is thriving at this time and this can be a very fun hunt. Landownership is 65% private and 35% BLM/SITLA.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn are concentrated on the northern part of this unit in the area north of Antelope Road up to the northern boundary, Lund Road. Pronghorn can also be found south of Antelope Road in the area west of Desert Mound out to the Antelope Range. Scout around water sources. Be mindful of private land and respect it. Keep closed gates closed!
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Expect warm dry conditions most years. Day time temperatures will be into the 80-90's Be prepared to quarter your animal and get it on ice as soon as possible to ensure you do not waste any meat.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a good unit with decent access in many places. The pronghorn population has been increasing steadily over the last several years.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There are a few groups of pronghorn north of highway 50, though most of those are often on private land. Written permission would need to be obtained before hunting private land. Most of the pronghorn are found south of highway 50. There is a pronghorn CWMU on the southern part of the unit that cannot be hunted on with this permit. There are areas with higher concentrations of pronghorn, however, pronghorn can be found scattered throughout the unit. The weather is still fairly warm and water can still be a decent place to focus. Some areas have lots of dips that can hide pronghorn and others are flat for a long way. While driving roads can be productive you should also plan to spend time glassing to locate pronghorn.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Roads can get slick after a rain storm. Bring plenty of water and fuel.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather is a little cooler than it was during the archery hunt, though lighting and rain storms are still possible.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt unit encompasses low elevation desert and higher mountainous sagebrush terrain, with the pronghorn distributed throughout the unit. Road access is good throughout the unit, with one area-Bare Top-closed to motorized vehicles. There is a migration study occurring to look at winter habitat use; it's asked that collared animals not be harvested if possible.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Scouting Tips: Pronghorn are fairly habitual and can be found in the same general area from late summer through the hunt. Pronghorn are best scouted from a distance using a spotting scope or binoculars so they don't leave the area. They are most active in the morning and evening when the temperatures are cooler; these are the best times to scout. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time they are in desert scrub/sagebrush flat areas. If the weather is extremely hot, they will often seek shade during the middle part of the day. Pronghorn are herd animals. You will often see groups of does and fawns with only a few bucks mixed in during the fall. During the rut, bucks will separate from other males to find does to mate with. The rest of the year, the bucks are usually with other pronghorn. Buck vs Doe: Hunters can tell bucks from does by several characteristics. Bucks will have larger horns and a black cheek patch. Pronghorn rut: The pronghorn rut usually starts the end of September so bucks will be mixed with doe herds. Where to find pronghorn: 90% of the pronghorn are found on public lands in desert scrub and sagebrush flat areas. They typically stay out of heavily treed and cliffy areas. Pronghorn are found near water sources. Recommended areas in the Three Corners/West Daggett: Good areas to hunt include Clay Basin, Goslin Mountain, Antelope Flat, Bare Top, and Lucerne Valley. Very few pronghorn are found in Browns Park.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Due to recent storms, several roads in the 3 Corners vicinity have washed out and are impassable to any vehicle, including side by sides and ATVs. Please do not harm the habitat by trying to drive off road around wash outs. Driving off road is illegal. Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October.
