hunt_bio_general_information: It is such a large area that hunter competition is really low. I would put a significant effort into pre-season scouting on this unit. Don't be afraid to ask the oil field workers where they have been seeing pronghorn. They drive the roads that go right through prime antelope habitat every day and can be a great resource. I would work on locating water sources, placing trail cameras. Unless it rains which has been a rare occurrence, antelope have to come to water. It is an extremely fun hunt, and you can see antelope all throughout the day. Spot and stalk techniques are effective as well. The pronghorn are used to vehicle traffic because of all the oil and gas production in the area. They rely on their eye sight and speed to avoid predation. As long as they don't see anything out of the ordinary they are fairly docile, and calm.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: The Vernal antelope herd does not show many signs of migration. Throughout the year they stay in the same general area. During the rut the larger herds tend to break up into smaller herds with one to two bucks in the herd. The great thing about hunting antelope is that you can hunt them all throughout the day. Vegetative communities that dominate the areas of the herd unit frequented by pronghorn include salt desert shrub types on the lower elevation zones grading upward in elevation to Wyoming sage habitats. Annual precipitation generally varies from 6 to 8 inches in these vegetation types. Forb production is important for healthy fawn survival. Water distribution can be limiting but has been provided by the BLM and other conservation interests through guzzlers or other devices. During the past decade of drought, the poor maintenance condition of many of these artificial water sources limited their effectiveness. Repairs have been made and are continuing. Natural gas and oil production is rapidly increasing on pronghorn range with subsequent vegetative removal limiting both forage availability and habitat effectiveness. Habitat loss and disturbance associated with drilling and other energy extraction activities may be a significant factor affecting pronghorn populations. I have seen antelope shade up during the day under the large tanks on oil well pads. I would focus on rangeland that boarder's private agricultural land. During late summer agricultural fields are essential for large herds of antelope. Ouray Valley and the Ashley Oil Field holds large groups of antelope. Hwy 88 near the Hwy 40 intersection is a great place to look. North of the Green River there are large salt desert shrub communities. Scouting Tips: A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential. Scouting is most effective right before the hunt opens. I would plan on covering a lot of ground to locate springs and guzzlers in the more arid areas on the northern part of the unit. Trail cameras can make a big difference in scouting these areas. Once you locate a buck there is a good chance he will stay in same vicinity. Behavior: Antelope are fairly solitary, and herd up in small groups during the rut. Bucks like to make scrapes in the dirt roads to make territories and warn off other competing bucks. I don't see large herds of antelope on this unit. A large group of antelope on the Vernal is 12-18 head. They have to stay relatively close to a sustainable water source. If it rains they are less likely to visit springs or guzzlers and more likely to drink out of hoof prints or natural water catches.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is a very remote location with some areas with limited access. Cellular phone coverage is very spotty on this hunt unit. Digital cell phones may show several bars but cannot always connect due to the distance to the cell towers. Satellite phones do work in the area. The biologist suggests hand held radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, and hot conditions. Storms can cause muddy road conditions and flash floods in this region.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Parker offers great opportunity to view and hunt pronghorn. The area of this hunt boundary that contains the highest densities of pronghorn is located roughly west and south of Loa and Bicknell. The pronghorn also use a smaller area north of Loa. Animals can occasionally be found on the west side of the unit in John's Valley crossing back and forth between the Parker and Mt Dutton units.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn on this unit love timbered areas! During the warmer weather they will lounge in small meadows in the aspen and spruce forests on the south and east portions of the Parker plateau. As hunting pressure increases on this unit, the pronghorn will also use the trees for security cover. Pronghorn can be found in the more traditional open areas of the Parker, but the greatest densities are found higher up along the tree lines. Access to these areas in a vehicle is limited. The pronghorn on the Parker are also wary of motorized vehicles and will go to great lengths to avoid them. It may be profitable for hunters to plan on walking away from roads and vehicles to glass for animals. There are many water sources on the Parker and pronghorn like to use these sources. They are accustomed to drinking every day and locating water sources and waiting in blinds for animals to show up is a good hunting strategy. Mature bucks are most likely to be found with larger herds of does and fawns but are frequently off on their own as well. Be prepared to seek out the highest densities of animals at a much higher elevation than one might expect.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some remote areas on this unit and the terrain is very similar throughout the Parker plateau. It is very easy to become disoriented.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms often occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Parker offers great opportunity to view and hunt pronghorn. The area of this hunt boundary that contains the highest densities of pronghorn is located roughly west and south of Loa and Bicknell. The pronghorn also use a smaller area north of Loa. Animals can occasionally be found on the west side of the unit in John's Valley crossing back and forth between the Parker and Mt Dutton units.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn on this unit love timbered areas! During the warmer weather they will lounge in small meadows in the aspen and spruce forests on the south and east portions of the Parker plateau. As hunting pressure increases on this unit, the pronghorn will also use the trees for security cover. Pronghorn can be found in the more traditional open areas of the Parker, but the greatest densities are found higher up along the tree lines. Access to these areas in a vehicle is limited. The pronghorn on the Parker are also wary of motorized vehicles and will go to great lengths to avoid them. It may be profitable for hunters to plan on walking away from roads and vehicles to glass for animals. There are many water sources on the Parker and pronghorn like to use these sources. They are accustomed to drinking every day and locating water sources and waiting in blinds for animals to show up is a good hunting strategy. Mature bucks are most likely to be found with larger herds of does and fawns but are frequently off on their own as well. Be prepared to seek out the highest densities of animals at a much higher elevation than one might expect.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some remote areas on this unit and the terrain is very similar throughout the Parker plateau. It is very easy to become disoriented. There is limited cell service in the area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions and check weather forecasts often. Late summer and early fall monsoonal rains are common in this area and they cause many roads to become muddy and impassible. Snow storms are also a possibility during this hunt. Drive cautiously on muddy or snowy roads, otherwise you may get a vehicle stuck.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) takes up parts of Weber, Morgan and Rich counties, with Rich county having the most area. The higher points on the Deseret CWMU are along Horse Ridge (8500 feet). On the west the Unit drops away to about 6400 feet in the south and 8000 feet in the north. On the eastside of Horse Ridge the Unit makes a less steep drop, dropping down to around 6400 feet in the north and 6800 feet in the south along the Utah - Wyoming state border. The most common elevation is 6400 feet but ranges from 6000 feet to 8700 feet with an elevation difference of 2700 feet. Fifty-two percent (52%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 6800 feet and 7800 feet an elevation difference of 1000 feet. The Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is much larger than other CWMUs in Utah, therefore land cover is more diversified. About half (50%) of the land cover on the Deseret CWMU is Inter-Mountain Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62). Towards the northeast and at lower elevation, there are large areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Steppe (66). Thet higher elevations on the west of the Unit, mixed with Sagebrush Steppe are extensive areas of Rocky Mountain Aspen Forest and Woodland (22). At lower elevations towards the northeast are several patches of Agriculture (114) land. At minor extents are Southern Rocky Mountain Montane-Subalpine Grassland (71), Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48), and Rocky Mountain Gambel Oak-Mixed Montane shrubland (41). One of the Deseret Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, WOODRUFF (429595), is about 10.5 km north from the north edge of the CWMU. WOODRUFF has one hundred eleven (111) years of records, 1897 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.64 inches, but it can be as high as 5.18 inches or as low as 0.64 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 8.7 inches but can be as high as 29.2 inches. FALL temperature at WOODRUFF averages 40.8 degrees F. but can be as high as 111.0 degrees F. or as low as -26.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 73 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 6 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This unit has opened private land for public use to help compensate the public for having public land in the CWMU. Here is a link to a map showing "trade lands" in CWMUs https://wildlife.utah.gov/cwmu.html . The Rabbit Creek Cooperative Wildlife Managment Unit (CWMU) is east of Bear Lake ten (10) km. Lake Ridge runs north too south on the eastside of the unit, ranging from 7200 feet in the north to 7000 feet in the south. Most elevation slope from this ridge to the east and west. On the east the unit bounday is 6800 feet in the north and 6400 feet in the south. Rabbit Creek cuts the CWMU starting in the west (7000 feet) and exiting in the southeast at 6400 feet. Elevation on the Wood Canyon CWMU ranges betwenn 6400 and 7200 feet a difference of 800 feet. The most common elevation on the CWMU is 6800 feet. On the Rabbit Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) forty-four percent (44%) of the land cover is Inter-Mountian Basins Montane Sagebrush Steppe (62), twenty-four percent (24%); Agriculture (114), eighteen percent (18%); Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Steppe (66), and twelve percent (12%) is Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). One of the Rabbit Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit's (CWMU) nearest weather stations, LAKETOWN (424856), is about 16.7 km southwest from the northeast edge of the CWMU. LAKETOWN has one hundred nine (109) years of records, 1900 - 2009. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.19 inches, but it can be as high as 6.53 inches or as low as 1.75 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 9 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. There can also be one day of precipitation of 1.0 inch. Snowfall during the FALL averages 8.3 inches but can be as high as 35.0 inches. FALL temperature at LAKETOWN averages 44.2 degrees F. but can be as high as 90.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 53 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 0 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Skull Valley South Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located in Tooele County in Skull Valley west of the Stansbury Mountains. The CWMU is about 22.5 km southwest of Timpie, Utah. Elevations in the east are around 5600 feet and 4300 feet in the west. The Skull Valley South Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit land cover is dominated by Invasive Annual Grassland (121), about 35%. This invasive is evident throughout the unit. In the northwest of the CWMU is mostly Inter-Mountain Basins Geasewood Flat (82), 15%. Down the middle of the CWMU are six patches of Agriculture (114) land, 12%. Finally, towards the southwest are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58), 11%. One of the Skull Valley South Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, IOSEPA SOUTH RANCH (424233), is near the middle of the CWMU. IOSEPA SOUTH RANCH has thirty-five (35) years of records, 1910 - 1958. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 1.61 inches, but it can be as high as 2.76 inches or as low as 0.35 inches. During the 91-day FALL period, 7 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 5 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 1.0 inch but can be as high as 5.5 inches. FALL temperature at IOSEPA SOUTH RANCH averages 50.5 degrees F. but can be as high as 109.0 degrees F. or as low as -9.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 43 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 10 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: Pronghorn can be difficult to locate on this unit. There are several places you can gain elevation and take advantage of using you optics to locate these animals. I would focus your efforts on the large flats above Willow Creek.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn are a challenging animal to hunt. They have great vision but are curious and will often respond to flagging or a decoy. During the rut the bucks become very territorial and will leave scrapes along the roads to warn off other males. During the peak rut you can expect to find the bucks in with the herds of does.

hunt_bio_weather_considerations: I would prepare for fair to cold weather conditions. The roads can be affected by rain and snow. There is a fair amount of oil field traffic that helps keep the roads open.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The West Lake Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located west and south of Utah Lake in Goshen Valley. Part of the northeast border is the shoreline of Utah Lake. This is a relatively flat Unit, about 4500 feet in the north, rising to 5000 feet in the middle and westside, then decreasing to 4700 feet in the south. Kimball Creek (4600 feet to 4900 feet) is probably the only major drainage on the Unit. The most common elevation is 4500 feet but ranges from 4400 feet to 5200 feet with an elevation difference of 800 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 4600 feet and 4900 feet an elevation difference of 300 feet. Over sixty percent (60%) of the West Lake Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Agriculture (114). Around the edges of the Unit are areas of Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48) and Invasive Annual Grassland (121). Inter-Mountain Basins Greasewood Flat (82) and Developed, Open Space - Low Intensity (111) add to the character of the Unit. One of the West Lake Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ELBERTA (422418), is 0.6 km north of the north edge of the south parcel of the CWMU. ELBERTA has ninety (90) years of records, 1902 - 1992. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.64 inches, but it can be as high as 7.49 inches or as low as 0.51 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 3.2 inches but can be as high as 15.0 inches. FALL temperature at ELBERTA averages 51.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 100.0 degrees F. or as low as -8.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 37 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 4 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Allen Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located on the south end of Cedar Valley and northwest of the Tinic Mountains. The terrain is relatively flat with a relief difference of only about 500 feet (4900 feet to 5400 feet). The lowest elevation is in a north with highest in the south. The most common elevation is 5000 feet but ranges from 5000 feet to 5400 feet with an elevation difference of 400 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5000 feet and 5200 feet an elevation difference of 200 feet. Agriculture (114) is the primary land cover type for the Allen Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU). Add Invasive Annual Grassland (121) and Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48) and about seventy percent of the land is covered. Add Inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58), Invasive Annual and Biennial Forbland (122), and Developed, Open Space - Low Intensity (111) and near ninety percent (90%) of the land is covered. One of the Allen's Ranch Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, ELBERTA (422418), is about 1.4 km to the southeast. ELBERTA has ninety (90) years of records, 1902 - 1092. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.64 inches, but it can be as high as 7.49 inches or as low as 0.51 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 15 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Total snowfall averages 3.2 inches but can be as high as 15.0 inches. FALL temperature at ELBERTA averages 51.0 degrees F. but can be as high as 100.0 degrees F. or as low as -8.0 degrees F. During the fall, 37 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 4 days above 90 degrees F.

CWMUs are managed separately from the larger units of which they are a part, but management objectives are the same. Specific information related to this CWMU should be directed to the CWMU operator before applying for the unit. Pronghorn in this unit will use irrigated agricultural fields as well as rangeland.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Services are located in Tremonton, Snowville, and Grouse Creek. Specific rules to maintain safe conditions while on the CWMU are part of the management plan. Hunters should contact the CWMU operator prior to applying for the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of December.

hunt_bio_general_information: Hunt is located in both the Mt Dutton and Paunsaugunt Units. Good numbers of pronghorn can be see with great bucks available. This hunt runs during the rut so bucks are often very active throughout the day. Mornings and evenings are generally best, but because of the need for water and the rut pronghorn can be found all day long. If it is a dry summer and fall pronghorn could be congregated around the water. Most hunters often harvest early in the hunt often the first morning. So generally by the second day you could literally have the entire unit to yourself. Cover some country and if you find a great buck they generally don't move very far if they have does with them.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: You may want to hunt water early in the hunt and then decoy or spot and stalk later in the hunt as bucks are rutting and chasing does. If it stays dry sitting water could be very effective, but if monsoon rains are occurring there could be a lot of water available so you may need to do more spot and stalk.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Basic hunting related safety concerns
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Usually very hot and dry, but afternoon thunderstorms could occur.

hunt_bio_general_information: Approximately 50% of this unit where pronghorn can be found is private property. Hunters should obtain written permission to access private lands before entering. Three pronghorn CWMUs exist on the Snowville unit. No hunting is allowed on CWMUs without the appropriate permit.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn in this unit are primarily found on private land near cultivated agriculture. Make sure to obtain written permission to hunt on private land before entering. Populations can be found west of Snowville, Wildcat Hill, Kelton, Baker Hills, Matlin Mtns, and west of the Locomotive Springs Road. Once livestock near Snowville are moved to the irrigated crop fields in late fall, pronghorn will move south onto the rangelands for the winter.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Caution should be used when taking aim at pronghorn in this unit to ensure a safe backstop. Long range shots are common when pursuing pronghorn and animals in this unit will be on or near agricultural fields. Cell phone coverage is good in this area but not complete. Ensure that someone else knows where you plan on camping and hunting, and when you will be returning. Nearest services are in Tremonton or Snowville.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until the first week of December.

hunt_bio_general_information: The area of this hunt boundary that contains pronghorn is located roughly west and south of Loa and Bicknell. The pronghorn also use a smaller area north of Loa.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn on this unit love timbered areas! During the warmer weather they will lounge in small meadows in the aspen and spruce forests on the south and east portions of the Parker. As hunting pressure increases on this unit the pronghorn will also use the trees for security cover. Access to these areas in a vehicle is limited. The pronghorn on the Parker are also wary of motorized vehicles and will go to great lengths to avoid them. It may be profitable for hunters to plan on walking away from roads and vehicles to glass for animals. There are many water sources on the Parker and pronghorn like to use these sources. They are accustomed to drinking every day and locating water sources and waiting in blinds for animals to show up is a good hunting strategy.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some remote areas on this unit and the terrain is very similar throughout the Awapa Plateau.It is very easy to become disoriented.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions. Check weather forecasts often. Snow storms often occur during this hunt. Most of the time snow will melt off within a day or so. Be prepared for muddy or snowy road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is comprised of approximately 95% private land. Hunters should obtain written permission from landowners prior to applying for this hunt. Most roads and ATV trails on this unit are managed by Box Elder County or BLM and are covered on their Travel Management Plans. Please direct all questions regarding which roads and trails ATVs can be operated on to their respective website: Box Elder County: http://www.boxeldercounty.org/box-elder-county-web-map.htm BLM: http://www.blm.gov/ut/st/en/fo/salt_lake.html No campgrounds on this unit are managed by the BLM. Camping outside of official campgrounds is permitted on most of the public lands. Please direct all questions regarding campground availability and other camping questions to the BLM. Maps and camping regulations are available on their website.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn in this unit are primarily found on private land near cultivated agriculture. Make sure to obtain written permission to hunt on private land before entering. Populations can be found northwest of Blue Creek Reservoir, in Hansel Valley, Salt Wells, Sage Valley, and east of the Locomotive Springs Road.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Caution should be used when taking aim at pronghorn in this unit to ensure a safe backstop. Long range shots are common when pursuing pronghorn and animals in this unit will be on or near agricultural fields. Cell phone coverage is good in this area but not complete. Ensure that someone else knows where you plan on camping and hunting, and when you will be returning. Nearest services are in Tremonton, Corinne, or Snowville.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until the first week of December.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Zane(CWMU) is located southwest of Lund, Utah. This mostly flat Unit ranges from 5100 feet in the south to 5300 feet in the north. Mountain Spring Wash the only substantial drainage cuts the unit also ranges from 5100 feet to 5300 feet. The most common levation is 5200 feet but ranges from 5100 feet to 5400 feet with an elevation difference of 300 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5200 feet and 5300 feet an elevation difference of 100 feet. Much of the Zane Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is dominated by Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). Most of this Sagebrush shrubland is in the northwest part. Inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58) is dominate in the southwest part, extending into the southeast. Patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Semi-Desert Shrub Steppe (67) occur across the unit, but there are large areas on the eastside of the Unit. In the middle of the Unit, are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Semi-Desert Grassland (76). One of the Zane Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, LUND (425247), is about 7.8 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. LUND has sixty-seven (67) years of records, 1900 - 1967. During thThe Zane Cooperative Wildlife Management Une FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 1.97 inches, but it can be as high as 4.37 inches or as low as 0.03 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 7 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 5 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 day of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 1.1 inches but can be as high as 7.0 inches. FALL temperature at LUND averages 50.3 degrees F. but can be as high as 104.0 degrees F. or as low as -9.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 47 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 5 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of the day. Most of the time they are in desert scrub/sagebrush flat areas. If the weather is extremely hot, they will often seek shade during the middle part of the day. Pronghorn are herd animals. You will often see groups of does and fawns with only a few bucks mixed in during the fall. During the rut, bucks will separate from other males to find does. 50% of the pronghorn are found on public lands in desert scrub and sagebrush flat areas. The other half can be found near irrigated agricultural areas. They typically stay out of heavily treed and cliffy areas. Pronghorn are found near water sources. Good areas to hunt include east Pilot Mtn near TL Bar Ranch, Lucin, Winter Cabin Road, South of Goose Creek, Yost, Rosebud, and Curlew Junction.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Caution should be used when taking aim at pronghorn in this unit to ensure a safe backstop. Long range shots are common when pursuing pronghorn and animals in this unit will be on or near agricultural fields. Cell phone coverage is spotty in this area. Ensure that someone else knows where you plan on camping and hunting, and when you will be returning. Nearest services are in Grouse Creek, Montello, Nevada, Wendover, Utah/Nevada, Oakley, Idaho, or Almo, Idaho.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically between the hunting seasons. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until the first week of December.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a great CWMU with good numbers of pronghorn.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There are a lot of pronghorn on the CWMU and lots of bucks to choose from. Pronghorn can be found in both the ag fields as well as on the range portion. The Pahvant Ensign Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is in the south Pahvant Valley, west of Kanosh, Utah and on the westside of Interstate Highway I-15. The most common elevation is 5800 feet but ranges from 4700 feet to 7100 feet with an elevation difference of 2400 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5500 feet and 6300 feet an elevation difference of 800 feet. Almost sixty percent (60%) of the Pahvant Ensign Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU)is dominated by Agriculture (114). On the north and south extremes there are areas dominated by Invasive Perennial Grassland (119) and Invasive Annual Grassland (121). In the areas that are not Agriculture, there are patches of inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58) and Inter-Mountain Basins Greasewood Flat (82). One of the nearest weather stations, KANOSH (424527), is about 5.0 km southeast from the southeast edge of the CWMU. KANOSH has one hundred (100) years of records, 1907 - 2007. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 3.52 inches, but it can be as high as 8.43 inches or as low as 0.69 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 9 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 12.0 inches but can be as high as 66.0 inches. FALL temperature at KANOSH average 53.6 degrees F. but can be as high as 99.0 degrees F. or as low as 1.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 27 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 4 days above 90 degrees F.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: A lot of pronghorn can be found in the agricultural fields. The roads get used regularly. Please be aware of the your surroundings to avoid harm to anyone or damaging equipment.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather should be good but be prepared for storms and slick roads.

hunt_bio_general_information: This hunt is comprised largely of private lands. It is highly recommended that hunters obtain written permission to access private lands before applying for this hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt is intended to reduce pronghorn densities in privately-owned, low-elevation agricultural areas where pronghorn are damaging crops. Hunters may target animals in morning and evening hours traveling to and from agricultural crops. Hunters should plan on being patient, scouting and spending some time patterning and hunting to harvest a doe. Some hunting opportunities exist on the Ouray National Wildlife Refuge, but there are many refuge-specific hunting regulations that hunters need to be aware of and follow. Please contact the Ouray refuge for more information on hunting activities at (435) 545-2522 or see their website .
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Much of the terrain in this hunt boundary is flat and in close proximity to roads, structures, equipment and livestock. Be 100% sure of your target and ensure you have a safe backstop for your bullet before shooting.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: October weather ranges from warm and sunny to cold and snowy. Be prepared for drastic temperature fluctuations. Rain and snow are possibilities.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Antelope Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is in the southeast part of Duchesne County, about 10.5 km from Duchesne, Utah. Higher elevations are in the southwest corner of the unit (6300 feet). Antelope Creek that cuts the CWMU ranges from 5300 feet to 5800 feet. Pleasant Valley in the east ranges from 5300 feet to 5800 feet. The most common elevation is 5500 feet but ranges from 5300 feet to 6300 feet with an elevation difference of 1000 feet. Fifty (50%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5600 feet and 6100 feet an elevation difference of 500 feet. About thirty-six perecent (36%) of the Antelope Creek Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is Colorado Plateau Mixed Low Sagebrush Shrubland (50), located on the westside of the unit. Another thirty-four percent (34%) is Inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58), located mostly on the eastside of the unit. Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (66), Inter-Mountain Basins Greasewood Flat (82), and Inter-Mountain Basins Semi-Desert Grassland (76) also figure into the mix. One of the Antelope Creek Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, DUCHESNE (422253), is about 6.0 km west from the west edge of the CWMU. DUCHESNE has eighty-three (92) years of records, 1906 - 2008. During the FALL (September, October and November) the average precipitation is 2.57inches, but it can be as high as 6.21 inches or as low as 0.25 inch. During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 8 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 1 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Total FALL snowfall averages 3.1 inches but can be as high as 17.1 inches. FALL temperature at DUCHESNE averages 46.4 degrees F. but can be as high as 93.0 degrees F. or as low as -17.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 49 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and less than 1 day above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The unit is managed as a limited entry unit but does not guarantee success. CWMUs are managed separately from the larger units of which they are a part, but management objectives are the same. Specific information related to this CWMU should be directed to the CWMU operator before applying for the unit. Pronghorn in this unit will use irrigated agricultural fields as well as rangeland.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to drive to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Services are located in Tremonton, Snowville, and Grouse Creek. Specific rules to maintain safe conditions while on the CWMU are part of the management plan. Hunters should contact the CWMU operator prior to applying for the unit.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of December.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The Zane Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is located southwest of Lund, Utah. This mostly flat Unit ranges from 5100 feet in the south to 5300 feet in the north. Mountain Spring Wash the only substantial drainage cuts the unit also ranges from 5100 feet to 5300 feet. The most common levation is 5200 feet but ranges from 5100 feet to 5400 feet with an elevation difference of 300 feet. Fifty-six percent (56%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5200 feet and 5300 feet an elevation difference of 100 feet. Much of the Zane Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is dominated by Inter-Mountain Basins Big Sagebrush Shrubland (48). Most of this Sagebrush shrubland is in the northwest part. Inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58) is dominate in the southwest part, extending into the southeast. Patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Semi-Desert Shrub Steppe (67) occur across the unit, but there are large areas on the eastside of the Unit. In the middle of the Unit, are patches of Inter-Mountain Basins Semi-Desert Grassland (76). One of the Zane Cooperative Wildlife Mangement Unit (CWMU) nearest weather stations, LUND (425247), is about 7.8 km northeast from the northeast edge of the CWMU. The Pahvant Ensign Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU) is in the south Pahvant Valley, west of Kanosh, Utah and on the westside of Interstate Highway I-15. The most common elevation is 5800 feet but ranges from 4700 feet to 7100 feet with an elevation difference of 2400 feet. Fifty-one percent (51%) of the CWMU elevation ranges between 5500 feet and 6300 feet an elevation difference of 800 feet. Almost sixty percent (60%) of the Pahvant Ensign Cooperative Wildlife Management Unit (CWMU)is dominated by Agriculture (114). On the north and south extremes there are areas dominated by Invasive Perennial Grassland (119) and Invasive Annual Grassland (121). In the areas that are not Agriculture, there are patches of inter-Mountain Basins Mixed Salt Desert Scrub (58) and Inter-Mountain Basins Greasewood Flat (82). During the 91-day FALL period, 14 days will experience greater than or equal to 0.01 inch of precipitation, 9 days of greater than or equal to 0.10 inch, or 2 days of the greater than or equal to 0.50 inch of precipitation. Snowfall during the FALL averages 12.0 inches but can be as high as 66.0 inches. FALL temperature at KANOSH average 53.6 degrees F. but can be as high as 99.0 degrees F. or as low as 1.0 degrees F. During the FALL, 27 days will be below freezing (32 degrees F.) and 4 days above 90 degrees F.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Parker offers great opportunity to view and hunt pronghorn. The area of this hunt boundary that contains the highest densities of pronghorn is located roughly west and south of Loa and Bicknell. The pronghorn also use a smaller area north of Loa. Animals can occasionally be found on the west side of the unit in John's Valley crossing back and forth between the Parker and Mt Dutton units.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Pronghorn on this unit love timbered areas! During the warmer weather they will lounge in small meadows in the aspen and spruce forests on the south and east portions of the Parker plateau. As hunting pressure increases on this unit, the pronghorn will also use the trees for security cover. Pronghorn can be found in the more traditional open areas of the Parker, but the greatest densities are found higher up along the tree lines. Access to these areas in a vehicle is limited. The pronghorn on the Parker are also wary of motorized vehicles and will go to great lengths to avoid them. It may be profitable for hunters to plan on walking away from roads and vehicles to glass for animals. There are many water sources on the Parker and pronghorn like to use these sources. They are accustomed to drinking every day and locating water sources and waiting in blinds for animals to show up is a good hunting strategy. Mature bucks are most likely to be found with larger herds of does and fawns but are frequently off on their own as well. Be prepared to seek out the highest densities of animals at a much higher elevation than one might expect.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some remote areas on this unit and the terrain is very similar throughout the Parker plateau. It is very easy to become disoriented. There is limited cell service in the area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions and check weather forecasts often. Late summer and early fall monsoonal rains can make roads incredibly muddy and impassible roads. Drive these roads with extreme caution, otherwise you may get vehicles stuck.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Parker offers great opportunity to view and hunt pronghorn. The area of this hunt boundary that contains the highest densities of pronghorn is located roughly west and south of Loa and Bicknell. The pronghorn also use a smaller area north of Loa on the Fishlake.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The terrain of this unit is very flat and open, which allows for great glassing opportunity but at the cost of pronghorn being able to spot you quite easily. Use limited cover, draws, and valleys to your advantage to view and approach animals while out of sight. The pronghorn on the Parker are also wary of motorized vehicles and will go to great lengths to avoid them. It may be profitable for hunters to plan on walking away from roads and vehicles to glass for animals. There are many water sources on the Parker and pronghorn like to use these sources. They are accustomed to drinking every day and locating water sources and waiting in blinds for animals to show up is a good hunting strategy. Mature bucks are most likely to be found with larger herds of does and fawns but are frequently off on their own as well.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Be prepared for some rough roads and rocky trails. Always carry plenty of water and tell someone where you are hunting. There are some remote areas on this unit and the terrain is very similar throughout the Parker plateau. It is very easy to become disoriented. There is limited cell service in the area.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for variable conditions and check weather forecasts often. Late summer and early fall monsoonal rains are common in this area and they cause many roads to become muddy and impassible. Snow storms are also a possibility during this hunt. The snow burns off in a day or two typically, but may leave roads muddy. Drive cautiously on muddy or snowy roads, otherwise you may get a vehicle stuck.

There are small isolated tracts of private lands representing less than 5% of the unit. These private lands include the mouths of most the major canyons coming out of the Book Cliffs and the irrigated fields near the town of Green River. These private lands will be more of an impact for deer hunters than pronghorn or bighorn sheep hunters. ","WMA_IN_UNIT":"Nash Wash WMA. It is accessed from Exit 204 off of Interstate 70. It is a good campground that is very near good sheep hunting opportunities. Dispersed camping opportunities on SITLA and BLM lands across the desert are abundant. Firewood and water are relatively scarce. Plan on bringing your own water. ","SUGGESTED_MAPS":"The yellow 1:100,000 scale BLM maps named Westwater, Huntington, and Moab.","COUNTY_ROAD_INFO":"Grand County: http://www.grandcountyutah.net/pdf/roads/broadmap.jpg ","ATV_VEH_ACCESS":"ATV and Vehicle Access: allowed on approved roads and trails

Bighorn Sheep: Most roads and ATV trails on this unit are managed by the BLM and are covered on its Travel Management Plan. There are only a few roads that go on or near bighorn sheep habitat on the unit. The Hastings Road just east of the Green River in the town of Green River will take you along the east side of the Green River for about 15 miles until the road dead-ends near Rattlesnake Canyon. This road will provide the closest access to where most of the sheep live. This road is graded by the county and is generally in good shape. There are some tight spots along the river that you should be wary of if there is snowy or icy conditions. The Tushar Canyon road will go northeast off of the Hastings Road about 9 miles north of the town of Green River. It will access the right and left fork of Tushar Canyon and loop around along the bench to the east and provide access to Coal, Horse, and Floy Canyons. The Coal Canyon Road is the first right hand turn off of the Hastings Road while still in the town of Green River. It will go through a bunch of alfalfa fields and then up on the cliffs. the Horse Canyon and Floy Canyon roads can be access by following the frontage road along I-70 to the east. Despite all of these directions, most of your time will be spent on foot.

Deer: The main areas with the highest concentrations of deer include Nash Wash (Exit 204 off of Interstate 70), Cottonwood Canyon (Exit 214), Hay Canyon (Exit 221), and Bitter Creek (Exit 227)

Pronghorn: Use any exit off of Interstate 70 or drive the frontage road along the Interstate. Major access points include Green River (Exit 164), Floy Wash (Exit 175), Crescent Junction, Thompson, Yellowcat, Nash Wash (Exit 204), Cottonwood (Exit 214), Sulphur Canyon (Exit 221), and Bitter Creek (Exit 227)","PRIV_TRIBE_LAND_ISSUES":"Bighorn Sheep: The northern boundary of this unit adjoins Ute Tribal lands along Coal Creek. This is good bighorn sheep habitat and bighorns have been seen on both sides of the boundary near the mouth of Coal Creek. Take great care not to hunt or trespass on these tribal lands. The upper Tribal Boundary at upper elevations near Sego Canyon generally doesn't have bighorn sheep during November. There are small isolated pieces of private property in the mouths of Coal, Horse, Floy, and Thompson Canyons. County roads go through these properties so it is best to simply travel through them and park on public lands if you do not have written permission to hunt on these private lands. Bighorn sheep generally do not spend a great deal of time on these private lands.

Pronghorn: There is a large block of private land on the alfalfa fields near the town of Green River. Antelope use this area. Please secure written permission prior to hunting these private lands. The remainder of the private lands on this unit either do not occur in Pronghorn habitat or are scattered and unmarked.

Deer: Deer concentrate on private lands at the mouths of Cottonwood, Hay, and Bitter Creek Canyons. Please secure written permission prior to hunting these private lands. They are relatively small parcels so they are easy to avoid but they do concentrate deer. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit is also known as the Rattlesnake Unit. Bighorn sheep populations have been stable in this area for several decades. Permit numbers have not changed dramatically over this time period. The unit boundary is relatively large however, the vast majority of the occupied bighorn sheep habitat is in the western third of the unit from Thompson west to Green River.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Over 80% of the bighorn sheep observed on this unit are found within 2 miles of the Green River. Sheep use the first 2 to 3 cliff bands above the river and the grassy benches between them. The core area where most sheep live can be found between Tushar Canyon north to Rattlesnake Canyon. Lower densities of bighorn sheep can be found north of Rattlesnake Canyon to the tribal boundary in Coal Creek. Lower densities of bighorn can also be found east of Tushar Canyon along the Book Cliffs to as far east as Thompson. Generally no bighorn sheep are found anywhere on the unit east of the town of Thompson. Scouting Tips: It is good to do pre-season scouting to learn country. However, it is very hot on this unit during the summer months so plan accordingly. You will need a good pair of binoculars and a spotting scope. This unit looks a lot more like desert bighorn sheep habitat than Rocky Mountain bighorn habitat. It is dry and cliffy. During the summer you will most likely see groups of ewes, lambs, and young rams. Many of the larger harvestable rams will not move on to public lands and be available for harvest until the rut begins in late October. Do not be alarmed if there are no big rams in the summer. They will show up by November. Hunting generally gets better the later you go. The peak of the rut tends to be the week of Thanksgiving. Find groups of ewes and lambs and often times a new ram will be with the ewe group each day as rams are moving alot in November between ewe groups. A way to cover lots of ground is to hike up on top of a canyon and glass the other side while having someone else hike the other side of the canyon and look back across the canyon toward you. Behavior: The month of November is during the bighorn sheep rut. Rams are moving from group to group looking for ewes. Rams can also be observed butting heads. It is advised to occasionally stop and listen for the sound of butting heads it can be a good tool for locating sheep that are otherwise difficult to see. Sheep are generally active throughout the day in November but activity is highest in morning and evening. Bighorn sheep will not be as tied to water in November as it is generally more available that time of year if it has snowed. Bighorn will generally avoid the flat mesa top areas where there is any sort of tree cover. They tend to be found on the steep open cliffs and are occasionally are feeding on the flat canyon bottoms or benches. Ram vs Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Many young rams will have a pronounced curl. The best way to recognize mature trophy class bighorn rams is to look for horn mass particularly out near the tip of the horn. Younger rams that are 3 to 5 years old will have plenty of horn length but the horn tips are very thin. Mature rams 6 years and older tend to have thicker horns out near the tips, and thicker bases. Often times if you are close enough you can count horn rings on rams to get an approximate age. Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep rut: The bighorn rut runs during late October and extends through early December with the peak being around Thanksgiving. Where to find Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep: Recommended areas: Highest density areas are Tushar Canyon, the Canyon above Swaseys Beach, the canyon above the Rock House, and Butler Canyon. Hike up through the first cliff band and hunt the upper cliff layers within 2 miles of the river and you will generally see sheep in these canyons.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This unit is steep and rough with very little cell coverage. As in most bighorn sheep habitat, hunters should be in excellent physical condition prior to the hunt as most hunters end up walking dozens of miles and climbing thousands of feet prior to harvesting their ram. As with most bighorn sheep habitat, there is an abundance of cliffs. Be very careful scaling cliffs. It is advised that you bring extra rope to assist with getting through difficult ledges. A GPS unit is very handy on this unit to not only mark sheep and routes but also places where you can get through the ledges as they are relatively rare. Hunters can sometimes spend hours hiking along trying to find a way through the ledges and wasting time and energy. Bring plenty of water. It can be warm in November and there is very little water on the unit. Water in the Green River is plentiful but is tough on most portable water filters as it generally runs pretty muddy. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather conditions in November are variable on this unit. Generally, plan on cold nights with mild days with little snow accumulation. Most of the occupied bighorn sheep habitat occurs at lower elevations between 4200 and 6000 feet where snow generally doesn't accumulate. Snow and bad weather is always possible in November. The roads can get icy as they rarely see sunlight in these dark canyons.

There are small isolated pieces of private property in the mouths of Coal, Horse, Floy, and Thompson Canyons. Bighorn sheep generally do not spend a great deal of time on these private lands.

Pronghorn: There is a large block of private land on the alfalfa fields near the town of Green River. Antelope use this area. Please secure written permission prior to hunting these private lands. They are relatively small parcels so they are easy to avoid but they do concentrate deer. hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The majority of sheep stay in the same general areas throughout much of the year. During summer months, sheep concentrate on the north end of the mountain range in conjunction with natural water availability. During the late fall and winter, sheep begin to spread south across the range. Miners Basin and Desert Peak hold the highest densities of sheep, but sheep will range in high densities south to Big Pass and to the military boundary. Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep are found in steep rocky terrain. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your bighorn sheep. If you cannot safely retrieve the bighorn sheep, do not shoot. Once the rut starts, the rams will be begin to move to where the ewes are. hunt_bio_general_information: This unit has spectacular scenery with many tourists, fishermen, and campers utilizing the area during the summer months. Many visitors to this area travel here specifically to view bighorn sheep. This hunt allows hunters to scout and hunt from land or from a boat. This unit is small with a low sheep population. Many of the mature rams congregate in 1 to 2 groups most of the year. Herd numbers have been declining and older rams have been dying before being harvested. Hunters should expect a class III or 3/4 curl (score 140-150) type ram.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep are found in steep rocky terrain. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your bighorn sheep. If you cannot safely retrieve the bighorn sheep, do not shoot. Scouting Tips: The bighorn sheep stay fairly consistently in the same general areas throughout much of the year. Once the rut starts, the rams will be begin to move to where the ewes are. Scouting is a good way to see what size of ram you can expect to harvest. Scores for sheep on Bare Top are usually in the 140s-150s and are 5.5-6.5 years old. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in steep terrain, but they occasionally move down to the shoreline or up on top of Bare Top where it's flat. Mature rams seem to hang out more in steeper cliffs than ewes. Ewes with lambs prefer areas that are a little less steep and where they can find better feed. Bighorn sheep will usually go to water at least once a day. Ram vs Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep rut: The bighorn rut runs during November. Where to find Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep: Bighorn sheep like steep cliffy areas because it provides an escape from predators. You can find them on grassy flats or near the shoreline when they are eating or come down to drink. Recommended areas: There are a couple of areas that the sheep use regularly. These areas include Hideout, Boars Tusk, along the Flaming Gorge Reservoir shoreline and along the Green River below the dam to Little Hole. Hunters that access the area by boat tend to have better success and satisfaction.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage is spotty on this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return. Camps should be kept clean to prevent bear incidents. Food should be kept inside vehicles or bear-proof containers. Coolers are not bear-proof. Bears have gotten into camps in the past. Number and severity of bear incidents differ by year depending on weather and other food availability. Meat and garbage should be put away inside a vehicle or hung in a tree above 8 feet off the ground and 3 feet away from the trunk or any branches of the tree.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, wind and heat. It is quite common on clear mornings for clouds to build through the morning and have thunderstorms in the afternoon. Be very cautious of lightning while hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October.

hunt_bio_biologist_notes: u>Location of harvest: The core area where most bighorn reside and are harvested is along the lower Price River and lower Green River in Gray Canyon. Probably 75% of the harvest occurs here. There are small concentrations of sheep near Lila Canyon where people can harvest sheep. Sheep can be found down along the river and canyon bottoms all the way up through the cliffs to the top. It is rare to find sheep on the juniper covered mesas on the top. The confluence of the Price River and Green River tends to have the highest concentrations of sheep. There are no known sheep north of Rabbit Valley along the Green River so I wouldn't spend much time there. Bighorn observations in lower Range Creek are also quite rare. Common spots where sheep are found from south to north include Blue Castle Canyon, Long Canyon, Short Canyon, Sand Knolls Canyon, the lower Price River, and Jenny Canyon. Sheep can also be found on Bighorn Mountain and along the face of the Book Cliffs facing SR-6 as far north as Sunnyside. Scouting Tips: It is good to do pre-season scouting to learn country. However, it is very hot on this unit during the summer months so plan accordingly. You will need a good pair of binoculars and a spotting scope. This unit looks a lot more like desert bighorn sheep habitat than Rocky Mountain bighorn habitat. It is dry and cliffy. During the summer you will most likely see groups of ewes, lambs, and young rams. Many of the larger harvestable rams will not move in with the ewes and be available for harvest until the rut begins in late October. Do not be alarmed if there are no big rams in the summer. They will show up by November. Hunting generally gets better the later you go. The peak of the rut tends to be the week of Thanksgiving. Find groups of ewes and lambs and often times a new ram will be with the ewe group each day as rams are moving alot in November between ewe groups. If you need to get a feel for how to judge a ram, it is advised that you go to the town of Sunnyside during the summer months. From April to September each year there is occasionally a group of 5 to 10 rams that reside in the east part of town and can be viewed at close range ( Behavior: The month of November is during the bighorn sheep rut. Rams are moving from group to group looking for ewes. Rams can also be observed butting heads. It is advised to occasionally stop and listen for the sound of butting heads it can be a good tool for locating sheep that are otherwise difficult to see. Sheep are generally active throughout the day in November but activity is highest in morning and evening. Bighorn sheep will not be as tied to water in November as it is generally more available that time of year if it has snowed. Bighorn will generally avoid the flat mesa top areas where there is any sort of tree cover. They tend to be found on the steep open cliffs and are occasionally are feeding on the flat canyon bottoms or benches. Ram vs Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Many young rams will have a pronounced curl. The best way to recognize mature trophy class bighorn rams is to look for horn mass particularly out near the tip of the horn. Younger rams that are 3 to 5 years old will have plenty of horn length but the horn tips are very thin. Mature rams 6 years and older tend to have thicker horns out near the tips, and thicker bases. Often times if you are close enough you can count horn rings on rams to get an approximate age. Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep rut: The bighorn rut runs during late October and extends through early December with the peak in late November
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: This is very remote, very steep, insanely rugged country. There is little to no cell coverage in most of the bighorn sheep habitat. As in most bighorn sheep habitat, hunters should be in excellent physical condition prior to the hunt as most hunters end up walking dozens of miles and climbing thousands of feet prior to harvesting their ram. As with most bighorn sheep habitat, there is an abundance of cliffs. Be very careful scaling cliffs. It is advised that you bring extra rope to assist with getting through difficult ledges. A GPS unit is very handy on this unit to not only mark sheep and routes but also places where you can get through the ledges as they are relatively rare. Hunters can sometimes spend hours hiking along trying to find a way through the ledges and wasting time and energy. Bring plenty of water. It can be warm in November and there is very little water on the unit. Water in the Green River is plentiful but is tough on most portable water filters as it generally runs pretty muddy. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.

hunt_bio_general_information: This is a very remote, very rugged hunt unit. Access is very difficult and will often require either a multiple day float trip down Desolation Canyon or long hikes which will require a descent of several thousand feet to the river bottom.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: There is a good population of bighorn sheep in this area of approximately 70 to 100 sheep. This resource has been underutilized so this hunt was created to provide sportsmen with an opportunity to exclusively hunt this area. Most of the sheep reside between Rockhouse Canyon on the North to Flat Canyon on the south with the highest concentrations of sheep near the mouth of Jack Creek. There are lots of layers to the canyon so sheep can be difficult to locate. There are also a few more trees in the canyon than in most bighorn sheep habitat. Most sheep tend to be in the bottom several layers of the canyon closer to the river, but they are occasionally seen on the ridgetops as well. Main access points are Cottonwood Ridge and the Peters Point wellpads accessed from the Nine Mile Canyon road. This will overlook Jack Creek from the north and will give you a good access point to hop in to the canyon. A second way is to continue driving to Cedar Ridge which is south of Jack Creek. There are locked gates on this road so your walk to the river will be much longer but it will be your closest access point to all points south of Jack Creek. You can reach lower Horse Bench (near Rockhouse Canyon) with an ATV by taking a trail from the Sand Wash boat ramp that crosses Nine Mile Creek and goes up on Horse Bench. The final access point would be floating the river. This takes 4 days and roughly 90 miles and can be a bit tricky at low water levels and a bit cold. Please consult the Price BLM office for permitting and regulations regarding float trips on Desolation Canyon.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The general area you will be hunting is called Desolation Canyon. It is appropriately named. You will be in the middle of nowhere. There is no cell coverage, no people, and no real roads to speak of. Make sure people know where you are and when you will return. Be very careful in attempting to navigate through the countless ledges in the canyon. Do not go down through something you don't feel you can get back up. This is a very deep canyon where the sun rarely shines in some portions. Some slopes may have snow and be slick. If you are planning to float the river, make sure you have an experienced oarsman and all of the correct equipment. The river will be running low in November and be rather technical. There are several Class 3 and 4 rapids along the 90 mile float trip required.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Highly variable. November is a volatile month. Prepare for winter-like conditions and be pleasantly surprised if the weather is nice. The main access road in to the area on Cottonwood Ridge will remain open even if the snow piles up but most of the side roads will not. There is the possibility that the river could freeze up in late November if it got really cold. Generally the slow parts of the Green River do not freeze until mid to Late December.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Oak Creek Bighorn Sheep hunt started in 2018. Several groups of sheep have been transplanted to the Oak Creeks since 2014 and have been successful. Translocated sheep were sourced from Antelope Island and the Newfoundland Mountains.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The core area for the sheep is the Oak Creek and Dry Creek drainages. Many different rams can be located by glassing the drainages that feed into Oak Creek and Dry Creek. Good starting points to find sheep: Fool Creek Peak, Cascade, Limekiln, and Walker canyons.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Sheep inhabit rugged terrain. Wear good boots and take caution when hiking around cliffs and rocks. Cell phone service is spotty up the canyons. Be sure to pack plenty of drinking water as there are not a lot of sources for water on the mountain.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: This time of year can be cold with possible rain or snow storms.

hunt_bio_general_information: Bighorn sheep on this unit are California Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep. The population is still growing and expanding. The Unit is a classic Great Basin mountain range. The terrain is steep and rocky. This unit has had several wildfires in the past decade, creating good bighorn habitat. The higher elevations have a mix of aspen and conifer forests. The mid elevations are juniper woodlands, and burned areas with grass. The lowest elevations are sagebrush and desert scrub.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The unit has an estimated 100 bighorn sheep. Most of the bighorns are on the very north end of the Stansbury Mountains, from Muskrat Canyon and north. There are a handful of bighorns further south on the west slope of the Stansbury Mountains. The unit produces rams in the 140 to 150 inch range. A good spotting scope and binoculars are essential for scouting bighorns in this area. Most hunters use the few roads to access the base of the mountain and use binoculars and spotting scopes to locate bighorns. Once a ram is located, they hike up after it. The rams will be fully in the rut during the hunt. Rams can move long distances during the rut trying to locate ewes. There are several recovering burned areas that are excellent for bighorns. There are very few signs on the trails. I would bring a good map, compass, GPS, and if possible someone who is familiar with the area. If you have never set foot in this unit, it might appear small on a map but on the ground it is quite a large area.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: The locations where bighorn sheep occur are very steep and rocky, with many cliffs. Come prepared in very good physical shape. Plan on hiking in very steep terrain. Snow can make hiking in the steep rocky terrain very difficult. There are very remote location with a few areas having limited access. Cellular phone coverage is fair over most this hunt unit. Satellite phones do work in the area. Handheld radios and even a "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and when you will return.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightening, snow, wind and heat. Snowstorms can cause muddy and slick road conditions.

hunt_bio_general_information: Military lands exist on this hunt unit and access in not permitted.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: This hunt is focused on giving more opportunity. If storms come in late it may be very difficult to access the area with muddy impassable roads. I would recommend getting out there early in the season or traveling roads when they are frozen early in the morning. The majority of sheep stay in the same general areas throughout much of the year. During summer months, sheep concentrate on the north end of the mountain range in conjunction with natural water availability. During the late fall and winter, sheep begin to spread south across the range. Miners Basin and Desert Peak hold the highest densities of sheep, but sheep will range in high densities south to Big Pass and to the military boundary. Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep are found in steep rocky terrain. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your bighorn sheep. If you cannot safely retrieve the bighorn sheep, do not shoot. Once the rut starts, the rams will be begin to move to where the ewes are. Scouting is a good way to see what size of ram you can expect to harvest. Sheep are most active in mornings and evenings. Using a spotting scope works well to find sheep in the steep rocky areas. Scores for sheep from the Newfoundlands have typically been in the 150s-160s. With increase in opportunity, these scores may be slightly lower now.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Cellular phone coverage on this hunt unit is spotty. Satellite phones do work in the area. A "Spot Tracker" type of satellite messaging device for safety can be used if you decide to camp in an area without cell phone service and do not wish to travel to reach service. Make sure someone knows where you plan to camp and hunt, and when you will return. Roads around the mountain can become very slick and muddy when wet, and access roads are rough and can cause tire damage. This unit is very isolated and is very far from the nearest services. The closest services are in Wendover, Utah/Nevada, Grantsville, or Snowville. Munitions from the active military base may be present on public property. If found, do not touch! Take a GPS location and report what you found.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: The weather on this hunt unit can vary dramatically during the hunting season. Be prepared for rain, lightning, snow, and wind. Typically by this hunting season, any precipitation that is received is freezing rain or snow and temperatures regularly fall below freezing at night. Be very cautious of lightning while scouting and hunting on high ridges or exposed slopes. Early fall snow storms occur occasionally in this area. Most years the snow will melt off within a day or two until through the first week of October. Any precipitation will cause the roads to become very slick and muddy.

hunt_bio_general_information: Rocky Mountain Bighorn sheep are scattered from Alpine on the north to Springville on the south. Population estimates for sheep on the unit is 90+ animals.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Rocky Mountain Bighorn can be found above Alpine in the old burn, in American Fork Canyon, Mt. Timpanogos, Rock Canyon and above Springville on the north end. Sheep can also be found in places in between. Rams are on the move during the hunt looking for ewes to breed. Spend time looking pre-season for sheep. Most sheep can be found on the mountain face.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Areas where Rocky Mountain Bighorn sheep hang out in is steep and rocky. Where good boots and where gloves bring lots of water to drink. Be prepared for rain and snow at this time of year. Carry cell phone for emergency.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: Weather is usually good at this time of year, but prepare yourself for bad weather.

hunt_bio_general_information: The bighorn population in this unit typically fluctuates between approximately 40 and 60 animals. Even in November sheep can be found near 11,000 feet. This is a very rugged and physically demanding hunt.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: Location of harvest: Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep are found in steep rocky terrain. Choose your shot wisely. Make sure it is in a safe place to harvest your bighorn sheep. If you cannot safely retrieve the bighorn sheep, do not shoot. Scouting Tips: The bighorn sheep stay fairly consistently in the same general areas throughout much of the year. Once the rut starts, the rams will be begin to move to where the ewes are. Scouting is a good way to see what size of ram you can expect to harvest. Behavior: Like other wildlife, they are most active in the early mornings and evenings, but they can be up and moving any time of day. Most of the time they are in steep terrain, but they occasionally move down to stream bottoms to water. Ram vs. Ewe: Both rams and ewes have horns. Ram horns are much larger than ewe horns and will form a curl. Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep rut: The bighorn rut peaks in November. Where to find Rocky Mountain Bighorn Sheep: Bighorn sheep like steep cliffy areas because it provides an escape from predators. Recommended areas: Willow Creek to North Creek near Mona, Bald Mtn, and basins near Nebo Peak are good spots to start looking.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Bighorn sheep live in steep, rugged, and cliffy areas. Use precaution while climbing and hunting these areas.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: This hunt takes place the month of November. This area can be very snowy and cold this time of year.

hunt_bio_general_information: The Oak Creek Bighorn Sheep hunt started in 2018. Several groups of sheep have been transplanted to the Oak Creeks since 2014 and have been successful. Translocated sheep were sourced from Antelope Island and the Newfoundland Mountains.
hunt_bio_biologist_notes: The core area for the sheep is the Oak Creek and Dry Creek drainages. Many different rams can be located by glassing the drainages that feed into Oak Creek and Dry Creek. Good starting points to find sheep: Fool Creek Peak, Cascade, Limekiln, and Walker canyons.
hunt_bio_safety_considerations: Sheep inhabit rugged terrain. Wear good boots and take caution when hiking around cliffs and rocks. Cell phone service is spotty up the canyons. Be sure to pack plenty of drinking water as there are not a lot of sources for water on the mountain.
hunt_bio_weather_considerations: This time of year can be cold with possible rain or snow storms.
